exercises.description: The reverse hyperextension on a 45-degree bench raises both straight legs behind the body while the torso rests on the pad and the hands hold the foot rollers. Extend through the hips until the legs align with the trunk, working the glutes and hamstrings, then lower with control.
instructions: Lie face down with your trunk supported by the pad of a 45-degree bench and your hips near its upper edge.
Hold the foot rollers firmly with both hands and let the straight legs hang behind the pad.
Brace your abdomen and keep the torso still.
Raise both legs together by extending the hips until the legs align with the trunk.
Pause briefly, then lower the legs slowly to the starting position without changing the knee angle.
Repeat with a controlled hip movement.
mistakes: Swinging the legs to create momentum instead of lifting them with the glutes and hamstrings.
Arching the lower back to lift the legs higher rather than extending at the hips.
Raising the legs far above torso level, which shifts the work into excessive lumbar extension.
Letting the pelvis rotate or lift off the pad during the movement.
Bending and straightening the knees during each rep instead of keeping a consistent knee position.
Dropping the legs too quickly instead of controlling the lowering phase.
exercises.name: 45-Degree Reverse Hyperextension
tips: Test your hand support before lifting the legs.
Keep a small space between the feet so both hips can move evenly.
Exhale during the lift and inhale as you lower.
Use a brief pause at the top to feel the glutes contract.
Use a smaller range if you cannot find a comfortable bottom position.

exercises.description: Position yourself sideways on a 45-degree back extension bench with your feet secured and hands behind your head. Bend your torso sideways toward the floor, then use your obliques to return to a straight line with your legs. Keep your pelvis stable and repeat on the other side after the set.
instructions: Set the 45-degree back extension bench so the hip pad sits just below your hip on the side you are training.
Stand sideways on the bench with your feet secured under the ankle pads and your body in a straight line from head to feet.
Place both hands lightly behind your head without pulling your neck.
Brace your abdominal muscles and keep your hips square against the pad.
Lower your torso sideways toward the floor in a slow, controlled motion. Move only as far as you can without twisting your torso or losing control.
Contract the muscles along the side of your waist to raise your torso back until your body is straight again.
Complete all repetitions on one side, then turn around and repeat on the other side.
mistakes: Letting the pelvis rotate forward or backward instead of keeping the hips stacked.
Twisting the torso during the lift instead of bending directly to the side.
Rounding forward as you lower instead of keeping the chest and spine aligned.
Rising past neutral and side bending to the opposite side at the top.
Using momentum or bouncing out of the bottom position.
Pulling with the arms or holding the head instead of using the obliques.
Dropping too low and losing control of the trunk position.
exercises.name: 45-Degree Side Bend
tips: Secure your feet in the supports before beginning the set.
Keep your hands lightly behind the head, elbows open and neck relaxed.
Exhale as you raise the torso and inhale as you lower it.
Use the same range and number of repetitions on both sides.
Adjust the bench before starting so the side of the pelvis stays comfortably supported.

exercises.description: The 90 To 90 Stretch is a seated static hip stretch. You sit tall with your front leg bent 90 degrees in front of you and your back leg bent 90 degrees out to the side, and hold the position. It stretches the glute and hip rotators of the front leg, opens the hip of the back leg and fits into a warm-up or cool-down.
instructions: Sit on the floor and place your right leg in front of you with the knee bent 90 degrees, the shin across your body and the outside of the leg on the floor.
Place your left leg out to the side with the knee bent 90 degrees, the thigh pointing sideways and the shin pointing back.
Rest your hands on the floor beside your front shin.
Sit up tall: lift your chest, keep your back straight and let both hips sink as close to the floor as you can.
Hold for 20-30 seconds and breathe slowly. You should feel the stretch in the glute and outer hip of the front leg.
Come out of the position and set it up on the other side, left leg in front and right leg to the side.
Hold the second side for the same time.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back and slumping over the front leg.
Leaning back or to the side to escape the stretch.
Letting the knees open far past 90 degrees, which takes the stretch out of the hips.
Pushing hard through the hands to prop yourself up instead of sitting on your hips.
Forcing the position when you feel pain in the knee rather than a stretch in the hip.
Holding your breath while you stretch.
Bouncing in the position instead of holding still.
Stretching only one side or holding one side much shorter.
exercises.name: 90 To 90 Stretch
tips: If you cannot sit upright, put a folded towel or cushion under your hips.
For a deeper stretch, hinge forward from the hips over the front shin while keeping your chest open.
Relax your glutes and let your hips sink a little lower as the hold goes on.
If one side feels tighter, give it an extra hold.
Use it in your warm-up before squats and deadlifts or after training to cool down.

exercises.description: Sit on the floor in a 90/90 with your palms pressed together in front of your chest and swing both knees from one side to the other without putting a hand down. Every switch turns one hip out and the other in, so a set of 90/90 hip switches trains hip external and internal rotation in both hips. You feel it deep in the hips and in the glute of the front leg, and your abs work to keep you upright. The static 90/90 stretch holds one side; here you keep moving, and unlike the 90/90 Hip Switch with Hand Support, your trunk does all the balancing.
instructions: Sit on the floor with your feet planted wider than your hips, knees bent about 90 degrees and heels down.
Lower both knees to the right into a 90/90: right shin across the front of your body, left shin out to the side and pointing back.
Press your palms together in front of your chest, elbows out, and sit tall with your hands off the floor.
Pivot on your heels and lift both knees until they point at the ceiling, feet flat in the middle.
Keep turning and lower both knees to the left into the opposite 90/90, left shin now in front.
Pause for a second with your chest up and both sit bones on the floor, then lift the knees and head back to the right.
Count one rep each time you arrive on a side and keep alternating to the end of the set.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back and sinking into the floor as the knees rise. Sit on the front of your sit bones and lead with your chest; if you still slump, set your feet a little wider.
Leaning far back or dropping a hand to catch your balance. Go back to the version with hand support until you can sit upright on your own.
Letting the knees fall to the floor. Lower them slowly over the last few centimetres so you could stop at any point.
Twisting the shoulders along with the knees. Keep your chest and hands facing forward so the turn comes from the hips.
Hitching one hip high off the floor to get the knees down. Let the knees stop higher and keep both sit bones near the floor.
Pushing the back knee down while you feel a twist in the knee. The pull belongs in the hip; if the knee complains, end the switch earlier on that side.
exercises.name: 90/90 Hip Switch
tips: Do 2-3 sets of 6-10 switches per side. Take 2-3 seconds to move from one side to the other and pause 1-2 seconds in each 90/90.
Use it in the warm-up before squats, deadlifts or lunges, between sets of lower-body work, or to open a hip mobility session. Five slow switches per side are enough before lifting.
Expect a stretch in the glute of the front leg and a pull at the front of the back hip. If one side is clearly stiffer, give it 3-5 extra switches or a 20-30 second hold in the 90 To 90 Stretch.

Progress in steps: hands on the floor behind you, then palms at your chest as here, then arms reaching straight forward. After that, hold each side for 5 seconds and lean your chest slightly over the front shin.
Breathe out as the knees settle on each side; the hips sink a little further when you do.

exercises.description: Sit on the floor in a 90/90 with your hands planted behind your hips and swing both knees from one side to the other. With your hands handling balance, the whole set goes into hip internal and external rotation, so this is where most people with stiff hips start their 90/90 work. You feel it in the glute of the front leg and at the front of the back hip as the knees settle. Next to the hands-free 90/90 Hip Switch your trunk works far less and you may lean back a little; unlike the static 90/90 stretch, you keep switching sides instead of holding one.
instructions: Sit on the floor with your feet wider than your hips, knees bent about 90 degrees and heels on the floor.
Place your hands on the floor behind your hips, arms straight, and lean back just enough to feel balanced.
Lower both knees to the right: right shin across the front of your body, left shin out to the side and pointing back.
Lift your chest so your lower back stays long even with the slight lean.
Pivot on your heels and raise both knees until they point up and both feet are flat.
Carry on turning and lower the knees to the left into the opposite 90/90, left shin in front.
Pause briefly on each side, then switch back, alternating to the end of the set.
mistakes: Bending the elbows and sinking between the shoulders. Straighten your arms and push the floor away so your chest stays lifted.
Leaning back so far that the knees just tip over and the hips barely turn. Bring your hands closer and sit more upright.
Lifting the hips and shoving through the hands to throw the legs over. Both sit bones stay on the floor; let the knees stop higher instead.
Dropping the knees onto the floor. Slow down for the last few centimetres of each side.
Letting the feet slide or lift off the floor. Pivot on the heels so the feet stay planted and only the knees travel.
Front shin sliding forward so the front knee opens far past 90 degrees. Set the shin back across your body after each switch.
exercises.name: 90/90 Hip Switch with Hand Support
tips: Do 2-3 sets of 8-10 switches per side at a slow pace, about 3 seconds from side to side. It fits the warm-up before squats and deadlifts, the start of a hip mobility session, or a few minutes on a rest day.
Plant your hands about a forearm's length behind your hips: close enough to sit up, far enough to take weight off the hips.
Make it harder over the weeks: walk your hands closer to your hips, then switch with one hand down, then move on to the hands-free 90/90 Hip Switch.
Stay 3-5 seconds at the bottom of each side and breathe out to sink a little deeper. Give the stiffer side a few extra reps.
If tight hips or hamstrings round your back, sit on a folded towel or a thin cushion. Raising the hips makes sitting tall much easier.

exercises.description: The Ab Wheel Rollout is a core strengthening exercise that primarily targets the rectus abdominis, obliques, and transverse abdominis. It also engages the shoulders, back, and hip flexors. This exercise requires an ab wheel, which is a small wheel with handles on either side. The movement involves rolling the wheel forward from a kneeling position while maintaining a straight line from head to knees, then returning to the starting position.
instructions: Start in a kneeling position on a mat to protect your knees.
Grip the handles of the ab wheel firmly with both hands.
Position the wheel on the floor in front of you, directly under your shoulders.
Engage your core and keep your back straight.
Slowly roll the wheel forward, extending your body as far as you can without losing form.
Pause briefly at the extended position, ensuring your core remains tight.
Reverse the movement by pulling the wheel back towards your knees, maintaining control throughout.
Return to the starting position and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Arching the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Allowing the hips to sag towards the floor during the rollout.
Rolling out too far beyond shoulder width, losing core engagement.
Using momentum rather than controlled movements.
Failing to engage the core muscles throughout the exercise.
Starting the rollout from a position too far away from the knees.
Not keeping the arms straight and locked during the rollout.
Allowing the shoulders to shrug up towards the ears.
Returning to the starting position too quickly, losing control.
Neglecting to breathe properly, holding the breath throughout.
exercises.name: Ab Wheel Rollout
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the entire movement to protect your lower back.
Avoid arching your back; maintain a neutral spine to prevent injury.
Start with shorter rollouts if you're new to this exercise and gradually increase the distance as you build strength.
Breathe steadily; inhale as you roll out and exhale as you return to the starting position.
Perform this exercise on a soft surface or use a mat to cushion your knees.
If you feel discomfort in your lower back, reduce the range of motion or check your form.

exercises.description: Abdominal crunches are a core exercise that primarily targets the rectus abdominis muscle. This exercise helps in strengthening the core, improving posture, and enhancing overall abdominal endurance. It is performed by lying on your back and lifting your upper body towards your knees using your abdominal muscles.
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Place your hands behind your head with elbows pointing outwards. Avoid pulling on your neck.
Engage your core by drawing your belly button towards your spine.
Lift your shoulder blades off the ground by contracting your abdominal muscles. Exhale as you lift.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring not to pull with your neck or arms.
Inhale as you slowly lower back down to the starting position without letting your shoulders touch the ground completely.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Pulling on the neck with hands instead of engaging the core.
Lifting the lower back off the ground, reducing core engagement.
Using momentum to lift the torso instead of controlled movement.
Not fully engaging the abdominal muscles throughout the motion.
Raising the shoulders too high, turning the crunch into a sit-up.
Tucking the chin too tightly to the chest, straining the neck.
Allowing the elbows to collapse inward, reducing effectiveness.
Failing to keep feet flat on the ground, leading to instability.
Holding the breath instead of maintaining steady breathing.
Performing the movement too quickly, sacrificing form for speed.
exercises.name: Abdominal Crunches
tips: Keep your movements controlled and avoid using momentum to lift yourself.
Focus on using your abs to lift rather than pulling with your neck or arms.
Keep a small space between your chin and chest to avoid straining your neck.
Exhale as you crunch up and inhale as you return to the starting position for better core engagement.
Ensure that your lower back remains in contact with the mat throughout the exercise to protect your spine.
Start with a manageable number of repetitions and gradually increase as you build strength.

exercises.description: The abdominal vacuum is an isometric exercise that targets the transverse abdominis, the deep core muscle responsible for stabilizing the spine and maintaining internal abdominal pressure. This exercise helps improve core strength, posture, and can contribute to a slimmer waist appearance by training the muscle to hold the abdomen in.
instructions: Stand upright with feet shoulder-width apart or kneel on the floor.
Exhale completely to empty your lungs of air.
Draw your belly button inward towards your spine as much as possible.
Hold this position for 15-30 seconds while maintaining normal breathing.
Release and relax your abdominal muscles.
Repeat for 3-5 sets, gradually increasing hold time as you progress.
mistakes: Not fully exhaling before drawing the abdomen in, leading to reduced muscle engagement.
Allowing the chest to rise during the contraction, which shifts focus away from the transverse abdominis.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine, causing unnecessary tension in the lower back.
Holding the breath instead of using controlled breathing, reducing the effectiveness of the exercise.
Engaging the rectus abdominis instead of the transverse abdominis, which diminishes the vacuum effect.
Performing the exercise with a forward head posture, straining the neck and reducing core engagement.
Rushing through the movement without holding the contraction, limiting muscle activation.
Using excessive force to pull the abdomen in, which can lead to muscle strain.
exercises.name: Abdominal Vacuum
tips: Perform the exercise on an empty stomach for better control and comfort.
Focus on pulling your navel inwards rather than sucking in air.
Keep your chest relaxed and avoid raising your shoulders during the contraction.
Practice regularly to improve muscle control and endurance.
Incorporate this exercise into your routine to enhance overall core stability.

exercises.description: Air Bike is the lying bicycle crunch, not the fan bike machine. On your back with your hands behind your head, you curl up and turn one elbow toward the opposite knee while the other leg straightens, then lower your shoulders and switch sides. It trains the obliques and the rectus abdominis, and the hip flexors keep the legs off the floor.
instructions: Lie on your back on a mat with your hands behind your head and your elbows wide.
Lift both legs off the floor with the knees almost straight and press your lower back into the mat.
Curl your shoulders up and twist to bring your right elbow toward your left knee as you pull that knee in toward your chest.
Keep your right leg straight and low, just above the floor.
Lower your shoulders back to the mat and straighten your left leg.
Repeat to the other side, left elbow toward right knee, and keep alternating.
Breathe out as you twist up and breathe in as you lower.
mistakes: Pulling on the head with the hands and straining the neck.
Moving only the elbow instead of rotating the upper back toward the knee.
Letting the lower back arch off the mat as the leg straightens.
Pedaling fast with momentum instead of controlling each rep.
Putting the feet down between sides and losing tension.
Straightening the extended leg only halfway.
exercises.name: Air Bike
tips: Turn your ribcage toward the knee so the shoulder leads, not just the elbow.
Keep your hands light on your head and leave a fist's width between chin and chest.
Keep your lower back on the mat for the whole set. If it lifts, raise the straight leg higher.
Work at a steady tempo and pause briefly at the top of each twist.
Keep your feet off the floor between sides so your abs stay under tension.

exercises.description: The Alternate Bent Over Dumbbell Reverse Fly is an isolation exercise targeting the rear deltoids, upper back, and rhomboids. It involves bending at the hips while maintaining a neutral spine and lifting dumbbells laterally in an alternating fashion.
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip.
Hinge at the hips to bend forward until your torso is almost parallel to the floor, keeping your back straight and knees slightly bent.
Let your arms hang down naturally with a slight bend in the elbows.
Engage your core and lift one dumbbell out to the side, keeping your elbow slightly bent, until it reaches shoulder height.
Lower the dumbbell back to the starting position while simultaneously lifting the opposite dumbbell.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Rounding the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Using too much momentum and swinging the weights.
Lifting the dumbbells too high, causing shoulder strain.
Not engaging the core, leading to instability.
Allowing the wrists to bend instead of keeping them straight.
Standing too upright, reducing the effectiveness of the exercise.
Failing to retract the shoulder blades fully.
Moving the elbows too far forward, reducing back muscle activation.
Not controlling the descent of the weights.
exercises.name: Alternate Bent Over Dumbbell Reverse Fly
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the movement to maintain stability.
Avoid using momentum; focus on controlled movements to isolate the target muscles.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows to reduce strain on the joints.
Ensure your back remains flat and avoid rounding your shoulders.
Breathe out as you lift the dumbbell and inhale as you lower it.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: The Alternate Biceps Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps brachii. It involves curling one dumbbell at a time, allowing for focused contraction and improved muscle symmetry. This exercise helps in developing arm strength and size, emphasizing the peak of the bicep.
instructions: Stand upright with a dumbbell in each hand, arms fully extended, and palms facing your body.
Keep your elbows close to your torso throughout the movement.
Curl the right dumbbell by contracting your bicep, rotating your wrist so that the palm faces up as you lift.
Continue lifting until your bicep is fully contracted and the dumbbell is at shoulder level.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, squeezing your bicep.
Slowly lower the dumbbell back to the starting position, rotating your wrist back to a neutral position.
Repeat the movement with the left arm while keeping the right arm stationary.
Continue alternating arms for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Swinging the weights, using momentum instead of controlled muscle engagement.
Lifting the elbows, turning the exercise into a shoulder movement.
Curling the wrists, reducing biceps activation and risking wrist strain.
Not fully extending the arms, limiting the range of motion and muscle engagement.
Leaning back, compromising posture and reducing biceps isolation.
Using weights that are too heavy, leading to compromised form and reduced control.
Rushing the movement, preventing full contraction and relaxation of the biceps.
Allowing the shoulders to round forward, reducing stability and biceps focus.
exercises.name: Alternate Biceps Curl
tips: Maintain a controlled motion; avoid swinging or using momentum to lift the weights.
Focus on squeezing your bicep at the top of each curl for maximum contraction.
Keep your core engaged and back straight to prevent any unwanted movement or strain.
Ensure a full range of motion by fully extending your arm at the bottom of each rep.
Start with lighter weights to perfect your form before progressing to heavier dumbbells.
Breath out as you curl the weight up and inhale as you lower it down.

exercises.description: The Alternate Dumbbell Hammer Curl is a strength training exercise targeting the biceps and forearms. It involves lifting dumbbells in a neutral grip, alternating arms, which helps in developing arm size and strength while also engaging the brachialis and brachioradialis muscles.
instructions: Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart and hold a dumbbell in each hand using a neutral grip, palms facing each other.
Keep your elbows close to your torso and maintain a straight back.
Curl the right dumbbell upward by bending your elbow, keeping your upper arm stationary.
Continue lifting until your forearm is vertical and the dumbbell is at shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, then slowly lower the dumbbell back to the starting position.
Repeat the movement with your left arm while keeping the right arm stationary.
Continue alternating arms for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Swinging the body or using momentum to lift the weights.
Allowing the elbows to flare out instead of keeping them close to the torso.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom of the movement.
Curling the wrists instead of keeping them neutral.
Lifting the shoulders or shrugging during the curl.
Using too heavy weights, leading to compromised form.
Rushing through the movement without controlled tempo.
Not engaging the biceps and brachialis effectively.
Leaning backward excessively to lift the weights.
exercises.name: Alternate Dumbbell Hammer Curl
tips: Maintain a controlled motion throughout the exercise to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid swinging or using momentum to lift the weights; focus on isolating the biceps.
Keep your wrists straight and avoid bending them during the curl to prevent strain.
Exhale as you lift the dumbbell and inhale as you lower it back down.
Ensure that your elbows remain close to your body to effectively target the biceps.

exercises.description: The Alternate Renegade Row is a compound exercise that targets the back, shoulders, and core. It involves performing a rowing motion while in a plank position, alternating arms to engage stabilizing muscles and improve balance and coordination.
instructions: Begin in a high plank position with your hands gripping dumbbells placed shoulder-width apart. Your body should form a straight line from head to heels.
Engage your core to maintain stability and prevent your hips from sagging or rotating.
Row one dumbbell towards your hip by retracting your shoulder blade and bending your elbow, keeping your elbow close to your body.
Lower the dumbbell back to the starting position with control.
Repeat the rowing motion with the opposite arm while maintaining plank form.
Continue alternating arms for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Allowing hips to sag or rise, compromising spinal alignment.
Rotating the torso excessively, reducing core engagement.
Using momentum instead of controlled movement, diminishing muscle activation.
Failing to stabilize the shoulder, increasing risk of shoulder strain.
Rowing the dumbbell too high, causing elbow to flare out.
Not maintaining a neutral neck position, leading to strain.
Placing feet too close together, reducing balance and stability.
Neglecting to engage the core, weakening the exercise's effectiveness.
Rushing the movement, sacrificing form and control.
exercises.name: Alternate Renegade Row
tips: Keep your feet slightly wider than shoulder-width apart for better stability.
Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together during each row to maximize back engagement.
Maintain a neutral neck position by looking slightly ahead of you, not down or up.
Avoid rotating your hips; keep them square to the ground throughout the exercise.
If maintaining balance is challenging, start with lighter weights or perform the exercise without dumbbells to build core strength first.
Breathe steadily, exhaling as you row the dumbbell upwards and inhaling as you lower it.

exercises.description: Stand with your feet side by side and your fists in front of your chest. Punch straight forward with alternating arms, letting your shoulders turn slightly with each punch. Return each fist to guard and keep your weight balanced without stepping or leaning into the punch.
instructions: Stand with your feet parallel, knees slightly bent and fists in front of your chest.
Keep your core braced, chest lifted, and chin slightly tucked while looking straight ahead.
Extend one arm straight forward at shoulder height, rotating the fist so the palm faces down at full extension.
Retract the punching hand quickly back to your guard position.
Immediately punch forward with the opposite arm, returning the first hand to guard as the second arm extends.
Continue alternating controlled punches at a steady pace, exhaling with each punch and keeping your shoulders relaxed.
mistakes: Dropping the hands between punches instead of returning to a guard position
Overextending the arm and locking the elbow at the end of the punch
Letting the knees collapse inward or standing with a narrow, unstable stance
Leaning forward or backward excessively instead of maintaining a tall, balanced posture
Flaring the elbow out to the side rather than driving the fist straight forward
Using uncontrolled, swinging punches instead of crisp, straight movements
exercises.name: Alternating Punches
tips: Turn the punching hand so the knuckles face forward near full extension, while keeping the wrist straight and aligned with the forearm.
Exhale sharply as you punch and inhale as you return to guard; avoid holding your breath during fast combinations.
Keep your chin slightly tucked and your eyes on the direction of the punches.
Keep the same rhythm for the left and right punches.
Extend one arm straight forward at a time, rotating the shoulder and torso slightly with each punch rather than reaching only with the arm.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/美式壶铃摆动

exercises.description: Hold one kettlebell with both hands and hinge at your hips to swing it between your thighs. Extend your hips powerfully to send the bell overhead, finishing with straight arms above your shoulders. Control the return into the next hinge while keeping your ribs down and your back neutral.
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder width apart, with the kettlebell on the floor slightly in front of you. Point your toes forward or slightly out, and keep the handle horizontal.
Hinge at your hips by pushing them back, then bend your knees slightly. Keep your chest long, back flat, and neck neutral as you grip the kettlebell handle with both hands.
Hike the kettlebell back between your thighs, keeping your arms straight and close to your body. Load your hamstrings and keep your weight balanced through your whole feet.
Drive forcefully through the floor by extending your hips and knees. Let the hip drive move the kettlebell forward and upward, rather than lifting it with your arms.

As the kettlebell rises, keep your ribs down and brace your abdominal muscles. Guide the bell overhead until your arms are straight, your biceps are close to your ears, and the kettlebell is directly above your shoulders.
At the top position, stand tall with your hips and knees fully extended. Do not lean back or let your lower back arch to reach overhead.
Let the kettlebell fall under control, keeping your arms straight. As it comes down, hinge at the hips and allow the bell to travel back between your thighs.
mistakes: Squatting the swing instead of hinging at the hips.
Rounding the lower back during the backswing.
Using the arms to lift the kettlebell overhead instead of driving with the hips.
Failing to fully extend the hips and knees at the top.
Overarching the lower back to force the kettlebell overhead.
Shifting weight onto the toes rather than keeping pressure through the mid-foot and heels.
exercises.name: American Kettlebell Swing
tips: Wrap both thumbs securely around the handle before the first backswing.
Guide the bell high between your thighs on the backswing rather than letting it hang near your knees.
Keep your shoulders active overhead, with your arms close to your ears and your elbows locked without forcing them backward.
Exhale sharply as you drive your hips forward, then inhale as the kettlebell returns into the backswing.
Keep your neck neutral and look forward or slightly down during the swing. Do not follow the kettlebell with your eyes by throwing your head back.

exercises.description: The Anderson Squat, also known as the pin squat, is a variation of the traditional squat where the barbell starts from a dead stop on safety pins or supports within a power rack. This exercise focuses on developing explosive strength from the bottom position, improving sticking points in the squat, and enhancing overall lower body power.
instructions: Set the safety pins in a power rack at a height where your thighs are parallel to the ground when you are in the bottom squat position.
Position the barbell on the safety pins and load it with an appropriate weight.
Stand under the barbell, positioning it across your upper back, and set your feet shoulder-width apart.
Engage your core and grip the bar firmly with both hands.
Drive through your heels to lift the barbell off the pins, extending your hips and knees until you reach a standing position.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower the barbell back to the pins with control.
Reset your position and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Starting with the bar too high, leading to improper depth and reduced range of motion.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine, increasing the risk of lower back strain.
Allowing knees to cave inward, which can lead to knee joint stress.
Not engaging the core, resulting in poor stability and control.
Using momentum to lift the bar instead of controlled muscle engagement.
Improper foot positioning, causing imbalance and ineffective force distribution.
Rounding the shoulders forward, compromising upper back engagement.
Neglecting to set the safety pins at the correct height, affecting starting position.
exercises.name: Anderson Squat
tips: Focus on maintaining a strong core throughout the lift to ensure stability and prevent injury.
Use a controlled tempo when lowering the barbell back to the pins to maximize muscle engagement.
Start with a lighter weight to master proper form before progressing to heavier loads.
Ensure your feet are firmly planted and drive through your heels to maximize power output.
Keep your chest up and shoulders back to maintain proper posture during the lift.
Practice breathing techniques: inhale before lifting off the pins and exhale as you complete the lift.

exercises.description: The lying torso twist is an abdominal exercise that targets the oblique muscles. It involves rotating the lower body while keeping the upper body stable, enhancing core strength and flexibility.
instructions: Lie flat on your back with your arms extended out to the sides, palms facing down for stability.
Bend your knees and lift your legs so that your thighs are perpendicular to the floor and your calves are parallel.
Engage your core muscles to stabilize your spine.
Slowly lower your legs to one side, keeping your shoulders flat on the ground.
Pause briefly when your legs are close to the floor, then return to the starting position using your core muscles.
Repeat the movement on the opposite side.
mistakes: Lifting the head too high off the ground, causing neck strain.
Failing to engage the core, leading to ineffective movement.
Reaching with the arms instead of using the obliques to twist.
Allowing the lower back to arch off the floor, reducing core activation.
Moving too quickly, sacrificing control and precision.
Not maintaining a consistent breathing pattern, affecting endurance.
Overextending the reach, leading to improper form and reduced effectiveness.
Keeping the feet too close together, limiting the range of motion.
exercises.name: Ankle Taps
tips: Maintain a slow and controlled motion to maximize muscle engagement.
Focus on keeping your shoulders and upper back pressed against the floor throughout the exercise.
Engage your core by pulling your belly button towards your spine.
Breathe out as you lower your legs and inhale as you return to the center position.
If you feel strain in your lower back, reduce the range of motion or keep your feet closer to the floor.

exercises.description: The archer pull-up shifts most of the pulling work to one arm while the other supports you along the bar. Take a wide overhand grip and pull your chest toward one hand, bending that elbow as the opposite arm straightens. Lower back to the center under control, keeping your legs and trunk steady.
instructions: Grip a secure pull-up bar with a wide overhand grip and enough clearance for your feet.
Hang with straight arms, legs together or slightly in front of you, and brace your abdomen to limit swinging.
Set your shoulders by pulling them down away from your ears and keeping your chest lifted.
Pull your body toward one hand, bending that elbow while allowing the opposite arm to straighten out to the side along the bar.
Continue until your chest is close to the working hand or as high as you can control. Keep your shoulders level and avoid twisting your torso excessively.
Lower slowly back to a centered dead hang, controlling the movement through both arms.
Repeat toward the other hand. Alternate sides each repetition, or complete the planned repetitions on one side before switching.
mistakes: Bending both elbows evenly instead of keeping the non-working arm nearly straight.
Pulling straight up in the center instead of moving the chest toward the working hand.
Letting the shoulder of the straight arm hang passively instead of keeping it active and down.
Using momentum, swinging the legs, or kipping to reach the top.
Twisting the torso too much instead of shifting sideways with the shoulders and chest under control.
Dropping too fast instead of controlling the lowering phase.
exercises.name: Archer Pull-Up
tips: Use a wide overhand grip that feels comfortable at both shoulders.
Wrap your thumbs around the bar for a secure grip.
Exhale as you pull toward the working hand.
Use the same range and repetition count on both sides.
Build up with an assisted version before attempting unassisted repetitions.

exercises.description: The Archer Push Up is an advanced bodyweight exercise that targets the chest, triceps, and shoulders while also engaging the core and stabilizing muscles. It involves a wider hand placement and shifting of body weight from one side to the other, mimicking the motion of drawing a bow.
instructions: Start in a standard push-up position with your hands placed wider than shoulder-width apart.
Extend one arm fully to the side, keeping it straight, while the other arm remains bent.
Lower your body towards the bent arm, keeping your core tight and back straight.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement, ensuring your chest is close to the ground.
Push through the bent arm to return to the starting position.
Shift your weight to the opposite side and repeat the movement with the other arm.
mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag or rise, leading to poor core engagement.
Failing to keep the elbows at a 45-degree angle, which can strain the shoulder joints.
Not fully extending the non-working arm, reducing the exercise's effectiveness.
Dropping the head instead of maintaining a neutral neck position.
Uneven weight distribution between arms, causing imbalance.
Rushing the movement, leading to poor control and reduced muscle activation.
Not lowering the chest close enough to the ground, limiting range of motion.
Letting the shoulders shrug, which disengages the chest muscles.
exercises.name: Archer Push-Up
tips: Ensure your hands are placed wider than shoulder-width to allow for proper weight shifting.
Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain stability and prevent sagging hips.
Focus on controlled movements rather than speed to maximize muscle engagement and reduce injury risk.
Breathe in as you lower your body and exhale as you push back up.
If you're new to this exercise, start with a modified version by performing it on your knees or using an elevated surface for support.

exercises.description: The Arm Blaster Biceps Dumbbell Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps brachii. Utilizing an arm blaster helps maintain proper form by preventing elbow movement, thus maximizing bicep engagement. This exercise is ideal for building bicep size and strength by focusing on strict form and muscle contraction.
instructions: Adjust the arm blaster so it fits comfortably around your neck and rests against your upper body.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand with an underhand grip.
Position your elbows against the arm blaster, ensuring they remain stationary throughout the movement.
Curl the dumbbells upward by contracting your biceps, keeping your upper arms stationary.
Continue lifting until your biceps are fully contracted and the dumbbells are at shoulder level.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement to maximize contraction.
Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position, maintaining control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using momentum to lift the weights instead of isolating the biceps.
Allowing the elbows to drift away from the arm blaster, reducing isolation.
Curling the wrists at the top of the movement, shifting tension away from the biceps.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom, limiting range of motion.
Leaning back or swaying the torso to assist the lift.
Gripping the dumbbells too tightly, causing forearm fatigue.
Rushing through reps without controlled movement.
Using excessively heavy weights, compromising form and control.
Neglecting to keep the shoulders down and relaxed.
exercises.name: Arm Blaster Biceps Dumbbell Curl
tips: Focus on keeping your elbows pinned to the arm blaster to prevent swinging.
Use a weight that allows you to maintain strict form throughout all repetitions.
Engage your core to stabilize your body and prevent any unnecessary movement.
Exhale as you lift the dumbbells and inhale as you lower them.
Avoid using momentum; concentrate on slow, controlled movements for maximum effectiveness.
Ensure a full range of motion by fully extending and contracting your biceps with each rep.

exercises.description: Arm Circles are a dynamic warm-up exercise that targets the shoulders, deltoids, and upper arms. This exercise helps improve shoulder mobility, increase blood flow, and prepare the upper body for more intense workouts. It involves rotating the arms in circular motions, which can be performed in both forward and backward directions.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and arms extended straight out to the sides at shoulder height.
Keep your palms facing down and your arms parallel to the ground.
Begin making small circles with your arms by rotating them forward.
Gradually increase the size of the circles while maintaining control and stability.
After completing a set number of rotations, reverse the direction and perform backward circles.
Maintain a steady breathing pattern throughout the exercise.
mistakes: Rotating arms too quickly, leading to loss of control and reduced muscle engagement.
Using too large a range of motion, causing strain on shoulder joints.
Allowing arms to drop below shoulder height, reducing effectiveness.
Failing to engage core muscles, leading to poor posture and balance.
Keeping arms too stiff, limiting fluidity and range of motion.
Not maintaining a consistent circular motion, causing uneven muscle activation.
Holding breath, which can increase tension and reduce endurance.
Leaning forward or backward, disrupting proper alignment and engagement.
exercises.name: Arm Circle
tips: Engage your core muscles to maintain balance and stability during the exercise.
Keep your movements controlled to avoid straining your shoulder joints.
Start with smaller circles to warm up the muscles before progressing to larger circles.
Focus on smooth, fluid motions rather than speed to maximize effectiveness.
Ensure that your shoulders remain relaxed and not hunched up towards your ears.
Perform arm circles as part of a comprehensive warm-up routine to enhance overall workout performance.

exercises.description: Shoulder circles are a dynamic warm-up exercise targeting the shoulder joints and surrounding muscles. This exercise helps improve mobility, flexibility, and blood flow to the shoulder area, reducing the risk of injury during more intense workouts.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and arms relaxed by your sides.
Lift your shoulders towards your ears in a shrugging motion.
Begin to move your shoulders in a circular motion, first moving them forward, up, back, and down.
Complete the desired number of repetitions in the forward direction.
Reverse the direction of the circles, moving your shoulders backward, up, forward, and down.
Maintain a smooth and controlled motion throughout the exercise.
mistakes: Performing circles too quickly, leading to loss of control and muscle engagement.
Using overly large circles, which can strain the shoulder joint.
Allowing the shoulders to hunch up towards the ears, causing tension in the neck.
Not maintaining a stable core, resulting in unnecessary torso movement.
Failing to keep arms fully extended, reducing the effectiveness of the exercise.
Neglecting to engage the shoulder muscles, relying too much on momentum.
Starting with arms too low, limiting the range of motion and shoulder activation.
Rotating arms unevenly, causing imbalance and uneven muscle work.
exercises.name: Arm Circles
tips: Keep your core engaged to maintain good posture during the exercise.
Perform the circles slowly to maximize the stretch and control.
Focus on making large circles to fully engage the shoulder joint.
Breathe naturally and avoid holding your breath.
Start with smaller circles if you feel any discomfort or tightness.

exercises.description: The Assault Air Bike is a high-intensity cardio machine that combines the benefits of cycling and upper body workouts. It uses air resistance, which increases with the speed and power of your pedaling, providing a scalable workout suitable for all fitness levels. The bike features moving handlebars, allowing for a full-body workout that engages both the lower and upper body muscles.
instructions: Adjust the seat height so that your legs are slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke.
Sit on the bike with your feet securely on the pedals and hands gripping the handlebars.
Start pedaling at a moderate pace to warm up, using both your legs and arms to move the pedals and handlebars.
Increase your speed and intensity by pedaling faster and pushing/pulling harder on the handlebars.
Maintain a steady breathing pattern, inhaling through your nose and exhaling through your mouth.
Cool down by gradually reducing your speed and intensity over the last few minutes of your workout.
mistakes: Leaning too far forward, causing poor posture and reduced efficiency.
Using only arms or only legs, leading to muscle imbalance and reduced power output.
Setting the seat too low, limiting leg extension and causing knee strain.
Gripping the handles too tightly, resulting in unnecessary tension in the upper body.
Pedaling too fast without control, increasing the risk of losing balance.
Neglecting to engage the core, reducing stability and power transfer.
Not maintaining a steady breathing pattern, leading to premature fatigue.
Allowing knees to flare outward, causing misalignment and potential knee discomfort.
exercises.name: Assault Air Bike
tips: Ensure the seat is adjusted properly to avoid strain on your knees.
Engage your core muscles to maintain stability while pedaling.
Use both arms and legs equally to distribute effort and maximize efficiency.
Focus on smooth, controlled movements rather than jerky or rushed motions.
Monitor your heart rate to ensure you are working within your target zone.
Incorporate interval training by alternating between high-intensity bursts and recovery periods.

exercises.description: Set the machine's assistance and kneel on its moving pad. Grip the central bar underhand, about shoulder-width apart, and pull until your chin passes the bar. Lower under control to straight arms while keeping your knees supported and your legs still.
instructions: Set the assistance weight so you can complete the set with controlled form. More selected weight provides more assistance.
Grip the central bar underhand, with your hands about shoulder-width apart.
Kneel on the moving pad while holding the bar and begin with straight arms.
Brace your stomach and keep your legs still. Start by pulling your shoulder blades down and back.
Pull your chest upward by driving your elbows down toward your sides. Keep your torso tall and avoid swinging or kicking.
Pull until your chin passes the bar without reaching forward with your neck.
Lower yourself slowly until your arms are straight again and your shoulders remain controlled. Do not drop into the bottom position.
mistakes: Kicking or swinging the legs to create momentum.
Letting the hips drift far forward or backward instead of keeping the torso stable.
Leading with the chin and craning the neck to reach the bar.
Stopping short of a full overhead stretch at the bottom.
Dropping too quickly into the bottom position instead of controlling the lowering phase.
Relaxing at the bottom and losing shoulder control before starting the next repetition.
exercises.name: Assisted Chin-Up
tips: Selecting more assistance weight makes the exercise easier.
Use an underhand grip about shoulder width apart.
Wrap your thumbs around the bar for a secure grip.
Exhale as you pull up and inhale as you lower.
Reduce the assistance gradually as your strength improves, while keeping the same range of motion and control.

exercises.description: Assisted Machine Dips target the triceps, chest, and shoulders. This exercise is performed on a dip machine with adjustable weight assistance, allowing for controlled movement and gradual strength development. It is suitable for beginners who may not yet have the strength to perform unassisted dips.
instructions: Adjust the weight stack to provide the desired level of assistance.
Step onto the machine platform and grip the handles firmly.
Position your knees on the knee pad or foot platform, ensuring your body is upright.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until your upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Press through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control throughout.
mistakes: Leaning too far forward, shifting focus from triceps to chest.
Allowing shoulders to shrug, reducing triceps engagement.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine, leading to poor posture.
Using too much assistance weight, minimizing muscle activation.
Not lowering body to a 90-degree elbow angle, limiting range of motion.
Rushing through reps, sacrificing control and form.
Locking elbows at the top, causing joint strain.
Allowing elbows to flare out excessively, increasing shoulder stress.
Not keeping wrists straight, risking wrist discomfort.
exercises.name: Assisted Machine Dips
tips: Ensure a full range of motion by lowering until your upper arms are parallel to the ground.
Keep your core engaged to maintain stability and prevent swinging.
Focus on a slow, controlled descent and ascent to maximize muscle engagement.
Adjust the assistance level as you gain strength to continue challenging your muscles.
Avoid locking out your elbows at the top of the movement to keep tension on the muscles.

exercises.description: The Assisted Pistol Squat is a single-leg squat variation that utilizes support to aid in balance and control. This exercise targets the quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings, and core muscles while improving unilateral strength and stability.
instructions: Stand upright next to a sturdy support, such as a squat rack or parallel bars, with your feet hip-width apart.
Hold onto the support with one hand for balance.
Lift one leg off the ground, extending it straight in front of you.
Engage your core and slowly lower your body into a squat on the supporting leg, keeping your chest up and back straight.
Descend as low as you can comfortably go while maintaining control and balance.
Push through the heel of your supporting foot to return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions before switching legs.
mistakes: Leaning too far forward, causing imbalance and strain on the knee.
Not keeping the supporting foot flat on the ground, leading to instability.
Allowing the knee to cave inward, increasing the risk of knee injury.
Failing to engage the core, resulting in poor balance and control.
Dropping too quickly into the squat, losing control and risking muscle strain.
Not extending the non-working leg fully, reducing the exercise's effectiveness.
Using too much assistance, which limits strength development.
Rounding the back, which can lead to poor posture and back strain.
Not maintaining an upright torso, affecting balance and squat depth.
Allowing the heel of the working leg to lift off the ground, compromising stability.
exercises.name: Assisted Pistol Squat
tips: Focus on keeping your core engaged throughout the movement to maintain stability.
Use the support only as much as needed to maintain balance; try to rely more on your leg strength over time.
Keep your knee aligned with your toes to prevent any inward or outward collapse.
Control the descent and ascent to maximize muscle engagement and reduce injury risk.
Start with a higher support if needed and gradually work towards using less assistance as you gain strength.

exercises.description: The Assisted Pull-Up is a strength training exercise that targets the muscles of the back, shoulders, and arms. It is performed using a machine that provides counterbalance weight to assist in lifting your body, making it suitable for those who are building strength to perform unassisted pull-ups. This exercise primarily engages the latissimus dorsi, biceps, and trapezius muscles.
instructions: Adjust the weight on the assisted pull-up machine to provide the necessary support.
Stand on the platform or kneel on the pad, depending on the machine design.
Grasp the pull-up handles with an overhand grip, slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
Engage your core and keep your body straight as you begin the movement.
Pull yourself upward by driving your elbows down and back until your chin is above the bar.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring full contraction of the back muscles.
Slowly lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using too much assistance, reducing muscle engagement and effectiveness.
Allowing the body to swing, leading to momentum-based movement instead of muscle activation.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom, limiting range of motion and muscle activation.
Pulling with the arms instead of engaging the back muscles, reducing back development.
Shrugging shoulders up towards ears, causing tension in the neck and shoulders.
Leaning back excessively, altering movement pattern and reducing effectiveness.
Not maintaining a stable core, leading to poor body alignment and control.
Gripping the bar incorrectly, causing wrist strain and reducing pulling efficiency.
Rushing through the movement, sacrificing control and form.
Failing to engage the scapulae, limiting back muscle activation and strength gains.
exercises.name: Assisted Pull-Up
tips: Ensure that your grip is firm but relaxed to prevent unnecessary tension in your forearms.
Focus on engaging your back muscles rather than pulling with your arms.
Maintain a steady and controlled movement throughout each repetition to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid swinging or using momentum to complete the pull-up; control is key.
Adjust the assistance weight as you gain strength to gradually reduce dependency on the machine.
Keep your shoulders down and away from your ears to prevent strain and promote proper form.
Breathe out as you pull up and inhale as you lower yourself back down.

exercises.description: A strongman lift in which you pick a heavy round stone up from the floor, rest it on your lap in a deep squat, then stand up and load it onto a chest-high platform. The legs and hips do most of the work, while the back, arms and grip hold the stone tight to your body.
instructions: Stand close behind the stone facing the platform, with your feet about shoulder-width apart.
Bend your hips and knees, bring your chest over the stone and wrap your forearms and hands under its lower half.
Pull the stone off the floor and roll it up onto your thighs, sitting into a deep squat.
With the stone on your lap, move your hands higher around it and squeeze it tightly against your torso.
Drive through your legs and stand up with the stone hugged high on your chest.
Push your hips forward, lean back slightly and roll the stone over the edge onto the platform.
Release the stone only when it rests securely on the platform.
mistakes: Starting with the stone too far in front of your feet
Trying to lift the stone from the floor to the platform in one pull without lapping it
Curling the stone with the arms instead of driving with the legs and hips
Leaving the hands low on the stone after the lap, so it slips as you stand
Letting the stone drift away from your chest as you stand up
Throwing the stone with a hard lean back instead of rolling it onto the platform with the hips
exercises.name: Atlas Stone Load
tips: Start with a light stone and a lower platform while you learn the lap and the regrip.
Take a fresh breath and brace again while the stone rests on your lap, before you stand up.
Look forward rather than down as you stand up, so your chest stays up behind the stone.
Tacky on your forearms improves the grip on the stone if your gym allows it.
Finish close to the platform with your feet flat, so a slight lean back is enough to roll the stone over.

exercises.description: The Australian Pull-Up Underhand Grip, also known as an inverted row with a supine grip, is a bodyweight exercise targeting the upper back, biceps, and forearms. It involves pulling your chest towards a bar while your body remains in a horizontal position, with feet on the ground and palms facing you.
instructions: Set a bar at waist height on a squat rack or Smith machine.
Lie under the bar with your chest directly beneath it.
Grab the bar with an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Extend your legs out in front of you, keeping your heels on the ground.
Engage your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Pull your chest towards the bar by bending your elbows and squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement when your chest touches the bar.
Lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
mistakes: Hips sagging, reducing core engagement and increasing strain on the lower back.
Elbows flaring out, which can lead to shoulder discomfort and inefficient pulling mechanics.
Pulling with the arms instead of initiating the movement from the back muscles.
Inadequate retraction and depression of the scapulae, limiting back muscle activation.
Inconsistent tempo, leading to poor control and reduced effectiveness of the exercise.
Chin not reaching the bar, resulting in incomplete range of motion.
Feet placed too far forward, reducing leverage and making the movement more difficult.
Wrists bending excessively, which can cause discomfort and reduce grip strength.
Neck craning forward, leading to potential neck strain and misalignment.
exercises.name: Australian Pull-Up Underhand Grip
tips: Ensure your body forms a straight line from head to heels throughout the exercise.
Keep your elbows close to your body as you pull up to engage the biceps effectively.
Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement for maximum back engagement.
Control the descent to maintain tension in the muscles and prevent injury.
If you find it too difficult, bend your knees to reduce the load or raise the bar higher.
To increase difficulty, elevate your feet on a bench or platform.

exercises.description: The B Stance Romanian Deadlift is a unilateral variation of the traditional Romanian Deadlift, designed to target the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back. This exercise involves a staggered stance where one foot is positioned slightly behind the other, allowing for greater emphasis on the front leg while maintaining balance and stability.
instructions: Stand with your feet hip-width apart. Shift your weight onto your right foot and place your left foot slightly behind you, toes touching the ground for balance.
Hold a dumbbell or barbell in front of your thighs with an overhand grip, keeping your arms straight.
Engage your core and keep your back straight as you hinge at the hips, lowering the weight towards the floor. Your right knee should have a slight bend.
Lower the weight until you feel a stretch in your right hamstring, ensuring your back remains flat and your shoulders are pulled back.
Push through your right heel to return to the starting position, keeping the movement controlled.
Complete the desired number of repetitions on one side before switching to the other leg.
mistakes: Leaning too far forward, causing excessive strain on the lower back.
Not keeping the back straight, leading to rounding of the spine.
Allowing the front knee to bend excessively, reducing hamstring engagement.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Using the back leg for support instead of balance, reducing load on the working leg.
Raising the torso too quickly, compromising control and muscle engagement.
Not hinging at the hips, resulting in a squat-like movement.
Allowing the shoulders to round forward, disengaging the upper back muscles.
Dropping the weights too low, causing unnecessary stress on the lower back.
Not engaging the core, leading to instability and poor balance.
Using momentum to lift the weight instead of controlled muscle activation.
Positioning the back foot too far behind, causing imbalance and reduced effectiveness.
exercises.name: B Stance Romanian Deadlift
tips: Focus on maintaining a neutral spine throughout the movement to prevent lower back strain.
Keep your core engaged to help stabilize your body and maintain balance.
Ensure that most of your weight is on the front leg to maximize muscle engagement.
Move slowly and with control to fully engage the hamstrings and glutes.
Avoid rounding your back as you lower the weight; keep your chest open and shoulders back.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: The Back Extension exercise targets the lower back muscles, specifically the erector spinae. It also engages the glutes and hamstrings. This exercise is typically performed on a hyperextension bench or Roman chair, allowing for controlled extension and flexion of the spine.
instructions: Position yourself face down on a hyperextension bench with your hips aligned with the edge of the pad.
Secure your feet under the foot pads to maintain stability.
Cross your arms over your chest or place your hands behind your head.
Start with your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Slowly lower your upper body towards the floor by bending at the hips, keeping your back straight.
Descend until you feel a slight stretch in your hamstrings or until your torso is approximately perpendicular to the floor.
Engage your lower back muscles and glutes to raise your torso back to the starting position.
Avoid hyperextending your back at the top of the movement.
mistakes: Hyperextending the lower back beyond its natural range of motion.
Using momentum instead of controlled movement.
Failing to engage the core muscles for stabilization.
Allowing the head to drop or extend excessively.
Arching the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Lifting the torso too high, causing spinal compression.
Positioning the feet too close together, reducing stability.
Neglecting to align the hips properly with the pad.
Rushing through repetitions without proper form.
Holding the breath instead of maintaining steady breathing.
exercises.name: Back Extension
tips: Maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise to prevent injury.
Control the movement speed; avoid using momentum to lift yourself.
Focus on squeezing your glutes and lower back muscles during the ascent.
Keep your neck in line with your spine to avoid strain.
Adjust the bench height so that it supports your hips comfortably without restricting movement.
Perform the exercise with slow, deliberate movements for maximum muscle engagement.
If new to this exercise, start with fewer repetitions and gradually increase as you build strength.

exercises.description: The Back Extension With Dumbbell is an exercise targeting the lower back muscles, specifically the erector spinae. It also engages the glutes and hamstrings. This exercise helps improve posture and strengthen the posterior chain.
instructions: Begin by lying face down on a hyperextension bench, securing your feet under the foot pads.
Hold a dumbbell with both hands against your chest.
Ensure your body forms a straight line from head to heels.
Slowly lower your upper body towards the floor by bending at the hips, keeping your back straight.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement.

Slowly tuck your knees to your chest to transition into an inverted hang.

exercises.description: Hang from the bar with an overhand grip and one foot supported by a resistance band. Pull your chest up to the bar, bring your shoulders over it and press into a straight-arm support. Lower through the same phases under control, keeping the band secure beneath your foot.
instructions: Secure a resistance band around the bar and place one foot in its hanging loop.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width with an overhand grip. Start in a dead hang with your arms straight, shoulders active, chest lifted, and legs kept under control by the band.
Begin by pulling the bar down toward your upper chest. Drive your elbows down and back, and lean your torso slightly behind the bar as you pull.
Pull explosively until your chest reaches bar height. Keep the bar close to your body and avoid swinging your legs forward.
As your chest comes over the bar, quickly rotate your wrists and elbows over it. Bring your shoulders forward above the bar while keeping pressure through the band-supported leg.
Finish the transition in the top support position with the bar near your lower chest or upper abdomen. Your elbows should be bent and pointing back, not flared far out to the sides.
Press down through the bar to perform a straight-bar dip until your arms are fully extended. Keep your shoulders stable and your body tight at the top.
Lower under control by bending your elbows, bringing your chest back to the bar, then returning to a full hang. Reset your body position before the next repetition.

Trying to transition before pulling high enough, causing the elbows to get stuck below the bar.
Keeping the elbows wide during the turnover instead of bringing them quickly over the bar.

Dropping too quickly through the transition and lowering phase instead of controlling the descent.

Start from a controlled dead hang with your shoulders active. Pull your shoulder blades down and keep your ribs from flaring excessively.
Exhale through the pull and press, then inhale as you lower.
Keep the band-supported leg long and let the free leg follow without kicking.

Focus on pulling with your back muscles rather than just your arms.
Keep your elbows slightly in front of you to engage your lats effectively.
Maintain a controlled movement throughout; avoid swinging or using momentum.
Gradually decrease band assistance as you build strength.

exercises.description: Hinge forward and pull a band from a mid-height anchor to your upper chest: a lat pulldown you can do at home with no high anchor point. Your lats do most of the work, helped by the small muscles around and below your shoulder blades (teres major and minor, infraspinatus), your lower traps and rear delts. Leaning forward puts your torso in line with the band, so the pull works like a pulldown, not a row. Your hamstrings, glutes and lower back only hold the hinge; if your lower back is tired, kneel under a high anchor instead. Light sets make a good warm-up before pull-ups and rows.
instructions: Loop the band around something solid at waist-to-chest height: a rack upright, a post or a door anchor at the middle hinge of a closed door.
Hold one end in each hand with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder width, and walk back until the band is taut with your arms straight.
Feet hip to shoulder width, knees bent: push your hips back until your torso is about 30–45° above horizontal, back flat and head in line.
Reach your arms toward the anchor so they line up with your torso, upper arms beside your head. You should feel a stretch under your armpits.
Start the pull by drawing your shoulders down away from your ears, then drive your elbows down and back toward your sides.
Stop when your elbows are beside your ribs and your hands sit just below your chin. Squeeze your shoulder blades down and together for a second.
Let your arms travel forward over 2–3 seconds until straight, band still taut. After the last rep, walk toward the anchor before standing up.
mistakes: Turning it into a row: arms hanging toward the floor at the start, hands pulled to your belly, elbows rising behind your back. Start with your arms reaching forward in line with your torso and drive your elbows down along your sides until your hands reach your chin.
Standing up as you pull, so your body stretches the band instead of your back. Set the torso angle before the first rep and keep it; if you can't, take a lighter band or step closer to the anchor.
Rounding your lower back or letting your head drop. Brace and keep your neck long; if your back still rounds, hinge a little less.
Letting the band yank your arms forward. Return over 2–3 seconds and stop at full reach while the band is still taut.
exercises.name: Band Bent Over Lat Pulldown
tips: Sets of 12–20 reps taken close to failure work well, with a one-second squeeze and a slow return; a heavy band suits sets of 8–12.

Earn each step with reps first. When you get 20 on each set with the full stretch and the same hinge, step 15–30 cm further from the anchor or move to the next band, and restart at the bottom of the range. Bands jump a lot between sizes, so use the step back before you change bands.

The work sits in the sides of your back from the armpits down, the area around your shoulder blades and the back of your shoulders. Your biceps help bend the elbows but shouldn't tire first: keep your wrists straight and lead with your elbows.
Lower back giving out before your lats? Use a lighter band or switch to the kneeling one-arm version. To make it harder, fold the band double or slow the return to 3 seconds.
The band runs at face height. Check it for nicks and the anchor for a firm wrap before each set, and never let go of a stretched band.

Substitutes: One-Arm Band Kneeling Lat Pulldown (no hinge to hold, needs a high anchor), Band Pulldown Behind Neck (high anchor and more shoulder mobility), Cable Lat Pulldown (the gym version, with small weight steps), Band Assisted Pull Up (needs a pull-up bar).

Maintain tension in the resistance band throughout the exercise for maximum effectiveness.

Keep your core engaged and hips pressed into the ground.
Flex your knees, pulling your heels towards your glutes against the band's resistance.

Hold the band with both hands, keeping your arms extended in front of your chest.

Engage your core and glutes to maintain a stable posture.
Press the band straight out in front of you, keeping your arms parallel to the floor.

exercises.description: The Band Pass Through Shoulders exercise is a mobility drill designed to improve shoulder flexibility and range of motion. Continue moving your arms backward until the band reaches behind your back, or as far as your shoulder mobility allows.

Keep your core engaged to maintain stability and prevent arching of the lower back during the movement.

exercises.description: A standing upper-back exercise: hold a resistance band in front of you with straight arms at shoulder height and pull it apart until your arms point out to the sides. Pull the band apart by moving your hands out to the sides in a wide arc, keeping your arms straight and level with your shoulders.

Start with a light band to learn its increasing resistance.
Step forward until there is a little tension at the start.
Exhale as you press and inhale on the return.
Change the leading foot between sets for a balanced stance.

exercises.description: A standing rotator cuff exercise with a loop band around both wrists. instructions: Place a loop band around both wrists and stand tall with your feet about hip-width apart.
Bend your elbows to 90 degrees and keep them lightly pressed against your sides.
Start with your forearms in front of your abdomen. Keep your shoulders down and relaxed and your wrists straight.
Keeping your elbows at your sides, rotate both forearms outward at the same time, away from your body, as far as you can without moving the elbows.

Picture your forearms as two doors swinging open on hinges at your elbows.
Keep your chest up and your shoulder blades gently drawn back.

instructions: Anchor the band to the base of a rack at ankle height and loop the other end around one ankle.
Stand facing the rack, step back until the band is taut and hold an upright with both hands.
Stand tall on the supporting leg with a slight bend in that knee and brace your core.
Keep the working knee next to the supporting knee, pointing down.
Bend the working knee and curl your heel back toward your glute against the band.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower the foot slowly until the knee is almost straight.
Complete all reps on one leg, then move the band to the other ankle.

Stopping short of a full knee bend because the band is too strong.

Use the rack for balance only. Do not pull on it to help lift the leg.
Squeeze your glutes lightly to keep the hips square and the torso upright.
Keep the working foot gently flexed so the band stays in place on the ankle.
Lower the foot over 2 to 3 seconds instead of letting the band pull it down.

exercises.description: A standing one-leg hamstring curl with no anchor: a loop band goes around the working ankle and under the other foot. Stand tall with your hands on your hips, keep the thighs side by side and curl the working heel back toward your glute, then lower it slowly under control.

Squeeze your glutes lightly to keep the pelvis level while you balance on one leg.

Lower the foot over 2 to 3 seconds instead of letting the band snap it down.

Engage your core and keep your back straight.
Slowly bend your torso to the right, pulling against the resistance of the band.

Overextending the side bend, risking strain on the lower back.
Not returning to a fully upright position between repetitions.

Avoid leaning forward or backward; focus on a pure lateral bend.
Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid shrugging them during the exercise.
Maintain a slight bend in your knees to reduce strain on your lower back.
Focus on using your oblique muscles to initiate and control the movement.
Exhale as you bend to the side and inhale as you return to the starting position.

exercises.description: Stand with your back to a high band anchor, hands at your neck, and curl one shoulder down toward the opposite hip to load your obliques. The sides of your waist do most of the work, and the effort runs diagonally from the shoulder that comes down to the opposite hip; your six-pack muscle (rectus abdominis) helps because the spine rounds. Think of it as a crunch with a twist, not a straight-arm rotation or a side bend. It suits home training with just a band and a high anchor, and anyone who can't kneel comfortably.
instructions: Loop the band around something high and solid behind you: the top of a power rack, a pull-up bar or a door anchor at the top of a closed door.
Stand with your back to the anchor, feet hip-width and knees soft.
Step forward until the band is taut while you stand tall, hips stacked over your feet.
Bring the band over your shoulders and hold the ends in your fists at the sides of your neck, just above the collarbones.
Point your elbows down in front of your chest; your hands stay parked there until the set is over.
Breathe out and curl your ribs toward your pelvis while turning one shoulder down and across, as if taking your right elbow to the outside of your left thigh.
Stop when your trunk is curled about 45° and clearly turned, and squeeze for a second. Hips, knees and feet don't move.
Breathe in and uncurl over 2–3 seconds, letting the band bring you back to tall standing but not past it into an arch.
On the next rep, curl and turn to the other side, or finish all reps to one side, then switch. Match the count and depth on both sides.
mistakes: Bowing forward from the hips with a flat back, so the hips and the band do the work. Keep your hips over your heels, think "ribs to pelvis" and let your spine round; if that won't happen, use a lighter band or stand a little closer to the anchor.
Pulling with your arms: the fists drift away from your neck or the elbows drive down on their own. Pin your fists to your collarbones so the elbows move only because your trunk curls.
Turning without curling, or curling without turning. Lead with one shoulder down and across toward the opposite hip and finish with that elbow outside the opposite thigh.
Letting your hips and knees twist with your trunk until your feet pivot. Keep your feet planted, the knee bend fixed and your belt line facing forward.
exercises.name: Band Standing Twisting Crunches
tips: This isn't a max-strength lift. For harder sets, pick a band that stops you at 8–12 slow reps per side; for muscle growth, 12–20 per side over 2–4 sets. Add reps at the same band and distance first. Once you get the top number on all sets with a one-second squeeze, make it harder and start again from the low end.

The next band up is often a big jump, roughly 5–10 kg at full stretch. Bridge it first: stand half a step (15–30 cm) farther from the anchor, add a light band to your current one or pause for 2 seconds at the bottom. Then move up a band.

Expect a hard squeeze along the side of your waist and diagonally across the front of your abs. Burning arms or neck mean your hands are pulling; a pinch in your lower back means you're hinging or arching instead of curling.

The band and your hands sit right next to your face, so check the band for nicks and the anchor for slipping before every set. Use a door anchor only on the hinge side of a closed door that opens away from you. If loaded twisting flares up a known disc problem, shorten the range or switch to a Pallof press.

Substitutes: Band Kneeling Twisting Crunch (same setup, but kneeling locks your hips), Cable Kneeling Side Crunch (heavier loads in finer steps) and Bicycle Crunches (no equipment). If your hips still turn with you, go back to Band Standing Crunches with a lighter band and add a small turn later.

Avoid using momentum; focus on slow and controlled movements for better muscle activation.
Adjust the resistance by stepping closer or further from the anchor point to increase or decrease tension.

exercises.description: Perform an underhand pull-up with a resistance band supporting one knee. Pull until the chin passes the bar, then lower to a controlled hang. The band assists the upward phase while the back and biceps work through the same pulling movement as an unassisted chin-up.
