Stand under the bar and take an underhand grip with your palms facing you. Place your hands about shoulder-width apart.
Hang with your arms straight, shoulders pulled slightly down away from your ears, and your body in a straight line. Keep your ribs down and brace your stomach.
Pull your elbows down toward your sides and raise your chest toward the bar. Let the band assist you, but keep the movement controlled.

Lower yourself slowly until your arms are fully straight again, keeping tension through your shoulders and core.

Pulling the chest forward while overextending the lower back.
Stopping short of bringing the chin clearly over the bar.
Dropping too quickly instead of controlling the lowering phase.
Failing to reach a full, controlled hang at the bottom.
Craning the neck toward the bar instead of keeping the head neutral.

Use a band that gives enough assistance to complete smooth reps with full control, but not so much that it pulls you up without effort.
Grip the bar with an underhand grip, hands about shoulder width apart. Wrap your thumbs around the bar for a secure hold.
End the set while you can still pull actively against the assistance.
Progress by using a lighter band, adding more controlled reps, or pausing briefly at the top and bottom positions.

exercises.description: Band-assisted dips use a resistance band under the knees to reduce the load as you press on parallel bars. Use a platform to enter the band without a jump, then settle both knees securely.
Progress by using a band with less assistance or adding repetitions while preserving the same range.

exercises.description: Lying on a flat bench, you lower a barbell to your lower chest and press it back to straight arms to build a bigger chest and a stronger press. The whole chest works, from the collarbone down to its lower edge, and you feel it most at the bottom. Your front delts help drive the bar off the chest and your triceps finish the lockout. With both hands on one bar you can handle more weight than with dumbbells and add it in small, exact steps, which is why it's the standard test of upper-body strength and one of the three powerlifting lifts.
instructions: Set the bar in the hooks at a height you can unrack with your arms almost straight, then lie down with your eyes under it.
Plant your feet flat and wide, under or a little behind your knees. They stay put until the bar is back in the hooks.
Take an overhand grip with your thumbs wrapped, hands a little wider than your shoulders. On an Olympic bar that's often near the ring marks.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down and pin them to the bench. A small lower-back arch is fine, but your glutes stay down.
Unrack on straight arms and bring the bar out until it sits over your shoulders. Breathe in and brace your stomach.
Lower the bar over 1–2 seconds to the bottom half of your chest, around nipple level, elbows 45–60° from your sides and forearms vertical.
Touch lightly without bouncing, then press up and slightly back toward your face until your elbows are straight and the bar is over your shoulders.
After the final rep, lock out, move the bar back until it touches the uprights, and only then set it down in the hooks.
mistakes: Bouncing the bar off your chest to get it moving. Lower it at an even pace and just touch; if the bounce keeps sneaking back, pause for a split second.
Elbows flared out to 90° with the bar landing high on the chest or near the neck. Tuck them to 45–60° and touch the bottom half of your chest.
Shoulder blades sliding apart so the shoulders roll forward at the top. Set the blades back and down before you unrack and stop at straight elbows instead of reaching for the ceiling.

Wrists bent back with the bar sitting in your fingers, sometimes with the thumbs off it. Hold it low in your palm over the forearm and wrap your thumbs, since a thumbless grip can let the bar roll onto your chest or neck.
Hips coming off the bench to grind out the last rep. Keep your glutes down and push your feet into the floor; if the rep won't move that way, the set is over.
Pressing straight up or toward your feet, so the bar finishes over your chest. Drive it up and slightly back until it's stacked over your shoulders.
exercises.name: Barbell Bench Press
tips: For strength, 3–5 sets of 3–6 reps are typical; for muscle size, 6–12, sometimes up to 15. End most sets with 1–3 reps left in the tank.

Add reps before weight. On 3 sets of 6–10, build up until all three sets hit 10, then add 2.5 kg (1.25 kg per side) and work up again from 6. Beginners can often add 5 kg a session at first; small 0.5–1 kg plates keep you moving later on.
A sharp or pinching pain at the front or top of the shoulder, or sore wrists, means stop and check three things: grip width, elbow angle and where the bar touches your chest.

For sets close to failure, set the safety arms just below chest height or have someone spot you. Training alone with no safeties? Leave the collars off so you can tip the plates off one side if you get stuck.
New to the lift? Groove it with the empty bar or start on the Machine Chest Press. Once it feels solid, make it harder by pausing the bar on your chest for 1–2 seconds every rep.
Substitutes: Dumbbell Bench Press if a fixed bar bothers your shoulders, Smith Bench Press when you train alone, Machine Chest Press, or Push-Up with no equipment.

exercises.description: The Barbell Bench Press with Chains is a variation of the traditional bench press that incorporates chains to add variable resistance. As the barbell is lifted, more chain links are lifted off the ground, increasing the load. This exercise targets the pectoral muscles, triceps, and shoulders, and helps improve strength and power by accommodating resistance throughout the range of motion.
instructions: Set up a flat bench and position a barbell with chains attached on a rack at an appropriate height.
Lie back on the bench with your feet flat on the ground and your eyes directly under the bar.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, ensuring your wrists are straight and elbows are under the bar.
Unrack the bar by straightening your arms and position it above your chest with elbows locked.
Lower the bar slowly to your chest, allowing the chains to pile on the floor, maintaining control and keeping elbows at a 45-degree angle to your body.
Press the bar back up explosively to the starting position, lifting more chain links off the ground as you extend your arms fully.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining form throughout.
mistakes: Allowing the barbell to bounce off the chest, reducing muscle engagement and control.
Failing to maintain a stable shoulder position, increasing the risk of shoulder strain.
Using too much chain weight, leading to compromised form and reduced range of motion.
Not keeping the feet planted on the floor, causing instability and loss of power.
Arching the back excessively, which can lead to improper load distribution.
Lowering the bar unevenly, causing imbalanced muscle activation.
Not engaging the core, leading to a lack of stability and control.
Failing to align wrists and elbows, increasing the risk of joint stress.
Rushing the lift, which can compromise form and control.
Neglecting to adjust chain length for proper load distribution throughout the lift.
exercises.name: Barbell Bench Press with Chains
tips: Ensure chains are evenly distributed on both sides of the barbell to maintain balance.
Focus on controlling the descent of the bar to maximize muscle engagement and safety.
Keep your core engaged throughout the movement to stabilize your body.
Use a spotter if lifting heavy weights to ensure safety during unracking and reracking.
Experiment with different chain lengths to adjust resistance levels according to your strength and goals.
Maintain a steady breathing pattern: inhale as you lower the bar and exhale as you press it back up.

exercises.description: Hinge forward until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor and row a barbell from a straight-arm hang to your stomach to build a stronger upper back. You feel it between and below your shoulder blades (middle and lower traps), in your rear delts and down the sides of your back in your lats, while your lower back holds the hinge and your forearms hold the bar. Once you can hold a flat-back hip hinge, it's the standard heavy back exercise and needs only a bar and plates. Unlike the Pendlay Row, the plates never touch the floor between reps, so your back stays loaded all set long.
instructions: Load the bar on the floor, or set it in a rack at mid-thigh height.
Take an overhand grip a little wider than your shoulders, thumbs wrapped around the bar.
Pick the bar up the way you start a deadlift: flat back, bar close to your legs. Feet end up hip-width apart, toes forward.
Soften your knees and push your hips back until your torso sits about 15–30° above parallel. That's the starting position: arms straight, bar hanging around mid-shin.
Breathe into your belly, pull your ribs down and brace. Look at the floor about a meter ahead so your head stays in line with your back.
Drive your elbows back toward your hips and pull the bar up along your thighs to your stomach, between your lower ribs and your navel.
In the top position your elbows are behind your torso, roughly 30–45° from your sides, and your shoulder blades are squeezed together. Hold it for a second.
Lower the bar in 1–2 seconds until your arms are straight again. Your torso, hips and knees stay put, and the plates don't touch the floor.
To finish, bend your knees and set the bar down with a flat back, or stand up and return it to the rack.
mistakes: Standing up a bit more with every rep and jerking the bar with your hips. Pick one torso angle and keep it to the last rep; if the bar only moves with a hip drive, strip some weight.

Rounding your back at the bottom as the bar pulls your shoulders toward the floor. Brace again before each rep and let only your shoulder blades spread. If your lower back still rounds, bend your knees a little more.
Rowing to your chest with your elbows flared out wide. Aim the bar at your navel and drive your elbows toward your hips.
Tapping or bouncing the plates on the floor between reps. That turns it into a Pendlay Row; here every rep starts from a dead hang with straight arms.
Cranking your neck up to watch yourself in the mirror. Look at the floor about a meter ahead with your chin slightly tucked.
exercises.name: Barbell Bent Over Row
tips: Sets of 8–12 suit muscle growth, 5–8 suit strength.
Stay at one weight and add reps; once each set hits the upper number without your torso rising, add 2.5 kg (1.25 kg per side) and build up again from the lower one.
Your lower back works here because it holds the hinge, and that's normal. If it aches before your upper back is tired, the weight is too heavy or your spine is rounding.

Overhand or underhand? With this overhand grip and slightly wider hands, your upper back and rear shoulders do more of the work. In the Barbell Reverse Grip Bent Over Row your elbows stay closer to your body and your arms help more.

Can't hold the hinge yet? Learn the pull with your chest on an incline bench, or row a lighter bar with your torso at about 45°. Once the full version feels easy, pause for 2 seconds with the bar on your stomach.

Substitutes: Pendlay Row if you want every rep to start from the floor, Double Dumbbell Bent Over Row for a longer pull, Incline Chest Supported Barbell Row when your lower back is tired, and Smith Machine Bent Over Row for a fixed bar path.

exercises.description: The Barbell Bent Over Row From Pin is a compound exercise targeting the back muscles, primarily the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and trapezius. instructions: Set the safety pins in a power rack to knee height or slightly below.
Place the barbell on the pins and stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the barbell with an overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Keep your back straight and core engaged as you lift the barbell off the pins.
Pull the barbell towards your lower chest or upper abdomen, keeping elbows close to your body.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Lower the barbell back to the pins in a controlled manner.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Rounding the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Pulling the bar with the arms rather than engaging the back muscles.
Elevating the shoulders instead of keeping them retracted.
Bouncing the bar off the pins instead of lifting with control.
Not setting the pins at the correct height for proper range of motion.
Standing too upright, reducing the effectiveness of the exercise.
Allowing the wrists to bend excessively, straining them.
Failing to engage the core for stability.
Using momentum instead of controlled muscle contraction.
exercises.name: Barbell Bent Over Row From Pin
tips: Ensure your back remains flat throughout the exercise to avoid injury.
Engage your core to maintain stability and support your lower back.
Focus on pulling with your back muscles rather than your arms.
Use a weight that allows you to maintain proper form throughout all repetitions.
Control the descent of the barbell to maximize muscle engagement.
Breath out as you pull the barbell up and inhale as you lower it back down.

exercises.description: Stand tall, hold a straight barbell palms-forward and curl it from your thighs to shoulder height: the standard barbell curl for bigger, stronger biceps. Both heads of the biceps lift the bar, with the brachialis underneath and the brachioradialis on the thumb side of your forearm pitching in. Two hands on one bar let you curl more total weight than with dumbbells, and the straight bar keeps your palms turned fully up, so the biceps works a little harder than on an EZ bar. The EZ-bar, wide-grip, close-grip and palms-down reverse curls are separate variations.
instructions: Take a straight bar you can curl without swinging from a mid-thigh rack, or deadlift it off the floor with a flat back.
Stand tall with your feet about hip-width apart, knees straight but soft and your weight over the middle of your feet.
Take an underhand grip, palms facing forward, hands about shoulder-width so your forearms hang straight just outside your thighs. Wrap your thumbs around the bar.
Start with straight arms, bar on your thighs, shoulders down and back. Lightly brace your abs and glutes so your torso can't rock.
Breathe out and bend both elbows, curling the bar up in an arc. Upper arms stay against your ribs; only your forearms move.
Stop with your forearms about vertical and the bar at shoulder height in front of your upper chest, below your chin. Squeeze for a second.
Take 2–3 seconds to lower the bar until your elbows are straight and the bar touches your thighs. Pause briefly, then curl again.
To end the set, put the bar back in the rack, or bend your knees and lower it to the floor with a flat back.
mistakes: Swinging: your hips drive forward and your torso leans back to get the bar moving. Take some weight off, squeeze your glutes and abs before each rep and keep your knees still; if the swing keeps sneaking in, curl with your back against a wall.
Elbows travel forward and up at the top, so your front delts lift the bar toward your chin. Keep your elbows by your ribs and stop once your forearms are vertical.
Wrists bending back under the bar or curling in at the top. Hold the bar firmly with your knuckles in line with your forearms from the first rep to the last.

Dropping the bar and bouncing it off your thighs into the next rep. Count 2–3 seconds on every lowering and start each rep from a short stop; a heavy bar slamming into straight elbows yanks on the biceps tendon.
exercises.name: Barbell Biceps Curl
tips: Curl for 8–15 reps, or 6–10 on heavier days.
Stay at one weight and add reps until you get the top number on every set with no swing, then add the smallest plates (1.25 kg per side) and build back up from the bottom of the range.

An empty 20 kg Olympic bar is already too heavy for many beginners, so a fixed-weight straight bar or a light technique bar is fine. Fixed bars usually go up in 2.5–5 kg steps, a big jump at curl weights: expect a few sessions at each one, or use 0.5–1 kg fractional plates if your gym has them.

The front of your upper arms works hardest from halfway up to the squeeze, plus the thumb side of your forearms and your grip. If your lower back or the front of your shoulders joins in, the bar is too heavy. If the straight bar pulls on your inner elbows or wrists, switch to an EZ bar or dumbbells.

Can't stop the swing? Do the Barbell Wall Curl with your back flat against a wall. To make it harder, lower in 3–4 seconds, pause for a second with your forearms level on the way up, or move on to the Barbell Preacher Curl.

Substitutes: EZ-Bar Biceps Curl (easier on the wrists), Dumbbell Biceps Curl (each arm lifts its own weight), Bar Cable Biceps Curl (steady pull at the bottom), Close Grip Biceps Curl (same bar, narrower hands).

exercises.description: A standing overhead press that alternates the bar position: from the front of your shoulders up to straight arms, down behind your neck onto the upper traps, then over your head and back to the front. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to keep your ribs down and your torso upright.
Press the bar straight up until your arms are fully extended, tilting your head slightly back to let it pass.
Lower the bar under control behind your head until it rests on your upper traps.
Press the bar overhead again to straight arms, then lower it in front of your head to your shoulders.
Keep alternating the front and back positions for the planned number of repetitions.
mistakes: Arching the lower back and pushing the ribs forward to get the bar overhead
Dropping the bar onto the neck instead of lowering it to the traps under control
Letting the bar drift forward, away from the head
Pushing the head forward and down as the bar passes behind it
Using a knee dip or leg drive to bounce the bar up
Stopping short of straight arms overhead

Use a much lighter load than in your regular overhead press, since the behind-the-neck position demands good shoulder mobility.
At the top, push your shoulders up toward the bar and finish with your biceps beside your ears.
Move your head only as much as needed to clear the bar, then bring it back to neutral once the bar is overhead.
If lowering behind your neck pinches your shoulders, stop the bar higher or switch to a regular overhead press.

exercises.description: The Barbell Bulgarian Squat is a unilateral lower body exercise that targets the quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings. It involves performing a squat with one leg elevated behind you on a bench or platform while holding a barbell across your upper back. This exercise enhances balance, stability, and muscular strength in the legs.
instructions: Begin by positioning a bench or platform behind you at knee height.
Place a barbell across your upper back, ensuring it is centered and secure.
Stand about two feet in front of the bench with your feet hip-width apart.
Lift one leg and place the top of your foot on the bench behind you.
Engage your core and keep your chest up as you begin to lower your body by bending the front knee.
Descend until your front thigh is parallel to the ground, ensuring your knee does not extend past your toes.
Press through the heel of your front foot to return to the starting position.
Complete the desired number of repetitions before switching legs.
mistakes: Allowing the front knee to cave inward, which reduces stability and increases strain on the knee joint.
Positioning the rear foot too high on the bench, leading to an unstable base and compromised balance.
Failing to maintain an upright torso, which shifts the focus away from the targeted muscles and increases lower back strain.
Dropping the hips too low, causing the front knee to travel excessively forward past the toes.
Neglecting to engage the core, resulting in poor balance and reduced control over the movement.
Using too heavy a weight, which can compromise form and lead to improper execution.
Not keeping the front foot flat on the ground, leading to instability and reduced force production.
Rushing through the movement, which decreases control and increases the likelihood of improper form.
Allowing the barbell to roll or shift on the back, which disrupts balance and focus.
exercises.name: Barbell Bulgarian Squat
tips: Maintain an upright torso throughout the movement to prevent leaning forward.
Focus on keeping your front knee aligned with your toes to avoid unnecessary strain.
Engage your core muscles to enhance stability and control during the exercise.
Start with a lighter weight to master the form before progressing to heavier loads.
Ensure that the bench height allows for comfortable placement of your rear foot without causing discomfort.
Perform the exercise in front of a mirror if possible to monitor form and alignment.

instructions: Position a barbell across your upper back, similar to a back squat setup. Ensure it is balanced and secure.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart on a flat surface or an elevated platform for greater range of motion.
Keep your core engaged and your back straight throughout the movement.
Slowly raise your heels off the ground by pushing through the balls of your feet, extending your ankles fully.
Pause at the top of the movement, squeezing your calf muscles.
Lower your heels back to the starting position in a controlled manner.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Failing to fully extend the ankles at the top of the movement.
Allowing the heels to drop too quickly, losing control during the descent.
Bouncing at the bottom of the movement instead of using a controlled motion.
Positioning the feet too wide or too narrow, affecting balance and muscle engagement.
Leaning forward or backward, causing imbalance and improper muscle activation.
Neglecting to engage the core, resulting in instability.
Locking the knees, which can strain the joints and reduce calf engagement.
exercises.name: Barbell Calf Raise

Focus on a full range of motion by allowing your heels to drop below the platform if using one.
Control the movement to maximize muscle engagement and prevent injury.
Use an appropriate weight that allows you to maintain proper form throughout the set.
Engage your core to stabilize your body and prevent swaying.
Exhale as you lift your heels and inhale as you lower them.

exercises.description: Stand with a wide stance and rest a barbell securely across your upper back. Shift your hips to one side, bending that knee while keeping the opposite leg straight and the heel on the floor. Keep your chest up, spine neutral, and the bent knee tracking over the toes. Lower under control as far as mobility allows, then drive through the bent-leg foot to return to the starting position and repeat on the other side.
instructions: Set a barbell in a squat rack at upper-chest height and load it lightly. Step under the bar, place it securely across your upper traps or rear shoulders, grip the bar firmly, brace your core, and walk back carefully into a wide stance with your toes turned slightly outward.
Stand tall with your feet wider than shoulder width, keep your chest lifted, and distribute your weight evenly through both feet before starting the movement.

Shift your body weight toward one leg while bending that knee and pushing your hips back and down. Keep the working foot flat on the floor and allow the knee to track in the same direction as the toes.

As you descend, keep the opposite leg straight and extend it out to the side. Keep the heel of the straight leg on the floor if your mobility allows; otherwise, allow the toes to point upward while maintaining control.
Lower only as far as you can while keeping your spine neutral, chest proud, and the barbell stable over your mid-foot. Avoid rounding your lower back or letting the working knee collapse inward.
Press firmly through the heel and mid-foot of the bent leg to return to the starting wide stance, keeping your core braced and the bar level throughout the ascent.
Repeat on the opposite side, alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions. Re-rack the barbell carefully when finished.
mistakes: Letting the working knee collapse inward instead of tracking over the toes
Rising onto the heel of the bent leg instead of keeping the foot planted
Allowing the straight-leg heel to lift or the toes to turn excessively upward
Rounding the lower back or collapsing the chest under the bar
Leaning too far forward and turning the movement into a hip hinge
Shifting weight onto the straight leg instead of loading the bent leg
Using a range of motion that the hips and ankles cannot control
Dropping into the bottom position without control
Bouncing out of the bottom instead of driving smoothly through the working foot
Losing barbell stability by letting the torso twist or tilt to one side
Failing to brace the core, causing the pelvis and spine to shift under load
Pushing off the toes rather than the midfoot and heel of the bent leg
exercises.name: Barbell Cossack Squat
tips: Use a light barbell at first and place it securely across your upper back in a high-bar or comfortable back-squat position, keeping your torso braced before each repetition.
Set your feet wider than shoulder width with toes turned slightly outward, allowing enough room to shift fully into each side.
Shift your hips toward one leg and bend that knee while keeping the opposite leg as straight as your mobility allows.
Keep the working foot flat on the floor and track the working knee in the same direction as the toes; do not let the knee collapse inward.
Keep your chest proud and spine neutral rather than rounding forward to reach depth.
Let the straight-leg foot stay planted with the toes pointing upward or forward according to your hip and ankle mobility, without forcing an uncomfortable position.
Descend only as far as you can control while maintaining heel contact, knee alignment, and a stable barbell position.
Drive through the heel and midfoot of the bent leg to return to the starting position, then repeat smoothly on the other side.
Move slowly and avoid bouncing at the bottom, especially when learning the exercise or using heavier weight.
Stop and reduce the range of motion or load if you feel sharp pain in the knees, hips, groin, or lower back.

exercises.description: The Barbell Drag Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps brachii. Not maintaining a straight wrist position, which can lead to wrist strain.
Rushing through the movement, reducing time under tension for the biceps.
Neglecting to contract the biceps fully at the top of the movement.
exercises.name: Barbell Drag Curl

Avoid using momentum; focus on a slow and controlled movement to maximize bicep activation.
Keep your elbows slightly behind your body to emphasize the long head of the biceps.
Ensure that your shoulders do not move forward during the curl to isolate the biceps effectively.
Use a weight that allows you to perform the exercise with proper form for all repetitions.

Lower the barbell until your upper arms touch the floor, keeping elbows at a 45-degree angle to your body.
Pause briefly, then press the barbell back up to the starting position by extending your arms.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Arching the lower back, which can disengage core muscles.

Ensure your wrists remain straight and aligned with your forearms to avoid strain.
Focus on controlled movements; avoid bouncing the barbell off the floor.

exercises.description: Stand tall with a barbell resting across your upper back, feet hip-width apart. Brace your core and take a controlled step forward. instructions: Set a barbell in a rack at upper-chest height, position it across your upper traps, and grip it securely just outside shoulder width.

Lower your body by bending both knees until your back knee is close to the floor and your front thigh is approximately parallel to the ground.

Drive through the heel and midfoot of the front foot to push yourself back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired repetitions on one side, then perform the same number of repetitions with the opposite leg forward.
Return the barbell to the rack safely after completing the set.

Taking a step that is too long, which limits depth and pulls the torso forward.
Letting the front knee collapse inward instead of tracking in line with the toes.
Pushing mainly from the back leg rather than driving through the full front foot to return to standing.
Allowing the front heel to rise off the floor during the descent.
Leaning the torso excessively forward or arching the lower back under the barbell.
Rotating or tilting the hips and shoulders instead of keeping them square.
Dropping the back knee straight down without controlling the descent.
Failing to lower until both knees are bent appropriately, resulting in a shallow lunge.
Bouncing out of the bottom position instead of using controlled leg strength.
Letting the barbell shift, roll, or sit unevenly across the upper back.

exercises.name: Barbell Forward Lunge
tips: Set the barbell securely across your upper traps, not on your neck, and grip it evenly with your chest lifted and shoulder blades gently pulled back.
Start with feet about hip-width apart, brace your core, and keep your spine neutral before each repetition.
Step forward far enough that both knees can bend to roughly 90 degrees without the front heel lifting or the back knee drifting too far behind your hips.
Lower under control by bending both knees and dropping the back knee toward the floor, rather than leaning your torso forward.
Keep most of your weight over the front foot, with the front heel firmly planted and the knee tracking in line with your toes.
Do not allow the front knee to collapse inward; actively keep it aligned over the second and third toes throughout the movement.
Push through the whole front foot, especially the heel and midfoot, to return to the starting position with control.
Keep your hips square and avoid twisting or shifting sideways as you lunge and return.
Use a step length and range of motion you can control; reduce depth if you cannot maintain balance, knee alignment, or a neutral spine.
Begin with a light barbell or an unloaded bar until your balance and technique are consistent, then increase load gradually.
Perform the same number of repetitions on each leg and stop the set if you feel sharp pain in the knees, hips, back, or ankles.
Use a rack with safety arms when possible so you can safely unrack and rerack the barbell without compromising your setup.

exercises.description: The Barbell Front Raise is an isolation exercise targeting the anterior deltoids. It involves lifting a barbell in front of the body to shoulder height, emphasizing shoulder strength and stability.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a barbell with an overhand grip in front of your thighs.
Keep your arms straight but not locked, and engage your core for stability.
Inhale and lift the barbell forward and upward until your arms are parallel to the ground.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring control and stability.
Exhale as you slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position.
mistakes: Using too much weight, leading to swinging and momentum instead of controlled lifting.
Lifting the barbell above shoulder height, causing unnecessary shoulder strain.
Bending the elbows excessively, turning the exercise into a partial upright row.
Failing to engage the core, resulting in an arched back and poor posture.
Allowing the wrists to bend backward, putting strain on the wrists.
Not maintaining a neutral neck position, leading to tension in the neck.
Rushing the movement, reducing time under tension and muscle engagement.
Neglecting to keep the shoulders down and back, causing shoulder elevation and tension.
exercises.name: Barbell Front Raise
tips: Start with a light weight to ensure proper form and avoid strain.
Maintain a slight bend in your elbows to reduce joint stress.
Keep your movements controlled; avoid using momentum to lift the barbell.
Engage your core throughout the exercise to support your lower back.
Focus on lifting with your shoulders, not your arms, to maximize deltoid engagement.

exercises.description: The Barbell Glute Bridge is a compound exercise targeting the gluteal muscles, primarily the gluteus maximus. It involves lifting the hips off the ground while supporting a barbell across the hips, effectively engaging the lower body and core.
instructions: Begin by sitting on the floor with your upper back resting against a bench and your feet flat on the ground, hip-width apart.
Roll a barbell over your legs until it is positioned directly above your hips. Use a pad to cushion your hips if necessary.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes as you drive through your heels to lift your hips towards the ceiling.
Ensure that your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees at the top of the movement.
Pause briefly at the top, then slowly lower your hips back to the starting position without touching the ground.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Placing the barbell too high on the hips, leading to discomfort and reduced effectiveness.
Arching the lower back excessively, causing strain and reducing glute activation.
Allowing knees to collapse inward, which decreases glute engagement and can strain the knees.
Failing to keep feet flat on the ground, reducing stability and power.
Using momentum to lift the barbell instead of controlled muscle contraction.
Not fully extending the hips at the top, limiting glute activation.
Positioning feet too far apart or too close together, affecting balance and muscle engagement.
Rushing through repetitions, which can compromise form and control.
Neglecting to engage the core, leading to instability and poor posture.
exercises.name: Barbell Glute Bridge
tips: Keep your chin tucked and gaze forward to maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Focus on squeezing your glutes at the top of each rep for maximum muscle engagement.
Avoid arching your lower back; maintain a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Ensure that your feet are placed firmly on the ground and do not shift during the exercise.
Start with a lighter weight to master form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: The Barbell Good Morning is a compound exercise that primarily targets the lower back, hamstrings, and glutes. It involves bending at the hips while maintaining a neutral spine, which helps in strengthening the posterior chain and improving hip hinge mechanics.
instructions: Begin by setting up a barbell on a squat rack at shoulder height.
Position yourself under the barbell, resting it across your upper back and shoulders. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
Lift the bar off the rack by extending your legs and stepping back to clear the rack.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, toes pointing slightly outward.
Engage your core and keep your chest up. Maintain a slight bend in your knees.
Hinge at the hips by pushing them backward while keeping your back straight and chest up.
Lower your torso until it is nearly parallel to the ground or as far as your flexibility allows without rounding your back.
Reverse the movement by driving through your heels and extending your hips to return to the starting position.
mistakes: Rounding the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Bending the knees excessively, turning it into a squat.
Allowing the barbell to roll up the neck instead of resting securely on the upper back.
Leaning too far forward, causing loss of balance.
Not engaging the core, leading to instability.
Using too much weight, compromising form.
Lowering the torso too quickly, losing control.
Failing to hinge at the hips, reducing hamstring activation.
Hyperextending the back at the top of the movement.
Not keeping the chest up, leading to a collapsed posture.
exercises.name: Barbell Good Morning
tips: Keep your core tight throughout the movement to protect your lower back.
Focus on hinging at the hips rather than bending at the waist to maintain proper form.
Start with a light weight to master the technique before progressing to heavier loads.
Ensure that your knees remain slightly bent throughout the exercise to avoid unnecessary strain.
Maintain a neutral spine by keeping your head in line with your torso; avoid looking up or down excessively.
Control the descent and ascent of the movement to maximize muscle engagement and minimize injury risk.

exercises.description: A flat barbell bench press in which the bar comes down to the base of your neck instead of your mid-chest, with the elbows flared out to the sides. The high bar path shifts the work toward the upper chest and front delts, so it is done with a light load and strict control.
instructions: Lie on a flat bench with your eyes under the racked bar and your feet planted on the floor.
Take an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width and pull your shoulder blades back and down.
Unrack the bar and hold it on straight arms above your neck and upper chest.
Lower the bar slowly toward the base of your neck, letting your elbows flare out to the sides.
Stop with the bar just above your collarbones without letting it rest on your throat.
Press the bar straight up to full arm extension, keeping it above your neck.
Complete the planned repetitions, then return the bar to the uprights.
mistakes: Letting the bar drift down to the mid-chest, which turns it into a regular bench press
Bouncing the bar off the collarbones or resting it on the throat
Letting the shoulders roll forward off the bench at the bottom
Bending the wrists back under the bar
Lifting the hips off the bench to push the bar up
Letting the bar drift toward the face during the press
exercises.name: Barbell Guillotine Bench Press
tips: Use a clearly lighter load than in your regular bench press and train with a spotter.
Squeeze the bar hard and wrap your thumbs around it.
At the bottom, keep your forearms vertical with your elbows directly under the bar.
Lower the bar more slowly than in a regular bench press so you can stop it exactly above your collarbones.
If the bottom position pinches the front of your shoulders, shorten the range of motion.

exercises.description: The Barbell Hack Squat is a compound lower body exercise that primarily targets the quadriceps, with secondary emphasis on the hamstrings, glutes, and calves. It involves lifting a barbell from behind the legs while maintaining an upright torso, similar to a reverse deadlift.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and position a loaded barbell behind your legs.
Bend at the knees and hips to lower your body, keeping your back straight and chest up.
Grip the barbell with an overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
Engage your core and drive through your heels to lift the barbell by extending your hips and knees.
Keep the bar close to your body as you stand up fully, maintaining an upright torso.
Lower the barbell back to the starting position in a controlled manner by bending your knees and hips.

Rising onto the toes instead of keeping the heels grounded.
Using the arms to lift the bar instead of focusing on leg drive.
Failing to engage the core for stability throughout the movement.
Descending too quickly, losing control of the weight.
Not squatting deep enough to achieve full range of motion.
Letting the bar drift away from the body during the lift.
Using excessive weight, compromising form and control.
exercises.name: Barbell Hack Squat
tips: Ensure your knees track over your toes to avoid unnecessary strain.
Keep your core engaged throughout the movement to protect your lower back.
Focus on driving through your heels to maximize quadriceps activation.
Maintain a neutral spine by keeping your chest up and shoulders back.
Start with a lighter weight to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
Avoid rounding your back; keep it straight to prevent injury.

exercises.description: The barbell hang high pull combines an explosive leg and hip extension with a high elbow pull. Start with the bar at thigh height, hinge slightly and drive through your feet to accelerate it. Keep the bar close as your elbows rise out to the sides, then lower it to the hang without catching it on your shoulders.
instructions: Stand with your feet about hip-width apart. Hold a barbell with an overhand grip just outside your thighs, arms straight.
Lift the bar to a hang position around mid-thigh. Bend your knees slightly and hinge at the hips, keeping your back flat, chest up and shoulders slightly in front of the bar.
Keep the bar close to your body. Brace your core and keep your weight balanced through the middle of your feet.
Drive forcefully through your feet, extending your hips, knees and ankles. Shrug your shoulders upward as the bar accelerates.
After the leg and hip drive, lift your elbows high and out as the bar rises toward chest height.
Do not curl the bar or catch it on your shoulders. Your elbows should finish high, with the bar below them.
Lower the bar under control back to the hang position, then reset your posture before the next repetition.
mistakes: Starting with the bar too far from the body, which makes the pull swing forward.
Bending the arms too early.
Failing to fully extend the hips, knees, and ankles before pulling the elbows up.
Rounding the lower back or losing a braced torso during the hinge.
Squatting the bar down.
Keeping the elbows low or pulling them backward.
exercises.name: Barbell Hang High Pull
tips: Start with the bar at mid-thigh, feet about hip width apart, and your weight balanced through the whole foot.
Use a shoulder-width or slightly wider overhand grip.
Exhale as you lift and inhale as you return.
Use the bar markings to set both hands the same distance from the center.
Choose a load you can move through the full range.

Place a barbell over your hips, using a pad for comfort if necessary.
Brace your core and drive through your heels to lift your hips upward.
Extend your hips until your thighs are parallel to the floor and your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Pause at the top of the movement, squeezing your glutes tightly.
Lower your hips back down to the starting position in a controlled manner.
exercises.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
tips: Ensure that your feet are positioned shoulder-width apart for optimal stability.
Keep your chin tucked and gaze forward to maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Focus on engaging your glutes rather than hyperextending your lower back at the top of the lift.
Control the descent to maximize muscle tension and prevent injury.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.

Pull the barbell towards your chest by retracting your shoulder blades and bending your elbows.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring your shoulder blades are fully contracted.
Slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position with controlled motion.

exercises.description: Kneel with a barbell secured across your upper back and your feet resting behind you. Move your hips back toward your heels, allowing a controlled forward lean of the torso. Start the descent by pushing your hips back toward your heels. Keep your torso controlled and avoid rounding your lower back.
Lower until your glutes lightly touch or come close to your heels, or stop earlier if you cannot maintain a neutral spine.

Losing balance by shifting the hips to one side during the descent or ascent.

Failing to fully extend the hips at the top of each repetition.

Keep your feet pointed behind you and use knee padding if needed for comfortable support.
Brace your abdomen before each repetition and keep your ribs stacked over your pelvis so your lower back does not overarch.
Use a lighter load than you would for a standing squat, since balance and trunk control are limiting factors in this exercise.
Inhale as you sit back and exhale as you extend your hips.

Press the barbell back up to the starting position by extending your arms, ensuring a controlled movement throughout.

Focus on controlling the descent of the barbell to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid arching your back excessively; maintain a natural spine position.
Ensure that your wrists remain straight and in line with your forearms during the lift.
Breathe in as you lower the barbell and exhale as you press it back up.

exercises.description: A split squat with a barbell locked out overhead. It trains the quads and glutes of the front leg while testing shoulder stability, core control and balance, because the bar has to stay stacked over your shoulders and hips for the whole set.

Dropping fast and bouncing out of the bottom.

exercises.description: The Z press is a barbell overhead press performed sitting on the floor with your legs straight and no back support. exercises.description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, and core braced while holding one end of a rope in each hand. Keep your chest up and shoulders down, then create alternating or simultaneous waves by moving your arms forcefully up and down. Maintain a stable torso and avoid rounding your back. Use controlled, rhythmic movements and adjust the pace or wave size to match your fitness level.
instructions: Secure the battle rope around a stable anchor point and stand facing the anchor with one rope end in each hand.
Walk backward until there is light tension in the ropes, then place your feet about shoulder-width apart with your knees softly bent.
Hinge slightly at the hips, keep your chest lifted, brace your core, and maintain a neutral spine.
Hold the rope ends with an overhand grip, keeping your arms extended slightly in front of your body without locking your elbows.
Create alternating waves by quickly lifting one hand as you lower the other, driving the movement from your shoulders and arms while keeping your torso stable.
Continue producing even, controlled waves that travel from your hands to the anchor point without allowing excessive slack in the ropes.
Breathe steadily throughout the set and keep your knees bent to absorb the movement rather than rounding your back or shrugging your shoulders.
To finish, gradually reduce the speed and size of the waves, then stand upright and place the ropes down under control.
mistakes: Using only the arms instead of driving the ropes from the shoulders, back, and legs
Standing too upright or locking the knees instead of maintaining a stable athletic stance
Letting the lower back arch or rounding the torso while creating waves
Using ropes that are too slack, which prevents consistent waves from traveling to the anchor
Making small, weak waves instead of using a controlled full range of motion
Lifting the shoulders toward the ears and keeping the neck tense
Moving both arms out of sync when performing alternating waves
Slamming the ropes without controlling the return phase
Allowing the hips and torso to twist excessively during double-arm waves
Losing rhythm and letting the rope waves become uneven or stop before reaching the anchor
exercises.name: Battle Ropes
tips: Choose ropes with a length and thickness appropriate for your strength level, and anchor them securely to a heavy fixed point before starting.
Stand with feet about shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, hips back, and keep your chest tall with a neutral spine.
Grip the rope ends firmly without squeezing excessively, keeping your shoulders down away from your ears.
Generate the movement from your shoulders and arms while maintaining a stable torso; avoid rounding your back or twisting uncontrollably.
For alternating waves, move one arm up as the other arm moves down, creating consistent waves that travel all the way to the anchor point.
For double-arm waves, raise and lower both arms together while keeping the knees soft and using a small athletic bounce if needed.
Keep the range of motion controlled and avoid lifting the arms excessively high, especially if it causes shoulder discomfort.
Maintain steady breathing by exhaling during the effort and avoid holding your breath during intense intervals.
Start with short work intervals, such as 15 to 30 seconds, and focus on clean, continuous waves before increasing speed or duration.
Stop or reduce intensity if you feel sharp pain in the shoulders, elbows, wrists, lower back, or knees.

exercises.description: The Bayesian Cable Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps, performed using a cable machine. This exercise emphasizes the stretch and contraction of the biceps by maintaining constant tension throughout the movement. It is ideal for enhancing bicep peak and overall arm development.
instructions: Set the cable machine to a low pulley position and attach a single handle.
Stand facing away from the machine, holding the handle with one hand, arm extended behind you.
Step forward slightly to create tension on the cable and stagger your stance for stability.
Keep your elbow fixed in place and curl the handle towards your shoulder by contracting your biceps.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring maximum contraction.
Slowly lower the handle back to the starting position, maintaining control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, then switch arms.
mistakes: Using too much weight, leading to momentum-based lifting instead of controlled movement.
Standing too far from the cable, causing excessive shoulder involvement and reducing bicep isolation.
Allowing the elbows to flare out, which decreases tension on the biceps.
Failing to fully extend the arms at the bottom, limiting range of motion and muscle engagement.
Curling the wrists at the top, shifting focus away from the biceps to the forearms.
Leaning back excessively, reducing bicep engagement and risking lower back strain.
Rushing through reps, sacrificing form and muscle contraction quality.
Not maintaining a stable core, leading to imbalance and improper form.
exercises.name: Bayesian Cable Curl
tips: Focus on keeping your elbow stationary to maximize bicep engagement.
Maintain a slight bend in your knees for better balance and support.
Avoid using momentum; control both the lifting and lowering phases.
Ensure your wrist remains neutral throughout the exercise to prevent strain.
Exhale as you curl up and inhale as you lower down to maintain proper breathing rhythm.
Adjust the weight so that you can perform each rep with proper form without compromising technique.

exercises.description: Curl a low cable handle in each hand with your back to the machine, starting from straight arms behind your body, to load your biceps from a deep stretch. The cables pull back and down, so the rep is hardest near the bottom, right where a standing dumbbell curl has almost no load. Both heads of the biceps do the work, while your forearm muscles help and hold the handles. With a cable for each arm, your torso stays square and nothing twists. The one-arm Bayesian Cable Curl uses a single cable, and the seated version moves this setup onto a bench.
instructions: On a two-stack cable station, set both pulleys to the lowest notch, clip a single D-handle to each and load both stacks equally.
Take a handle in each hand, palms facing forward, and stand between the pulleys with your back to the machine.
Walk out about one step, until both stacks stay lifted with your arms straight and drawn slightly behind your hips.
Stagger your feet with one foot a stride ahead, rear heel up and knees soft. Chest up, shoulder blades back and down, abs braced.
Curl both handles at once, bending only at the elbows. The elbows stay back while your forearms swing forward and up.
Stop with your hands in front of your lower chest, palms facing you and elbows still behind your torso. Squeeze for about a second.
Lower over 2–3 seconds until both elbows are fully straight and the cables draw your arms back. Pause in the stretch, shoulders still back.
When the set is over, walk back toward the machine until the plates rest, and only then let go of the handles.
mistakes: Elbows drifting forward as the hands rise until the upper arms hang vertical. Now it's an ordinary cable curl. Keep the elbows behind your torso and stop at your lower chest, not your chin.
Standing so close that the plates touch down at the bottom and the stretch disappears. Walk out until both stacks stay up with straight arms, and keep that spot for the whole set.

Rocking forward to start each rep or leaning back at the top; if you feel it in your lower back, this is why. Brace in the staggered stance and keep your chest still, and go one plate lighter if it keeps happening.
Ending the lowering with the elbows still bent. That skips the stretch this exercise is built around, so straighten both arms fully and pause on every rep.
One arm running ahead of the other. Move both handles at the same speed and end the set when one arm can't keep up.
exercises.name: Bayesian Cable Curl (Face Away)
tips: Go for 2–4 sets of 10–15 reps close to failure.
Add reps at the same weight first; once you get 15 clean reps in all sets, move the pin down one hole on both stacks (usually 2.5–5 kg each) and build back up from 10.

Start lighter than on a regular cable curl, since the stretched bottom is the hardest part. Change both stacks together and log the weight the same way every session: many crossover stations have a 2:1 pulley, so the number on the stack isn't what you actually lift.

At the bottom you should feel a strong stretch along the front of your upper arm, from the elbow crease toward the shoulder, and at the top a hard squeeze. A mild pull across the front of the shoulder is normal. A sharp pinch there or in the elbow crease means take half a step back toward the machine or go lighter.
To make it harder without adding weight, lower over 3–4 seconds and pause for 1–2 seconds in the bottom stretch.

Substitutes: Bayesian Cable Curl (one arm at a time, for when only one pulley is free), Bayesian Cable Curl Seated (the same two-handle setup on a bench), Seated Incline Biceps Curl (dumbbells, a similar stretched start). If your shoulders hurt with the arms behind you, switch to the Bar Cable Biceps Curl facing the machine.

exercises.description: A bodyweight crawl on hands and feet with the knees bent and lifted off the floor. Move forward by stepping the opposite hand and foot together while keeping your back flat and your hips slightly above shoulder height. instructions: Start on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips.
Tuck your toes under, brace your core and lift your knees off the floor. Keep them bent so your hips sit slightly above shoulder height.
Keep your arms straight, your back flat and your eyes on the floor just ahead of your hands.
Step your right hand and left foot forward at the same time, using a short step.
Step your left hand and right foot forward in the same way, keeping your hips level.
Keep alternating sides without letting your knees touch the floor.
Crawl for the set time, then lower your knees to the floor under control.

Moving the same-side hand and foot together instead of opposite limbs

exercises.description: Stand on the belt squat platform facing the machine and hold the V-grip with both hands. Set your feet about hip-width apart, keep your arms straight, brace your core, and maintain a neutral spine. Push your hips back while slightly bending your knees, lowering the load under control until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings. Drive through your feet and extend your hips to return to standing, squeezing your glutes at the top. instructions: Set the belt squat machine to a light starting load and attach the V-grip handle to the machine’s designated lifting point according to the equipment design.
Stand on the platform facing the machine with your feet about hip-width apart, toes pointing forward or slightly outward.
Hinge at your hips and take the V-grip with both hands using a neutral grip, keeping your arms straight and shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Stand tall to lift the load, positioning the handle close to your body with your knees softly bent, chest proud, and spine neutral.
Begin the repetition by pushing your hips backward while allowing the handle to travel downward close to your legs.
Keep your shins nearly vertical, maintain a slight bend in the knees, and lower only until you feel a strong stretch through your hamstrings without rounding your lower back.
Drive your feet into the platform and extend your hips to return to standing, keeping the handle close and your arms relaxed.

Rounding the lower back as the torso lowers.
Overarching the lower back at the top instead of finishing with the glutes.

Lowering past the point where spinal neutrality can be maintained.
Losing tension at the bottom or bouncing out of the stretched position.
Shifting weight into the toes instead of keeping pressure through the midfoot and heels.
Moving too quickly and using momentum rather than controlled hip extension.

Begin with a soft bend in the knees, then push your hips backward as if reaching your glutes toward the wall behind you.
Keep your chest open, spine neutral, and neck aligned with your torso; avoid rounding your lower back or looking excessively upward.
Lower the handle by hinging at the hips, keeping it close to your legs and maintaining pressure through your whole foot, especially the mid-foot and heel.
Descend only as far as you can while keeping your back position stable and feeling a strong stretch in the hamstrings and glutes.
Drive your hips forward to stand up, squeezing your glutes at the top without leaning back or overextending the lower back.

instructions: Begin on all fours with your hands directly under your shoulders and knees under your hips.
Engage your core to maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Simultaneously extend your right arm forward and left leg backward until they are parallel to the floor.
Hold this position for a moment, ensuring your hips remain level and your back does not arch.
Return to the starting position with control.
Repeat the movement with your left arm and right leg.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.

exercises.description: A single-leg hip hinge with no added weight. Standing on one leg, you tip your torso forward until it is about parallel to the floor while the free leg rises straight behind you, then return to standing. It works the hamstrings and glutes of the standing leg and builds the balance you need before adding a dumbbell.
instructions: Stand tall with your feet close together and your arms hanging by your sides. Shift your weight onto one foot and keep a slight bend in that knee.
Brace your core and start the movement by pushing your hips back while the free leg slides straight back behind you.
Lower your torso and lift the back leg at the same time. Let your arms hang straight down toward the floor.
Keep both hips level and facing the floor, with the toes of the raised foot pointing down.
Go down until your torso and raised leg are about parallel to the floor, or until you feel a strong stretch in the back of the standing thigh. Keep your back flat.

Finish all reps on one leg, then switch sides.

exercises.description: The Bodyweight Windmill is a dynamic exercise that targets the core, shoulders, and hips. Shift your weight onto your right leg, bending your right knee slightly while keeping your left leg straight.
Rotate your torso to the right, lowering your left hand towards your right foot while keeping your right arm extended upwards.

Initiate the movement by pushing your hips back and bending your knees to lower yourself towards the box.

Lie on the bench with your feet flat on the floor, ensuring your back is in contact with the bench.
Grab each handle with an overhand grip and position your hands at chest level, elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees.
Press the handles upward by extending your arms, keeping your wrists straight and aligned with your forearms.

Slowly lower the handles back to the starting position, maintaining control and tension in the cables.

Using too much weight, compromising form and control.
Neglecting to keep feet planted, affecting stability and power.
exercises.name: Cable Bench Press
tips: Maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise to prevent lower back strain.
Focus on squeezing your chest muscles as you press the handles upward for maximum engagement.
Keep your elbows slightly tucked in to reduce stress on the shoulder joints.

exercises.description: Sit at a high pulley, take the lat bar overhand with your hands a fist apart and pull it from straight arms down to your chin to build your lats. Your lats do most of the work, helped by the teres major and teres minor, while the lower traps pull your shoulder blades down. Biceps and forearms help, and this grip makes your forearms work harder than the standard pulldown does. It uses the same bar as the regular and wide-grip versions, so you can change grips between sets without swapping the attachment. Use it for variety, or when a wider grip bothers your shoulders at the top.
instructions: Sit facing the stack and set the thigh pad so your legs are locked in, feet flat on the floor and knees bent about 90°.
Stand up and grab the bar overhand in the middle, one hand on each side of the cable clamp, about a fist's width apart.
Sit back down with the bar at arm's length and let your shoulders rise. Chest up, lean back only 5–10° from the hips.
Start the pull by drawing your shoulders down, then drive your elbows down; they travel in front of your ribs and slightly out.
Bring the bar straight down close to your face until it reaches your chin, a few centimeters above the collarbones, without changing your torso angle.
Pause briefly with your shoulder blades down, then let the bar rise over 2–3 seconds until your arms are fully straight.
At the end of the set, let go only when the bar is back overhead or you've stood up with it, so the stack doesn't slam.
mistakes: Hands creeping out toward shoulder width until you're doing the standard pulldown. Before every set, put one hand on each side of the clamp, a fist apart.
Wrists bent back, or the bar rolling into your fingertips, so the forearms quit before your back does. Keep the wrists straight, seat the bar in the base of your fingers and use your hands as hooks.
Leaning far back and rowing the bar down to your stomach. Hold the slight lean you set at the start, stop at the chin or the top of the chest, and take a plate off if you have to swing.
Bending the elbows before the shoulders move, so the arms start the pull. Get the shoulders down first, then think about driving your elbows toward your ribs.
Cutting the top short. Let the bar rise until your elbows are straight and your shoulders lift a little on every rep.
exercises.name: Cable Close Grip Lat Pulldown
tips: Use 8–15 reps for muscle and 5–8 for strength; beginners do well with 10–15 on a weight they can pull to the chin without leaning back.
Progress with reps first: once you hit the top number in all sets at the same torso angle, move the pin one plate down (usually 5 kg) and drop back to the bottom of the range.

Feel it along the sides of your back, down toward the lower ribs, and between your shoulder blades, with a stretch under the armpits at the top. Your forearms will burn more than on a wide grip, but your back should be the main thing you notice.

If the narrow overhand grip hurts your wrists or elbows, switch to the V-handle or an underhand grip instead of grinding through it. To make this version harder, take 3–4 seconds to let the bar up or pause for 2 seconds at your chin; the bodyweight version of this grip is the Close Grip Pull Up.

Substitutes: Cable Lat Pulldown (same bar, hands about 1.5 shoulder widths apart), Cable Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown (V-handle, palms facing, easier on the wrists), Cable Reverse Grip Pulldown (underhand, more biceps), Lat Pulldown Machine.

Adjust the weight so that you can perform the exercise with proper form for all repetitions.

Shift your weight onto the standing leg without locking the knee.

Step far enough from the pulley to keep the cable lightly tensioned at the start.
Begin with a light load to learn the diagonal path.
Exhale as the leg moves out and inhale as it returns.
Use the same number of repetitions on both sides.

exercises.description: A standing rotator cuff exercise done side-on to a cable set at elbow height. With the elbow bent to 90 degrees and tucked against your side, you rotate the forearm from across your abdomen outward, away from your body. It works the shoulder's external rotators: infraspinatus, teres minor and rear deltoid.
instructions: Set the pulley at about elbow height and attach a single handle.
Stand side-on to the machine with the working arm farther from the pulley, so the cable pulls your hand across your body.
Hold the handle with a neutral grip, thumb up. Bend your elbow to 90 degrees and keep it lightly pressed against your side.
Start with your forearm across your abdomen. Stand tall with your shoulders down and relaxed.
Keeping the elbow at your side, rotate your forearm outward, away from your body, as far as you can without moving the elbow.
Pause briefly, then return the forearm slowly across your abdomen.
Finish all reps on one side, then turn around and work the other arm.
mistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from your side to make the movement look bigger.
Twisting the torso or leaning away from the cable instead of rotating at the shoulder.
Shrugging the shoulder up toward your ear.
Bending the wrist back to move the handle farther instead of keeping it in line with the forearm.

exercises.name: Cable External Rotation
tips: Use a light weight and higher reps, around 12 to 20 per set. The external rotators are small muscles and respond best to slow, clean reps.
Stand far enough from the machine that the cable stays taut even when your forearm is across your abdomen.
Picture your forearm as a door swinging open on a hinge at your elbow.
Hold the handle loosely so the shoulder does the work, not the hand and forearm.
Breathe out as you rotate outward and breathe in on the way back.
Start with your weaker arm and match its reps on the stronger side.

exercises.description: Pull a rope from a head-height cable pulley to your face, finishing with your hands beside your head, to build your rear delts and upper back. Your rear delts take most of the load. The middle traps squeeze your shoulder blades together, the infraspinatus (a rotator cuff muscle on the back of the shoulder blade) turns your upper arms out at the finish, and the upper traps help a little. Easy to learn and kind to the joints, it works as a warm-up before pressing or as a finisher. Unlike a rear delt fly, your elbows bend and your arms rotate out at the end.
instructions: Clip a rope to one pulley of a cable station and set it at forehead height or a notch above, not at the top.
Hold one rope end in each hand just inside the stoppers, overhand: knuckles up, palms down, hands close together, wrists straight.
Face the pulley and walk back until your arms are straight at face height and the plates lift off the stack.
Set your feet hip-width apart, one foot half a step ahead, knees soft.
Stand tall, chest up, ribs down; your legs and torso stay put from here on.
Draw your shoulders down, then pull the rope toward your face with your elbows leading out to the sides at shoulder height.
In the last third, pull the rope ends apart so your hands finish beside your head at eye level, forearms vertical, knuckles up and back.
Pause for a second with the middle of the rope in front of your nose, elbows bent about 90° and shoulder blades squeezed.
Take 2–3 seconds to straighten your arms, plates still off the stack. After the last rep, step in before you set the weight down.
mistakes: Rowing to your chin or chest. Your elbows sink below shoulder height and your lats and biceps take over. Aim the middle of the rope at your nose or forehead and finish with your hands beside your head.
Leaning back or stepping back on every rep to get the stack moving. Set your stance before the first rep and keep your torso still; if it rocks anyway, the weight is too heavy.
Stopping with your hands in front of your face and the rope ends still together. Split the rope until your forearms stand vertical beside your head.

Running the cable from the top or the bottom of the column. From above it turns into a pulldown, from below into an upward row. Set the pulley at head height so the cable runs almost level from your face.
exercises.name: Cable Face Pull
tips: Aim for 2–4 sets of 12–20 reps, stopping 1–3 reps short of failure; the set is over when your hands can't get back to head height. Add reps first. When all sets reach 20 with a one-second pause and no sway, move the pin down one plate (usually 2.5–5 kg) and start again at 12. With loads this light, one plate is often a 10–20% jump, so plan on a few sessions per weight. Pulley ratios vary, so compare weights only on the same station.

You should feel it in the back of your shoulders and between your shoulder blades, and on the back of the shoulder blade as your hands turn up. Neck burning first? You're shrugging. Biceps and lats doing the pulling? You're rowing to your chest.

If the front of your shoulder pinches at the finish, stop with your hands slightly in front of your ears and take some weight off. Once the full turn feels easy, hold the finish for 2 seconds and take 3 seconds on the way back before you add load.

Substitutes: Seated Face Pull if you catch yourself leaning back to move the weight; Banded Face Pull at home or as a warm-up; Cable Rear Delt Fly or Machine Reverse Flyes to isolate the rear delts with straight arms and no rotation.

exercises.description: Sit under a high pulley and pull a long bar from straight arms down to your upper chest to build a wider, stronger back. Your lats are the main movers, helped by the teres major and minor and by the lower and middle traps, which pull your shoulder blades down and together. Your biceps and forearms assist, but they shouldn't give out first. This is the standard lat pulldown: the load can start far below body weight and go up one plate at a time, so it fits beginners working toward their first pull-up as well as advanced lifters adding back volume.
instructions: Sit facing the stack and set the thigh pad so your thighs are locked in, feet flat and knees bent about 90°.
Stand back up and take the bar overhand on the straight part just inside the bends, about one and a half shoulder widths apart, thumbs around it.
Sit down with the bar at arm's length and let your shoulders rise. Chest up, lean back 10–15° from the hips, and keep that angle until the set is done.
Start each rep by pulling your shoulders down, away from your ears, before your elbows bend.
Drive your elbows down and slightly back toward your sides until the bar passes in front of your face and reaches your upper chest, just below the chin.
Pause for a moment with your shoulder blades down and together, then let the bar rise over 2–3 seconds until your arms are straight and you feel a stretch under your armpits.
At the end of the set, let the bar go all the way up (or stand up with it) before you let go, so the plates don't slam into the stack.
mistakes: Leaning further back with every rep until the pulldown turns into a row. Set a slight lean at the start, hold it, and take a plate off if you can't finish the set without swinging.
Pulling with your hands and curling the wrists, so your biceps and forearms quit before your back does. Keep the wrists straight, pull the shoulders down first, then drive the elbows to your sides.
Forcing the bar lower than your upper chest and letting your shoulders roll forward toward your ears. Stop at the upper chest with your chest up and shoulder blades down.
Half reps at the top, where the elbows never straighten and the lats never stretch. Let the bar rise all the way on every rep, taking 2–3 seconds instead of letting the stack yank your arms up.
exercises.name: Cable Lat Pulldown
tips: Sets of 8–15 build muscle and sets of 5–8 build strength; beginners do well with 10–15 on a weight they can pull to the chest without leaning back. Progress the reps before the plates. When you can do the top number in each set with the same torso angle, move the pin down one plate (usually 5 kg) and go back to the bottom of the range. If the stack jumps in 7 kg plates or more, stay on each weight longer or use the small add-on weight if the machine has one.

The sides of your back and the area under your shoulder blades should do the work, with a stretch under the armpits at the top; the back of your shoulders works too. If your biceps and forearms burn out first, you're pulling with your hands. Treat them as hooks and lead with your elbows.

Can't feel your back yet? Learn the shoulders-down start on the Lat Pulldown Machine, where the path is fixed, or pause for a second at the chest with a lighter weight. To make it harder, take 3–4 seconds on the way up or pause 2 seconds at the bottom. Assisted pull-ups bridge the gap to pull-ups; as a rough guide, clean sets of 8–10 with close to your body weight mean you're ready to try unassisted pull-ups.
Substitutes: Wide Grip Lat Pulldown (hands at the ends of the bar), Cable Wide Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown (easier on the wrists and shoulders), Lat Pulldown Machine, Assisted Pull-Up.

exercises.description: Stand side-on to a shoulder-high cable and press one handle forward and across your body until your hand is in front of the opposite shoulder. The chest on the pressing side does most of the work, hardest near the breastbone as your hand passes the midline; the triceps straighten the elbow and the serratus anterior lets the shoulder reach at the end. Use it as a second chest exercise after a bench or machine press. Pick it over the One-Arm Cable Fly when you want a bent elbow and more weight, and over a two-handed cable press when you want that squeeze across the middle.
instructions: Set one pulley at about shoulder height and clip on a single D-handle.
Stand side-on to the column with your working arm nearest the stack. Step away until the weight stays lifted with the handle beside your chest.
Stagger your feet: the cable-side leg back on the ball of the foot, the other foot forward and flat, knees soft.
Hold the handle palm down beside your chest, elbow out to the side and just below shoulder height.
Rest your free hand on your stomach, hips and shoulders square to the front. That hand feels it the moment your torso turns.
Press on a level arc forward and across, as if around a post, until your hand sits in front of the opposite shoulder.
With the elbow almost straight and your chest still facing forward, squeeze for a second.
Take 2–3 seconds to return along the same arc, stopping beside your chest. After the last rep, turn around for the other arm.
mistakes: Turning your torso toward the far side to reach further. Hips and shoulders stay square, the hand on your stomach keeps you honest, and if you still can't cross without turning, the weight comes down.
Pressing straight ahead and stopping in front of the working shoulder. Aim the hand at the opposite shoulder and get it past the middle of your chest on every rep.
Standing so close that the stack touches down between reps. Step out until the weight stays up with the handle at your chest.
Dropping the elbow to your ribs so the rep turns into a low punch, or lifting it above the shoulder. Keep it just under shoulder height and move the hand on a flat arc.

Letting the cable yank your arm back behind the line of your torso. That loads the front of the shoulder and adds nothing for the chest; take 2–3 seconds to return and stop with the hand beside your chest.
exercises.name: Cable Press Around
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 10–15 reps per arm, up to 20 as a finisher; loading it for fewer than 8–10 reps buys you little here. Grow the reps first. Once both arms reach 15 in every set with a full cross, move the pin down one plate (usually 2.5–5 kg) and build the reps back up.
The chest on the working side does the work, most of all toward the breastbone. If the front of your shoulder or your lower back takes over, the stack is too heavy or your torso is turning.

Can't cross without twisting? Drop a plate and stop the hand at the middle of your chest for a few weeks. Too easy, but the next plate is too big a jump? Hold the cross for 2 seconds, take 3 to return, or bring your back foot level with the front one.

Substitutes: One-Arm Cable Fly (straighter arm, longer stretch), Standing Cable Chest Press (both arms, heavier), Cross Body One-Arm Strength Press (the same cross on a machine) and Cable Middle Chest Fly.
