exercises.description: Face a cable crossover, hold the high cables crossed in front of your chest and sweep your arms out into a T to build the backs of your shoulders. The rear delts do most of the work, with help from the middle traps between your shoulder blades and the infraspinatus that sits on them. Crossing the cables starts each rep with your hands on the far side of your chest for a longer arc, and the stack pulls from the first inch, where a bent-over dumbbell raise has almost no load. Unlike a face pull, the elbows never bend: your arms stay long and only sweep out and back.
instructions: Set both pulleys at the top, well above your head. Hold the bare cable ends or clip a single D-handle to each.
Cross the cables: right hand on the left pulley's cable, left hand on the right one. Thumbs up, elbows slightly bent.
Face the machine from the middle and step back until the cables are taut, wrists crossed in front of your chest at shoulder height.
Set your feet hip- to shoulder-width apart, knees soft, ribs down and glutes lightly squeezed so the high cables can't tip you forward.
Keeping that elbow angle fixed, sweep your arms out and back at shoulder height, as if the backs of your hands push the cables apart.
Stop once your arms line up with your shoulders and your body forms a T. Hold a second, shoulder blades together, shoulders low.
Take 2–3 seconds to follow the same arc back until your wrists cross again. The plates stay off the stack between reps.
When the set is done, bring your hands back to the crossed start and lower the stacks before letting go, so the cables don't snap back.
mistakes: Bending the elbows and pulling your hands toward your shoulders like a row. Set the slight bend at the start, keep it to the last rep and think "push the cables apart", not "pull".
Hands sinking toward your hips as the arms open, so the fly turns into a straight-arm pulldown. Finish in a T, not a Y pointing down, and go one plate lighter if your arms keep sinking.
Shrugging as the arms open. Keep your neck long and let the shoulder blades travel back, not up toward your ears.
Taking each cable in the hand on its own side, or standing too close, so the cables hang slack at the start. Cross them and step back until they're taut with your wrists crossed.
Leaning back or rocking to swing the arms open. Stand tall with your ribs down, or use a short split stance; if you still need the rock, the weight is too heavy.
Pulling the arms behind your body at the end and pushing your chest forward. Stop at the T, arms in line with your shoulders, and hold there.
exercises.name: Cable Rear Delt Fly
tips: Take 2–4 sets of 12–20 reps close to failure here; the rear delts recover fast, so two or three sessions a week are fine. Add reps at the same pin until you get 20 in each set with a one-second hold at the T, then move each stack up one plate and drop back to 12.

Go light at first. Both stacks add up, and many dual-pulley stations use 2:1 or 4:1 pulleys, so pin numbers don't carry over from one machine to another. If one plate is too big a jump, use the add-on weights or hold the T longer before you move the pin.
Rear shoulders and the area between your shoulder blades should do the work. Burning in your neck means you're shrugging, and a pinch at the front of the shoulder means your arms went past your body.
Can't hold the T yet? Use the lightest pin and open only until your hands are about 45° out. Once the full arc is easy, a 2-second hold and a 3-second return come before more weight.

Substitutes: Machine Reverse Flyes if you want your chest on a pad and the simplest setup, One-Arm Cable Rear Delt Fly when only one column is free (your other hand can brace), and Bent Over Dumbbell Lateral Raise if all you have is dumbbells.

exercises.description: Sit tall at a cable row station and pull a shoulder-width, palms-in row bar to your lower ribs with a still torso to build your mid-back and rear delts. The work lands between and on your shoulder blades: middle and lower traps, rear delts and two small muscles on the blade, the infraspinatus and teres minor, while your upper traps, lats and forearms chip in. The handles sit wider than the close V-handle of the Seated Cable Low Row Neutral Grip, so your elbows travel slightly out and the lats do less. Palms facing in is easy on wrists and elbows, and the seat spares your lower back.
instructions: Clip the neutral-grip row bar to the cable: the curved bar with an upright handle at each end, about shoulder-width apart.
Sit facing the stack with your feet on the foot plate and your knees softly bent, roughly 15–30°.
Take the handles palms-in and slide back on the seat until your arms are straight and your plates hang clear of the stack.
Sit tall: torso vertical, chest up, ribs down. The handles start at about lower-chest height and the cable runs close to level.
Draw your shoulder blades back first, then drive your elbows behind your torso with your upper arms about 20–40° out from your sides.
Stop the handles at your lower ribs, just above your stomach, and hold for a second with your shoulder blades squeezed together and slightly down.
Take 2–3 seconds to let the handles forward until your arms are straight and your shoulder blades spread. The plates never touch down between reps.
When the set is done, bend your knees and bring the bar back to the foot plate with a flat back, then let go.
mistakes: Reaching for the stack at the start. Your torso tips forward and your lower back rounds; sit further back so your arms straighten while you stay upright, and let only your shoulder blades slide forward.
Swinging back past vertical to finish the rep. Hips and torso stay put from the first rep to the last; if the handles reach your ribs only with a lean, take a plate off.

Losing the elbow path, either pinned to your ribs with the bar headed for your navel or flared up toward shoulder height. Aim at the lower ribs with your upper arms about 20–40° out and your forearms in line with the cable.
exercises.name: Cable Seated Row Neutral Grip
tips: Row 10–15 reps for muscle and 6–10 for strength; go much heavier on a stack row and the torso tends to rock. Add reps at the same weight until all your sets reach the top number with a still torso and a one-second hold, then move the pin down one plate (usually 2.5–5 kg) and build back up from the bottom of the range.

Feel it between your shoulder blades, across the blades and at the back of your shoulders. If your forearms tire first, keep your wrists straight, treat your hands as hooks and pull with your elbows. A working lower back means your torso is moving.

Torso won't stay still even with a light stack? Learn the pull on the Chest Supported Machine Row, where the pad holds your chest. Before you add weight here, stretch the hold at your ribs to two seconds and the return to three; Barbell Bent Over Row is the free-weight next step, the same pull from a hip hinge.
No row bar at your gym? Clip two single D-handles onto the carabiner and hold them shoulder-width apart, palms facing each other.
Substitutes: Seated Cable Low Row Neutral Grip (close V-handle, elbows tucked, more lats), Seated Cable Row, Chest Supported Machine Row and Barbell Bent Over Row.

Pull the bar upward close to your body by driving your elbows up and out to the sides. Your elbows should stay higher than your hands during the lift.
Raise the bar only as high as you can without shoulder discomfort, usually to lower-chest or upper-chest height. Pulling all the way to the chin is not necessary and can irritate some shoulders.
Pause briefly at the top while keeping your shoulders down away from your ears, then lower the bar slowly and under control to the starting position.
Use a moderate load that allows controlled repetitions. If you need to swing, shrug aggressively, or lean backward, reduce the weight.
Keep your wrists neutral and avoid bending them excessively as you pull. Think about leading with the elbows rather than yanking the bar with your hands.

If you feel pinching in the front or top of the shoulder, widen your grip, reduce the range of motion, try an EZ-bar or rope attachment, or choose a more shoulder-friendly exercise such as cable lateral raises.

exercises.description: The Cable Wide Grip Behind Neck Pulldown is an upper body exercise targeting the latissimus dorsi, trapezius, and rhomboids. It involves pulling a cable bar down behind the neck while seated, emphasizing the upper back and shoulder muscles.
instructions: Adjust the seat height so your feet are flat on the floor and your thighs are secured under the pad.
Attach a wide grip bar to the high pulley of a cable machine.
Sit down facing the machine and grasp the bar with a wide overhand grip, palms facing forward.
Lean slightly forward at the hips, keeping your back straight and core engaged.
Pull the bar down behind your neck by squeezing your shoulder blades together and bending your elbows.
Pause briefly when the bar reaches just below ear level.
Slowly return to the starting position with controlled movement, fully extending your arms.

Leaning excessively forward, compromising spine alignment and reducing lat engagement.
Using too much weight, leading to momentum-based movement rather than controlled muscle contraction.
Failing to engage core muscles, resulting in an unstable torso position.
Allowing elbows to flare out excessively, reducing lat activation and increasing shoulder joint stress.
Neglecting to retract shoulder blades, limiting upper back muscle involvement.

Pulling the bar down with the arms instead of focusing on the back muscles.
Using a jerking motion to initiate the pull, reducing control and muscle engagement.
exercises.name: Cable Wide Grip Behind Neck Pulldown
tips: Ensure your grip is wide enough to engage the lats effectively but not so wide that it causes discomfort.
Maintain a slight forward lean to avoid excessive strain on the shoulders and neck.
Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together during the pull to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid using momentum; control the movement throughout to prevent injury.
Keep your core tight to stabilize your torso during the exercise.
Exhale as you pull down and inhale as you return to the starting position.

exercises.description: Pull a wide parallel-grip bar from the high pulley down in front of your face, palms facing each other, to build your lats with a wrist-friendly grip. The lats along the sides of your back do most of the work. Your rear delts and teres major join in, the lower and middle traps pull the shoulder blades down and together, and the biceps and forearms assist. For most people it's the strongest pulldown grip, so the back tires first. Pick it over the overhand bar when that bothers your wrists, elbows or shoulders. Unlike the close V-handle version, your elbows come down at your sides and you lean back less.
instructions: Hang the wide parallel-grip bar on the high pulley; its short end handles sit at right angles to the bar, so your palms face each other.
Lower the thigh pad until it locks your thighs in, feet flat and knees bent about 90°, so you can't rise off the seat.
Stand, take one end handle in each hand and sit down with the bar, the cable hanging just in front of your face.
Start with straight arms and let your shoulders ride up. Sit tall, chest lifted, leaning back only about 10° for the whole set.
Pull your shoulders down away from your ears first, then drive your elbows down and in toward your ribs.
Stop with the handles beside your head at shoulder or collarbone height, forearms vertical. The bar passes in front of your face, never behind your neck, so keep your head still.
Pause briefly, shoulder blades down and together, then let the bar rise over 2–3 seconds until your arms are straight and your armpits stretch.
Let go only once your arms are straight again, or stand up with the bar. Dropped at the bottom, it shoots up and slams the stack.
mistakes: Swinging the torso back on every rep and rowing the bar to your chest. Set the slight lean once and keep it; if you can't finish the set without rocking, take a plate off.
Bending the elbows before the shoulders move, so your biceps and forearms give out before your back does. Shoulders down first, then elbows to your ribs, wrists straight.
Gripping the straight middle of the bar or the bent sections instead of the end handles. Hold the parallel handles, palms facing, the same distance from the center on each side.
Cutting the top short. Let the bar rise until your elbows are straight and your shoulders lift a little on every rep, because that stretch is half the exercise.
exercises.name: Cable Wide Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown
tips: For size, sets of 8–15 work for most lifters; for strength, 6–8. If you're new, use 10–15 with a weight you can bring to shoulder height without leaning back. Reps come before weight. When all your sets reach 15 with the same torso angle, put the pin one plate lower (usually 5 kg or 10 lb) and drop back to 8.

Expect to feel it along the sides of your back from the armpits down, at the back of your shoulders and under your shoulder blades, plus a stretch under the armpits at the top. If your biceps burn more than your back, think of your hands as hooks and lead with the elbows.

Struggling with the shoulders-down start? Practice it on the Lat Pulldown Machine, whose fixed lever path makes it easier to learn, or go lighter with a 1-second pause at the bottom. To make it harder, let the bar rise over 3–4 seconds or pause for 2 at the bottom. Clean sets of 8–10 with close to your body weight are a rough sign you're ready for the Assisted Pull-Up on neutral handles, then the Neutral-Grip Pull-Up.

Substitutes: Cable Lat Pulldown (straight overhand bar), Cable Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown with the close V-handle (use it if your gym has no parallel-grip bar), Lat Pulldown Machine, Neutral-Grip Pull-Up.

Start with a lighter weight to ensure proper form and gradually increase as you build strength.

exercises.description: On a flat bench, lower a barbell to your forehead, bring it over to your lower chest and press it up with a close grip to train your triceps heavy. Each rep is a skull crusher on the way down and a close-grip bench press on the way up, in that order. Behind your head the long head of the triceps gets a deep stretch, and because you lift with a press, you can handle more weight than in a skull crusher. Your lats and teres major move the bar from head to chest, and your chest helps the press. Good for intermediate lifters whose skull crushers have stalled.
instructions: Lie on a flat bench with your head, upper back and hips on the pad, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat on the floor.
Grip the bar overhand at shoulder width or a touch narrower, hands not touching. Wrap your thumbs around it; it sits low in your palms.
Get the bar to lockout over your shoulders: unrack it, take it from a spotter, or lie back with it on your thighs and press.
Lower the bar like a skull crusher, elbows pointing at the ceiling, until it reaches your forehead and just past the top of your head (about 2 seconds).
Keep that elbow angle and pull your upper arms down to your sides; the bar travels back over your face to just above your lower chest.
Press straight up from there, exactly like a close-grip bench press, and breathe out as your elbows lock out over your shoulders.
Start each rep from straight arms. After the last, rack the bar, hand it to your spotter, or lower it to your thighs and sit up.
mistakes: Doing the phases in reverse: lowering to the chest first and then sliding the bar toward your forehead. The bar goes to your head first, then to your chest, and the way up is always a press.

Elbows flaring out as the bar comes over to your chest, so the press turns into a wide-grip bench press. Bring them down close to your ribs, about 30 to 45 degrees from your torso, pointing at your hips.
Straightening your elbows on the way from your head to your chest. That's a pullover, and the bar tends to crash onto your breastbone; keep the elbow angle fixed and move the bar slowly.
Bouncing the bar off your chest to get the press going. Stop it just above your lower chest and press from a dead stop.
Wrists bent back under the load. Keep the bar low in your palm, over the forearm bones, with your knuckles in line with your forearms.
exercises.name: California Press
tips: Use 3 or 4 sets of 5 to 8 reps for strength or 8 to 12 for size; with a lighter bar you can go up to 15.
Add reps first: when you get the top number on all sets with the bar going all the way behind your head, add 2 to 2.5 kg (1 to 1.25 kg per side) and drop back to the low end.

Behind your head you should feel a deep stretch along the back of your upper arm, then your lats working as the bar comes over to your chest. Sore elbows mean the skull-crusher half is too deep or too heavy: stop at your forehead, switch to an EZ bar, or train the two halves separately for a while.

The bar passes over your face, so never use a thumbless grip, and have a spotter or a bench rack once the sets get heavy. If a rep stalls behind your head, don't try to straighten your elbows from there. Bring the bar to your chest and finish it as a press.
To make it harder before adding weight, pause for 1 to 2 seconds with the bar behind your head, or take 3 to 4 seconds to lower it.

Substitutes: Lying Barbell Triceps Extension for the first half on its own, Close Grip Bench Press for the second half, JM Press if your elbows prefer a shorter skull crusher, and Lying EZ-Bar Triceps Extension if a straight bar bothers your wrists.

exercises.description: The Cat-Cow exercise is a dynamic stretch that targets the spine, improving flexibility and promoting spinal health. Neglecting to keep the wrists aligned under the shoulders, affecting balance.

exercises.description: Sit chest-to-pad on a plate-loaded machine and row the neutral handles to your lower ribs to build your back while your lower back rests. Most of the pull comes from your lats and teres major along the sides of your back, the middle and lower traps between your shoulder blades, and the rear delts with the small infraspinatus and teres minor behind each shoulder; biceps and forearms only assist. The pad holds your torso in place, so there's nothing to swing. That suits beginners and days when squats or deadlifts have already worn out your lower back. Elbows kept close give the lats more work than the wide overhand version.
instructions: Load the same plates on both horns while the handles rest in their start position. The arms move independently, so mismatched plates mean mismatched sides.
Set the seat so the top of the chest pad sits at your breastbone, below the collarbones, with the handles level with your lower chest.
Sit tall with your feet on the foot plate, knees bent about 90°, and lean your chest lightly into the pad.
Take the vertical handles with a neutral grip, hands about shoulder-width apart. If you can't reach them with straight arms, adjust the chest pad.
Start the pull with your shoulder blades: draw them back and down, then drive your elbows back along your sides, about 30–45° from your body.
Row until your elbows pass your torso and your hands reach your lower ribs. Squeeze for a second, chest still on the pad.
Take 2–3 seconds on the return, until your arms are straight and your shoulder blades spread. Don't let the plates touch down between reps.
At the end of the set, walk the handles back to their resting spot before you let go and stand up.
mistakes: Peeling your chest off the pad and leaning back to heave the last reps in. Keep your breastbone on the pad; once it lifts, take off a plate or call the set.
Short reps at the front, with bent arms and shoulder blades that never spread. Let the handles go forward until your elbows are straight.

Pulling with your hands: the wrists curl, the elbows stay in front of your body and the biceps take over. Treat your hands as hooks and lead with the elbows. Lifting straps help if your grip quits before your back does.
One handle leading or finishing further back than the other. Check the plates match, then slow down until both handles arrive level, at the same point.
exercises.name: Chest Supported Machine Row
tips: Row 3–4 sets of 8–15 reps, or 6–8 when the goal is strength.

Pick a range such as 8–12 and add reps at the same load until you get 12 on every set with a one-second squeeze. Then add the smallest plate pair, usually 2.5 kg per side, and go back to 8. The lever changes how heavy a plate feels, so only compare loads on the same machine.

Most of the work happens between and below your shoulder blades, across the backs of your shoulders and along the sides of your back under the armpits. A tired lower back means your chest is coming off the pad. A burning neck means you're shrugging, and a pinch at the front of the shoulder means your elbows are traveling too far back; stop them just behind your torso.

Shoulder blades won't move? Do a few sets of scapular rows on the same machine first: arms straight, only the shoulder blades pull back and return. Once regular reps get easy, add a 2-second pause at the ribs and a 3-second return, or switch to the One-Arm Seated Row on this machine.

Substitutes: Dumbbell Neutral Grip Incline Bench Row or Incline Chest Supported Barbell Row when the machine is taken; Seated Cable Low Row Neutral Grip when you want a longer stretch at the front and don't mind your trunk doing some of the holding.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/back/t杠胸部支撑划船

exercises.description: Lie chest-down on the incline pad of a T-bar machine and pull the wide handles to your lower chest, elbows flared, to build your upper back and rear delts. The middle and lower traps between and below your shoulder blades do the most work, along with your rear delts and the small muscles over each shoulder blade: infraspinatus and teres major and minor. Your lats help only a little. You stand on a footplate with your torso on the pad, so nothing can swing and your lower back gets a break. Pick it over the bent-over T-bar row when your lower back is the weak link.
instructions: Load plates onto the horn at the front of the lever while it sits on its stop, evenly if both sides take plates.
If the footplate adjusts, set it so the top edge of the pad meets your lower chest and your shoulders clear the front of the pad.
Step onto the angled footplate with your knees well bent and lie onto the pad, chest and upper stomach supported. Eyes on the floor.
Grip the horizontal handles overhand, thumbs wrapped, hands wider than your shoulders, and lift the lever off its stop with straight arms.
Start each rep from that full reach, shoulder blades spread: pull them back first, then drive your elbows up and out, roughly 60–80° from your sides.
Stop when your hands reach the front edge of the pad at lower-chest height and your elbows are level with your back. Squeeze and hold a second.
Lower over 2–3 seconds until your arms hang straight, and start the next rep just before the plates touch the stop.
When you're done, set the lever down on its stop before you let go or step off the footplate.
mistakes: Peeling your chest off the pad and pushing through your legs to heave the lever up. Your breastbone stays on the pad and your legs stay still; if that's impossible, the load is too heavy.

Tucking your elbows and rowing to your stomach. With handles this wide, that's a cramped lat row. Keep your upper arms 60–80° out and finish at the pad edge, or use the Chest Supported Machine Row when you want the tucked version.

Half reps: the arms never straighten at the bottom, or the shoulder blades never meet at the top. Let the lever go all the way down, hold the squeeze for a second, and drop a plate if you can't do both.
Lifting your head to look ahead as you pull. Keep your chin tucked and your eyes on the floor in front of the machine.
exercises.name: Chest Supported T-Bar Row
tips: Plan on 3–4 sets of 8–15 reps.

The upper back and rear delts usually do well with 10–15, while 6–8 is enough for strength work. Add reps at the same load until you get 15 on all sets with straight arms at the bottom and a one-second squeeze at the top. Then add the smallest plate the horn takes, usually 2.5 kg, and go back to 8. The lever changes how heavy a plate feels, so compare numbers only on the same machine.

It should burn across the middle of your upper back and on the backs of your shoulders. A burning neck means you're shrugging, a tired lower back means your chest is lifting off the pad, and a pump under the armpits means your elbows have dropped to your sides.

If your shoulder blades barely move, warm up with a couple of light sets where your arms stay straight and only the shoulder blades pull back and return. When the top of your range comes easily, add a 2-second hold and a 3-second lowering before you add plates. A pinch at the front of the shoulder? Bring your elbows in to about 45°.

Substitutes: Wide Grip Chest Supported Row (the same wide pull, seated), Chest Supported Machine Row (neutral handles and more lats), and Incline Bench Dumbbell Wide Row or Barbell Incline Wide Grip Row when there's no T-bar machine.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/臀部/婴儿式

exercises.description: Child’s Pose, or Balasana, is a resting yoga posture that gently stretches the hips, thighs, and ankles while calming the mind and relieving stress. It is often used as a counterpose to more strenuous exercises or as a resting position during a workout.
instructions: Begin by kneeling on the floor with your big toes touching and knees spread apart about hip-width.
Sit back on your heels and slowly bend forward, extending your arms in front of you on the floor.
Lower your torso between your thighs and rest your forehead on the mat.
Keep your arms extended forward with palms facing down or alongside your body with palms facing up.
Hold the position for several breaths, focusing on deep, even breathing.
mistakes: Knees too close together, limiting hip and back stretch.
Hips not reaching towards heels, reducing lower back release.
Arms fully extended with tension, instead of relaxed.
Forehead not resting on the ground, causing neck strain.
Shoulders hunched up towards ears, creating tension.
Breathing shallowly, limiting relaxation and stretch.
Feet not touching, leading to imbalance.
Lower back excessively arched, risking strain.
exercises.name: Child’s Pose
tips: If you have tight hips, keep your knees closer together for comfort.
To deepen the stretch in your shoulders, keep your arms extended forward.
Use a cushion or folded blanket under your torso or forehead for added support if needed.
Focus on relaxing your entire body and breathing deeply to enhance the calming effects of the pose.
If you experience discomfort in your knees, place a rolled towel behind them for additional support.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/back/反握引体向上

exercises.description: The chin-up is a compound upper-body exercise that primarily targets the latissimus dorsi muscles in the back, along with the biceps, forearms, and shoulders. It involves pulling your body up to a bar using a supinated or underhand grip, with hands typically shoulder-width apart.
instructions: Stand beneath a pull-up bar and grasp it with an underhand grip, palms facing you, hands shoulder-width apart.
Hang from the bar with your arms fully extended and feet off the ground. Engage your core and keep your body straight.
Initiate the movement by pulling your shoulder blades down and back, then pull your chest towards the bar by bending your elbows.
Continue pulling until your chin is above the bar. Pause briefly at the top of the movement.
Lower yourself back to the starting position in a controlled manner, fully extending your arms.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using momentum by swinging the body to complete the movement.
Failing to fully extend the arms at the bottom of the movement.
Pulling with the arms instead of engaging the back muscles.
Allowing the shoulders to shrug up towards the ears.
Not keeping the core engaged, leading to excessive arching of the back.
Gripping the bar too tightly, causing forearm fatigue.
Not bringing the chin above the bar at the top of the movement.
Letting the elbows flare out excessively to the sides.
Rushing through the movement without controlled tempo.
Neglecting to breathe properly, holding breath throughout the exercise.
exercises.name: Chin-Up
tips: Focus on engaging your back muscles rather than just pulling with your arms to maximize lat activation.
Keep your core tight throughout the movement to prevent swinging or kipping.
If you're unable to perform a full chin-up, use resistance bands for assistance or perform negative chin-ups by jumping to the top position and lowering yourself slowly.
Ensure a full range of motion by fully extending your arms at the bottom of each rep.
Avoid using momentum; perform each rep in a controlled manner to increase strength effectively.

exercises.description: A bodyweight hip exercise done lying on your side with your knees bent and feet together. You open the top knee like a clamshell by rotating the thigh outward while your pelvis stays still. The small, controlled movement targets the gluteus medius and the other hip stabilizers.
instructions: Lie on your side on the floor and extend your bottom arm along the floor above your head. Rest your head on that arm and place your top hand on the floor in front of your chest.
Bend your hips slightly and your knees to about 90 degrees, with your hips, knees and feet stacked.
Brace your abs lightly to keep your pelvis still.
Keeping your feet together, rotate your top thigh outward and lift the knee as high as you can without your pelvis rolling back.
Pause for a moment at the top.
Lower the knee slowly until it rests on the bottom knee.
Finish all reps on one side, then roll over and repeat on the other side.
mistakes: Rolling the pelvis and torso backward to lift the knee higher
Letting the feet come apart or the top foot rise with the knee
Swinging the knee up with momentum and letting it drop on the way down
Arching or twisting the lower back as the knee opens
Pushing off the floor with the top hand to help lift the leg
Letting the top hip roll forward so the hips are no longer stacked
exercises.name: Clamshell
tips: Rest your head on your bottom arm and use your top hand on the floor for balance, so your neck and shoulders stay relaxed.
Think of turning the thigh outward in the hip socket. Your feet are the hinge and the knee opens like the top of a shell.
Hold the top position for one or two seconds and feel the work on the side of your hip, not in the front of your thigh.
When learning the movement, lie with your back against a wall so you feel right away if your pelvis starts to roll back.
Breathe out as you open the knee and breathe in as you lower it.
Do the same number of reps on each side, and start with the side that tires sooner.

exercises.description: The Clap Push Up is an advanced plyometric exercise that enhances upper body strength, explosiveness, and coordination. It primarily targets the chest, triceps, and shoulders, while also engaging the core for stability.
instructions: Start in a standard push-up position with your hands shoulder-width apart and your body forming a straight line from head to heels.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until your chest nearly touches the floor.
Explosively push yourself upwards with enough force to lift your hands off the ground.
Quickly clap your hands together while in the air.
Return your hands to the starting position to catch yourself and immediately proceed to the next repetition.
mistakes: Failing to engage core muscles, leading to a sagging lower back.
Allowing elbows to flare out excessively, reducing power and control.
Inadequate push-off force, resulting in incomplete clap or missed clap.
Landing with locked elbows, increasing joint stress.
Neglecting to maintain a straight body line from head to heels.
Performing the exercise too quickly, sacrificing form for speed.
Not achieving full range of motion, limiting muscle activation.
Inconsistent hand placement on landing, causing imbalance.
Insufficient shoulder stability, risking shoulder strain.
exercises.name: Clap Push-Up
tips: Ensure your core is engaged throughout the movement to maintain a straight body line.
Focus on generating power from your chest and triceps during the push-off phase.
Practice regular push-ups first to build foundational strength before attempting clap push-ups.
Start with small claps if you're new to this exercise and gradually increase the height of your jump as you become more comfortable.
Maintain a controlled descent to prevent injury and ensure smooth transitions between repetitions.

exercises.description: The Clean and Jerk is a two-part Olympic weightlifting exercise that involves lifting a barbell from the floor to an overhead position. It combines strength, power, coordination, and technique, making it a comprehensive full-body workout. The exercise is divided into two phases: the Clean, where the barbell is lifted from the floor to the shoulders, and the Jerk, where the barbell is driven overhead.
instructions: Start with your feet shoulder-width apart, barbell over mid-foot.
Grip the barbell with a hook grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Lower your hips with a straight back and chest up.
Initiate the lift by extending your knees and hips explosively.
Pull the bar close to your body, shrugging your shoulders as it passes your knees.
Drop under the bar into a front squat position as you catch it on your shoulders.
Stand up from the squat to complete the Clean phase.
For the Jerk, dip slightly by bending your knees and then drive upward explosively.
Push the bar overhead while splitting your legs into a lunge position.
Lock out your arms with the barbell overhead and stabilize.
Bring your feet together to finish in a standing position with control.
mistakes: Starting with hips too low or too high in the setup position.
Pulling with the arms too early instead of driving with the legs.
Not keeping the barbell close to the body during the pull.
Failing to fully extend the hips before initiating the drop under the bar.
Catching the barbell in a forward position instead of directly above the shoulders.
Not achieving full depth in the squat during the clean.
Pressing the barbell instead of driving it with the legs during the jerk.
Allowing the elbows to drop during the clean, leading to a loss of control.
Jumping forward or backward excessively during the lift.
Not maintaining a stable core throughout the movement.
Landing with feet too narrow or too wide in the split jerk.
Failing to lock out the elbows fully in the overhead position.
exercises.name: Clean and Jerk
tips: Focus on keeping the barbell close to your body throughout the lift to maintain control and efficiency.
Use a hook grip for better grip security during heavy lifts.
Engage your core throughout both phases to maintain stability and prevent injury.
Practice each phase separately before combining them to ensure proper technique.
Ensure proper warm-up and mobility exercises before attempting heavy lifts to prevent injury.
Keep your elbows high during the Clean catch to secure the bar on your shoulders effectively.
During the Jerk, ensure a quick transition from dip to drive for maximum power transfer.

exercises.description: A deadlift from the floor that uses the clean grip and the clean start position, with the hips low, chest up and shoulders slightly in front of the bar. You pull to a full standing lockout without jumping or shrugging, which builds the strength and positions of the first pull of the clean.
instructions: Stand with your feet about hip-width apart and the bar over the middle of your feet.
Squat down and take an overhand grip about shoulder-width apart, with your hands just outside your knees.
Set your hips low, chest up and back flat, with your shoulders slightly in front of the bar and your arms straight.
Brace your core and pull the slack out of the bar without lifting it off the floor.
Push the floor away with your legs and keep the bar close to your shins. Raise your hips and shoulders together until the bar passes your knees.
Drive your hips forward and stand tall with your knees and hips fully extended. Do not lean back or shrug.
Lower the bar along the same path under control and set it on the floor before the next repetition.
mistakes: Starting with the hips high, as in a conventional deadlift, instead of the low clean start position.
Letting the hips shoot up first so the chest drops toward the bar.
Letting the bar drift away from the shins and thighs.
Rounding the lower back under the load.
Bending the arms during the pull.
Leaning back, shrugging or jumping at the top.
Dropping the bar instead of lowering it under control.
exercises.name: Clean Deadlift
tips: Use the same grip width and foot position as in your clean, so the pull carries over to the lift.
Keep your weight over the whole foot, not on your toes.
Pull your shoulders down and tense your lats to keep the bar against your legs.
Keep your head neutral and your eyes forward.
Lift at a steady, controlled speed. This is a strength pull, not an explosive one.

exercises.description: Lift the barbell from the floor with a clean grip, then extend your hips and knees dynamically and shrug your shoulders. This clean pull finishes with the bar near the hips and a slight bend of the elbows, without catching the bar on the shoulders.
instructions: Stand with your feet about hip-width apart, with the barbell positioned over the middle of your feet.
Grip the bar just outside your legs using a clean grip, with your hands far enough apart to allow the bar to pass close to your thighs.
Bend your knees and hips to reach the bar, keep your chest up, brace your core, and maintain a neutral spine.
Start the pull by pushing the floor away with your legs, keeping your hips and shoulders rising together and the bar close to your shins.
As the bar passes your knees, sweep it slightly back toward your thighs while continuing to extend your knees and hips.
Drive forcefully through the floor and extend your hips, knees, and ankles explosively, finishing tall with the bar close to your upper thighs.
At full extension, shrug your shoulders and allow a slight outward elbow bend as the bar rises near the hips.
Guide the bar back down under control, reset your starting position, and repeat each repetition with consistent posture and bar path.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back during the initial pull.
Raising the hips faster than the shoulders and turning the lift into a stiff-leg pull.
Bending the elbows early rather than keeping the arms long through the extension.
Failing to fully extend the hips, knees, and ankles before the shrug.
Leaning backward excessively at the top of the pull.
Jumping forward or backward instead of maintaining balanced pressure through the feet.
exercises.name: Clean Pull
tips: Start with the bar over the midfoot, feet about hip-width apart, and use the same grip and setup you would for a clean.
Start each repetition from a still bar on the floor before accelerating it.
Keep your shoulders over the bar during the first pull, then bring the bar into the upper thigh or hip area under control.
Lower the bar with control, reset your position between repetitions, and maintain consistent technique rather than rushing the set.
Choose a load you can accelerate with the legs rather than merely lift slowly.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/抓举深蹲

exercises.description: The Clean Squat is a compound exercise that combines elements of the clean and the squat. It targets multiple muscle groups, including the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, core, and shoulders. This exercise enhances strength, power, and coordination.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and position a barbell over your mid-foot.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the barbell with an overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Keep your chest up, back straight, and engage your core.
Initiate the lift by extending your hips and knees explosively to pull the barbell off the ground.
As the bar reaches your thighs, shrug your shoulders and pull yourself under the bar into a front squat position.
Catch the bar on your shoulders with elbows high and upper arms parallel to the ground.
Lower into a deep squat by bending at the hips and knees while keeping your chest up.
Drive through your heels to stand back up, maintaining control of the barbell on your shoulders.
Lower the barbell back to the ground with control to complete one repetition.
mistakes: Failing to keep the barbell close to the body during the pull phase, leading to inefficient movement and potential loss of balance.
Not fully extending the hips and knees in the catch phase, resulting in a weak squat position.
Allowing the knees to cave inward during the squat, which can strain the knee joints.
Dropping the elbows too low in the front rack position, causing instability and poor bar control.
Rounding the back during the lift, increasing the risk of lower back injury.
Not engaging the core throughout the movement, leading to a lack of stability and control.
Using too much arm pull instead of relying on the power from the hips and legs.
Starting with feet too wide apart, which can limit squat depth and power.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine, compromising posture and efficiency.
Rising onto the toes during the squat, which can destabilize the lift and reduce power.
exercises.name: Clean Squat
tips: Focus on keeping your core tight throughout the movement to maintain stability.
Ensure that your elbows remain high during the catch phase to properly support the barbell.
Practice with lighter weights initially to perfect form before progressing to heavier loads.
Use a hook grip for better control of the barbell during the pull phase.
Keep your weight centered over your mid-foot to maintain balance during both the clean and squat phases.
Engage in proper warm-up exercises to prepare your muscles for this compound movement.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/肱三头肌/窄握卧推

exercises.description: Lie on a flat bench with your feet planted firmly on the floor. Grip the barbell slightly narrower than shoulder width, keeping your wrists straight and elbows close to your torso. Unrack the bar and lower it under control to the lower chest, then press it back up by extending your elbows. Keep your shoulder blades retracted, chest lifted, and avoid flaring the elbows excessively.
instructions: Set a barbell in a bench press rack at a height you can safely unrack while lying on a flat bench, then load the desired weight and secure the plates with collars.
Lie on the bench with your eyes under the bar, feet planted firmly on the floor, and your head, upper back, and glutes in contact with the bench.

Grip the bar with both hands approximately shoulder-width apart or slightly narrower, keeping your wrists straight and stacked over your forearms. Avoid an extremely narrow grip that causes wrist discomfort.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down, brace your core, and create a stable upper-back position while maintaining a natural, slight arch in your lower back.
Unrack the bar with straight arms and position it over your lower chest or upper abdomen, keeping your elbows close to your sides.
Inhale and lower the bar under control toward your lower chest, allowing the elbows to bend backward at roughly a 30–45 degree angle from your torso.
Lightly touch the bar to your chest without bouncing, then press it upward while exhaling, driving through your palms and keeping your elbows close to your body.

Finish with the elbows extended without forcefully locking them out, stabilize the bar above your lower chest, and repeat for the desired number of repetitions before carefully returning the bar to the rack.
mistakes: Grip is excessively narrow, forcing the wrists into extreme extension and making the bar unstable.
Elbows flare wide to the sides instead of tracking relatively close to the torso.
Wrists bend backward or sideways instead of staying stacked over the forearms.
Lowering the bar too high on the chest or toward the neck rather than to the lower chest or upper sternum area.
Bouncing the bar off the chest instead of pausing or controlling the descent.
Using a partial range of motion by stopping short of the chest or failing to fully extend the elbows.
Losing upper-back tension and allowing the shoulders to roll forward at the bottom.
Raising the shoulders off the bench or shrugging them toward the ears during the press.
Letting the hips lift excessively off the bench to compensate for insufficient pressing strength.
Allowing the bar to drift forward or backward instead of pressing in a controlled, consistent bar path.
Relaxing the triceps at lockout and losing control of the bar between repetitions.
Using momentum or uneven pressing, causing one side of the bar to rise faster than the other.
exercises.name: Close Grip Bench Press
tips: Use a grip slightly narrower than shoulder width; placing the hands extremely close together can stress the wrists and reduce control.
Set your shoulder blades back and down against the bench, keep your chest lifted, and maintain a small natural arch in your lower back.
Keep your feet firmly planted on the floor throughout the lift to create a stable base and avoid shifting on the bench.
Lower the bar under control toward the lower chest or upper sternum, keeping the bar path steady and close to vertical.
Keep your elbows tucked at roughly 30–45 degrees from your torso rather than letting them flare wide.
Stack your wrists over your forearms and keep the wrists as neutral as possible; do not let the bar bend the wrists backward.
Grip the bar tightly and use a full thumb wrap for better control and safety.
Press the bar up by driving through the triceps while keeping the shoulders stable and avoiding excessive elbow flare near lockout.
Do not bounce the bar off your chest; pause briefly or lightly touch the chest before pressing back up.
Use a spotter or safety arms when training heavy, especially because the narrower grip can make the bar less stable.
Start with a lighter load than your regular bench press and prioritize smooth, pain-free repetitions before adding weight.
Stop the set if you feel sharp pain in the wrists, elbows, or shoulders, and adjust grip width or range of motion as needed.

exercises.description: The Close Grip Biceps Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps brachii, particularly emphasizing the short head of the biceps. This exercise involves using a barbell or an EZ curl bar with a narrow grip to maximize bicep engagement and minimize forearm involvement.
instructions: Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a barbell or EZ curl bar with an underhand grip. Your hands should be positioned close together, about 6-8 inches apart.
Keep your elbows close to your torso and maintain a slight bend in your knees for stability.
Exhale as you curl the bar upwards by flexing your elbows, keeping your upper arms stationary. Focus on contracting your biceps throughout the movement.
Continue lifting until your biceps are fully contracted and the bar is at shoulder level.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, then inhale as you slowly lower the bar back to the starting position, maintaining control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using too much weight, leading to swinging or jerking motions.
Allowing elbows to flare out, reducing bicep engagement.
Failing to fully extend arms at the bottom of the curl.
Curling wrists instead of keeping them neutral, causing strain.
Leaning back excessively, shifting focus from biceps to back.
Moving elbows forward during the curl, reducing tension on biceps.
Rushing through reps, sacrificing control and form.
Not maintaining a consistent grip width, affecting muscle activation.
exercises.name: Close Grip Biceps Curl
tips: Ensure that your grip is narrow but comfortable to avoid unnecessary wrist strain.
Keep your elbows tucked in and stationary to isolate the biceps effectively.
Focus on a slow and controlled movement to maximize muscle tension and avoid using momentum.
Maintain a neutral spine and engage your core throughout the exercise to support proper posture.
Avoid locking out your elbows at the bottom of the movement to keep constant tension on the biceps.
Use a weight that allows you to perform the exercise with proper form for all repetitions.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/chest/窄握哑铃卧推

exercises.description: The Close Grip Dumbbell Bench Press is a compound exercise targeting the triceps, chest, and shoulders. It involves pressing dumbbells from a supine position on a bench with hands positioned closer together than in a standard bench press. This exercise emphasizes the triceps while also engaging the pectoral muscles and anterior deltoids.
instructions: Lie back on a flat bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with your feet flat on the floor.
Position the dumbbells directly above your chest with palms facing each other and elbows close to your body.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly towards your chest by bending your elbows, keeping them tucked in.
Pause briefly when the dumbbells are near your chest.
Exhale and press the dumbbells back up to the starting position by extending your arms fully.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control throughout the movement.
mistakes: Elbows flaring out excessively, reducing triceps engagement.
Dumbbells drifting too far apart, losing control and stability.
Arching the lower back excessively, risking lower back strain.
Pressing the dumbbells too high above the chest, reducing triceps activation.
Failing to keep wrists straight, leading to potential wrist strain.
Lowering the dumbbells too quickly, compromising muscle tension.
Not maintaining a consistent grip, risking dumbbell slippage.
Allowing shoulders to shrug, reducing focus on the triceps.
exercises.name: Close Grip Dumbbell Press
tips: Keep your elbows close to your body to maximize triceps engagement.
Maintain a neutral wrist position to avoid unnecessary strain.
Focus on controlled movements rather than speed to ensure proper form.
Engage your core throughout the exercise to stabilize your body.
Avoid locking out your elbows completely at the top of the movement to maintain tension on the muscles.
Ensure that your shoulder blades are retracted and remain in contact with the bench for stability.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/肱三头肌/窄握上斜哑铃卧推

exercises.description: The close grip incline dumbbell chest press is a compound exercise targeting the upper portion of the pectoral muscles, triceps, and anterior deltoids. By using a close grip, this variation emphasizes the triceps while also engaging the chest and shoulders. Performing this exercise on an incline bench further targets the upper chest.
instructions: Set an incline bench to a 30-45 degree angle.
Sit on the bench with a dumbbell in each hand, resting them on your thighs.
Lie back on the bench and bring the dumbbells to shoulder height with palms facing each other.
Position your feet flat on the floor for stability.
Press the dumbbells upward by extending your elbows until your arms are fully extended above your chest.
Pause briefly at the top, ensuring your arms are straight but not locked.
Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position at shoulder height.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Elbows flaring outwards instead of staying close to the body.
Arching the back excessively during the lift.
Using too heavy weights, compromising form and control.
Failing to maintain a neutral wrist position, leading to wrist strain.
Lowering the dumbbells too quickly, losing muscle tension.
Not bringing the dumbbells down to the chest, reducing range of motion.
Allowing the shoulders to shrug upwards, disengaging the chest.
Pressing the dumbbells unevenly, causing imbalance.
Not engaging the core, leading to instability on the bench.
exercises.name: Close Grip Incline Dumbbell Bench Press

instructions: Position a barbell in a landmine attachment or securely anchor one end in a corner.
Stand over the barbell with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent.
Bend at the hips to lower your torso until it is nearly parallel to the floor, maintaining a neutral spine.
Grip the barbell close to the weighted end with both hands using an overhand grip.
Engage your core and pull the barbell towards your lower chest by retracting your shoulder blades and bending your elbows.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position with control.

exercises.name: Close Grip Landmine Row
tips: Keep your back straight and avoid rounding your shoulders to prevent injury.
Focus on pulling with your back muscles rather than relying solely on your arms.
Maintain a slight bend in your knees to support balance and stability.
Control the movement throughout; avoid using momentum to lift the weight.
Ensure that your grip is firm but not excessively tight to reduce forearm fatigue.
Exhale as you pull the barbell towards you and inhale as you lower it back down.

exercises.description: The Close Grip Pull-Up is a bodyweight exercise targeting the upper back, biceps, and forearms. It involves pulling your body upward using a narrow grip on a pull-up bar, emphasizing the inner back muscles and arm flexors.

Hang from the bar with your arms fully extended and feet off the ground. Engage your core and keep your body straight.
Initiate the pull by squeezing your shoulder blades together and pulling your elbows down towards your sides.
Continue to pull until your chin is above the bar, keeping your elbows close to your body.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, then slowly lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

exercises.name: Close Grip Pull Up
tips: Ensure a full range of motion by fully extending your arms at the bottom of each rep.
Focus on engaging your lats and biceps throughout the movement for maximum effectiveness.
Avoid swinging or using momentum to lift yourself; maintain control throughout the exercise.
If you're unable to perform a full pull-up, use resistance bands or an assisted pull-up machine to build strength.
Keep your core tight to prevent excessive arching of the lower back during the exercise.

instructions: Start in a plank position with your body straight from head to heels.
Place your hands directly under your chest, closer than shoulder-width apart.
Keep your elbows tucked close to your body throughout the movement.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until your chest nearly touches the floor.
Push through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Maintain a straight line from head to heels throughout the exercise.

tips: Focus on keeping your core engaged to maintain a straight body line.
Ensure your elbows stay close to your sides to maximize tricep engagement.
Control the movement both on the way down and up for better muscle activation.
If it's too challenging, perform the exercise on your knees while maintaining proper form.
Breathe in as you lower yourself and exhale as you push back up.

exercises.description: A close-grip bench press on a Smith machine. With your hands about shoulder-width apart and your elbows close to your sides, the triceps take on more of the work, while the chest and front delts still help. The guided bar path lets you push hard without having to balance the bar.
instructions: Set a flat bench under the Smith machine. Adjust the bar height so you can comfortably un-rack it with your arms fully extended.
Lie back on the bench and position yourself so that your eyes are directly under the bar. Grip the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip.
Un-rack the bar and lower it towards your lower chest, keeping your elbows tucked close to your body.
Stop when the bar is about an inch above your chest, then press it back up by extending your elbows until your arms are fully extended.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control of the bar throughout the movement.
mistakes: Hands placed too wide, reducing triceps activation.

Start with a lighter weight to master the form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: Curl an EZ bar from thighs to shoulders with your hands underhand on the inner bends, close together: the close-grip version of the standard EZ-bar curl. Both biceps heads drive the curl, helped by the brachialis underneath and the thumb side of your forearm. In the standard version your hands sit on the outer bends at about shoulder width. Use it for variety or when narrow hands feel better on your shoulders; if your wrists or inner elbows complain, move back out. Close relatives: the straight-bar close-grip curl and the EZ preacher curl.
instructions: Load a weight you can curl without hip drive. Take the bar from a mid-thigh rack, or deadlift it up with a flat back.
Stand tall with your feet about hip-width apart, toes turned out slightly, knees straight but not locked.
Take the two inner bends, next to the center, palms forward and thumbs wrapped. Your hands end up 6–8 in (15–20 cm) apart.
Arms hang straight, bar on your thighs, elbows at your sides. Your forearms angle in toward your hands in a V; that's normal here.
Brace lightly, breathe out and curl the bar in an arc toward your upper chest. Elbows point down and stay by your ribs, never flaring.
Stop when your forearms are vertical and the bar is at shoulder height, just under your chin. Squeeze your biceps there for about a second.
Take 2–3 seconds to lower to straight elbows, pause a beat at your thighs, then curl again. Rack the bar after the last rep.
mistakes: Gripping the outer bends, or one inner and one outer, so the grip isn't close and the bar tilts. Set both hands on the inner bends, equally far from the center, before the bar leaves the rack.
Elbows flaring out as the bar rises because your hands are close together. Keep them pointed down and brushing your ribs, and let your forearms angle in instead.
Leaning back and driving your hips forward to get the bar moving. Take weight off, brace your abs and glutes and keep your knees still; if you still swing, do the set with your back on a wall.
Pulling the bar to your chin as your elbows rise and the front of your shoulders takes over. Finish each rep when your forearms are vertical and the bar is level with your shoulders.
Short reps at the bottom, or letting the bar drop and bounce off your thighs. Lower to straight elbows every time and start each rep from a brief stop.
exercises.name: Close-grip EZ Bar Curl
tips: Sets of 8–15 suit this curl, or 6–10 on a heavier day. Keep the same bar until you can do the top number on all sets without swinging, then add 2.5 kg (1.25 kg or 2.5 lb per side) and work back up from the bottom. Expect to handle about what you use on the standard EZ curl, or a little less.

Your upper arms should burn at the front, hardest from halfway up to the squeeze. A mild stretch along the inside of your forearms is normal with hands this close; sharp pain in your wrist or inner elbow is your cue to switch to the outer bends.

If your torso still rocks with a lighter bar, try the Barbell Wall Curl, which works with an EZ bar and a close grip too. Once the reps come easily, slow the lowering to 3–4 seconds or move on to the EZ-Bar Preacher Curl.

Substitutes: EZ-Bar Biceps Curl (outer bends, easier on sore wrists), Close Grip Biceps Curl (straight bar, for when the EZ bar is taken), Barbell Biceps Curl, Bar Cable Biceps Curl (hands close on the bar, and the cable keeps pulling at the bottom).

exercises.description: The Cobra Push Up is a dynamic bodyweight exercise that combines elements of a traditional push-up with a back extension movement, targeting the chest, triceps, shoulders, and lower back. It enhances upper body strength and flexibility while engaging the core.
instructions: Start in a prone position on the floor with your legs extended and feet together.
Place your hands under your shoulders, palms flat on the ground.
Engage your core and press through your palms to lift your chest off the ground, extending your arms fully while keeping your elbows close to your body.
Simultaneously, arch your back and lift your head towards the ceiling, resembling a cobra pose.
Hold the top position briefly, then slowly lower your chest back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Flaring the elbows out too wide, increasing shoulder strain.

Arching the lower back excessively, leading to potential lower back discomfort.
Rushing through the movement, sacrificing control and form.
Neglecting to engage the glutes and thighs, reducing overall stability.
exercises.name: Cobra Push-Up
tips: Keep your elbows close to your body throughout the movement to maximize triceps engagement.
Focus on controlled movements to enhance muscle activation and prevent injury.
Ensure that your core is engaged to maintain stability and protect your lower back.
Breathe out as you push up and inhale as you lower down.

instructions: Sit on a bench with your feet flat on the floor, legs spread slightly apart.

Lean forward slightly and rest the elbow of the working arm against the inner thigh of the same side leg.
Keep your back straight and core engaged throughout the movement.
Slowly curl the dumbbell upwards by flexing your elbow, keeping your wrist straight.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement when your forearm is vertical or slightly beyond.
Lower the dumbbell back to the starting position in a controlled manner.
Complete the desired number of repetitions before switching arms.

Failing to keep the shoulder stable, which can lead to strain or discomfort.
Rushing through the eccentric phase, minimizing muscle tension and growth potential.
exercises.name: Concentration Hammer Curl
tips: Focus on using a slow and controlled motion to maximize muscle tension.
Avoid swinging or using momentum to lift the weight; keep the movement strict.
Ensure your elbow remains stationary against your thigh to isolate the target muscles effectively.
Maintain a neutral wrist position throughout to prevent strain and ensure proper form.
Breathe out while lifting the weight and inhale while lowering it.
Start with a lighter weight to master the form before progressing to heavier dumbbells.

exercises.description: A side plank on your forearm with your top foot resting on a flat bench, in which you lift your hips and raise the bottom leg up to the underside of the bench. Pressing the top leg down into the bench loads the inner thigh adductors, while the obliques hold your trunk in line.
instructions: Lie on your side next to a flat bench, with your forearm on the floor and your elbow directly under your shoulder.
Place the inside of your top foot on the bench with the leg straight, and rest the bottom leg on the floor under the bench.
Rest your free hand on your opposite shoulder and brace your core.
Press the top leg down into the bench and lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from head to feet.
As your hips rise, raise the straight bottom leg until it meets the underside of the bench.
Pause briefly, then lower your hips and bottom leg under control until your hips are just above the floor.
Complete all reps, then switch sides.

Rotating the chest toward the floor or letting the top hip roll backward
Bending at the waist so the hips stay behind the line of the shoulders and feet

exercises.name: Copenhagen Adduction
tips: Drive the top leg down into the bench. That pressure from the inner thigh is what lifts your hips.
Keep both legs straight throughout the set, including the bottom leg as it rises.
Keep your elbow directly under your shoulder and push the floor away so your shoulder does not sink.
Exhale as you lift your hips and inhale as you lower them.
If you cannot keep your hips up with your foot on the bench, start with your knee on the bench. The shorter lever makes the exercise easier.

exercises.description: The Cossack Squat is a lower body exercise that targets the muscles of the legs, particularly the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and adductors. It also enhances flexibility, balance, and mobility in the hips and ankles. This exercise involves a lateral movement pattern, which helps in developing strength and stability in the lower body.
instructions: Stand with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart and toes slightly pointed out.
Shift your weight onto your right leg, bending your right knee while keeping your left leg straight.
Lower your hips down towards the right heel, keeping your chest up and back straight.

Repeat on the left side by shifting your weight onto your left leg.

Twisting the torso instead of keeping it aligned with the hips.

exercises.name: Cossack Squat

Focus on keeping your core engaged to enhance stability.
Start with a wider stance if you find it difficult to balance initially.

exercises.description: A kneeling stretch for the hip flexors and quadriceps of the rear leg, done with the rear shin upright against a flat bench and the top of the foot on it. Tuck your pelvis slightly and squeeze the glute of the rear leg.

exercises.name: Couch Stretch

exercises.name: Crab Pose

Engage your glutes and core to maintain stability throughout the pose.
Keep your chest open and shoulders away from your ears to avoid tension.
Focus on maintaining a straight line from shoulders to knees for proper alignment.
If you experience discomfort in your wrists, adjust hand positioning or take breaks as needed.
Practice controlled breathing to help maintain balance and focus during the pose.

Keep your elbows close to your body as you lower yourself to maximize tricep engagement.
Focus on controlled movements; avoid rushing through repetitions to maintain form and effectiveness.

exercises.description: A bodyweight lunge in which one leg steps diagonally behind the other, as in a curtsy, and you lower until the back knee is close to the floor. Step the other leg diagonally back behind the standing leg, as in a curtsy, and land on the ball of that foot.
Bend both knees and lower until the back knee is just above the floor. Keep most of your weight on the front foot.

Drive through the front foot to stand up and bring the back leg forward without setting it down.

exercises.description: Sit upright in a decline press machine and push the handles forward and slightly down from your lower chest to build the lower part of your chest. The muscles worked are mainly the lower chest, the fibers that run toward your breastbone, and then the middle chest; your triceps take over near lockout and the front delts help only a little. You get the decline angle without lying head-down on a bench, with no bar to unrack and no spotter needed, so beginners and people training alone can push their sets close to failure. The independent levers also show you if one side is weaker.
instructions: Load the same plates on both levers, or set the pin on a stack machine, and adjust the seat so the handles start level with your lower chest, just below the nipples.
Sit with your hips all the way back and your back and head on the pad. Feet flat, about hip to shoulder width apart, knees bent close to 90°.
Take the handles overhand, hands a little wider than your shoulders, knuckles up and wrists stacked straight over your forearms.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the pad. Your elbows sit about 45–60° from your sides, slightly behind the handles.
Press both handles forward and down along the machine's arc until your arms are almost straight in front of your lower chest. Shoulders stay on the pad and the elbows never lock.
Take about 2 seconds to bring the handles back beside your lower chest, where you should feel a stretch across the bottom of your chest. Touch lightly without resting the plates, then press again.
When the set is done, guide the handles back onto their stops before you let go, so the levers don't slam.
mistakes: Setting the seat too low, so the handles start at shoulder height and the lift turns into a flat or incline press with lots of front-delt work. Raise the seat until the handles line up with your lower chest.
Rolling your shoulders forward off the pad at the top to reach a few more inches. Keep your shoulder blades pinned back and stop when your arms are almost straight.
Bringing the handles only halfway back, so your lower chest never gets stretched. Return them beside your chest on every rep, and drop a plate if you can't get there.

One lever running ahead of the other because the plates don't match or your stronger arm takes over. Load both sides the same and move the handles at the same speed; when one arm slows down, the set is over.
exercises.name: Decline Chest Press
tips: It fits as a second or third chest exercise: 3–4 sets of 8–12 reps, or 5–8 for strength.

Add reps first. Once you get 12 on all sets with your shoulders still on the pad, add the smallest plate per side (2 × 1.25 kg or 2 × 2.5 kg) or move the pin one hole. Log plates per side and your seat setting; the lever changes the real resistance, so the total won't match your barbell numbers.

Expect to feel it along the bottom edge of your chest toward the breastbone, and in your triceps near the top. If the front of your shoulders does most of the work, the seat is too low or your shoulders are leaving the pad. A pinch at the front of the shoulder at the bottom means shorten the stretch or go lighter.

New to it? Use lighter plates and stop a little short at the bottom for the first few weeks. To make it harder without more weight, take 3–4 seconds on the way back or pause for 1–2 seconds at the bottom.

Substitutes: Decline Barbell Bench Press for heavy low-rep sets with a spotter, Decline Dumbbell Bench Press when all you have is a decline bench, Chest Dips for a bodyweight lower-chest press, and Plate-Loaded Chest Press when the decline machine is taken.

exercises.description: The Decline Push-Up is a bodyweight exercise that targets the upper chest, shoulders, and triceps by elevating the feet on a stable surface. This variation increases the difficulty compared to a standard push-up by shifting more weight onto the upper body.
instructions: Begin by placing your feet on an elevated surface such as a bench or step, ensuring it's stable and secure.
Position your hands shoulder-width apart on the floor, directly under your shoulders.
Engage your core to maintain a straight line from head to heels.
Lower your body by bending your elbows, keeping them at a 45-degree angle to your torso.
Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor, maintaining control throughout the movement.
Push through your palms to extend your elbows and return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Hands placed too wide, reducing chest engagement.
Hips sagging, leading to lower back strain.
Feet positioned too high, causing shoulder strain.
Failing to maintain a straight line from head to heels.
Elbows flaring out excessively, increasing shoulder stress.
Not lowering the chest fully to the ground, limiting range of motion.
Rushing through repetitions, compromising control and form.
Neck craning forward, causing neck strain.
Inadequate core engagement, resulting in poor stability.
Uneven weight distribution between hands, leading to imbalanced muscle activation.
exercises.name: Decline Push-Up
tips: Ensure your core remains tight throughout the exercise to prevent sagging hips.
Keep your head in a neutral position by looking slightly ahead of you, not down at the floor.
Control the descent to maximize muscle engagement and prevent injury.
Adjust the height of the elevated surface to modify the difficulty level; higher surfaces increase difficulty.
Breathe in as you lower your body and exhale as you push back up.
Focus on maintaining even weight distribution between both hands.

exercises.description: A full sit-up on a decline bench with your feet hooked under the pads and your hands behind your head. You rise from lying flat on the bench until your torso is upright, then lower back down under control. Because of the decline it is harder than a floor sit-up, and it trains your abs and hip flexors through a long range.
instructions: Set the decline bench to an angle you can control and hook your feet under the foot pads.
Lie back with your knees bent until your back and head rest on the bench.
Place your hands behind your head with your elbows out to the sides.
Brace your abs and exhale as you curl up, lifting your head and shoulders first, then the rest of your back.
Keep rising until your torso is upright, with your elbows still wide.
Inhale and lower yourself slowly, rolling your back down onto the bench from the lower back to the shoulders.
Let your upper back and head touch the bench, then start the next rep.
mistakes: Pulling on your head with your hands to help yourself up
Swinging your arms or jerking your torso to get up
Rising with a stiff, flat back so your hip flexors do most of the work instead of your abs
Stopping before your torso is upright
Bouncing off the bench at the bottom to start the next rep
Letting your lower back arch away from the bench at the bottom
Holding your breath through the whole set
exercises.name: Decline Sit-Up
tips: Start with a gentle decline and make the bench steeper only when you can do every rep smoothly.
Hook your feet firmly under the pads before you lie back so your hips stay fixed throughout the set.
Keep your chin slightly tucked, about a fist's width from your chest, so your neck stays neutral.
Take 2 to 3 seconds to lower yourself, since the lowering phase works your abs as hard as the rise.
If you cannot finish your reps with your hands behind your head, cross your arms over your chest. This shortens the lever and makes each rep easier.

exercises.description: The Decline Smith Bench Press is a compound exercise targeting the lower portion of the pectoral muscles, with secondary involvement of the triceps and anterior deltoids. Utilizing the Smith machine provides stability and control, allowing for a focused contraction of the chest muscles while minimizing the risk of injury. This exercise is performed on a decline bench set at an angle, which shifts emphasis to the lower chest.
instructions: Set the decline bench at a 15-30 degree angle under the Smith machine bar.
Lie back on the bench with your feet secured under the footpads or firmly planted on the floor.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, ensuring wrists are straight and aligned with forearms.
Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists or releasing the safety catches, keeping your arms extended.
Lower the bar slowly towards your lower chest, maintaining control and keeping elbows at a 45-degree angle to your body.
Pause briefly when the bar is just above your chest, ensuring tension in the muscles.
Press the bar back up to the starting position by extending your arms, without locking elbows at the top.
Repeat for desired repetitions, then safely re-rack the bar.
mistakes: Setting the bench at too steep of a decline, which shifts focus away from the chest to the shoulders.
Placing hands too wide or too narrow on the bar, leading to improper muscle engagement.
Failing to maintain a stable shoulder position, which can lead to shoulder strain.
Not keeping the feet firmly planted on the ground, reducing stability and power.
Allowing the bar to bounce off the chest, reducing muscle tension and control.
Lowering the bar too quickly, compromising control and increasing the risk of losing balance.
Not fully extending the arms at the top of the movement, limiting range of motion.
Arching the back excessively, which can strain the lower back.
Engaging the triceps too much by flaring the elbows out instead of keeping them at a 45-degree angle.
Neglecting to engage the core, leading to instability and poor form.
exercises.name: Decline Smith Bench Press
tips: Ensure your back remains flat against the bench throughout the movement to avoid strain.
Focus on controlled movements; avoid bouncing the bar off your chest to prevent injury.
Keep your core engaged for stability and to support proper form during each repetition.
Adjust hand placement if necessary to ensure comfort and optimal muscle engagement.
Warm up thoroughly before performing heavy sets to prepare muscles and joints.
Breathing is crucial: inhale as you lower the bar and exhale as you press it back up.

exercises.description: The Deep Push Up On Parallel Bars is an advanced upper body exercise that targets the chest, triceps, and shoulders. By performing this exercise on parallel bars, you increase the range of motion compared to standard push-ups, which enhances muscle engagement and strength development.
instructions: Position yourself between two parallel bars with your hands gripping the bars slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
Extend your legs behind you, keeping your body straight from head to heels.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until your chest is below the level of the bars.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement, ensuring a deep stretch in the chest muscles.
Push through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions while maintaining proper form.
mistakes: Allowing elbows to flare out excessively, reducing shoulder stability.
Dropping shoulders too low, risking shoulder impingement.
Not keeping the core engaged, leading to a sagging lower back.
Failing to maintain a neutral neck position, causing neck strain.
Using a limited range of motion, preventing full muscle activation.
Rushing the movement, sacrificing control and form.
Letting the wrists bend excessively, increasing wrist strain.
Not aligning the wrists directly under the shoulders, causing imbalance.
Neglecting to engage the chest muscles, reducing push-up effectiveness.
Allowing the body to dip unevenly, creating asymmetrical muscle development.
exercises.name: Deep Push Up On Parallel Bars
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain a straight body line.
Avoid flaring your elbows too wide; keep them at about a 45-degree angle to protect your shoulders.
Control the descent to maximize muscle tension and prevent injury.
Focus on a full range of motion to enhance muscle activation and growth.
Breathe in as you lower down and exhale as you push back up.
If you're new to this exercise, start with a smaller range of motion and gradually increase as you build strength.
