exercises.description: A compound exercise that links a dumbbell front squat and an overhead press into one movement. You squat with a dumbbell at each shoulder, then use the drive from your legs to press both weights overhead as you stand. It works the quads, glutes and shoulders and is often used for conditioning.
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and your toes turned slightly out. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your shoulders, palms facing each other and elbows pointing forward.
Brace your abs, lift your chest and look straight ahead.
Push your hips back and bend your knees to squat down, keeping your heels on the floor and the dumbbells at your shoulders.
Lower yourself until your thighs are about parallel to the floor, with your back flat and your knees in line with your toes.
Drive through your whole foot and stand up powerfully, straightening your hips and knees.
As your legs straighten, carry that drive into the press and push both dumbbells overhead until your arms are straight and the weights are over your shoulders.
Lower the dumbbells under control to your shoulders and move straight into the next squat.
mistakes: Letting the knees cave in during the squat.
Lifting the heels and shifting the weight onto the toes.
Cutting the squat short, well above parallel.
Rounding the lower back or letting the chest drop forward at the bottom.
Pausing at the top of the squat and pressing with the arms alone, which wastes the leg drive.
Leaning back and arching the lower back as the dumbbells go overhead.
Finishing the press with bent elbows.
Dropping into the squat or letting the dumbbells crash onto the shoulders.
exercises.name: Dumbbell Thruster
tips: In the squat, rest one end of each dumbbell on the front of your shoulders and keep your elbows forward, so the weights stay put and your chest stays up.
Take a breath and brace your abs before each squat, then breathe out as you press the dumbbells overhead.
Press the dumbbells straight up past your face and finish with your arms by your ears and the weights over your shoulders.
Look straight ahead throughout the rep. Looking down pulls your chest forward and looking up arches your back.
Choose the weight by your overhead press, not your squat, because the press is the weaker part of the movement.
Learn the timing with light dumbbells first and add load once the squat and press flow into one movement.

instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand with an overhand grip.
Let the dumbbells hang at arm's length in front of you, palms facing your body.
Keep your back straight, chest up, and core engaged throughout the movement.
Lift the dumbbells vertically by bending your elbows, keeping them higher than your forearms.
Continue lifting until the dumbbells reach chest level or slightly below your chin.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring your elbows are pointing outwards.
Lower the dumbbells back to the starting position in a controlled manner.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Using momentum or swinging the weights, reducing muscle engagement.
Failing to keep the wrists straight, leading to unnecessary wrist strain.
Allowing the shoulders to shrug, which shifts focus away from the target muscles.
Letting the dumbbells drift away from the body, which puts extra strain on the shoulders.
Not engaging the core, resulting in poor posture and balance.
Positioning the hands too close together, causing excessive internal shoulder rotation.
Ignoring controlled movement during both the lift and descent phases.
exercises.name: Dumbbell Upright Row
tips: Maintain a neutral spine and avoid leaning backward or forward during the lift.
Focus on lifting with your shoulders and not pulling with your arms or wrists.
Keep your movements smooth and controlled to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid using excessive weight to prevent strain on your shoulders and wrists.
Ensure your elbows remain higher than your wrists throughout the exercise.
Breathe out as you lift the dumbbells and inhale as you lower them back down.

exercises.description: Dumbbell Walking Lunges are a compound lower body exercise targeting the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. instructions: Stand upright with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.

Step forward with your right foot, lowering your hips until both knees are bent at approximately 90-degree angles. Ensure your front knee is directly above your ankle and your back knee hovers just above the ground.
Push through the heel of your right foot to rise and bring your left foot forward, stepping into the next lunge.
Continue alternating legs for the desired number of repetitions or distance.
Maintain an upright torso throughout the movement, keeping your core engaged.
mistakes: Allowing the front knee to extend past the toes, increasing strain on the knee joint.
Leaning the torso too far forward, reducing engagement of the glutes and core.
Using too much weight, compromising form and control.
Taking steps that are too short, limiting range of motion and muscle activation.
Failing to keep the back knee close to the ground, reducing the effectiveness of the lunge.
Letting the front foot collapse inward, causing ankle instability.
Not maintaining a straight back, leading to poor posture and reduced core engagement.
Rushing the movement, sacrificing balance and control.
Holding the dumbbells incorrectly, leading to shoulder strain.
Neglecting to engage the core, resulting in less stability and balance.
exercises.name: Dumbbell Walking Lunges
tips: Keep your chest up and shoulders back to maintain proper posture.
Focus on a controlled descent to maximize muscle engagement.
Ensure your front knee does not extend past your toes to prevent strain on the knee joint.
Use a mirror to check form and alignment during the exercise.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier dumbbells.

exercises.description: The dumbbell Z press trains the shoulders and triceps while your trunk holds an unsupported seated position on the floor. Keep your legs straight and heels down, press both dumbbells from shoulder height to above your shoulders with a neutral grip, then lower them without leaning back.
instructions: Sit on the floor with straight legs and heels down, holding a dumbbell at each shoulder with palms facing each other.
Sit tall with your chest up and your ribs stacked over your hips. Brace your abdominal muscles and keep your legs straight, with your heels on the floor.
Press both dumbbells overhead in a controlled motion. Keep your forearms close to vertical and avoid leaning your torso backward.
Finish with the dumbbells over your shoulders and your elbows straight but not forcefully locked. Keep your head neutral and your ribs down.
Lower the dumbbells slowly back to shoulder height while staying upright. Do not let your lower back round excessively or your torso rock backward.
Repeat for the planned number of repetitions, using a weight that allows you to maintain a tall seated position throughout.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back instead of maintaining a tall, neutral seated posture.
Leaning back to turn the press into an incline press.
Starting with the dumbbells too far in front of the shoulders.
Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides instead of keeping them slightly forward.
Pressing the dumbbells forward rather than stacking them over the shoulders at the top.
Using momentum or bouncing the dumbbells out of the bottom position.
exercises.name: Dumbbell Z Press
tips: Exhale through the hardest part of the upward movement.
Choose a load that allows the same range on every repetition.
Use two weights of equal mass to balance the load on both sides.
Keep the palms facing each other as shown in the video.
Press your heels gently into the floor to stabilize the seated base.

exercises.description: Place both hands on the floor and brace your bent elbows against the sides of your abdomen to form a support. Lean forward, lift the feet and extend the legs behind you until the body is horizontal, holding the balance on your palms with small fingertip adjustments.
instructions: Place your palms on a firm floor at shoulder width with fingers spread and knees bent.
Bend your elbows and place them against the sides of your abdomen, usually near the hip bones or lower stomach.
Lean your shoulders forward over your hands until your weight is supported through your palms and elbows.
Brace your abdomen, bring the legs together and shift forward until both feet lift off the floor.
Straighten your legs behind you until your body is as parallel to the floor as your strength and balance allow.
Press actively through your hands and keep your fingers gripping the floor to control balance.
Hold the position briefly with steady breathing.
To come down, bend your knees and place your feet on the floor under control.
mistakes: Letting the elbows slide during the hold instead of keeping firm, consistent contact with the torso.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears instead of actively pushing the floor away.
Collapsing through the shoulder blades instead of keeping the upper back engaged.
Bending at the hips or letting the legs hang instead of holding the body in one straight line.
Lifting the hips too high, turning the position into a tucked or diagonal balance.
Holding the breath and losing trunk tension during the balance.
exercises.name: Elbow Lever
tips: Place your hands shoulder-width apart with fingers spread wide.
Explore a small forward weight shift with both feet still on the floor before lifting them.
Start with one foot lightly on the floor, then lift it for short holds.
Use a soft surface in front of you while learning, but keep your hands on a firm, non-slip floor.
If you tip forward, press harder through your fingertips.

Neglecting to keep the neck relaxed, which can lead to unnecessary tension.
Holding the breath, which can reduce oxygen flow and increase tension in the body.
exercises.name: Elbow Out Chest Stretch

Ensure your elbow remains at shoulder height to effectively target the chest muscles.
Focus on a gentle stretch; avoid pushing too hard to prevent injury.
Maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise to support proper posture.
Perform this stretch after workouts or during breaks to relieve muscle tension.

instructions: Step onto the elliptical trainer and place your feet on the pedals.
Grip the handles firmly with both hands.
Start pedaling forward by pushing down with one foot while pulling up with the other.
Adjust the resistance and incline settings to match your desired intensity level.
Maintain an upright posture with your core engaged throughout the workout.
Use a smooth and controlled motion, avoiding bouncing or jerky movements.
To stop, gradually slow down your pace until the machine comes to a complete stop.

Setting resistance too low, resulting in minimal muscle activation.
Pedaling backwards without maintaining proper form, risking knee discomfort.
Overextending knees at full stride, increasing strain on joints.
Neglecting to engage core muscles, reducing stability and overall workout quality.
Using only arms or only legs, failing to achieve a balanced full-body workout.
exercises.name: Elliptical Trainer

Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid gripping the handles too tightly.
Focus on a consistent breathing pattern to enhance endurance.
Vary your workout by adjusting resistance and incline for different muscle engagement.
Monitor your heart rate to stay within your target cardiovascular zone.
Incorporate interval training by alternating between high and low intensity periods.

exercises.description: Hold an EZ bar underhand on its outer bends and curl it from your thighs to shoulder height: the standard standing EZ-bar curl for bigger, stronger biceps. Both heads of the biceps do the bulk of the work, with help from the brachialis underneath and the brachioradialis on the thumb side of your forearm. The zig-zag bar turns your palms slightly inward, so most people feel less strain in their wrists and inner elbows than with a straight bar. For a different angle, try the straight-bar curl, the close-grip EZ curl on the inner bends, the EZ preacher curl or the palms-down reverse curl.
instructions: Pick a load you can curl without swinging, then take the bar from a mid-thigh rack or deadlift it up with a flat back.
Stand with your feet about hip-width, toes slightly out, knees straight but soft. Lightly brace your abs and glutes so your torso can't rock.
Hold the outer angled bends underhand, thumbs wrapped, hands about shoulder-width and equally far from the center. Palms face forward and tilt slightly in.
Breathe out and curl the bar up in an arc from your thighs. Only your forearms move; your upper arms stay against your ribs.
Stop when your forearms are about vertical and the bar is level with your shoulders, just below your chin, and squeeze for a second.
Take 2–3 seconds to lower until your elbows are fully straight, then pause briefly before the next rep.
When the set is over, put the bar back in the rack, or bend your knees and lower it to the floor with a flat back.
mistakes: Throwing the bar up with your hips and leaning back. Take some weight off, squeeze your abs and glutes and keep your knees still; if the rocking continues, do the set with your back against a wall.
Elbows drifting forward and up at the top while the front of your shoulders lifts the bar toward your chin. Keep your elbows by your ribs and stop once your forearms are vertical.
Stopping short at the bottom, so your arms never straighten. Lower to straight elbows on every rep, even if that means a lighter bar.

Hands on mismatched bends or off-center, so the bar tilts and one arm does more. Set both hands on the outer bends, the same distance from the middle, before you lift; the inner bends belong to the close-grip curl.
Wrists bending back under the bar or curling in at the top. Grip hard and keep your knuckles in line with your forearms on every rep.
Letting the bar drop and bounce off your thighs. Count 2–3 seconds on every descent and start each rep from a short stop; a heavy bar slamming into locked elbows strains the biceps tendon.
exercises.name: EZ-Bar Biceps Curl
tips: Curl 8–15 reps a set, or 6–10 on a heavier day. Keep the weight and add reps until the top number comes in all sets without swinging, then add the smallest plates (1.25 kg per side). Fixed EZ bars jump 2.5–5 kg at a time, so expect a few sessions at each one.

You should feel the front of your upper arms, most of all from halfway up to the squeeze, with some burn on the thumb side of your forearms. If your lower back or the front of your shoulders starts working, the bar is too heavy.

Still rocking with a lighter bar? Curl with your back flat against a wall, as in the Barbell Wall Curl. To make it harder, take 3–4 seconds on the way down, pause a second with your forearms level on the way up, or move on to the EZ-Bar Preacher Curl.

Substitutes: Barbell Biceps Curl (straight bar, palms fully up), Dumbbell Biceps Curl (each arm lifts its own weight, handy if one side is weaker), Bar Cable Biceps Curl (the cable keeps pulling at the bottom), Close-grip EZ Bar Curl (same bar, hands on the inner bends).

Shrugging the shoulders or leaning back as fatigue builds.
Bending the wrists back or allowing them to collapse under the bar.
Snapping the elbows straight at the bottom.
exercises.name: EZ-Bar Bottom-Half Biceps Curl

Keep pressure evenly distributed between both hands.
Exhale as you curl and inhale as you lower.
Use the forearms' horizontal position as the top marker.
Reset your stance before starting another set.

exercises.description: The EZ Bar Preacher Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps brachii. Position your upper arms on the pad, ensuring your armpits are snug against the top edge.

Continue curling until your forearms are vertical or slightly beyond vertical, without lifting your elbows off the pad.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, squeezing your biceps.
Slowly lower the bar back to the starting position, fully extending your arms.

Keep your wrists straight and avoid bending them during the curl to prevent strain.
Focus on a slow and controlled motion, especially during the lowering phase, to maximize muscle engagement.

exercises.description: Stand tall and curl an EZ bar to your upper chest with your palms facing down to build thicker forearms and stronger elbow flexors. Most of the work lands on the brachioradialis, the muscle on the thumb side of your forearm; your biceps help, and you'll feel the brachialis on the outer upper arm too. The back of your forearm works just to hold the wrists straight. Your hands sit on the angled sections, which is kinder to the wrists than a straight bar. Expect roughly half to two thirds of your regular curl weight.
instructions: Load the bar lighter than for a regular curl and pick it up like a deadlift, not by curling it off the floor.
Stand with your feet about hip-width and knees straight but soft, the bar resting against the front of your thighs.
Take an overhand grip on the angled sections, hands about shoulder-width so your forearms run parallel, thumbs wrapped around the bar.
Tuck your elbows against your ribs, pull your shoulders down and lock your wrists so the knuckles line up with your forearms.
Curl the bar up in an arc with your knuckles leading. Your upper arms stay vertical beside your body.
Stop when your forearms are vertical and the bar is at upper-chest height, knuckles pointing at the ceiling, and hold for a second.
Take 2–3 seconds to lower it to fully straight elbows, then start the next rep without bouncing off your thighs.
mistakes: Wrists bending back as the bar rises, so your knuckles tip toward you. Drop the weight, squeeze the bar harder and finish with the knuckles pointing at the ceiling.
Elbows drifting forward until your front delts are lifting the bar to your chin. Keep the elbows by your ribs and stop at upper-chest height.
Hands on the inner bends almost touching, or out on the straight ends. Both twist the wrists and let the bar tilt. Hold the angled sections at shoulder width.
Quick half reps that never reach straight arms. Lower for 2–3 seconds until your elbows are fully extended on every rep.
exercises.name: EZ-Bar Reverse Grip Biceps Curl
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 10–15 reps; for heavier work 6–10, as this curl rarely feels good below 6. Stay at one weight and add reps. Once all sets hit 15 with straight wrists and a still torso, add the smallest plates (1.25 kg per side) and work up again from 10. On a light bar that jump is big, so expect a few sessions per step.

The thumb side of your forearm just below the elbow and the outer front of the upper arm do the work, and the forearm pump is solid. A sharp pain on the bony point on the outside of the elbow means stop.
Prone to tennis elbow or sore wrists? Go light, or swap in the Dumbbell Hammer Curl for a few weeks. When this one gets easy, try the EZ-Bar Reverse Spider Curl or slow the lowering to 3–4 seconds.
Substitutes: Barbell Reverse Grip Forearm Curl if there's no EZ bar, Dumbbell Reverse Curl, Reverse Grip Cable Curl, Dumbbell Hammer Curl.

exercises.description: Sit at a preacher bench with your upper arms supported on the pad and hold an EZ-bar with an overhand grip. exercises.description: The Farmer Walk is a strength and conditioning exercise that involves walking while holding heavy weights in each hand. Engage your core muscles to maintain a straight posture.
Lift the weights off the ground by extending your hips and knees while keeping your back straight.

exercises.description: Place your hands on a bench behind you and your heels on a second bench in front, keeping your legs straight. Bend your elbows to lower your body close to the rear bench, then press through your palms to return to straight arms. Use a controlled depth and keep your shoulders down throughout.
instructions: Place two sturdy benches parallel to each other, far enough apart that you can rest your heels on one bench while supporting yourself with your hands on the other.
Sit on the edge of the bench behind you and place your hands beside your hips, fingers pointing toward your feet. Grip the bench edge firmly.
Extend your legs and place your heels on the opposite bench. Lift your hips off the supporting bench and keep them close to its edge.
Start with your arms straight but not forcefully locked, chest open, shoulders down and core braced.
Bend your elbows straight behind you and lower your body in a controlled motion. Keep your hips close to the bench and avoid letting your shoulders roll forward.

instructions: Sit upright on a sturdy chair with your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Lift your right foot and place your right ankle on your left knee, forming a 'figure 4' shape with your legs.
Keep your back straight and gently lean forward from the hips until you feel a stretch in your right hip and glute.
Hold the stretch for 20-30 seconds, breathing deeply and maintaining a relaxed posture.
Return to the starting position and repeat on the opposite side.

exercises.description: A bodyweight exercise on all fours that adds a side kick to the fire hydrant. You lift the bent leg out to the side to hip height, straighten the knee until the leg is fully extended, then bend it and lower it. exercises.description: A balance on straight arms with no wall for support. From a forward fold with your palms on the floor, you lean onto your hands, tuck both legs up together and extend them into one vertical line, hold the balance, then lower back down. It builds shoulder and wrist strength, full-body tension and balance.
instructions: Stand with your feet together, fold forward and place your palms flat on the floor shoulder-width apart, a little in front of your feet. Spread your fingers wide and point them forward.
Straighten your arms and lean forward until your shoulders are over your hands and most of your weight rests on them.
Bend your knees and lift both feet off the floor at the same time with a small hop. Pull your knees toward your chest until your hips are above your shoulders.
Extend your legs straight up, keeping them together, until your body forms one vertical line from your hands to your toes.
Push the floor away with locked elbows and lift your shoulders toward your ears. Squeeze your glutes and legs, point your toes and keep your ribs pulled in.
Balance through your hands. If your legs tip past vertical, press your fingertips into the floor; if you start falling back the way you came up, shift the pressure to the heels of your hands.
After the planned time, bend your knees, lower both feet to the floor together with control and return to the forward fold.
mistakes: Placing the hands too narrow, too wide or unevenly, which makes the balance harder to control

exercises.name: Freestanding Handstand
tips: Learn the straight body line in a chest-to-wall handstand before you try it freestanding.
Practice on a non-slip floor with open space around you. If you overbalance, turn one hand and step out sideways into a cartwheel instead of falling onto your back.
Look at the floor between your hands so your head stays between your arms.
Practice holding the tuck with your hips over your shoulders before you extend your legs. The shorter lever makes the balance point easier to find.
Do several short attempts with full rest instead of one long struggle for balance.
Breathe steadily during the hold. Holding your breath stiffens your body and makes your corrections jerky.

exercises.description: The Frog Crunch is an abdominal exercise that targets the rectus abdominis and obliques. It involves a crunching motion while maintaining a frog-like leg position, which increases core engagement and challenges stability.
instructions: Lie flat on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall outward, forming a diamond shape with your legs.
Place your hands behind your head with elbows wide, or cross them over your chest.
Engage your core by drawing your navel towards your spine.
Exhale as you lift your head, shoulders, and upper back off the ground in a controlled crunching motion.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, squeezing your abdominal muscles.
Inhale as you slowly lower back to the starting position without letting your head touch the ground.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Feet positioned too high or too low, disrupting balance and core engagement.
Allowing knees to collapse inward, reducing hip and core activation.
Neck strain from pulling on the head instead of lifting with the core.
Failing to keep the lower back pressed into the ground, leading to an arched back.
Using momentum to swing the upper body instead of controlled core contraction.
Inadequate range of motion, not fully lifting the shoulders off the ground.
Rushing through reps, compromising form and muscle engagement.
Holding breath, which can reduce oxygen flow and increase tension.
exercises.name: Frog Crunch
tips: Keep your chin slightly tucked to avoid straining your neck during the crunch.
Focus on using your abdominal muscles to lift rather than pulling on your neck or head.
Ensure that your lower back remains in contact with the floor throughout the exercise.
Control the movement both on the way up and down to maximize muscle engagement.
Breathe out as you crunch up and inhale as you return to the starting position.
If you feel discomfort in your neck, try placing a small towel under it for support.

exercises.description: Jump vertically from a deep, wide squat with the hands reaching down between the knees. Extend the hips and knees to leave the floor, then return to the same squat with a cushioned landing. This bodyweight jump trains leg power and control through a larger squat range.
instructions: Stand with your feet wider than shoulder width and toes turned out.
Lower into a deep squat and reach your hands down between your knees.
Push through both feet and extend your hips and knees to jump vertically.
Land in the same area and bend the hips and knees to absorb the impact.
Return to the deep squat with your hands between your knees.
Repeat once your balance is stable, keeping both feet coordinated.
mistakes: Starting with the knees collapsing inward instead of tracking over the toes.
Letting the heels lift in the squat instead of keeping the feet grounded before takeoff.
Rounding the lower back excessively at the bottom of the squat.
Jumping mostly from the knees instead of driving through the hips, knees, and ankles together.
Not reaching a controlled squat depth before each jump.
Rushing consecutive jumps without resetting a stable squat position.
exercises.name: Frog Jump
tips: Use a wide stance that leaves room for the hands between the knees.
Land through the forefoot and bring the heels down smoothly.
Keep the head in line with the upper back throughout the jump.
Keep the hands low rather than swinging them forward.
Use a clear, non-slip surface.

exercises.description: The Frog Planche is an advanced bodyweight exercise that focuses on building strength and balance in the upper body and core. It involves supporting the body parallel to the ground with only the hands, while the knees rest on the elbows. This exercise targets the shoulders, chest, triceps, and core muscles, enhancing stability and control.
instructions: Begin in a squat position with your feet close together and hands placed shoulder-width apart on the ground.
Lean forward, bending your elbows slightly, and place your knees on the back of your upper arms near the elbows.
Shift your weight forward onto your hands while lifting your feet off the ground, maintaining balance.
Engage your core and keep your back flat, ensuring that your body remains parallel to the ground.
Hold this position for as long as possible while maintaining steady breathing.
To exit, gently lower your feet back to the ground and return to a squat position.
mistakes: Hands placed too far apart, reducing stability and control.
Elbows not fully locked, leading to insufficient arm engagement.
Hips sagging below shoulder level, causing poor alignment.
Head positioned too low, disrupting balance.
Failing to engage core muscles, resulting in a lack of body tension.
Allowing knees to rest on elbows, reducing the challenge and effectiveness.
Rushing into the position without proper warm-up, increasing strain risk.
Neglecting to spread fingers for better weight distribution.
Holding breath, which can cause loss of focus and stability.
exercises.name: Frog Planche
tips: Warm up thoroughly before attempting the Frog Planche to prevent injury.
Focus on engaging your core muscles to maintain balance and stability.
Practice holding the position for short periods initially, gradually increasing duration as you build strength.
Keep your gaze slightly forward to help maintain balance and alignment.
If you're struggling with balance, try practicing against a wall for additional support.
Ensure that your wrists are directly under your shoulders to distribute weight evenly.

exercises.description: The Frog Pump is an effective glute activation exercise that targets the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus. It is performed by lying on your back with your feet together and knees bent outward, resembling a frog's position. instructions: Lie on your back on a mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Bring the soles of your feet together, allowing your knees to fall outward to the sides.
Position your arms at your sides with palms facing down for stability.
Engage your core and squeeze your glutes as you lift your hips off the ground.
Raise your hips until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Hold the top position for a moment, squeezing your glutes tightly.
Slowly lower your hips back to the starting position without touching the ground.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Feet positioned too far from the body, reducing glute activation.
Knees not flaring outward, limiting hip external rotation.
Arching the lower back excessively, leading to poor glute engagement.
Lifting the hips too high, shifting focus away from the glutes.
Using momentum instead of controlled movements, decreasing muscle activation.
Failing to squeeze the glutes at the top of the movement.
Allowing the knees to collapse inward, reducing exercise effectiveness.
Performing the exercise too quickly, compromising control and form.
Not maintaining a neutral neck position, causing unnecessary strain.
exercises.name: Frog Pump
tips: Focus on squeezing your glutes throughout the movement to maximize activation.
Keep your core engaged to maintain stability and prevent lower back strain.
Ensure that your feet remain together and knees stay wide apart during the exercise.
Perform the movement slowly and with control to enhance muscle engagement.
Avoid arching your lower back; maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise.
Start with body weight and progress to adding resistance, such as a band or weight plate, as you become more comfortable.

exercises.description: Front crawl is the most common pool stroke and a cardio workout for the back, shoulders, arms, core and legs. You swim face-down, pulling with alternating arms while the legs keep up a continuous flutter kick. The body stays long and level and rolls from side to side, and you breathe by turning your head to the side.
instructions: Push off the wall face-down with your arms extended in front, your body long and level, and your eyes looking down and slightly ahead.
Kick continuously from the hips with long legs, soft knees and pointed feet, keeping the kick small and close to the surface.
Reach one arm forward in line with your shoulder, then bend the elbow slightly so your hand and forearm face backward and catch the water.
Pull the water back under your body with a high elbow and push it past your hip, letting the hand leave the water by your thigh.
Bring the arm forward over the water with a relaxed, bent elbow leading, and enter the hand in front of your shoulder without crossing your centerline.
Alternate your arms without pausing, letting your shoulders and hips roll together from side to side while your body stays level.

Exhale steadily into the water. To breathe, turn your head with the body roll as that arm finishes its pull, inhale quickly with one goggle lens still underwater, and turn your face back down as the arm comes forward.
Keep an even rhythm of strokes, kicks and breaths for the planned time.
mistakes: Lifting the head forward to breathe instead of turning it to the side, which makes the hips and legs sink.
Holding your breath underwater, so you have to exhale and inhale in the short moment your mouth is above the water.
Swimming flat without rolling the shoulders and hips, which shortens the stroke and strains the shoulders.
Crossing the hand over the centerline on entry, which makes you snake through the water and loads the shoulder.
Dropping the elbow during the catch and pressing the water down instead of pushing it back.
Cutting the pull short and lifting the hand out before it passes the hip.
Kicking from the knees with big, bicycle-like movements that slow you down.
Swinging the arm forward straight and stiff, or slapping the hand onto the water.
exercises.name: Front Crawl Swimming
tips: Press your chest slightly into the water so your hips and legs stay near the surface.
Keep the leading arm extended until the other hand is about to enter. This keeps the stroke long and the body balanced.
Breathe every two or three strokes. Breathing to both sides every three strokes keeps the stroke even.
Keep your ankles relaxed so your feet flick like fins. Stiff ankles add drag.
Count your strokes per length. Fewer strokes at the same pace mean a more efficient stroke.
Start with short intervals and rest between them, and swim longer only once your technique holds up when you are tired.

exercises.description: The Front Lever is an advanced calisthenics exercise that requires significant core, back, and shoulder strength. instructions: Begin by hanging from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Engage your core and lats to lift your legs and torso until your body is parallel to the ground.
Keep your arms straight and maintain a hollow body position with your shoulders retracted.
Hold the position for as long as possible while maintaining control and proper form.
Slowly lower your body back to the starting position.
mistakes: Bending the elbows instead of keeping them straight, reducing leverage and effectiveness.

exercises.name: Front Lever
tips: Start with tuck front levers to build strength before attempting the full front lever.
Focus on engaging your core and lats throughout the movement to maintain stability.
Practice scapular retraction by pulling your shoulder blades down and together.
Keep your body in a straight line from head to toes to ensure proper form.
Incorporate negative reps by lowering slowly from the front lever position to build strength.

instructions: Begin by hanging from a pull-up bar with a shoulder-width grip, palms facing forward.
Engage your core and lats to lift your legs and torso into a horizontal position, parallel to the ground.

Neglecting to keep the head in a neutral position, causing neck strain.
Starting with an incorrect grip width, affecting leverage and muscle activation.
Not maintaining a hollow body position, reducing core tension and control.
Overextending the range of motion, risking shoulder strain.
exercises.name: Front Lever Pull-Up
tips: Ensure your body remains straight and parallel to the ground throughout the exercise.
Focus on engaging your core and lats to maintain stability in the front lever position.
Start with tuck front lever pull-ups if you are new to this exercise to build strength gradually.
Use a spotter or resistance bands for assistance if you struggle to maintain form.
Incorporate exercises like planks and hollow holds into your routine to strengthen your core for better performance.

exercises.description: The front squat is a compound lower body exercise that primarily targets the quadriceps, glutes, and core. It involves holding a barbell across the front of your shoulders while performing a squat, requiring greater core stability and mobility compared to the back squat.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and position the barbell on the front of your shoulders, resting it on your deltoids.
Cross your arms over the barbell or use a clean grip with your fingertips under the bar for support.

Engage your core and begin the squat by bending at the hips and knees, lowering your body until your thighs are parallel to the ground.

Push through your heels to return to the starting position, keeping your core engaged throughout the movement.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Heels lifting off the ground, shifting weight forward and compromising balance.

Not squatting to full depth, limiting muscle engagement and effectiveness.
Allowing the chest to fall forward, shifting the load away from the legs.
Using excessive weight, leading to compromised form and reduced range of motion.
Engaging the lower back instead of the core, leading to instability and potential strain.
Rushing the movement, resulting in poor control and lack of muscle activation.
exercises.name: Front Squat
tips: Focus on keeping your elbows high throughout the movement to prevent the bar from rolling forward.
Maintain an upright torso by engaging your core muscles; this helps in balancing the weight effectively.
Warm up with mobility exercises for wrists and shoulders to improve grip comfort and range of motion.
Start with lighter weights to perfect form before progressing to heavier loads.
Use lifting shoes or flat-soled shoes for better stability during the squat.
Keep a neutral spine position by looking straight ahead or slightly upward.

Lift your feet off the ground by engaging your core and lower back muscles.

exercises.description: The glute bridge march trains the glutes and trunk to maintain a bridge while the legs lift alternately. Place your feet close enough to your hips that your shins are nearly vertical at the top of the bridge.
Brace your stomach and gently tuck your pelvis so your lower back does not arch.
Press through both heels and lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from your shoulders to your knees.
Keep your ribs down, squeeze your glutes, and hold your hips level at the top position.
Without letting your hips drop or twist, lift one foot from the floor and bring that knee toward your chest.
Lower that foot back to the floor with control, keeping your hips lifted.

exercises.description: The Glute Cable Kickback is an isolation exercise targeting the gluteus maximus. It involves extending the hip against resistance, typically using a cable machine, to enhance glute strength and definition.
instructions: Attach an ankle strap to a low pulley cable machine and secure it around your ankle.
Stand facing the machine, holding onto the frame for support.
Shift your weight onto your non-working leg and slightly bend your knee.
With a slight bend in your working leg's knee, extend your leg backward in a controlled motion.
Squeeze your glutes at the top of the movement, ensuring your back remains straight.
Slowly return to the starting position without letting the weight stack touch.
Complete the desired number of repetitions before switching legs.
mistakes: Using too much weight, leading to momentum-based movement instead of controlled muscle engagement.
Arching the lower back excessively, which shifts focus away from the glutes and increases stress on the spine.
Failing to keep the core engaged, reducing stability and control during the exercise.
Allowing the knee of the working leg to bend excessively, which decreases the effectiveness of the glute activation.
Not maintaining a neutral spine, which can lead to improper form and reduced glute engagement.
Swinging the leg instead of performing a controlled kickback, which diminishes muscle activation.
Positioning the body too upright, which can shift focus to the lower back instead of the glutes.
Not achieving full hip extension, limiting the range of motion and glute activation.
Letting the supporting leg lock out, reducing balance and stability.
Failing to keep the foot flexed, which can decrease the engagement of the glutes.
exercises.name: Glute Cable Kickback
tips: Focus on squeezing your glutes at the peak of each kickback for maximum contraction.
Maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise to avoid lower back strain.
Keep your core engaged to stabilize your body during the movement.
Avoid swinging your leg; control the motion to maximize muscle engagement.
Start with a lighter weight to perfect your form before increasing resistance.
Ensure that the movement comes from the hip joint, not from arching your back.

exercises.description: Lean your hips into the pad and push the roller back with one foot until your hip is fully extended, building your glutes one leg at a time. The main muscle worked is the gluteus maximus of the kicking leg, while the gluteus medius keeps your pelvis level. Your hips and forearms rest on pads, so your spine carries no load and you don't have to fight for balance. Pick it over the cable kickback when you want a fixed path and quick weight changes, usually after squats, hip thrusts or Romanian deadlifts, or as low-fatigue glute work on an upper-body day.
instructions: Set the lever so the roller meets the middle of your sole when your thigh is under your hip and your knee is bent about 90°.
Step onto the platform facing the pads, weight behind you, and lean the front of your hips into the upright pad with both hip bones square to it.
Rest your forearms on the arm pads and hold the handles. They keep you in place; you don't pull on them.
Stand on one leg, foot flat under your hip and knee soft. Put the heel and arch of the other foot on the roller, toes pointing down.
Brace your abs, ribs down, and push the roller back through your heel. Hip and knee straighten together, as if you were pushing the floor away behind you.
Stop when your thigh is about 30° behind vertical and squeeze your glute for half a second. The foot stays low; height isn't the goal.
Take about 2 seconds to bring the knee back to 90° and stop just before the weight touches down.
Finish every rep on one leg, then switch, starting with the weaker side if there is one. Step off only once your foot is off the roller.
mistakes: Arching your lower back to get the leg higher. Stop at full hip extension, thigh about 30° behind vertical, hips on the pad and ribs down. If the arch keeps creeping in, drop the weight.
Your pelvis twists open toward the working side as the leg goes back. Keep both hip bones on the pad and the knee pointing at the floor, and shorten the kick if the hips still turn.

Curling the heel toward your butt instead of pushing the roller back. You'll usually feel a cramp in the back of the thigh. Drive through the heel and let the knee straighten as the hip opens: the roller travels back, not up.
Pushing your body away from the pad and yanking on the handles. Leave your forearms relaxed on the pads; only the working leg moves.
Letting the weight slam down and bouncing out of the bottom. Take about 2 seconds on the way back and stop just before it touches.
exercises.name: Glute Machine Kickback
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 10–15 reps per leg, stopping 1–2 reps short of failure. Add reps before load. When both legs reach 15 in all sets with the half-second squeeze, add the smallest weight step and go back to 10. That step is often 2.5–5 kg, a big jump for one leg, so spending a few sessions at the same weight is normal.
The buttock of the working leg should do the work, hardest in the last third of the kick. Sharp pain in your lower back or the front of the hip means stop and shorten the range.
To make it harder without adding weight, slow the return to 3 seconds and hold the end for 1–2 seconds. If you can't straighten the hip without arching, learn the pattern with the Donkey Kick first.

Substitutes: Glute Cable Kickback, Band Standing Balance Glute Kickback, Kneeling Resistance Band Glute Kickback, Donkey Kick. The cable version is the closest swap with real load; the band versions work at home.

exercises.description: The Glute-Ham Raise 1/2 is a strength exercise targeting the posterior chain, specifically the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back. It involves lowering the body from a kneeling position to a horizontal position and returning halfway up, focusing on eccentric control and muscle activation.
instructions: Begin by securing your feet under the footplate of a glute-ham developer (GHD) machine, with your knees resting on the pad.
Ensure your body is straight from head to knees, with your hands crossed over your chest or placed behind your head.
Engage your core and glutes as you slowly lower your torso forward by extending at the knees, keeping your back straight.
Lower your body until it is parallel to the ground or slightly below, maintaining tension in the hamstrings.
Pause briefly at the bottom position to maximize muscle engagement.
Initiate the upward movement by contracting your hamstrings and glutes, raising your body halfway back to the starting position.
Hold this halfway position for a moment before repeating the lowering phase.
mistakes: Starting with hips too far back, reducing hamstring engagement.
Allowing the hips to sag, causing lower back strain.
Using momentum to rise instead of controlled muscle contraction.
Failing to keep the core engaged, leading to instability.
Rising too high, placing undue stress on the knees.
Not aligning the knees properly with the pad, causing discomfort.
Neglecting to maintain a straight line from head to knees.
Rushing the eccentric phase, diminishing muscle activation.
Incorrect foot placement on the footplate, affecting leverage.
exercises.name: Glute-Ham Raise 1/2
tips: Focus on controlled movements to maximize muscle activation and prevent injury.
Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain proper alignment and support.
Avoid using momentum; instead, rely on muscle contraction to perform each repetition.
Start with a limited range of motion if you're new to this exercise and gradually increase as you build strength.
Ensure that the GHD machine is adjusted correctly for your height to provide optimal support and leverage.

exercises.description: The Glutes Roll is a self-myofascial release exercise targeting the gluteal muscles. It involves using a foam roller to apply pressure to the glutes, helping to release tension, improve flexibility, and enhance muscle recovery.
instructions: Sit on the floor with your legs extended and place a foam roller under your glutes.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor.
Cross your right ankle over your left knee to target the right glute.
Place your hands on the floor behind you for support.
Shift your weight onto the right glute and slowly roll back and forth from the top of the glute to the bottom.
Continue rolling for 30-60 seconds, focusing on any tight or tender areas.
Switch sides by crossing your left ankle over your right knee and repeat the process for the left glute.
mistakes: Arching the lower back excessively instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Using momentum to roll instead of controlled movements.
Not engaging the core muscles to stabilize the pelvis.
Placing feet too close or too far from the glutes, affecting leverage.
Allowing knees to collapse inward or splay outward.
Failing to maintain even pressure on both feet throughout the movement.
Rolling too quickly, reducing muscle engagement.
Not aligning the body properly on the foam roller, leading to imbalance.
Neglecting to breathe steadily, causing tension and reduced effectiveness.
exercises.name: Glutes Roll
tips: Maintain a steady pace while rolling to effectively target muscle tension.
If you find a particularly tight spot, pause and hold pressure for 20-30 seconds to help release tension.
Keep your core engaged to maintain stability during the exercise.
Breathe deeply and relax your muscles as much as possible while rolling.
Adjust the pressure by shifting more or less of your body weight onto the foam roller.

exercises.description: The Goblet Squat is a lower-body exercise that primarily targets the quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings. It involves holding a weight, typically a dumbbell or kettlebell, close to the chest while performing a squat. This exercise helps improve core stability, balance, and overall leg strength.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and hold a dumbbell or kettlebell with both hands at chest level.
Keep your elbows close to your body and ensure the weight is secure.
Engage your core and keep your chest up as you begin to lower your body by bending at the hips and knees.
Descend until your thighs are parallel to the floor or as low as your flexibility allows.
Ensure your knees track over your toes and do not cave inward.
Push through your heels to return to the starting position, fully extending your hips and knees.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Holding the dumbbell too far from the chest, causing imbalance and strain on the arms.
Allowing the knees to cave inward, increasing stress on the knee joints.
Not squatting deep enough, limiting engagement of the glutes and hamstrings.
Rounding the back, leading to potential lower back strain.
Lifting the heels off the ground, reducing stability and power.
Allowing the elbows to flare out, compromising control and form.
Leaning too far forward, shifting weight away from the heels.
Failing to engage the core, reducing overall stability and control.
Descending too quickly, losing control and risking improper form.
Not maintaining a neutral spine, increasing the risk of spinal stress.
exercises.name: Goblet Squat
tips: Maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement to avoid injury.
Focus on keeping your weight distributed evenly across your feet.
Avoid letting your knees extend past your toes during the descent.
Keep the weight close to your body to maintain balance and control.
Breathe in as you lower into the squat and exhale as you push back up.
If you're new to this exercise, start with a lighter weight to master the form before progressing.

exercises.description: The Gorilla Row is a unilateral back exercise that targets the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and traps while also engaging the core. It is performed with dumbbells and involves a bent-over stance, mimicking the posture of a gorilla. This exercise helps in building strength and stability in the upper back and shoulders.
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Bend your knees slightly and hinge at the hips to lower your torso until it is almost parallel to the floor.
Keep your back straight and engage your core throughout the movement.
Let your arms hang straight down from your shoulders with palms facing each other.
Row one dumbbell towards your hip by bending your elbow and squeezing your shoulder blade towards your spine.
Lower the dumbbell back to the starting position and repeat with the opposite arm.
Continue alternating arms for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Hunching the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Using momentum instead of controlled movements.
Allowing the elbows to flare out excessively.
Pulling the weight too high, causing shoulder strain.
Not engaging the core to stabilize the torso.
Dropping the chest too low, losing proper posture.
Neglecting to keep the shoulders retracted.
Rounding the shoulders forward during the row.
Failing to keep the feet firmly planted for stability.
Overextending the arm at the bottom of the row.
exercises.name: Gorilla Row
tips: Maintain a neutral spine by keeping your head aligned with your spine.
Engage your core to prevent lower back strain.
Focus on pulling with your back muscles rather than using momentum.
Keep your elbows close to your body during the row for maximum lat engagement.
Control the weight throughout the movement, especially when lowering the dumbbell.
Ensure even distribution of weight on both feet to maintain balance.

exercises.description: Position your back against the hack squat machine pad with your shoulders under the supports and forefeet on the platform edge. Keep your legs straight as you lower your heels, then rise onto the balls of your feet. Pause at the top and lower with control, keeping your back against the pad throughout.
instructions: Set the hack squat machine to a light starting load and adjust the shoulder pads so you can stand securely with your shoulders under them.
Place the balls of both feet on the lower edge of the foot platform, about hip-width apart. Let your heels extend off the platform so they can move freely.
Stand tall with your back supported against the pad, brace your abdomen, and keep your knees straight but not locked.
Release the machine safety handles, then lower your heels slowly toward the floor until you feel a stretch in your calves.
Press through the balls of your feet and raise your heels as high as possible, squeezing your calves at the top.
Pause briefly at the top without bending your knees or pushing with your thighs.
Lower your heels under control and repeat for the planned number of repetitions. Re-engage the safety handles before stepping out of the machine.
mistakes: Letting the heels drop only partway instead of using a controlled full stretch.
Stopping short at the top instead of rising fully onto the balls of the feet.
Bending and straightening the knees to move the weight instead of isolating the calves.
Bouncing out of the bottom position instead of controlling the stretch.
Rolling onto the outside or inside edges of the feet instead of pressing evenly through the forefoot.
Allowing the hips or lower back to shift away from the pads during the movement.
exercises.name: Hack Squat Machine Calf Raise
tips: Set the hack squat machine so the shoulder pads sit securely on your shoulders and the safety stops allow a full, controlled calf range of motion.
Place the balls of your feet on the lower edge of the platform, about hip-width apart, with your heels free to move below the platform level.
Choose a manageable load before releasing the machine safeties.
Keep your feet pointing mostly forward. A small natural toe angle is fine, but avoid excessive turning in or out to chase different calf areas.
Finish the set by returning the safety catches before stepping out of the machine. Do not try to exit while the load is still supported only by your calves.

exercises.description: The Half Kneeling Quad Stretch is a flexibility exercise targeting the quadriceps muscles. It is performed in a half-kneeling position, which allows for a deep stretch of the front thigh muscles while also engaging the hip flexors. This stretch is beneficial for improving flexibility, reducing muscle tightness, and enhancing overall lower body mobility.
instructions: Begin in a half-kneeling position with your right knee on the ground and your left foot flat in front of you, forming a 90-degree angle at both knees.
Keep your torso upright and engage your core muscles to maintain balance.
Reach back with your right hand and gently grasp your right ankle or foot.
Slowly pull your right foot towards your glutes, feeling a stretch in the front of your right thigh.
Hold the stretch for 20-30 seconds, ensuring you maintain steady breathing.
Release the stretch and switch sides to repeat with the left leg.
mistakes: Leaning too far forward, reducing the stretch on the quad.
Arching the lower back excessively, causing strain.
Not keeping the hips square, leading to misalignment.
Failing to engage the glutes, decreasing stretch effectiveness.
Allowing the knee of the stretching leg to flare outwards.
Not maintaining a stable base with the front foot.
Pulling the foot too aggressively, risking knee strain.
Neglecting to keep the torso upright and stable.
Holding the stretch for too short a duration to be effective.
Allowing the pelvis to tilt anteriorly, reducing stretch intensity.
exercises.name: Half Kneeling Quad Stretch
tips: Ensure your front knee is aligned over your ankle to maintain proper form and prevent strain.
Keep your hips square and facing forward to maximize the effectiveness of the stretch.
If you have difficulty reaching your ankle, use a strap or towel looped around your foot for assistance.
Focus on keeping your back straight and avoid arching to prevent lower back strain.
Perform this stretch after workouts or during cool-downs to help reduce muscle tightness.

exercises.description: The Half Kneeling Shoulder Dumbbell Press is an exercise that targets the shoulder muscles, particularly the deltoids, while also engaging the core for stability. This movement is performed in a half-kneeling position, which helps to improve balance and unilateral strength.
instructions: Begin in a half-kneeling position with your right knee on the ground and left foot flat in front of you, forming a 90-degree angle at both knees.
Hold a dumbbell in your right hand at shoulder height with your palm facing forward.
Engage your core to maintain stability and keep your torso upright.
Press the dumbbell overhead by extending your elbow until your arm is fully extended.
Slowly lower the dumbbell back to the starting position at shoulder height.
Complete the desired number of repetitions before switching sides.
mistakes: Allowing the back knee to collapse inward, reducing stability and core engagement.
Overarching the lower back, leading to poor spinal alignment and potential strain.
Pressing the dumbbell too far forward instead of directly overhead, compromising shoulder mechanics.
Failing to keep the core engaged, resulting in loss of balance and reduced power.
Using too heavy a weight, causing compensatory movements and loss of form.
Allowing the front knee to move excessively, reducing stability and control.
Rushing the movement, leading to poor control and reduced muscle activation.
Holding the dumbbell too far away from the body at the start, increasing shoulder strain.
Neglecting to keep the shoulder blades retracted, reducing shoulder stability.
Failing to maintain a neutral head position, causing neck strain.
exercises.name: Half Kneeling Shoulder Dumbbell Press
tips: Ensure your core is engaged throughout the exercise to prevent leaning or arching your back.
Keep your gaze forward and maintain a neutral spine to promote proper posture.
Use a controlled motion when pressing and lowering the dumbbell to maximize muscle engagement.
Start with a lighter weight to focus on form and gradually increase as you become more comfortable with the movement.
Switch legs after completing a set on one side to ensure balanced development.

exercises.description: The Half Squat is a compound lower body exercise that targets the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. It involves bending the knees to a partial depth, typically stopping when the thighs are parallel to the floor. This exercise is beneficial for building strength and muscle endurance while reducing stress on the knees compared to a full squat.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly pointed out.
Engage your core and keep your chest up.
Begin the movement by pushing your hips back as if sitting in a chair.
Lower your body until your thighs are parallel to the floor.
Ensure your knees track over your toes and do not extend past them.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement.
Push through your heels to return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Knees collapsing inward, leading to improper alignment.
Heels lifting off the ground, reducing stability and engagement.
Leaning too far forward, causing strain on the lower back.
Not squatting low enough, limiting muscle activation.
Allowing the chest to drop, compromising posture.
Rounding the lower back, increasing risk of injury.
Failing to engage the core, reducing overall control.
Placing weight on the toes instead of the heels.
Moving too quickly, sacrificing form for speed.
Not keeping the knees in line with the toes.
exercises.name: Half Squat
tips: Maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise to avoid injury.
Focus on keeping your weight distributed evenly across your feet.
Avoid letting your knees collapse inward; keep them aligned with your toes.
Control the descent and ascent to maximize muscle engagement.
Use a mirror or partner to check form and ensure proper technique.
Start with body weight or light weights before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: The Hammer Grip Dumbbell Bench Press is a chest exercise that targets the pectoral muscles, triceps, and anterior deltoids. It involves pressing dumbbells upward while maintaining a neutral grip, which can reduce strain on the shoulders and wrists compared to traditional bench press variations.
instructions: Lie flat on a bench with your feet firmly planted on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip, palms facing each other.
Position the dumbbells at shoulder width, elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees.
Engage your core and press the dumbbells upward until your arms are fully extended but not locked.
Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position, maintaining control throughout the movement.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Allowing elbows to flare out, reducing triceps engagement.
Arching the lower back excessively, compromising stability.
Lowering dumbbells too fast, losing control and risking shoulder strain.
Not fully extending arms at the top, limiting range of motion.
Failing to keep wrists aligned with forearms, increasing wrist strain.
Letting dumbbells drift too far forward or backward, affecting shoulder positioning.
Using momentum to lift, reducing muscle activation.
Not retracting shoulder blades, leading to poor chest engagement.
exercises.name: Hammer Grip Dumbbell Bench Press
tips: Keep your shoulder blades retracted and pressed against the bench to stabilize your upper body.
Maintain a neutral wrist position to avoid unnecessary strain.
Focus on controlled movements, both during the pressing and lowering phases.
Exhale as you press the dumbbells up and inhale as you lower them.
Ensure your feet remain flat on the ground to provide stability and support.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: Lower from a straight-arm plank until your chest rests on the floor, then briefly lift both hands completely clear of the surface. Replace your palms and press back to the plank with the trunk and legs moving together, resetting the bottom position on every repetition.
instructions: Start in a high plank with your hands under or slightly wider than your shoulders, legs straight, and feet about hip-width apart.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes, and keep your body in a straight line from your head to your heels.
Lower your chest to the floor under control by bending your elbows.
Once your chest, thighs, and hips are on the floor, briefly lift both hands off the ground by squeezing your upper back.
Replace both palms in their starting positions and press your body up as one unit until the arms are straight.
Keep your hips from sagging or rising ahead of your chest, then repeat for the required number of repetitions.
mistakes: Letting the hips sag or rise instead of keeping a straight line from head to heels.
Failing to lower the chest all the way to the floor before lifting the hands.
Lifting only the palms while keeping the fingers or forearms pressed into the floor.
Pushing up before both hands are fully returned to the floor and set under the shoulders.
Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides instead of keeping them angled slightly back.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears instead of keeping the neck relaxed and shoulders controlled.
exercises.name: Hand-Release Push-Up
tips: Spread your fingers to distribute pressure across the palms.
Keep your neck neutral by looking slightly ahead of your hands, not craning your head forward or dropping it between your shoulders.
Exhale during the press and inhale while lowering the chest.
If full reps are difficult, perform the exercise from your knees while maintaining a straight line from your head to your knees.
Use a brief pause after lifting your hands to remove momentum and make every repetition consistent.

exercises.description: The Handstand Hold is an advanced bodyweight exercise that primarily targets the shoulders, arms, and core. It involves balancing the body upside down with hands placed on the ground and feet elevated, requiring strength, stability, and control.
instructions: Start in a standing position facing a wall.
Place your hands shoulder-width apart on the ground about 6-12 inches from the wall.
Kick up one leg at a time to bring your feet to the wall, achieving an inverted position.
Engage your core and glutes to maintain a straight line from hands to feet.
Keep your head neutral, looking slightly between your hands.
Hold this position for the desired duration, focusing on balance and control.
To exit, gently lower one leg at a time back to the ground.
mistakes: Arching the back excessively, leading to poor alignment and balance.
Failing to engage the core muscles, resulting in instability.
Allowing the shoulders to shrug, which reduces control and strength.
Not stacking the wrists, elbows, and shoulders in a straight line, causing imbalance.
Kicking up with too much force, leading to over-rotation and loss of control.
Placing hands too wide apart, affecting balance and shoulder positioning.
Neglecting to engage the glutes, causing the legs to sag or separate.
Failing to distribute weight evenly across the hands, leading to wrist strain.
Holding the breath, which can reduce stability and increase tension.
Looking at the ground instead of between the hands, disrupting neck alignment.
exercises.name: Handstand Hold
tips: Ensure your hands are firmly planted on the ground for stability.
Engage your core muscles to help maintain balance and prevent arching of the back.
Keep your elbows slightly bent to reduce strain on the joints.
Practice against a wall initially to build confidence and strength.
Focus on breathing steadily throughout the hold to maintain calmness and control.
Gradually increase hold duration as you build strength and stability.

exercises.description: Handstand Push Ups are a challenging bodyweight exercise that targets the shoulders, triceps, and upper chest. This exercise requires significant upper body strength and balance as it involves performing a push-up while in a handstand position, either against a wall or freestanding.
instructions: Begin by positioning yourself in a handstand against a wall, with your hands shoulder-width apart and fingers spread for stability.
Ensure your body is in a straight line from head to heels, engaging your core to maintain balance.
Slowly lower your body by bending your elbows, keeping them close to your body, until your head nearly touches the ground.
Press through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Maintain control throughout the movement and focus on using your shoulder and tricep muscles.
mistakes: Arching the back excessively, leading to poor core engagement.
Flaring the elbows out too wide, reducing shoulder stability.
Not maintaining a straight line from wrists to hips, causing imbalance.
Lowering too quickly, resulting in loss of control and potential head impact.
Failing to engage the scapulae, compromising shoulder support.
Inadequate head positioning, causing neck strain.
Limited range of motion, not achieving full depth.
Over-reliance on momentum, reducing muscle activation.
Inconsistent hand placement, affecting balance and alignment.
exercises.name: Handstand Push-Up
tips: Warm up thoroughly before attempting handstand push-ups to prevent injury.
Practice holding a stable handstand against the wall before incorporating the push-up motion.
Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain balance and stability.
If you're new to this exercise, start with partial range of motion and gradually increase depth as strength improves.
Focus on slow, controlled movements to maximize muscle engagement and reduce risk of injury.

exercises.description: Kick up into a freestanding handstand with your hands about shoulder-width apart. Keep your arms straight and shoulders active, then shift onto one hand and place the other a short step forward. Alternate the hands to travel forward while controlling balance with your palms and fingers.
instructions: Stand in a clear area and fold forward to prepare to place your hands on the floor.
Place your hands on the floor shoulder-width apart and kick one leg up, then bring the other leg up to reach a controlled handstand.
Stack your shoulders over your hands, keep your elbows locked and push tall through your shoulders.
Brace your core, squeeze your glutes and keep your legs together with pointed toes. Avoid arching your lower back.
Shift your body weight slightly onto one hand, then lift the opposite hand and place it a small step forward.
Transfer your weight onto the hand you just placed, then repeat with the other hand. Take short, controlled steps rather than reaching too far.
To finish safely, lower one leg at a time into a lunge or cartwheel out to the side if you lose balance.
mistakes: Starting with shoulders behind the hands instead of stacked over the wrists.
Letting the lower back overarch and the ribs flare instead of keeping a tight hollow body position.
Taking steps that are too large and losing control of the weight shift.
Moving the hands before fully shifting the shoulders over the supporting hand.
Keeping the hands too narrow or crossing them over the center line while walking.
Kicking up with too much force and overshooting the balanced handstand position.
exercises.name: Handstand Walk
tips: Use a clear, flat surface with enough space in front of you. Keep mats, benches and other people out of your walking path.
Spread your fingers and use small changes in fingertip pressure to adjust your balance.
Keep your elbows straight and push tall through your shoulders. Avoid sinking between the shoulders, which makes the position less stable.
Look slightly ahead of your hands, not directly at your feet. This helps you see where you are moving while keeping your neck in a comfortable position.
Learn a safe bailout before practicing away from a wall. Turn out to the side into a cartwheel style exit rather than trying to save every loss of balance.

exercises.description: A hang variation of the clean that starts with the barbell at mid-thigh instead of the floor. You extend the hips, knees and ankles explosively, pull yourself under the bar and catch it on the front of your shoulders in a squat, then stand up. It builds leg and hip power and the timing of the catch.
instructions: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and hold the barbell against your thighs with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder-width apart and arms straight.

Open your knees wider than your torso and pull them towards your armpits.
Ensure your ankles are directly over your knees, creating a 90-degree angle at the knee joint.
Gently press your tailbone down towards the floor while keeping your head and shoulders relaxed.
Hold the pose for 30 seconds to 1 minute, breathing deeply.
mistakes: Pulling the knees too wide apart, causing strain on the hips.
Allowing the lower back to lift off the floor, reducing the stretch's effectiveness.
Gripping the feet too tightly, creating unnecessary tension in the hands and arms.
Forcing the head and neck to lift, leading to strain in the cervical spine.
Failing to engage the core, resulting in an unstable position.
Holding the breath instead of maintaining a steady breathing pattern.
Overextending the legs, causing discomfort in the hamstrings.
exercises.name: Happy Baby Pose
tips: Focus on keeping your back flat on the ground to maximize the stretch in your lower back.
If you can't reach your feet, hold onto a strap looped around each foot.
Engage your core slightly to stabilize your spine during the pose.
Relax your shoulders away from your ears to avoid tension in the neck.
Breathe deeply and evenly to enhance relaxation and flexibility benefits.

exercises.description: Stand with your hips hinged, knees bent and hands supported on your knees. Wear a head harness with a weight plate suspended on a chain, then raise your lowered head through a controlled neck extension. Lower it slowly again, keeping your torso still and the plate from swinging.
instructions: Inspect the head harness, chain and weight attachment. Use a very light load the first time, because the neck muscles fatigue quickly.
Fit the harness securely and attach a light plate to its chain. Stand with your knees bent and feet planted.
Hinge forward at your hips and support your hands on your knees, leaving the plate free to move.
Start with your head lowered slightly, allowing your chin to move toward your chest without forcing the stretch.
Raise your lowered head slowly using the muscles at the back of your neck, within a comfortable range you can control and without moving your torso.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower your head slowly to the starting position.
mistakes: Using momentum or jerking the weight instead of moving the neck slowly.
Letting the torso rock or hinge forward and back to move the load.
Forcing the head backward beyond a comfortable, controlled range.
Dropping the weight quickly on the way down instead of controlling the lowering phase.
Allowing the harness to shift or sit loosely, which makes the load pull unevenly.
Turning or tilting the head during the rep instead of keeping the movement straight forward and back.
exercises.name: Head Harness Neck Extension
tips: Use a light load that lets you complete each repetition at the same slow pace.
Set up so the resistance pulls from in front of your head while you are bent forward at the hips, with your torso supported and stable.
Distribute your support evenly through both hands and keep your feet firmly planted.
Leave enough space for the plate to hang clear of your knees and the floor.
Keep your jaw relaxed and avoid clenching your teeth during the set.

exercises.description: The High Cable Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps brachii. It is performed using a cable machine with the pulley set at a high position. This exercise emphasizes the peak contraction of the biceps, promoting muscle growth and definition.
instructions: Attach a handle to each side of the high pulley on a cable crossover machine.
Stand in the center of the machine with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Grasp the handles with an underhand grip, arms extended out to your sides, parallel to the floor.
Keep your elbows stationary and curl the handles towards your head by flexing your elbows.
Squeeze your biceps at the top of the movement, then slowly return to the starting position.
Maintain control throughout the movement and avoid swinging or using momentum.
mistakes: Swinging the weights instead of using controlled movements.
Allowing the elbows to flare out, reducing bicep engagement.
Using momentum to lift the weights, not isolating the biceps.
Leaning back excessively, straining the lower back.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom of the movement.
Curling the wrists, which shifts tension away from the biceps.
Using weights that are too heavy, compromising form.
Not keeping the shoulders down and back, leading to shoulder involvement.
exercises.name: Hercules Curl
tips: Focus on keeping your elbows fixed in place to maximize bicep engagement.
Control the weight during both the lifting and lowering phases to enhance muscle tension.
Exhale as you curl the handles towards you and inhale as you return to the starting position.
Ensure your wrists remain straight to prevent unnecessary strain.
Adjust the weight so that you can perform 8-12 repetitions with proper form.

exercises.description: Running in place with each knee driven up to your hands, held palms down in front of you at hip height. Keep a quick alternating rhythm, stay tall and land lightly on the balls of your feet. It trains the hip flexors and quads and raises your heart rate fast.
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your weight on the balls of your feet.
Bend your elbows and hold your hands in front of you at about hip height, palms facing down.
Drive one knee up until your thigh touches your hand and is about parallel to the floor.
Bring that foot down under your hip onto the ball of the foot and drive the other knee up right away.
Keep alternating legs in a fast running rhythm, heels off the floor and torso upright.
Continue for the set time, keeping your hands at the same height throughout.
mistakes: Leaning the torso back to get the knees higher
Lowering the hands to meet the knees instead of keeping them at hip height
Landing heavily on the heels instead of lightly on the balls of the feet
Letting the knees cave inward on landing
Landing with the feet in front of the body instead of under the hips
Rounding the shoulders and dropping the chest as you tire
Twisting the torso or swaying side to side with each step
exercises.name: High Knees
tips: Use your hands as a target: a light touch of the thigh on each palm tells you the knee reached hip height.
Drive the knee straight up and let the shin hang below it. Don't kick the foot forward.
Keep a quick, springy rhythm with short ground contacts.
Start at a pace where every knee reaches your hands, and speed up only while that height holds.
Keep your shoulders relaxed and down. Tense arms make the rhythm stiff.
Breathe in a steady rhythm instead of holding your breath.
