exercises.description: The Landmine Squat is a compound exercise that targets the quadriceps, glutes, and core. It involves using a landmine attachment, which is a barbell anchored at one end, allowing for a unique range of motion. This exercise is beneficial for building lower body strength and improving balance and coordination.
instructions: Position the barbell in the landmine attachment, ensuring it is securely anchored.
Stand facing the barbell with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the end of the barbell with both hands, holding it close to your chest.
Engage your core and keep your chest up as you begin to lower into a squat by bending your knees and pushing your hips back.
Descend until your thighs are parallel to the ground or as low as your mobility allows.
Drive through your heels to return to the starting position, extending your hips and knees fully.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Feet positioned too close together, limiting stability and range of motion.
Barbell held too far from the chest, reducing control and increasing lower back strain.
Knees caving inward during the squat, leading to poor alignment and potential joint stress.
Heels lifting off the ground, reducing stability and shifting weight forward.
Back rounding at the bottom of the squat, risking spinal alignment issues.
Failing to engage the core, leading to poor posture and balance.
Descending too quickly, compromising control and increasing risk of injury.
Not squatting to a sufficient depth, limiting muscle engagement and effectiveness.
Allowing the elbows to flare out, reducing upper body stability.
exercises.name: Landmine Squat
tips: Maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement to avoid unnecessary strain on your back.
Keep your weight distributed evenly across your feet to ensure stability.
Focus on engaging your core muscles to support your lower back during the squat.
Ensure that your knees track over your toes as you descend to prevent knee injuries.
Control the movement both on the way down and up to maximize muscle engagement.
Adjust your stance width if necessary to find a comfortable position that allows for optimal squat depth.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腹肌/杠铃地雷旋转

exercises.description: The Landmine Twist is a core exercise that targets the obliques, abdominals, and shoulders. It involves rotating the torso while holding a barbell anchored at one end, providing a unique rotational movement that enhances core stability and strength.
instructions: Secure one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or corner of the room.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding the other end of the barbell with both hands at chest level.
Extend your arms fully in front of you, keeping a slight bend in the elbows.
Engage your core and rotate your torso to one side, pivoting on the opposite foot.
Return to the starting position by rotating back to the center.
Repeat the movement to the other side, maintaining control throughout.
Perform the desired number of repetitions on each side.
mistakes: Rotating the hips instead of keeping them stable.
Allowing the knees to cave inward during the twist.
Twisting the spine excessively instead of maintaining a controlled range of motion.
Using the arms to move the barbell instead of engaging the core muscles.
Leaning forward or backward instead of maintaining an upright posture.
Failing to keep the shoulders down and back, leading to poor shoulder positioning.
Moving too quickly, sacrificing control and stability.
Not keeping the feet firmly planted, causing imbalance.
Overarching the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Neglecting to breathe properly, leading to tension and reduced effectiveness.
exercises.name: Landmine Twist
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the movement to protect your lower back.
Focus on controlled movements rather than speed to maximize muscle engagement.
Ensure your shoulders and hips move together to maintain proper form.
Start with a lighter weight to master the technique before increasing resistance.
Breathe out as you rotate and inhale as you return to the center position.
Maintain a slight bend in your knees for better balance and stability.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/肩部/地雷管维京式推举

exercises.description: The landmine Viking press trains the shoulders and triceps using two neutral-grip handles on a pivoting barbell. Stand facing the loaded end and press from shoulder height along the bar's upward arc. Keep your trunk steady as you extend your arms, then lower the handles under control.
instructions: Set a barbell securely into a landmine base or anchored corner and load an appropriate amount of weight onto the free end.
Attach a Viking press handle to the sleeve of the barbell and make sure the attachment is locked in place and balanced.
Stand facing the loaded end of the barbell with your feet about shoulder-width apart, positioning yourself so the handles start at upper-chest or shoulder height.
Grip the handles firmly with both hands, keep your wrists neutral, brace your abdominal muscles, and maintain a slight bend in your knees.
Press the handles upward and forward by extending your elbows, allowing the barbell to travel along its natural arc.
Finish with your arms nearly straight overhead in front of you, keeping your shoulders controlled and avoiding an exaggerated lower-back arch.
Lower the handles slowly and under control back to shoulder height, keeping your core braced and elbows tracking comfortably.
mistakes: Using excessive lower-back arch.
Flaring the elbows too far out, reducing a strong pressing path.
Letting the elbows drift behind the torso at the bottom position.
Using leg drive or bouncing when the movement is intended to be a strict press.
Lowering the weight too quickly and losing control through the eccentric phase.
Using an uneven stance or shifting body weight from side to side during the press.
exercises.name: Landmine Viking Press
tips: Set the landmine pivot securely and use a Viking press handle that is firmly attached to the barbell before loading weight.
Use the neutral handles and keep your wrists aligned with your forearms.
Press the handles upward and slightly forward along the bar’s natural arc until your arms are nearly straight overhead.
Let your shoulder blades move naturally with your arms.
Choose a load you can move through the full range.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/back/坐姿下拉机

exercises.description: Sit with your thighs locked under the pad and pull two separate lever handles from straight arms to collarbone height to build a wider, stronger back. Your lats lead the pull, with the teres muscles and infraspinatus on the outer edge of the shoulder blade and your lower and middle traps pitching in. Each arm runs on its own plate-loaded lever along a fixed arc, so there is no bar to balance and your stronger side can't drag the weaker one along. It suits beginners, and it's a better choice than the cable pulldown when one side lags or you want the same path on every rep.
instructions: Load the same plates on both horns. The two arms move independently, so uneven loading shows up as one handle lagging behind.
Set the seat so you can just reach the handles with straight arms while your thighs sit snug under the pad. Feet flat, knees bent about 90°.
Take one angled handle in each hand, overhand with your thumbs wrapped around, then sit tall with your chest up. On many machines you half-stand to reach them.
Start every rep by pulling your shoulders down, away from your ears. Only then drive your elbows down and slightly back toward your sides.
Follow the machine's arc down past your face to chin or collarbone height. Both handles stay level, your head stays neutral and your torso doesn't move.
Pause for a beat with your shoulder blades down and back, then let the handles rise over 2–3 seconds until your arms are straight and you feel a stretch under your armpits.
To finish, ride the handles all the way up before you let go. Released at the bottom, the loaded levers snap up past your face.
mistakes: Setting the seat wrong: you can't reach the handles at the top, or your thighs float under the pad and your hips lift on heavy reps. Adjust the seat and pad before you load any plates.
One handle leading or finishing lower because the stronger side takes over. Pull both together and check they stop at the same height; if one side keeps lagging, add some one-arm sets.
Leaning back and swinging your torso to get each rep moving. Keep your chest up and your torso still, and strip plates until the pull starts from your shoulders again.
Pulling with your arms first: elbows drift forward, wrists bend and your biceps tire before your back does. Drop the shoulders, then drive the elbows to your sides with straight wrists.
Shrugging or rolling your shoulders forward at the bottom to force the handles lower. The rep ends where the machine's arc ends, at chin or upper-chest height with your shoulder blades down.
Cutting the top short or letting the levers fly up. Return over 2–3 seconds all the way to straight arms and catch the plates just before the arms hit the stops.
exercises.name: Lat Pulldown Machine
tips: Pull 8–15 reps for muscle and 6–8 for strength; if you're new, start with 10–15 at a load you can pull to your upper chest without leaning back. Add reps before plates: when all your sets reach the top number with straight arms at the top, level handles and no torso swing, add the smallest plate to each horn (usually 2.5 kg a side, or 1.25 kg if your gym has them) and drop back to the bottom of the range.
Lever ratios vary from one machine to the next, so the plates on the horns aren't the weight you actually move. Compare your numbers only on the same machine.

The work runs along the sides of your back from the armpits down and at the outer edge of your shoulder blades, plus a stretch under the armpits at the top. If your biceps and forearms give out before your back, use your hands as hooks and pull with your elbows.

Can't feel your back working? Drop some plates, pause 1–2 seconds at the bottom, and warm up with a few straight-arm reps where only your shoulders move down. If the empty levers are already too heavy, use the Cable Lat Pulldown, whose stack starts lighter.

To make it harder, take 3–4 seconds on the way up, or work one arm at a time with the free hand off its handle from the first rep. Off the machine, the next steps are the Assisted Pull-Up and then the Pull-Up.
Substitutes: Cable Lat Pulldown, Cable Wide Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown (easier on wrists and shoulders), One-Arm Lat Pulldown (each side pulls its own load), Assisted Pull-Up.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/侧向跳跃

exercises.description: Hop a short distance from side to side with both feet together. Keep the hops low and use a slight knee bend to absorb each landing before reversing direction. This bodyweight drill trains quick lateral movement and coordination while the torso stays facing forward.
instructions: Stand with your feet together on clear floor.
Bend your knees slightly and keep your arms relaxed by your sides.
Push off both feet and hop a short distance to one side.
Land on both feet with a slight bend in the knees.
Hop back to the other side without turning your torso.
Continue with low, quick hops and controlled landings.
mistakes: Letting the knees collapse inward when landing or pushing off
Jumping too high instead of moving quickly and laterally
Failing to push off evenly through both feet
Allowing the torso to twist or lean excessively to one side
Pausing too long between hops and losing the rhythm
Using a range that is too wide to control the landing position
exercises.name: Lateral Hops
tips: Keep the feet close together for a compact hop.
Land softly on both feet with your knees bent. Let your hips move back slightly to absorb the landing.
Use your arms naturally for balance, but avoid swinging them wildly to create momentum.
Use a similar hopping distance in both directions.
Use a firm, flat surface with reliable grip.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/臀部/侧向怪兽步行

exercises.description: The Lateral Side (Monster) Walk Squat is a dynamic exercise that targets the gluteus medius, hip abductors, and quadriceps. It involves performing a squat while simultaneously stepping laterally, often using a resistance band to increase intensity. This exercise enhances hip stability, strengthens the lower body, and improves lateral movement capabilities.
instructions: Place a resistance band around your legs just above your knees.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and lower into a squat position, keeping your chest up and back straight.
Engage your core and maintain tension in the band throughout the movement.
Step laterally to the right with your right foot, followed by your left foot, maintaining the squat position.
Take 3-5 steps to the right, then reverse the movement by stepping to the left with your left foot, followed by your right foot.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions or time.
mistakes: Allowing knees to cave inward, reducing glute engagement.
Taking steps that are too wide, causing loss of control.
Leaning forward excessively, shifting focus away from hip muscles.
Failing to maintain a slight bend in the knees, reducing stability.
Not keeping feet parallel, leading to improper muscle activation.
Rising up during the movement, decreasing tension on target muscles.
Using momentum instead of controlled movements, risking loss of balance.
Neglecting to keep core engaged, compromising posture and alignment.
exercises.name: Lateral Monster Walk
tips: Keep your knees aligned with your toes to prevent inward collapse during the movement.
Maintain a low squat position to maximize engagement of the glutes and thighs.
Focus on controlled movements rather than speed to ensure proper muscle activation.
Use a mirror or ask for feedback to ensure you are maintaining proper form throughout the exercise.
Start with a lighter resistance band if you're new to this exercise and gradually increase resistance as you become more comfortable.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/臀部/侧向滑步

exercises.description: Take a low athletic stance with your knees bent, hips back and feet apart. Shuffle sideways by stepping with the lead foot and bringing the other foot toward it without crossing. Travel back in the opposite direction, keeping your hips level and your chest facing forward.
instructions: Stand tall with your feet about shoulder-width apart. Bend your knees slightly and shift into an athletic stance with your hips back and chest up.
Keep your core braced, your back neutral, and your weight balanced over the middle of your feet.
Step sideways with the lead foot in the direction you are moving. Do not cross your feet.
Bring the trailing foot in toward the lead foot, returning to your starting stance width. Stay low throughout the movement.
Continue taking controlled side steps for the planned distance or number of repetitions, keeping your knees tracking in line with your toes.
Move back in the opposite direction by leading with the other foot. Keep your hips level, avoid bouncing up and down, and maintain control until you finish.
mistakes: Standing too tall instead of keeping a low athletic stance.
Crossing the feet instead of using short side steps.
Letting the knees collapse inward during the shuffle.
Allowing the hips to rise and fall with each step.
Pushing off only with the leading foot instead of driving from the trailing leg.
Turning the torso and hips instead of keeping the body facing forward.
exercises.name: Lateral Shuffle
tips: Use a clear, level surface that gives your shoes reliable traction.
Keep your core braced and your weight balanced through the middle of each foot, not on your toes only.
Take quick, controlled steps and keep your feet pointed mostly forward.
Use a shorter range and slower pace until you can maintain a stable knee and hip position.
If you are shuffling for conditioning, focus on clean movement first, then increase speed or distance.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/肩部/侧平举转前平举

exercises.description: Raise two dumbbells out to your sides, sweep them forward at shoulder height and lower them in front to train your side and front delts in one move. The side delts do most of the lifting on the way out, the front delts take over as your arms come forward and down, and the rear delts help a little. Your arms stay at shoulder height for the whole sweep, so even a light pair gets heavy fast. That makes it a good home exercise and a shoulder-day finisher. Pick the plain Dumbbell Lateral Raise when the side delts are the priority and you want to load them heavier.
instructions: Stand tall with your feet between hip and shoulder width, knees soft, a dumbbell hanging beside each thigh and palms facing in.
Pull your shoulders down away from your ears and set a slight bend in your elbows. That angle stays the same until the last rep.
Raise both dumbbells out to the sides until your arms are parallel to the floor, elbows leading, palms turning to face down.
Without letting them dip, sweep both arms forward in a wide arc at shoulder height until they point straight ahead, about shoulder width apart.
Lower the dumbbells straight down in front of you, taking 2 to 3 seconds to reach the front of your thighs.
Let them drift back to your sides, palms in, and start the next rep without a bounce. Set them down after the last one.
mistakes: Dumbbells sagging below shoulder height during the forward sweep. One rep turns into two half raises. Keep your hands level with your shoulders all the way across; if you can't, the weight is too heavy.

Leaning back or dipping the knees to swing the weights up, usually just as the arms come forward. Stand tall with a light brace; if you still sway, drop the weight, sit down or put your back against a wall.
Dropping the dumbbells from the front position. Take 2 to 3 seconds to lower them, because that part works your front delts too.
exercises.name: Lateral to Front Raise
tips: Use this at the end of a shoulder or upper-body day for 2 to 4 sets of 12 to 20 reps. Add reps with the same pair until all sets reach 20 with your hands level through the sweep and no lean back. Then move up the smallest step you have, ideally 1 kg per dumbbell, and drop back to 12. If your gym only jumps in 2 kg steps, earn a few reps past the range first.

The burn travels around the shoulder: the side while your arms rise, then the front as they come forward and lower. If it's mostly your neck that burns, you're shrugging. A sharp pinch at the top of the shoulder means the set is over.
Shoulder pinching with your arms out to the sides? Raise them about 30° in front of your body instead of straight out, stop at or just below shoulder height and go lighter.

Can't stop swaying? Sit on a bench, or bend your elbows to about 90° to shorten the lever. When the full version gets easy, pause for 2 seconds at the sides and again in front, or take 3 seconds over the forward sweep, before you add weight.

Substitutes: Dumbbell Lateral Raise to load the side delts heavier, Dumbbell Front Raise for the front half on its own, Dumbbell Alternate Front Raise if both arms at once keep pulling you into a sway.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/chest/前倾平板支撑

exercises.description: The Lean Planche is an advanced bodyweight exercise that targets the shoulders, chest, and core. It requires significant strength and balance, as it involves holding the body parallel to the ground with only the hands touching the floor. This exercise is a progression towards the full planche, emphasizing shoulder strength and core stability.
instructions: Begin in a push-up position with your hands shoulder-width apart and fingers pointing forward.
Lean your body forward by shifting your weight onto your hands, keeping your arms straight.
Engage your core and glutes to maintain a straight line from head to heels.
Keep your feet together and lift them slightly off the ground, balancing on your hands.
Hold this position for as long as possible, maintaining control and stability.
Slowly return to the starting position by reversing the movement.
mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag, losing the straight line from shoulders to feet.
Failing to protract the scapula, resulting in shoulder instability.
Placing hands too far forward, reducing leverage and control.
Bending the elbows, leading to insufficient arm engagement.
Not engaging the core, causing lower back strain.
Leaning too far forward, risking wrist strain.
Neglecting to maintain tension in the legs, causing loss of balance.
Rushing the movement, leading to poor form and control.
exercises.name: Lean Planche
tips: Focus on engaging your core muscles to maintain stability throughout the exercise.
Start with short holds and gradually increase the duration as you build strength.
Ensure your shoulders are protracted and depressed to protect them from injury.
Practice leaning forward incrementally to find your balance point without overextending.
Use parallettes or yoga blocks if wrist flexibility is a limiting factor.
Incorporate wrist strengthening exercises into your routine to support this movement.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/肩部/绳索侧身侧平举

exercises.description: Hold the cable column with one hand, lean away from it and raise a low-pulley handle out to the side with the other arm to build wider shoulders. Your side delts do most of the work, the rear delts help a lot and the front delts a little, and you'll feel the serratus anterior along the side of your ribs. The lean is what sets it apart: the cable meets your arm at a wider angle, so the raise is loaded right from the bottom, where a dumbbell feels almost weightless. Your support hand keeps the body still, so it's easier not to sway than in the upright version.
instructions: Set the pulley to the lowest notch and clip on a single D-handle.
Stand side-on to the column with your feet together right at its base, so the pulley sits next to your near foot.
With your near hand, grab a fixed upright of the frame at about head height. Never hold the moving pulley carriage or the cable.
Take the handle in your far hand. The cable runs diagonally across the front of your thighs, not behind you.
Lean away until your support arm is almost straight and your body forms one line from feet to head, about 15–20° off vertical.
Pull the working shoulder down, then raise the arm out to the side in a wide arc, elbow slightly bent and leading.
Stop when your upper arm is roughly parallel to the floor and your palm faces down. Hips and support arm stay where they are.
Take 2–3 seconds to lower back in front of your hip without letting the plates touch. Do all your reps on one side, then switch.
mistakes: Standing upright or leaning toward the machine. The lean away is the whole point: feet at the column base, support arm straight, then tip away before the first rep.
Swinging back toward upright as the arm comes up. Lock the support arm and hips, keep one body angle for the whole set and drop the pin a plate.
Bending and straightening the elbow until the raise turns into an upright row. Set a slight bend at the start and keep it; the elbow leads and the hand never rises above it.
Letting the stack crash at the bottom and starting each rep from a slack cable. Lower slowly and stop with the plates still apart.
exercises.name: Lean-Away Cable Lateral Raise
tips: Aim for 12–15 reps here, and anything from 10 to 20 works; below about 8, the shrug and the sway take over.
Stay on the same pin until you get the top number in every set with the lean held still, then go up one plate and start again lower in the range.

One stack plate is often 2.5–5 kg (5–10 lb), which on a one-arm raise can mean 25–50% more weight. Use an add-on weight if the stack has one; if not, first stretch the lowering to 3–4 seconds and add a one-second pause at the top.

The side of the working shoulder should burn from the first few inches of the raise. If it's mostly the top of your shoulder and your neck, you're shrugging or the pin is too heavy. A pinch at the top of the shoulder means stop a little lower and raise slightly in front of your body.
Can't keep your body still? Lean less, or go back to the upright one-arm raise with a lighter pin. Once your reps look clean, a slightly bigger lean loads the bottom of the range more.

Substitutes: Cable Lateral Raise if you'd rather stand upright, One-Arm Cable Lateral Raise, One-Arm Dumbbell Lateral Raise holding a post and leaning away the same way, Dumbbell Lateral Raise when every cable is taken.

exercises.description: The 'In And Out' exercise is a core-focused movement that targets the abdominal muscles, particularly the rectus abdominis and obliques. It involves a seated position where the legs are extended and then brought in towards the chest, engaging the core throughout the motion.
instructions: Sit on the floor with your legs extended in front of you and your hands placed slightly behind your hips for support.
Lean back slightly, keeping your back straight and your core engaged.
Lift your feet off the ground, balancing on your sit bones.
Simultaneously bring your knees towards your chest while keeping your core tight.
Extend your legs back out to the starting position without letting them touch the ground.
Repeat the movement for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control and balance throughout.
mistakes: Not maintaining a straight back, leading to rounding of the spine.
Allowing the feet to touch the ground between reps, reducing muscle engagement.
Failing to fully extend the legs, limiting range of motion.
Using momentum instead of controlled movement, reducing effectiveness.
Not engaging the core, resulting in poor stabilization.
Placing hands too far back, causing strain on the wrists.
Allowing knees to flare outward, misaligning the movement pattern.
Holding breath, leading to unnecessary tension and reduced endurance.
exercises.name: Leg In and Out
tips: Keep your core engaged at all times to protect your lower back and maximize abdominal activation.
Focus on controlled movements rather than speed to ensure proper form and effectiveness.
If you find it difficult to balance, try placing your hands further back or slightly bending your elbows for additional support.
To increase difficulty, perform the exercise without using your hands for support or add ankle weights for added resistance.
Maintain a steady breathing pattern; exhale as you bring your knees in and inhale as you extend them out.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/仰卧腿举

exercises.description: Sit back in a 45-degree leg press and drive the loaded sled up its rails with both feet to build your quads and glutes without a bar on your back. The quads, on the front of your thighs, do most of the work; the glutes kick in hard at the bottom, where your hips fold deepest. Your back and head stay on the pad, so you can take heavy sets close to failure even when your back or shoulders limit heavy squats. Pick it over the horizontal press for heavier loads and a deeper hip bend, and over the hack squat when you want your torso fully supported.
instructions: Load the same plates on both sides of the sled so it runs evenly on the rails.
Sit all the way back, hips down in the seat, with your back and head on the pad.
Set your feet flat in the middle of the platform, about hip-width apart, toes turned slightly out.
Press the sled just off the stops, turn the safety handles out to free it, then take hold of the seat handles beside your hips.
From the top, legs almost straight, bend your knees and hips and lower the sled over about 2 seconds, knees tracking over your toes.
Keep going until your thighs near your ribs, about 90 degrees at the knee or a bit deeper. Stop before your hips curl off the seat.
Without bouncing, drive the sled back up through your whole foot, heels down, and stop just short of locking your knees.
At the top of the final rep, turn the safety handles back in while the sled is at the top, then let it down onto them.
mistakes: Hips and lower back peeling off the seat at the bottom as your tailbone tucks under. Stop the descent just before that point, or set your feet a little higher on the platform.
Knees caving in as you press. Push them out in line with your second and third toes, turn your toes slightly out and take some weight off if they still drift.
Snapping the knees straight at the top. Stop just short of lockout and keep the legs working; a locked knee under a heavy sled is the main injury risk on this machine.
Quarter reps with a tall stack of plates. Strip weight until you reach about 90 degrees at the knee on every rep, and keep the same depth from set to set so the progress you log is real.
Pushing on your knees with your hands. Keep your hands on the seat handles; if you need them to finish a rep, that rep ends the set.
exercises.name: Leg Press
tips: For strength, use sets of 5–8; for muscle, 8–15, and many push the last set to 20 because the sled is safe to take close to failure.

Once all your sets hit the top number, add 10 kg (a 5 kg plate per side) and drop back to the bottom of the range; switch to 5 kg jumps when progress slows. Count the load the same way every session, since the empty sled weighs something different on every machine.

Foot placement changes the work. Higher on the platform means more hip bend and more glutes; lower means more knee bend and more quads, but your heels lift sooner. Narrow and wide stances are listed as separate exercises.

Expect to feel it mostly in the front of your thighs, plus the glutes near the bottom. Lower-back pressure or your tailbone lifting means you went deeper than your hips allow. If the front of the knee hurts, check that your knees follow your toes and your heels stay down.

To make it easier, cut the depth to about 90 degrees at the knee, or use the Lever Horizontal Leg Press: it's easier to get in and out of, and its pin stack allows small jumps. To make it harder without adding plates, pause for 2 seconds at the bottom of every rep or move to the Single Leg Press.
Substitutes: Lever Horizontal Leg Press, Machine Hack Squat, Smith Squat, Dumbbell Goblet Squat.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/宽距腿举

exercises.description: Press the sled of a 45-degree leg press with your feet set wide and your toes turned out to train your quads and glutes without loading your spine. Most of the work lands on the front of your thighs, the glutes help out of the bottom, and many lifters feel a stretch along the inner thighs at full depth. Machine, seat and foot height match the regular leg press; only the width changes. Because your knees travel out, your thighs pass beside your ribs instead of into your belly, so most people sink deeper before the hips roll. Pick it if a hip-width stance feels cramped.
instructions: Load the plates evenly on both sides of the sled, then sit all the way back with your hips down in the seat and your head on the pad.
Place your feet flat at mid-height on the platform, clearly wider than your shoulders, each one near a side edge but fully on it.
Turn your toes out about 15–30° so your feet point where your knees are going to travel.
Press the sled off the stops, turn the safety handles out to free it, and hold the seat handles beside your hips.
Bend your knees and let the sled come down over about two seconds, knees opening out in line with your toes.
Stop at roughly 90° at the knee, or sooner if your tailbone starts to lift. Your thighs should pass beside your ribs.
Drive back up through the whole foot with your heels down and knees pushed out, stopping just short of locking out.
At the top of the final rep, turn the safety handles back in before you let the sled down onto them.
mistakes: Knees caving in as you push out of the bottom. Keep them over your second or third toe all the way up, and drop the weight if they still drift.
Toes pointing straight ahead with the feet this wide. The knees can't follow the feet, so the groin and the inside of the knee take the strain. Turn them out 15–30°.
Feet hanging off the edges of the platform or rolling onto their inner edges. Bring them in until the whole foot stays flat at the bottom.
Chasing depth until your tailbone curls off the pad. Stop just before the hips roll, or move your feet a little higher.
Snapping the knees straight at the top. Stop a hair short of lockout so your legs stay loaded.
exercises.name: Leg Press Wide Stance
tips: Sets of 10–15 reps suit most people here, often as the second leg exercise after squats or a regular leg press. Once all sets hit 15 at the same depth and foot position, add 10 kg (5 kg per side) and start again at 10. The empty sled weighs a different amount on every machine, so count the load the same way each time.

Foot height is a separate dial. Higher on the platform bends your hips more and brings in more glutes; lower bends your knees more and loads the quads, as long as your heels stay down. "High and wide" is the usual glute setup.
A pull in the groin or a pinch at the front of the hip means your feet are too wide or your toes aren't turned out enough. New to wide stances? Build depth over a few sessions before you go heavy.

Substitutes: Leg Press with a hip-width stance if this one bothers your groin, Lever Horizontal Leg Press, and Sumo Squat With Smith or Sumo Squat once your hips like the position. To make this one harder without changing machines, pause for 2 seconds at the bottom.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/腿部摆动

exercises.description: Leg Swings are a dynamic stretching exercise that targets the hip flexors, hamstrings, and glutes. They are commonly used as a warm-up to increase flexibility and range of motion in the lower body, preparing it for more intense physical activity.
instructions: Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart next to a wall or sturdy object for support.
Place your left hand on the wall for balance.
Shift your weight onto your left leg and lift your right leg slightly off the ground.
Swing your right leg forward and backward in a controlled manner, keeping your torso upright.
Perform 10-15 swings, then switch legs and repeat the movement with your left leg.
Maintain a steady pace and avoid jerky movements to prevent injury.
mistakes: Swinging the leg too high, causing loss of control and balance.
Not maintaining a stable core, leading to excessive torso movement.
Failing to keep the standing leg straight, resulting in poor balance.
Allowing the swinging leg to bend, reducing the effectiveness of the exercise.
Not engaging the hip flexors and glutes, limiting range of motion.
Performing the exercise too quickly, sacrificing form for speed.
Incorrect foot positioning, causing misalignment and reducing stability.
Neglecting to maintain an upright posture, leading to lower back strain.
exercises.name: Leg Swings
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain balance.
Start with small swings and gradually increase the range of motion as you become more comfortable.
Focus on smooth, controlled movements rather than speed.
Ensure your standing foot is firmly planted on the ground to provide stability.
Use this exercise as part of a dynamic warm-up routine to enhance lower body mobility.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/back/杠杆式背部伸展

exercises.description: The Lever Back Extension is a strength training exercise targeting the lower back muscles, specifically the erector spinae. It is performed using a lever machine designed to support the body while allowing controlled extension of the spine. This exercise helps improve posture, enhance core stability, and strengthen the lower back.
instructions: Adjust the lever machine to fit your height, ensuring that the pads rest comfortably on your upper thighs.
Position yourself face down on the machine with your feet secured under the footpads.
Cross your arms over your chest or place your hands behind your head.
Engage your core and slowly lower your upper body towards the floor by bending at the hips.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement, ensuring you do not round your back.
Raise your upper body back to the starting position by extending at the hips until your body forms a straight line.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Arching the back excessively instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Using momentum to lift the torso rather than controlled muscle engagement.
Positioning the pad too high, causing discomfort and limiting range of motion.
Hyperextending the spine at the top of the movement.
Not aligning the hips properly with the pivot point of the machine.
Failing to engage the core muscles, leading to instability.
Allowing the shoulders to round forward during the exercise.
Rushing through the movement without proper control.
Not adjusting the machine to fit individual body dimensions.
Neglecting to engage the glutes and hamstrings effectively.
exercises.name: Lever Back Extension
tips: Ensure that the machine is adjusted properly to avoid strain on your lower back.
Keep your movements slow and controlled to maximize muscle engagement and reduce injury risk.
Focus on engaging your core throughout the exercise to maintain stability.
Avoid hyperextending your back at the top of the movement; stop when your body is in a straight line.
Exhale as you lift your body up and inhale as you lower it down.
Start with a lighter weight to perfect your form before increasing resistance.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/back/杠杆高位划船

exercises.description: Sit chest-to-pad on a plate-loaded high row machine and pull the handles from above your head down to your upper chest to build your lats and upper back. Your teres major and lats along the sides of your back do most of the work, helped by the lower traps low between your shoulder blades and the small infraspinatus and teres minor behind each shoulder. The chest pad and thigh roller lock you in, so your lower back rests and nothing swings. The high-to-low angle sits between a pulldown and a flat row, with more lat and lower-trap work than the Chest Supported Machine Row.
instructions: Set the seat so you reach the handles with almost straight arms while your chest is on the pad.
If you have to shrug or rise off the seat to get them, raise it.
Lock your thighs under the roller pad just above the knees, feet flat on the floor and knees bent about 90°.
Your lower chest rests on the vertical pad and stays there until the set is over.
Take the vertical handles with a neutral grip, palms facing, about shoulder-width apart. Wrists straight: your hands are just hooks.
Begin each rep by pulling your shoulders down, away from your ears, before your elbows bend.
Drive your elbows down and back toward your back pockets, so the handles sweep in an arc from above your forehead to your upper chest.
At the finish, your hands are at upper-chest height and your elbows just behind your torso, about 30–45° from your sides. Squeeze your shoulder blades together and down for a second.
Take 2–3 seconds on the way back, until your arms are long and your shoulder blades spread. After the last rep, ride the handles to the start before you let go.
mistakes: Elbows already bent at the start, or shrugging and rising off the seat to reach the handles. Reset the seat until your arms are almost straight at full reach with your chest on the pad and thighs under the roller.
Peeling your chest off the pad and leaning back to finish the rep. Your breastbone stays on the pad for every rep; if it can't, take a plate off.
Curling the wrists and hauling the handles to your chin. Treat your hands as hooks, lead with the elbows and stop when your hands reach your upper chest.
Half reps at the top: the arms never get long and the lats never stretch. Let the handles rise until only a soft bend is left in your elbows and your shoulder blades spread.
exercises.name: Lever High Row
tips: Do 3–4 sets of 8–12 reps (up to 15), or 6–8 when the goal is strength. Add reps at the same load until you get 12 on every set with a full reach and a one-second squeeze, then add 2.5–5 kg in total and go back to 8. Plate jumps are big, so if the next one is too much, add a 2-second hold at the chest first.

The sides of your back under the armpits should work, along with the area low between your shoulder blades and the back of each shoulder blade. A burning neck means you're shrugging; arms tiring before your back means you're pulling with your hands. A sharp pinch at the front of the shoulder in the top stretch means stop the return a little short of full reach.
Can't feel your shoulder blades move? Go lighter and pause for a second at the chest on every rep. When the machine feels easy, slow the return to 3 seconds or move on to the One-Arm Lever High Row.

Substitutes: Cable Neutral Grip Lat Pulldown (same grip and elbow path, finer weight steps), Chest Supported Machine Row (a flat pull with more mid-back) or One-Arm High Row Cable when your gym has no high row machine.

exercises.description: Sit upright with your feet on a fixed footplate and straighten your legs so the seat slides back on its rails: hard quad work with no bar on your back. The front of your thighs does most of the pushing, including the inner part just above the knee, and your glutes help in the bottom half, where your hips are deeply bent. With nothing to unrack or balance, it suits beginners, works as a back-friendly squat substitute and makes a good high-rep finisher after squats. Compared with the 45-degree Leg Press you move less weight over a shorter range, but setup and weight changes take seconds.
instructions: Set the weight first: move the pin in the stack, or load plates if your machine takes them.
Sit with your hips all the way back and your back on the pad. There is no headrest, so hold your head level.
Put both feet flat in the middle of the footplate, about hip-width apart, toes pointing up or slightly out, heels down.
Set the seat position so your knees start bent about 90 degrees with your feet on the plate.
Hold the handles beside the seat with straight arms. They keep your hips down; don't pull on them.
Breathe out and press through your heels and midfoot. The plate stays put while you and the seat roll back.
Keep your knees tracking over your second toe and pause for a beat just before they straighten fully.
Ride the seat forward over 2–3 seconds until your knees are back at about 90 degrees, touch the bottom lightly and press again.
When the set is over, let the seat settle against the stops before you take your feet off the plate.
mistakes: Seat set too close, so your knees start bent well past 90 degrees and your lower back curls off the pad at the bottom. Move the seat back until your hips and lower back stay put on every rep.
Snapping the knees straight at the top. Finish with a soft bend and keep pressure on the plate before you let the seat roll forward.
Knees caving in as you press. Point them over your second toe, turn the toes out slightly if needed, and drop the weight if they still collapse.
Heels peeling off the plate at the bottom so you push through your toes. Place your feet a little higher or move the seat back.
Yanking on the handles and lifting your hips to grind out a heavy rep. The handles only keep you seated; lighten the load until your hips stay down on every rep.
exercises.name: Lever Horizontal Leg Press
tips: Sets of 10–15 reps are the usual choice for size (some people go up to 20); for strength, 6–10 reps over 3–4 sets. Add reps before weight: when all sets hit the top of the range with your knees back to about 90 degrees, move the pin down one plate (usually 5–10 kg, or 5 kg per side on a plate-loaded version) and restart at the bottom of the range.

The front of your thighs takes most of it, with the glutes joining in at the bottom. Lower back doing the work? The seat is too close. A sharp pain at the front of the knee means stop, shorten the range or move your feet a little higher.

Feet lower on the plate bend the knees more and load the quads harder, but the heels lift sooner; feet higher bend the hips more and bring in a bit more glute. Keep the heels down either way. If 90 degrees at the knee is too much for now, set the seat so they bend only to about 100–110 degrees and go deeper as you get stronger.

Substitutes: Leg Press (heavier loads and a deeper range), Single Leg Press (one side at a time), Machine Hack Squat, or a Dumbbell Goblet Squat when there is no machine. To make this one harder without adding weight, pause 1 second at the bottom and take 3 seconds on the way back.

exercises.description: The Lever Low Row is a strength training exercise targeting the muscles of the back, specifically the latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, and trapezius. This exercise is performed using a lever machine designed to simulate the rowing motion, providing a controlled environment to focus on muscle contraction and form.
instructions: Adjust the seat height so that your chest is comfortably against the chest pad and your feet are flat on the floor.
Select an appropriate weight on the machine that allows you to perform the exercise with proper form.
Sit on the machine with your chest against the pad and grasp the handles with a neutral grip (palms facing each other).
Keep your back straight and core engaged throughout the movement.
Begin by pulling the handles towards your torso, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the movement.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring full contraction of the back muscles.
Slowly return to the starting position, fully extending your arms while maintaining control of the weight.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Rounding the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Using momentum by swinging the torso instead of controlled movement.
Pulling with the arms rather than engaging the back muscles.
Shrugging the shoulders up instead of keeping them down and back.
Allowing the elbows to flare out too wide, reducing back engagement.
Failing to fully retract the shoulder blades at the end of the pull.
Leaning too far forward or backward, affecting balance and form.
Not adjusting the seat height, leading to improper alignment.
Pulling the bar too high or too low, missing optimal range of motion.
Gripping the handles too tightly, causing forearm fatigue.
exercises.name: Lever Low Row
tips: Ensure your movements are slow and controlled to maximize muscle engagement and minimize risk of injury.
Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together at the peak of each repetition to enhance muscle activation.
Avoid using momentum or leaning back excessively; keep your torso stable throughout the exercise.
Adjust the seat and chest pad as needed to ensure proper alignment and comfort during the exercise.
Breathe out as you pull the handles towards you and inhale as you return to the starting position.
Start with a lighter weight to master form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: The Lever Seated Hammer Grip Shoulder Press is a machine-based exercise targeting the deltoid muscles, particularly the anterior and lateral heads. It involves pressing weights upward using a neutral grip, which can reduce strain on the shoulder joints compared to traditional grips. This exercise is beneficial for building shoulder strength and muscle mass.
instructions: Adjust the seat height so that the handles are at shoulder level when seated.
Sit down and firmly plant your feet on the ground, maintaining a slight arch in your lower back.
Grasp the handles with a neutral grip (palms facing each other).
Engage your core and press the handles upward by extending your elbows until your arms are fully extended but not locked.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring not to shrug your shoulders.
Slowly lower the handles back to the starting position with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Failing to adjust the seat height properly, leading to improper alignment of the handles with the shoulders.
Allowing the elbows to flare out excessively, which can reduce shoulder engagement and increase strain on the joints.
Using momentum to lift the weight instead of controlled muscle contraction, reducing effectiveness and increasing injury risk.
Not maintaining a neutral spine, which can lead to poor posture and reduce core engagement.
Locking out the elbows at the top of the movement, causing unnecessary joint stress.
Allowing the wrists to bend excessively, which can lead to discomfort and reduce control.
Not engaging the core, leading to instability and reduced power output.
Lowering the handles too quickly, which can compromise muscle tension and control.
Starting with too heavy a weight, leading to compromised form and reduced range of motion.
exercises.name: Lever Seated Hammer Grip Shoulder Press
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain stability.
Avoid locking your elbows at the top of the movement to reduce joint stress.
Focus on a slow and controlled descent to maximize muscle engagement.
Ensure your wrists remain in a neutral position to prevent strain.
Maintain a steady breathing pattern; exhale while pressing up and inhale while lowering.
Adjust the weight appropriately to ensure proper form is maintained throughout all repetitions.

exercises.description: Lizard Pose, or Utthan Pristhasana, is a yoga posture that targets the hip flexors, hamstrings, and quadriceps. It enhances flexibility in the hips and groin while also strengthening the core and improving balance.
instructions: Begin in a downward-facing dog position with your hands and feet on the mat.
Step your right foot forward to the outside of your right hand, aligning your knee over your ankle.
Lower your left knee to the mat and slide it back slightly to extend your leg.
Keep your hands on the mat or lower onto your forearms for a deeper stretch.
Hold the pose for several breaths, keeping your gaze forward or down.
To release, press back into downward-facing dog and repeat on the other side.
mistakes: Hands placed too far forward, reducing stability and engagement.
Front knee collapsing inward, straining the knee joint.
Back leg not extended fully, limiting hip flexor stretch.
Hips lifted too high, decreasing stretch effectiveness.
Shoulders hunching, causing tension and misalignment.
Neck craned forward, leading to strain and discomfort.
Core not engaged, resulting in loss of balance and support.
Breath holding, reducing oxygen flow and relaxation.
exercises.name: Lizard Pose
tips: Ensure your front knee is aligned over your ankle to avoid strain.
Engage your core to maintain stability and support the lower back.
If lowering onto forearms is challenging, use yoga blocks for support.
Keep your back leg active by pressing the top of the foot into the mat.
Focus on deep, even breathing to help relax into the stretch.

exercises.description: A strongman lift in which you clean a log from the floor to your chest and drive it overhead. From the chest you dip, drive the log up and bend your knees again to get under it, then stand up with your arms locked. Lower it to the chest, then to the thighs and the floor.
instructions: Stand close to the log with your feet about shoulder-width apart. Squat down and take the handles with a neutral grip.
Brace your core, keep your back flat and drive through your legs to lift the log to your thighs.
Keep the log tight to your body and roll it up onto your upper chest, driving your elbows high.
Stand tall with the log resting on your chest and your elbows up.
Dip by bending your knees, then drive hard with your legs to send the log upward.
Bend your knees again to get under the log and catch it on straight arms.
Stand up with your elbows locked and the log over your midfoot.
Lower the log to your chest, then to your thighs and back to the floor under control.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back when lifting the log off the floor
Pulling the log up with the arms instead of driving with the legs
Letting the log drift away from the body during the clean
Holding the log on the chest with the elbows low
Pressing the log out slowly with the arms instead of driving it with the legs
Leaning back with the ribs flared at lockout
Letting the log drift forward of the midfoot overhead
Dropping the log from overhead instead of lowering it in stages
exercises.name: Log Clean and Press
tips: Learn the lift in parts first: the clean to the chest, then the dip and drive.
Squeeze the handles hard and keep your wrists straight.
Keep the first dip short and straight down, with your torso upright and heels on the floor.
Push your head through between your arms at lockout.
Reset your grip and breath before every clean.

exercises.description: A seated yoga pose with each foot resting high on the opposite thigh, soles facing up. You sit tall with your hands on your knees and hold the position while breathing slowly. It needs a lot of external rotation at the hips, so build up to it gradually from half lotus.
instructions: Sit on the floor with your legs straight in front of you.
Bend one knee and place that foot high on the opposite thigh, close to the hip crease, sole facing up.
Bend the other knee and place that foot on the opposite thigh in the same way.
Let both knees sink toward the floor without pushing them down.
Sit tall with your weight even on both sitting bones and rest your hands on your knees.
Relax your shoulders and breathe slowly for the planned time.
To come out, lift the top foot off first, then straighten both legs slowly.
mistakes: Forcing the feet onto the thighs and twisting the knees
Staying in the pose despite pain or pinching in the knees
Pushing the knees down with the hands
Rounding the lower back and collapsing the chest
Leaning to one side instead of sitting evenly on both sitting bones
Holding the breath or tensing the shoulders
exercises.name: Lotus Pose
tips: Sit on a folded blanket or cushion if your knees stay high or your lower back rounds.
Let the movement come from rotation at the hips; your knees should feel no strain.
Loosen your hips first with a few minutes of easy cross-legged sitting or a butterfly stretch.
Switch which leg goes on top from one session to the next.
Practise half lotus until the first side feels easy before adding the second foot.

exercises.description: The Low Cable Horizontal Pallof Press is an anti-rotational core exercise that targets the obliques, transverse abdominis, and rectus abdominis. It involves pressing a cable horizontally from a low pulley position while resisting rotational forces, promoting core stability and strength.
instructions: Attach a handle to a low pulley cable machine and set the desired weight.
Stand sideways to the machine with feet shoulder-width apart, holding the handle with both hands close to your chest.
Step away from the machine to create tension in the cable. Ensure your body is aligned and your knees are slightly bent.
Engage your core and press the handle straight out in front of you, keeping your arms extended at shoulder height.
Hold the extended position briefly, resisting any rotation or movement in your torso.
Slowly return the handle to your chest while maintaining control and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Switch sides and repeat the exercise to ensure balanced development.
mistakes: Allowing the hips to rotate instead of keeping them square to the front.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine, leading to excessive arching or rounding.
Letting the shoulders shrug up towards the ears, causing tension in the neck.
Using momentum to press the cable instead of controlled muscle engagement.
Standing too far from the cable machine, reducing tension on the core.
Allowing the elbows to flare out instead of keeping them close to the body.
Incorrectly aligning the cable handle with the center of the chest.
Neglecting to engage the core muscles fully throughout the movement.
Starting with the feet too close together, reducing stability.
Rushing the press and return phases, compromising control and effectiveness.
exercises.name: Low Cable Horizontal Pallof Press
tips: Focus on keeping your core tight throughout the movement to maximize stability.
Ensure your shoulders remain level and avoid leaning towards the cable machine.
Control your breathing by exhaling as you press out and inhaling as you return to the starting position.
Start with a lighter weight to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
Maintain a slight bend in your knees to enhance stability and balance during the exercise.
Keep your movements slow and controlled to effectively engage your core muscles.

exercises.description: The Low Cable Incline Bench Press is a compound exercise targeting the upper chest muscles, specifically the clavicular head of the pectoralis major. This exercise also engages the anterior deltoids and triceps. By using cables, it provides constant tension throughout the movement, enhancing muscle activation and growth.
instructions: Set an incline bench at a 30-45 degree angle in front of a cable machine.
Attach handles to the low pulleys on each side of the machine.
Sit on the bench with your back firmly against it and feet flat on the floor.
Grab the handles with an overhand grip, palms facing forward.
Position your hands at chest level, elbows bent at approximately 90 degrees.
Press the handles upward and slightly inward until your arms are fully extended but not locked.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, squeezing your chest muscles.
Slowly lower the handles back to the starting position, maintaining control.
mistakes: Allowing the elbows to flare out excessively, reducing chest engagement and increasing shoulder strain.
Arching the lower back excessively, compromising spinal alignment and stability.
Using too much weight, leading to uncontrolled movement and reduced muscle activation.
Failing to maintain a stable shoulder position, causing excessive shoulder movement and potential joint stress.
Lowering the cables too quickly, reducing time under tension and control.
Not fully extending the arms at the top of the movement, limiting range of motion and muscle activation.
Positioning the bench at too steep an incline, shifting focus away from the upper chest.
Allowing the wrists to bend backward, increasing strain on the wrists and forearms.
Neglecting to engage the core, leading to instability and reduced power transfer.
Letting the cables move out of alignment with the chest, causing uneven muscle engagement.
exercises.name: Low Cable Incline Bench Press
tips: Ensure that your back remains firmly against the bench to prevent strain.
Maintain a controlled motion throughout to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid locking your elbows at the top to keep tension on your muscles.
Focus on squeezing your chest muscles at the peak of each rep for better activation.
Keep your core engaged to stabilize your body during the exercise.
Adjust the bench angle if necessary to target different areas of the chest.

exercises.description: The Dumbbell Incline Low Fly is an isolation exercise targeting the upper portion of the pectoral muscles. It is performed on an incline bench, which emphasizes the clavicular head of the pectoralis major. This exercise also engages the anterior deltoids and stabilizes the shoulder joint.
instructions: Set an incline bench to a 30-45 degree angle.
Sit on the bench with a dumbbell in each hand, resting them on your thighs.
Lie back on the bench and lift the dumbbells above your chest, palms facing each other.
Slightly bend your elbows and lower the dumbbells in an arc motion until you feel a stretch in your chest.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement.
Bring the dumbbells back to the starting position using the same arc motion, focusing on squeezing your chest muscles.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Allowing elbows to drop too low, causing excessive shoulder strain.
Using too heavy weights, leading to uncontrolled movements.
Failing to maintain a slight bend in the elbows, increasing joint stress.
Not keeping the shoulder blades retracted, reducing chest engagement.
Bringing dumbbells too close together at the top, losing tension on the chest.
Arching the back excessively, compromising core stability.
Using momentum to lift the weights instead of controlled muscle action.
Letting wrists bend backward, causing strain on the forearms.
Not aligning the bench properly, altering the angle of the exercise.
exercises.name: Low Incline Dumbbell Fly
tips: Maintain a slight bend in your elbows throughout the exercise to reduce stress on your joints.
Keep your movements controlled and avoid using momentum to lift the weights.
Focus on feeling a stretch in your chest at the bottom of the movement and a contraction at the top.
Ensure your back and head remain firmly against the bench to maintain proper form.
Start with lighter weights to master the form before progressing to heavier loads.
Exhale as you lift the weights and inhale as you lower them.

exercises.description: Stand between the low pulleys of a cable crossover and sweep two handles from your hips up and in to shoulder height to build your upper chest. You feel it mostly just below the collarbones, spreading toward the breastbone as the hands meet, with the middle chest, front delts and serratus anterior helping. The cables pull from below, so the top of the rep stays hard, right where a dumbbell fly goes slack. The low pulleys don't make it a lower-chest move: for the lower chest, set the pulleys high and do the High Low Cable Chest Fly instead.
instructions: Set both pulleys of the crossover to the lowest notch, clip a single D-handle to each cable and pick the same weight on both stacks.
Take the handles underhand, palms forward, and stand in the middle, half a step in front of the pulleys, with both stacks lifted.
Stagger your feet half a step, knees soft. Chest up, shoulder blades back and down, hands by your hips, elbows slightly bent.
Lock that elbow bend in and sweep both hands forward, up and in along a wide arc, as if scooping something up toward your chin.
Stop when your hands meet in front of the upper chest at shoulder height, palms up, and squeeze for about a second without shrugging.
Take 2–3 seconds to bring your hands down until they are back by your hips and the upper chest feels a light stretch.
Only your shoulders move. Torso, hips and feet stay put, and the weights don't touch the stack until the set is done.
When you finish, step back toward the pulleys so the stacks settle before you let go of the handles.
mistakes: Bending the elbows on the way up until the handles get curled toward your shoulders. Set a slight bend before the first rep and keep it; if it keeps creeping, the weight is too heavy.
Raising the hands to face height or overhead. Stop where they meet at shoulder height. Above that, your front delts do the lifting and your shoulders start to shrug.
Lifting straight forward like a front raise, with the hands staying shoulder-width apart. Think "up and in" so they meet at the middle of your chest.

Standing behind the pulleys, so the cables drag your arms behind your body at the bottom. Start half a step in front of them and finish each lowering with your hands by your hips: a deep stretch under a heavy stack strains the front of the shoulder.
exercises.name: Low-to-High Cable Fly
tips: Sets of 12–20 reps work for most people, 2–4 of them taken close to failure. If a weight won't give you about 8 clean reps, the fly turns into a curl or a press. Add reps at the same weight until you get 20 in every set with the same arc, then go up one stack step on both sides and start again at 12.
Many crossover stations run a 2:1 pulley ratio, so the number on the stack is more than you're holding. If one stack step is too big a jump, earn it with extra reps or use the add-on weight.
Biceps burning? Your elbows are bending and you're curling. If the fronts of your shoulders take over, your hands are finishing too high or the weight is too heavy.

Can't find your upper chest yet? Learn the arc one arm at a time with your free hand on the frame. Once that's easy, add a 1–2 second squeeze at the top and a 3–4 second lowering before you add weight.
The load is light and your shoulders never go into a deep stretch, so it's easy on the joints at any training level. It works well as a finisher after incline presses.

Substitutes: One-Arm Low-to-High Cable Fly; Dumbbell Low to High Fly when no cable station is free; Incline Bench Cable Fly to load the upper chest harder with your body supported; Incline Dumbbell Chest Fly.

exercises.description: The Lowbar Squat is a compound exercise primarily targeting the muscles of the lower body, including the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and lower back. It involves placing the barbell lower on the back compared to the high bar squat, typically across the posterior deltoids and just below the spine of the scapula. This positioning allows for a more horizontal back angle and greater hip flexion, emphasizing posterior chain engagement.
instructions: Set up a barbell in a squat rack at about chest height.
Position yourself under the bar, placing it across your posterior deltoids just below the spine of your scapula.
Grip the bar with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, keeping your wrists straight.
Step back from the rack with feet shoulder-width apart and toes slightly pointed out.
Take a deep breath, brace your core, and initiate the squat by pushing your hips back and bending your knees.
Lower yourself until your hip crease is below your knee level while maintaining a neutral spine.
Drive through your heels to return to the starting position, extending your hips and knees simultaneously.
Exhale at the top of the movement and repeat for desired repetitions.
mistakes: Bar placed too high on the back, leading to improper weight distribution.
Feet positioned too narrowly, limiting stability and depth.
Knees caving inward, increasing stress on knee joints.
Back rounding or excessive forward lean, risking spinal strain.
Hips rising faster than the chest, causing loss of balance.
Insufficient hip hinge, reducing glute and hamstring engagement.
Failing to maintain a tight core, compromising overall stability.
Not reaching proper depth, limiting muscle activation.
Allowing the wrists to bend, causing unnecessary strain.
Lack of control during descent, leading to a bounce at the bottom.
exercises.name: Lowbar Squat
tips: Ensure that the barbell is positioned securely on your back to avoid slipping during the lift.
Maintain a tight core throughout the movement to support your lower back.
Focus on pushing through your heels to maximize glute and hamstring activation.
Keep your chest up and eyes forward to help maintain proper spinal alignment.
Warm up thoroughly before performing heavy sets to reduce injury risk.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
Consider using lifting shoes for better stability and ankle support.

exercises.description: Raise a light plate in each hand out to your sides and on up until your arms are vertical overhead, building your side delts and overhead strength. Up to shoulder height the side delts do most of the work; above it the front delts help more and your traps rotate the shoulder blades upward. That overhead half sets it apart from the regular lateral raise, which stops at shoulder height. The lift is named after the Chinese weightlifter Lu Xiaojun, and weightlifters and CrossFit athletes use it as a warm-up or a shoulder-day finisher. You need pain-free overhead mobility: your arms should reach vertical without your back arching.
instructions: Hold a light plate in each hand (1.25–5 kg) upright by its inner edge, fingers hooked through the center hole. Light dumbbells held thumbs forward work the same way.
Stand tall with your feet hip- to shoulder-width apart and knees soft, plates together in front of your thighs, faces pointing forward.
Pull your ribs down, squeeze your glutes and unlock your elbows slightly. That elbow angle stays the same until the set is over.
Sweep both arms out to the sides in one wide arc, thumbs leading, in line with your body or slightly in front. No pause at shoulder height.
Keep going until your arms are vertical, plates side by side overhead and a few inches apart so they don't clash. Hold one second without leaning back.
Lower along the same arc over 2–3 seconds, stop just short of your thighs and start the next rep from a dead stop.
mistakes: Stopping at shoulder height. That's a plain lateral raise; go lighter and finish every rep with your arms vertical.
Leaning back or arching your lower back to get the plates overhead. Keep your ribs down and glutes squeezed, and if your arms still can't reach vertical, end the arc where your back stays neutral.
Bending the elbows on the way up until the raise turns into a press or an upright row. Set a soft elbow at the start, leave it alone and keep the plates on a wide arc, far from your head.

Thumbs and palms turning down in the top half. That can pinch the front of the shoulder; lead with your thumbs so the plate faces point forward, and keep your palms facing forward once your arms are overhead.
exercises.name: Lu Raises
tips: Sets of 10–15 reps work well, up to 20. This isn't a low-rep lift, so stay at 8 or more. Keep the same plates until you reach 15 on every set with arms fully vertical and no lean-back, then move up one weight and drop back to 10.
Going from 2.5 to 5 kg doubles the load. Bridge the jump with light dumbbells or fractional plates (1–1.25 kg per hand), or first add a 2–3 second pause overhead and a 3–4 second lowering.

The burn belongs on the outside of your shoulders and peaks around shoulder height; higher up, the front of the shoulder and your upper back between neck and shoulder blades join in. Feeling your neck from the first inch means you're shrugging. A pinch on top of the shoulder with your arms overhead? Check that your thumbs point up and use only the pain-free part of the arc.
Substitutes: Dumbbell Lateral Raise when going above shoulder height hurts, Cable Y Raise for an overhead finish with tension at the bottom, Band Lateral Raise at home.

exercises.description: The Lunge Stretch is a dynamic exercise that targets the hip flexors, quadriceps, and glutes. It is effective for improving flexibility, balance, and overall lower body strength. This stretch is often used as part of a warm-up routine to prepare the body for more intense physical activity.
instructions: Begin by standing upright with your feet hip-width apart.
Step forward with your right foot, lowering your hips until both knees are bent at approximately a 90-degree angle.
Ensure your right knee is directly above your ankle and your left knee hovers just above the ground.
Keep your torso upright and engage your core throughout the movement.
Hold the stretch for a few seconds, then push off your right foot to return to the starting position.
Repeat on the opposite side by stepping forward with your left foot.
mistakes: Knee extends beyond toes, increasing knee strain.
Back leg is not straight, reducing hip flexor stretch.
Front foot is not flat on the ground, compromising balance.
Torso leans forward excessively, disengaging core muscles.
Hips are not square, limiting stretch effectiveness.
Front knee collapses inward, risking knee joint strain.
Weight is not evenly distributed, causing instability.
Back heel lifts off the ground, reducing stretch in calf.
exercises.name: Lunge Stretch
tips: Maintain a straight back and avoid leaning forward during the stretch.
Focus on keeping your front knee aligned with your ankle to prevent injury.
Engage your core muscles to maintain balance and stability.
Perform the stretch slowly and with control to maximize its effectiveness.
If you feel discomfort in your knees, adjust the depth of the lunge or consult a fitness professional.

exercises.description: Lunges are a compound lower-body exercise that targets the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves. This exercise also engages the core for stability and balance. Lunges can be performed with body weight or additional resistance such as dumbbells or a barbell.
instructions: Stand upright with feet hip-width apart and hands on your hips or holding weights at your sides.
Step forward with your right foot, lowering your hips until both knees are bent at about a 90-degree angle.
Ensure your front knee is directly above your ankle and your back knee hovers just above the ground.
Push through the heel of your front foot to return to the starting position.
Repeat the movement with your left leg to complete one full repetition.
mistakes: Allowing the front knee to extend past the toes, which can strain the knee joint.
Failing to maintain a straight torso, leading to an imbalance and reduced core engagement.
Stepping too narrow, causing instability and improper alignment.
Not lowering the back knee close enough to the ground, limiting range of motion and muscle activation.
Letting the front heel lift off the ground, reducing stability and power.
Pushing off with the toes instead of the heel, which can decrease glute activation.
Allowing the back leg to remain too straight, reducing the effectiveness of the lunge.
Twisting the hips or torso, which can lead to poor balance and uneven muscle engagement.
Rushing the movement, which compromises control and form.
exercises.name: Lunges
tips: Keep your torso upright throughout the movement to maintain balance and engage the core.
Avoid letting your front knee extend past your toes to reduce stress on the knee joint.
Focus on a controlled descent and ascent to maximize muscle engagement.
For added intensity, hold dumbbells in each hand or place a barbell across your upper back.
Maintain a steady breathing pattern; inhale as you lower down and exhale as you push back up.

exercises.description: The Lying Barbell Triceps Extension, commonly known as the Skullcrusher, is an isolation exercise targeting the triceps brachii. It involves extending the elbows to lift a barbell from behind the head to above the chest while lying on a flat bench. This exercise emphasizes the long head of the triceps and is effective for building muscle mass and strength in the upper arm.
instructions: Lie flat on a bench with your feet firmly planted on the ground.
Grip a barbell with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Extend your arms fully, holding the barbell directly above your chest.
Slowly lower the barbell towards your forehead by bending your elbows.
Keep your upper arms stationary and close to your head throughout the movement.
Pause briefly when the barbell is just above your forehead.
Extend your elbows to lift the barbell back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Allowing elbows to flare out, reducing triceps engagement.
Lowering the barbell too far, risking shoulder strain.
Using momentum to lift the bar, compromising control.
Positioning elbows too far back, shifting focus away from triceps.
Failing to maintain a neutral wrist position, increasing strain on wrists.
Not keeping upper arms stationary, reducing exercise effectiveness.
Arching the back excessively, leading to poor form.
Rushing the movement, leading to improper muscle contraction.
exercises.name: Lying Barbell Triceps Extension
tips: Ensure your elbows remain stationary to maximize triceps engagement.
Use a spotter if lifting heavy weights to ensure safety.
Control the descent of the barbell to prevent injury and maintain tension on the triceps.
Avoid flaring your elbows out to maintain proper form and focus on the triceps.
Start with a lighter weight to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
Keep your core engaged and back flat on the bench for stability.

exercises.description: The Lying Butterfly Pose, also known as Supta Baddha Konasana, is a restorative yoga posture that focuses on opening the hips and stretching the inner thighs and groin. This exercise is performed while lying on your back, allowing gravity to assist in deepening the stretch. It is beneficial for improving flexibility, reducing tension, and promoting relaxation.
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs extended.
Bend your knees and bring the soles of your feet together, allowing your knees to fall open to the sides.
Position your heels comfortably close to your pelvis.
Rest your arms alongside your body with palms facing up or place them on your abdomen.
Close your eyes and take slow, deep breaths, allowing your body to relax into the pose.
Hold the position for 3-5 minutes or as long as comfortable.
mistakes: Allowing the knees to drop too low, causing strain on the inner thighs.
Failing to keep the back flat on the ground, leading to an arched lower back.
Not engaging the core, resulting in a lack of stability and support.
Positioning the feet too far from the body, reducing the stretch in the hips.
Pulling the feet too close to the body, causing discomfort or overstretching.
Neglecting to relax the shoulders, which can lead to unnecessary tension.
Holding the breath instead of maintaining a steady, relaxed breathing pattern.
exercises.name: Lying Butterfly Pose
tips: Ensure that your back remains flat on the ground to avoid strain.
If you feel discomfort in your knees or hips, place cushions or blocks under your thighs for support.
Focus on relaxing your inner thighs and letting gravity gently deepen the stretch.
Keep breathing deeply and evenly to enhance relaxation and flexibility.
To exit the pose, use your hands to gently bring your knees together before extending your legs back out.
