Keep your shoulders down and back to maintain proper form and avoid strain.
Use a box or step that allows you to start at the top position comfortably.
Breathe steadily throughout the exercise, exhaling as you lower yourself.

Keep your core engaged throughout the movement to maintain stability and protect your lower back.

exercises.description: Perform this exercise by gripping the pull-up bar with your palms facing each other (neutral grip). Engaging the arms primarily and neglecting to activate the back muscles

exercises.description: Hinge toward a high pulley with your free hand braced on the frame and push a single rope grip down to a straight elbow, training one triceps at a time. You feel it along the back of your upper arm, hardest at lockout. The pulley sits in front of you, so the cable still pulls at an angle when the arm is straight and the bottom of the rep stays loaded. Pick it over a two-arm pushdown when one arm lags or the stronger side does more than its share. The braced hinge keeps your torso still, which makes this a good place to learn a strict pushdown.
instructions: Set one pulley at the top of the column and clip on a single rope grip. A triceps rope works too; hold just one end.
Take it in your working hand with a neutral grip: palm toward your thigh, thumb toward the cable, little finger by the knob, wrist straight.
Face the machine from a long step away, feet hip-width, and grab an upright of the frame at shoulder height with your free hand.
Push your hips back until your torso leans about 30–40 degrees forward, back flat and both shoulders square to the machine.
Bring the rope to the start: upper arm against your ribs, elbow bent about 90 degrees, hand in front of your lower ribs.
Straighten the elbow, pushing down and slightly back until your hand reaches your thigh and the rope lies flat under your fist. Hold half a second.
Let the forearm rise over 2–3 seconds to 90 degrees. After the last rep, let the rope rise to the start before you let go, then switch arms.
mistakes: Letting the elbow wander: forward on the way up until the hand reaches your chest, or out to the side as the stack gets heavy. Keep the upper arm against your ribs, point the elbow back and end the return at 90 degrees.
Bobbing the torso, hinging deeper on each push and standing up on each return so body weight moves the stack. Set the hinge once, press your free hand into the frame and move only the forearm.
Bending the wrist or turning the hand palm-down at the bottom. Keep the wrist straight and the thumb toward the cable; the rope turns in your fist, your hand doesn't.
Hanging on the bracing arm and twisting toward the working side. The free hand only steadies you: both shoulders stay square to the machine, and the working shoulder stays down, away from your ear.
exercises.name: One-Arm Cable Pushdown
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 10–15 reps per arm, a rep or two short of failure. Start with your weaker arm and give the other one the same number.
Add reps before weight. Once both arms get 15 on all sets with a full lockout and a still upper arm, add the smallest weight step and start again at 10.
One plate is a big jump for a single arm, so expect a few sessions at each weight. Functional trainers often run a 2:1 pulley ratio, so compare numbers only on the same machine.

You should feel this only in the back of the working arm; the bracing arm and your abs just hold you in place. If the front of the shoulder or the chest joins in, the elbow is drifting forward or body weight is pushing, so take a plate off. A sharp twinge at the point of the elbow means too much load or a hard snap into lockout.
Weight getting easy? Take 3–4 seconds on the way up and hold the lockout for a full second before you add load. If the elbow won't stay pinned, do the two-handed rope version for a few weeks.

Substitutes: One-Arm Triceps Cable Pushdown, done upright with a D-handle, when there is nothing to hold on to; Rope Triceps Pushdown for both arms at once with the same neutral grip; Cable Triceps Pushdown with a straight bar to move the most weight; One-Arm Reverse Grip Triceps Cable Pushdown for a palm-up variation.

exercises.description: Sit on the floor facing a cable column with your legs straight and row a single handle from a long forward reach back to your lower ribs. Your lats do most of the pulling, helped by the muscles around the shoulder blade (teres major, infraspinatus, middle and lower traps) and, at the finish, the rear delt. One arm at a time lets you reach farther in front and drive the elbow deeper behind you than a bar allows, and a weaker side shows up fast. All you need is an adjustable cable column, no row station.
instructions: Slide the pulley down to chest height for someone sitting on the floor (about knee height when you stand) and clip on a single D-handle.
Sit on the floor facing the column, legs straight, feet together and heels down. Scoot back until your arm is straight and the plates still hang above the stack.
Hold the handle with a neutral grip, thumb up and wrist straight. Sit tall on your sit bones and rest the free hand on the floor by your hip or on your thigh.
Start from a long reach: the working shoulder travels toward the pulley, your torso leans forward about 15–20° and turns slightly away from that arm.
You'll feel a stretch down the side of your back.
Drive the elbow straight back along your ribs while your torso comes up to vertical. The cable should run roughly level.
Stop with the handle beside your lower ribs and the elbow just behind your body. Pull the shoulder blade back and down and hold a second; your chest turns only slightly toward the working side.
Let the arm travel forward over about 2 seconds until it's straight and the shoulder reaches again. The plates don't touch down between reps.
Do every rep on one arm, then switch, starting with your weaker side. Never let go of the handle at full reach, or it snaps back to the column; pass it to your other hand.
mistakes: Rocking the torso: folding far forward at the start and leaning back to finish. Keep the lean to a small reach and come back only to upright; if you can't, the weight is too heavy.
Twisting your trunk to get the handle home. Let your chest open just a little, drive the elbow toward your back pocket and keep both hips flat on the floor.
Lower back rounding because tight hamstrings tuck your pelvis under. Bend your knees slightly or sit on a low step or a weight plate so you can sit tall.
Flaring the elbow out so the handle ends up at your chest. That turns it into a rear-delt pull; keep the elbow close to your ribs and finish beside the lower ribs.
exercises.name: One-Arm Cable Row
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 8–15 reps per arm; for strength, 6–8 is about as low as this floor-seated version goes. Add reps first: once both arms hit 15 on all sets with a full reach and a still torso, move the pin down one plate (usually 2.5–5 kg) and restart at 8.

You should feel it along the side of your back up into the armpit and over the shoulder blade. If your biceps or lower back give out first, the hand is pulling instead of the elbow, or your torso is rocking.

Before adding weight, slow the return to 3 seconds and pause 2 seconds at the ribs. The next step up is the One-Arm Cable Low Row, done standing, where your hips and legs also have to brace against the pull.

Substitutes: Seated Cable Low Row Neutral Grip (both arms, feet on the foot plate, so the torso doesn't get pulled into a twist), One-Arm Low Cable Seated Row, and Dumbbell Bent Over Row when the cables are taken.

exercises.description: With your back to a low pulley, straighten one arm from behind your head until it points up, training your triceps from a deep stretch, one side at a time. Many lifters just call it the katana extension. Your free arm crosses in front of your face and holds the working arm below the elbow, so only the forearm moves. All three triceps heads work, and with the arm overhead the long head is stretched the most. The cable keeps pulling right up to lockout. Pick it when one arm lags or when two-arm overhead extensions bother your shoulders, since each arm finds its own elbow line.
instructions: Set one pulley of a cable station to the lowest notch and clip on a single D-handle.
Grab the handle, turn your back to the machine and stand a short step in front of it: feet hip-width, knees soft, ribs down.
Bring the handle up behind your head. Upper arm vertical by your ear, elbow pointing at the ceiling, hand behind your head toward the opposite shoulder.
Reach your free arm across in front of your face and hold the working arm just below the elbow.
Straighten the elbow so your hand travels up and over until the arm points straight above your shoulder. Squeeze there for about a second.
The lowering takes about 2 seconds and ends when the elbow is fully bent and the handle is back behind your head, upper arm still pinned.
Do all your reps on one arm, then switch and match the count.
To finish, lower the handle past your shoulder and step back to set the weight down; never let go of it behind your head.
mistakes: Elbow drifting forward toward your face on the way down, so the rep turns into a press and the stretch gets shorter. Brace the arm just below the elbow with your free hand and keep the elbow pointing at the ceiling.
Elbow flaring out to the side, away from your head. Keep the upper arm by your ear; if it only stays there for the first few reps, the weight is too heavy.
The stack touching down at the bottom of every rep, so the stretch carries no load. Step a little further from the machine until the plates stay up with your elbow fully bent.

Leaning forward or arching your lower back to drive the handle up once you tire, while the cable pulls you back toward the machine. Ribs down, glutes tight, a short staggered stance if you still tip, and end the set as soon as your torso starts to move.
Reversing the rep while your hand is still above your head. Lower until it sits behind your head toward the other shoulder, with a weight you can handle in that position.
exercises.name: One-Arm Katana Triceps Overhead Extension
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 10–20 reps per arm, the last few close to failure.

Add reps before weight: once both arms reach 20 in every set with the upper arm still, move the pin one step (often 2.5–5 kg; on many functional trainers it feels smaller because of the 2:1 pulley) and drop back to 10.

At the bottom you should feel a long stretch down the back of the working arm, strongest near the armpit and just above the elbow, and a hard squeeze at the top. A pinch at the front of the shoulder means your elbow is drifting back or out. A sharp ache in the elbow at the bottom means the weight or the depth is too much.
Easier: go lighter and shorten the bottom, stopping when your hand is level with the back of your head. Harder: lower over 3 seconds and pause for a second in the stretch before you add weight.

Substitutes: One-Arm Overhead Triceps Extension, the same rep with a dumbbell and no cable station, though it goes light near lockout; Cable Overhead Triceps Extension to work both arms at once; Standing One Dumbbell French Press, the simplest overhead extension to set up anywhere; Katana Triceps Extension to train both arms together on crossed cables.

exercises.description: Kneel tall and press the end of a landmine bar up and forward with one arm: shoulder pressing that doesn't demand full overhead mobility. Your front and side delts carry the press, the upper chest helps off the bottom and the triceps finish the lockout. At the top, your shoulder blade glides forward around the ribs. With both knees down you can't drive with your legs or hide a lean-back, so your glutes and abs work hard just to keep the hips straight and the torso square. Pick it over the standing version when you want strict reps, and expect to use less weight.
instructions: Slide one end of a barbell into the landmine pivot (or a towel-wrapped corner), load the free end and put a pad down for your knees.
From half-kneeling, bring the bar end to the front of your working shoulder, then lower the other knee: both knees down, hip-width apart, facing the plate.
Wrap your whole hand around the tip of the sleeve beyond the plate, palm turned in. The bar sits deep in your palm, wrist straight.
Point the elbow down in front of your ribs with the bar end between collarbone and chin. Rest your free hand on your stomach.
Squeeze your glutes until your hips are straight: shoulders over hips over knees, thighs vertical, ribs pulled down.
Press up and forward along the bar's arc until your elbow is straight and your hand sits just above and in front of your head.
At the top, let your shoulder blade reach up and forward around the ribs while your chest stays square to the bar.
Lower it back to the front of your shoulder in about 2 seconds, without bouncing.
To finish, go back to half-kneeling to switch hands or set the bar down. Never drop it from the top.
mistakes: Leaning back and arching your lower back to get the bar up: ribs flare and the hips drift behind the knees. Squeeze your glutes, pull the ribs down and take weight off until you stay stacked.
Sitting back toward your heels so the hips bend. Push your hips forward until the thighs are vertical before the first rep, and keep the glutes tight until the set is done.
Twisting toward the pressing side. Both hips and both shoulders face the bar; the free hand on your stomach tells you right away if your torso turns. If it keeps turning, go lighter.
Elbow flared straight out to the side at the bottom. Start every rep with the elbow down in front of your ribs and your forearm under the bar end.
Stopping with the elbow still bent, or with the shoulder blade pinned back. Straighten the arm fully on every rep and reach the bar end a little further up and forward.
exercises.name: One-Arm Landmine Kneeling Shoulder Press
tips: Press 5–8 reps per arm for strength and 8–15 (often 10–12) for size, usually after your main press.
Add reps first: once both arms reach the top of the range in every set with a straight elbow and no lean-back, add weight and go back to the low end.
Go up 1.25–2.5 kg at a time on the sleeve. The pivot carries part of the load, so each jump feels smaller in your hand than the plate suggests.

The front and side of your shoulder work, along with the back of your arm and, at the top, the muscle along your ribs under the armpit. If your lower back is working, you're leaning back. A pinch on top of the shoulder means end the set and lighten the load.

Can't stay upright? Drop to half-kneeling or use the empty bar. When strict reps get easy, move to the standing version for heavier sets, or to the One-Arm Kettlebell Overhead Press if you can get your arm straight overhead without arching.

Substitutes: One-Arm Landmine Half Kneeling Shoulder Press (the closest swap, with a wider base), One-Arm Landmine Standing Shoulder Press (takes more weight) and Dumbbell Half Kneeling Shoulder Press if your gym has no landmine.

exercises.description: Sit tall with a dumbbell in one hand overhead, lower it behind your head and straighten the arm again to train your triceps one side at a time. All three heads of the triceps work. The long head crosses the shoulder, so with your arm up it starts out lengthened and the bottom of the rep is the hard part. With one arm, the forearm folds toward the other side instead of straight down, which many people find easier on the elbow than the two-hand version. It also shows quickly if one arm lags. You need one light dumbbell, and without a bench you can stand.
instructions: Sit near the end of a flat bench or any sturdy seat, feet flat and wider than your hips, knees at about 90 degrees.
Grip the middle of the handle, bring the dumbbell to your shoulder and press it straight up until your arm is locked out, palm forward.

Bend only the elbow and lower for about 2 seconds. Your forearm folds behind your head toward the opposite shoulder; the handle turns upright.
Stop when your forearm is about horizontal and the back of your arm is fully stretched, or higher if that hurts. No bounce.
Straighten the elbow along the same arc until the dumbbell is directly over your head. Hold the lockout for a second.
Do every rep on one arm, weaker arm first, then switch. Afterward, bring the dumbbell forward to your shoulder and down to your thigh.
mistakes: Elbow drifting out to the side as the dumbbell comes down. Keep the upper arm beside your ear with the elbow pointing up; if it still wanders, go lighter or hold it with your free hand.
Upper arm swinging forward and down until the rep turns into a press. Reset it beside your head before every rep and let only the forearm move.
Cutting the rep short when the dumbbell reaches the top of your head. Lower until the forearm is about horizontal behind your head; that stretch is the reason to do this exercise.
Wrist bending back so the dumbbell hangs behind your hand. Hold the middle of the handle, wrist straight, knuckles pointing at the ceiling at lockout.
exercises.name: One-Arm Overhead Triceps Extension
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 10–15 reps per arm, stopping one or two reps short of failure with the same reps on both sides.

Add reps first: once both arms reach 15 in all sets with a full stretch and no leaning, take the next dumbbell and go back to 10. One dumbbell step is a big jump for one arm (8 kg to 10 kg is 25%), so expect a few sessions at each weight.

At the bottom you should feel a strong pull along the back of your upper arm up toward the armpit, and a hard squeeze at lockout. Feel it in your lower back or neck? Sit taller and go lighter. Sharp elbow pain in the stretch means shorten the bottom; a pinch at the front or top of the shoulder means do a cable pushdown instead today.

Easier: hold the working upper arm in place with your free hand, or sit on a bench with an upright backrest so your back can't arch. Harder: lower over 3 seconds and pause 1–2 seconds in the stretch before you add weight.
The plates pass right behind your head and neck. Tighten the collars on an adjustable dumbbell, and always bring it down in front of you; never let it drop behind you.

Substitutes: Standing One Dumbbell French Press or Dumbbell Seated Triceps Extension to load a heavier dumbbell with both hands; One-Arm Katana Triceps Overhead Extension, the cable version that still pulls at lockout and comes in small weight steps; Cable Overhead Triceps Extension to stretch both arms at once with a rope.

exercises.description: Stand facing a high pulley and sweep one straight arm from head height down to your thigh to train one lat at a time, with no help from the biceps. The work runs from your armpit down the side of your back: the lat first, then the teres major at the back of the armpit and the infraspinatus and teres minor on the shoulder blade. Your free hand on your hip tells you if your torso twists. Pick it if you can't feel your lats in pulldowns and rows or one side lags. Want the elbow to bend and the handle to reach your shoulder? That's the One-Arm Lat Pulldown.
instructions: Clip a single handle to the high pulley and pick a light weight; one arm moves far less than two arms on a bar.
Hold the handle like a ski pole: thumb toward the pulley, palm facing in, wrist straight. No need to squeeze it hard.
Face the tower with the pulley in line with your shoulder and step back until the stack lifts, arm straight and hand at head height.
Stand tall with feet hip-width, knees soft and ribs down, and rest your free hand on your hip.
Pull the shoulder down first, then sweep the straight arm down in front of you until your hand is beside your thigh.
Hold a second, then take 2–3 seconds to let the arm rise along the same arc until you feel a stretch under your armpit.
Do every rep on one arm, then switch. Start with your weaker side and match its reps on the other.
mistakes: Bending the elbow on the way down until it turns into a one-arm pulldown or a triceps pushdown. Set a soft elbow at the top and keep that angle; hand and upper arm move as one piece from the shoulder. Can't do it? Lighten the weight.
Twisting toward the working side or leaning back to finish the rep. Keep the free hand on your hip and both hips and shoulders square to the tower. If the torso has to move, the weight is too heavy.

Shrugging, or letting the shoulder roll forward at the bottom. Pull the shoulder down before the arm moves and finish with the arm by your side, chest tall, hand next to the thigh rather than pushed forward or behind your hip.
Cutting the top short: the hand stops at chest height and the lat never gets a stretch. Let it rise to about head height on every rep, and step back if the weight touches down.
exercises.name: One-Arm Straight-Arm Cable Lat Pulldown
tips: Two or three sets of 10–15 reps per arm suit this lift, or up to 20 when you let the arm rise slowly.

Going heavier than about 8–10 clean reps per arm rarely pays off here. Add reps before weight: when both arms reach 15 on all sets with a straight elbow, a still torso and a one-second hold at the thigh, move the pin down one plate (usually 2.5–5 kg) and restart at 10. One arm feels a 5 kg jump far more than two do, so on a stack with big plates use the add-on weight or stay longer on reps.

Most of the work lands from your armpit down the side of your back toward your waist, and at the back of the armpit and over the shoulder blade. Some work at the back of the upper arm is normal; if your triceps burn more than your back, the elbow is bending and straightening.

If raising the arm to head height pinches the front of your shoulder, or the elbow and torso won't stay still, start the arc at shoulder height with less weight, or do the two-arm rope version for a while. To make it harder, take 3 seconds to let the arm rise and hold 2 seconds at the thigh; later, hinge forward about 30° so the arm starts in line with your torso and the stretch gets longer.

Use this one-arm version to work each lat on its own and even out your sides, and the two-arm versions to move more weight in less time. Substitutes: Straight-Arm Lat Pulldown, Rope Straight-Arm Lat Pulldown (the closest two-arm version, same neutral grip), Dumbbell Pullover (no cable needed), Machine Pullover (the seat holds your torso still).

Straighten your elbows until your arms are vertical and locked out, and hold for half a second.
Only your forearms move; your upper arms stay by your ears.
Take 2–3 seconds to lower the bar along the same arc until it is behind your head again, without letting the plates touch down.
When you finish, step back toward the stack with your elbows still bent until the weight rests, then bring the bar down in front of you.
mistakes: Elbows flaring wide as the bar drops behind your head. Point them up and slightly forward, about shoulder-width apart, and take a slightly narrower grip or less weight if they keep drifting out.
Upper arms swinging forward on the way up until the rep turns into a press. Keep them beside your head and move only your forearms; if you can't, the weight is too heavy.
Arching your lower back to drive the bar up while the cable pulls you back. Ribs down, abs braced, feet staggered, and lean your whole body forward a little instead of just your chest.
Standing in the wrong spot: too close and the plates touch down in the stretch, too far and the cable tips you backward. Find the spot where the stack stays up with your elbows fully bent.

Reversing the rep with the bar at the top of your head. Lower until your elbows are fully bent and the bar is behind your head on every pain-free rep; that stretch is the reason to pick this exercise.
Wrists bending back under the bar. Set it in the heel of your palm with your thumbs wrapped, wrists in line with your forearms.
exercises.name: Overhead Cable Triceps Extension (Bar)
tips: Two to four sets of 10–15 reps suit this lift, most of them ending one or two reps short of failure.

Add reps first: once all sets reach 15 with a full stretch and a full lockout, move the pin down one plate and start again at 10. One plate is a big jump on a two-arm triceps lift, so use the stack's add-on weight if it has one, or expect a few sessions at each weight.

At the bottom you should feel a strong pull along the back of your upper arm toward the armpit, and at lockout a hard squeeze down the whole back of the arm. Lower back working? Your ribs are flaring, so brace harder or go lighter. Sharp pain at the tip or inner side of the elbow means shorten the stretch or switch to the rope, and a pinch at the top of the shoulder means today is a pushdown day.
Easier: use the same setup in tall kneeling with your back to the stack, so your hips can't sway and your lower back arches less. Harder: pause 1–2 seconds in the stretch and take 3 seconds to lower.

Substitutes: Cable Overhead Triceps Extension, the same lift with a rope, if the bar bothers your wrists or elbows; Standing One Dumbbell French Press when all you have is one dumbbell; Standing Overhead Barbell Triceps Extension, which gets easy near lockout; High Pulley Overhead Triceps Extension, where the cable pulls hardest in the stretch.

exercises.description: The Overhead Triceps Stretch is a static stretch exercise targeting the triceps brachii muscles. It helps improve flexibility and range of motion in the shoulders and arms, reducing the risk of injury and aiding in muscle recovery.
instructions: Stand or sit with your back straight and feet shoulder-width apart.
Raise your right arm overhead, bending the elbow to bring your right hand down towards the middle of your upper back.
Use your left hand to gently push on your right elbow, deepening the stretch.
Hold the position for 15-30 seconds, feeling the stretch in your triceps and shoulder.
Release and switch arms, repeating the stretch on the opposite side.
mistakes: Failing to keep the elbow pointed directly upwards, causing misalignment and reduced stretch effectiveness.
Allowing the back to arch excessively, which can lead to lower back strain.
Not engaging the core muscles, resulting in poor posture and stability.
Pulling the elbow too aggressively, risking shoulder strain.
Holding the stretch with a bent wrist, reducing the stretch on the triceps.
Failing to keep the head in a neutral position, leading to neck discomfort.
Allowing the shoulder to elevate towards the ear, reducing stretch isolation on the triceps.
exercises.name: Overhead Triceps Stretch
tips: Keep your core engaged to maintain a stable posture throughout the stretch.
Avoid arching your back; keep it straight to prevent strain.
Breathe deeply and consistently to help relax your muscles during the stretch.
If you feel any pain or discomfort, ease off slightly until you find a comfortable stretch.
Perform this stretch after workouts to aid in muscle recovery and flexibility.

exercises.description: The Patrick step loads one leg as its knee moves forward over the toes on a low step. Bend the standing knee to lower the free heel toward the floor in front, keeping the working heel planted. Touch down lightly, then straighten the working leg without pushing off with the free foot.
instructions: Stand on a low step or sturdy platform with one foot fully supported near the front edge. Let the other leg hang straight in front of the platform.
Keep your standing knee tracking in line with your toes and hold your chest tall. Lightly brace your abdomen.
Slowly bend the standing knee and lower your body straight down until the heel of the free leg gently touches the floor in front of the platform.
Keep most of the pressure through the whole foot of the working leg. Do not let the knee collapse inward or the heel lift off the step.
Press through the working foot to straighten the leg and return to the starting position without pushing off the floor with the free leg.
Complete all repetitions on one side, then switch legs. Use a lower step or hold a support if you cannot control the descent.
mistakes: Letting the working knee collapse inward.
Dropping the pelvis on the non-working side during the descent.
Pushing off the floor with the free foot.
Lowering too quickly and bouncing off the floor.
Using a step that is too high, causing the pelvis to twist or the back to round.
Leaning the torso excessively forward to avoid loading the working leg.
exercises.name: Patrick Step
tips: Place the entire supporting foot on the step before lowering.
Keep the working heel planted on the step throughout the movement.
Exhale as you lift and inhale as you return.
Hold a fixed support while learning the single-leg balance.
Use the same range and repetition count on both sides.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/chest/停顿式杠铃卧推

exercises.description: The paused bench press trains the chest and triceps while removing the bounce at the bottom. Lie on a flat bench, lower the bar to your lower chest and hold it still while maintaining body tension. Press up and slightly back toward your shoulders, keeping your feet planted and hips on the bench.
instructions: Set a barbell in a rack above a flat bench. Load it evenly and use collars. Set the safety pins just below the bar path if available.
Lie on the bench with your eyes under the bar. Place your feet flat on the floor, slightly behind your knees, and keep them planted throughout the set.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench. Keep your upper back, head and glutes in contact with the bench, with a small natural arch in your lower back.
Grip the bar evenly, slightly wider than shoulder width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar and keep your wrists stacked over your forearms.
Take a deep breath, brace your torso, and unrack the bar with straight arms. Move the bar until it is balanced over your shoulders.
Lower the bar under control to the lower chest or sternum area. Keep your elbows at a comfortable angle, not flared straight out to the sides.
Let the bar touch your chest lightly and hold it completely still for the planned pause. Maintain full-body tension and do not relax on the bench.
Press the bar up after the pause, driving through your feet and keeping your shoulder blades set. Press the bar slightly back toward the rack until your elbows are locked.
mistakes: Bouncing the bar off the chest.
Letting the bar sink into the chest during the pause.
Relaxing the upper back or losing shoulder blade retraction at the bottom.
Flaring the elbows too early or excessively during the descent.
Lowering the bar to the neck or upper chest.
Lifting the hips or losing stable foot pressure during the press.
exercises.name: Paused Bench Press
tips: Grip the bar evenly, with wrists stacked over your forearms. Use a grip width that lets your forearms stay close to vertical at the bottom.
Unrack the bar with straight arms and bring it over your shoulder joints before starting the rep.
Exhale as you lift and inhale as you return.
Use less weight than for a normal touch and go bench press, especially while learning to maintain a true pause.
Use a spotter or safety arms when training close to failure, and agree on the pause length before the set.

exercises.description: Perform a barbell back squat and hold the bottom position before standing up, keeping tension through the pause. The stop removes the rebound from the descent and makes you initiate the ascent from a stable squat position with the bar supported across the upper back.
instructions: Place the bar across your upper back, grip it firmly and extend your legs to lift it out of the rack.
Step back one or two small steps and place your feet about shoulder width apart, with your toes turned slightly out.
Take a deep breath into your abdomen and brace your trunk as if preparing for a punch.
Start the squat by bending at the hips and knees together.
Lower under control until your hip crease is at least level with the top of your knee, or to the deepest position you can maintain without losing spinal position or foot contact.
Hold the bottom position for the prescribed pause, usually one to three seconds.
Drive up by pushing the floor away through your midfoot.
Finish standing tall with your knees and hips fully extended.
mistakes: Letting the knees cave inward during the descent, pause, or ascent.
Rising onto the toes or letting the heels lift off the floor.
Losing a neutral spine and rounding the lower back at the bottom.
Dropping too quickly into the bottom position and losing control before the pause.
Shifting the hips to one side or loading one leg more than the other.
Letting the chest collapse forward and turning the squat into a good morning.
exercises.name: Paused Squat
tips: Take a full breath into your abdomen before each rep and keep your chest, ribs, and pelvis stacked as you descend.
Keep the pause consistent, usually one to three seconds, and do not use a bounce out of the bottom.
Exhale only after you are through the hardest part of the ascent, then reset your breath and brace before the next rep.
Use less weight than your regular squat at first, since the pause removes momentum and makes the bottom position more demanding.
Set the safety pins just below your lowest controlled squat depth, especially when training heavy paused squats without a spotter.

exercises.description: Sit with your back on the pec deck, forearms against the pads, and squeeze the pads together in front of your chest to build your pecs. Your elbows stay bent at about 90° and your hands only rest on the handles, so your forearms do the pushing, not your grip. The whole chest works, the middle near the breastbone hardest, while the front delts help only a little. The short lever and the backrest make it easy to learn and easy on the elbows, so many lifters use it to finish chest day after presses.
instructions: Set the seat so that, sitting tall, your elbows are level with your shoulders or slightly below and your shoulders sit right under the machine's pivots.
Before you sit, set the start-position adjuster, if there is one, so your elbows open only to the line of your body. Pick the weight now too.
Sit with your back and shoulder blades flat on the backrest, chest up, and feet flat on the floor a little wider than your hips.
Put your forearms upright against the pads with your elbows at the bottom end, bent about 90°. Your hands just rest on the top handles.
Breathe out and drive your elbows toward the middle of your chest until the pads touch. Squeeze for a second while your upper back stays on the backrest.
Breathe in as the pads open over about 2 seconds, back to the line of your body with a stretch across your chest. Keep the stack off its rest until the last rep.
mistakes: Pushing with your hands: a tight grip, bent wrists, forearms drifting off the pads. Hold the handles loosely, or open your hands, and press through your forearms and elbows.

Elbows sliding down the pads until the fly turns into a press and the front of your shoulder takes over. Set the seat so your upper arms are close to level, and keep your elbows at the bottom of the pads at the same height on every rep.
Rounding your shoulders off the backrest to make the pads meet. Your upper back and shoulder blades stay on the pad; if the pads won't touch that way, the weight is too heavy.
Opening too far or bouncing out of the stretch until the front of the shoulder pinches. Set the start so your elbows stop in line with your body, and turn around slowly at the open end.
Slamming the pads together, leaning back and letting the stack crash between reps. Go lighter and count it out: about 1.5 seconds in, a one-second squeeze, 2 seconds out.
exercises.name: Pec Deck Chest Fly
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 10–15 reps, sometimes up to 20, stopping 0–2 reps short of failure. Sets heavier than about 8–10 reps rarely pay off on this machine.

Add reps at the same weight until you get 15 on every set with the pads touching, a one-second squeeze and a 2-second return. Then move the pin down one plate (usually 2.5–5 kg) and work up again from 10. If a plate is too big a jump, use the add-on weight or hold the squeeze longer first.

The chest does the work: near the breastbone as the pads meet, and as a stretch toward your armpits when they open. Tired forearms or fingers mean you're pushing with your hands. A pinch at the front of the shoulder in the open position means the arms open too far or the seat is at the wrong height, so fix that before you add weight.

New to the machine? Use a light weight and set the start so your elbows open only to a hand's width in front of your body, then widen it as the movement gets familiar. Once the full range feels easy, make the same weight harder with a 3-second return and a one-second pause in the stretch.

Substitutes: Machine Chest Fly if your machine has handles and long arms instead of pads, Seated Cable Fly as the closest cable version with back support, Cable Middle Chest Fly for constant tension over a longer arc, and Dumbbell Chest Fly when all you have is dumbbells. Machine Reverse Flyes are a different exercise: you sit facing the backrest of a similar (often combination) machine and open your arms backward.

exercises.description: The Pendlay Row is a barbell exercise that targets the upper back, lats, and traps. It emphasizes strict form and explosive power from a dead stop position, making it an effective movement for building strength and muscle mass in the back.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and position a loaded barbell on the floor in front of you.
Bend at the hips and knees to lower your torso until it is nearly parallel to the ground, maintaining a neutral spine.
Grip the barbell with an overhand grip, slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Engage your core and retract your shoulder blades.
Lift the barbell explosively from the floor to your lower chest, keeping your elbows close to your body.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, then lower the barbell back to the floor under control.
Reset your position and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using momentum to lift the bar instead of controlled muscle engagement.
Not maintaining a neutral spine, leading to excessive rounding of the back.
Lifting the bar too high, causing shoulder strain.
Allowing the hips to rise, reducing the focus on the back muscles.
Failing to fully return the bar to the ground between reps, leading to partial range of motion.
Not engaging the core, resulting in instability and reduced power.
Pulling with the arms instead of initiating the movement with the back muscles.
Positioning the feet too close together, compromising balance and stability.
Not keeping the elbows close to the body, which can lead to shoulder stress.
exercises.name: Pendlay Row
tips: Ensure your back remains flat throughout the movement to avoid injury.
Keep your head in a neutral position by looking slightly ahead on the ground.
Focus on pulling with your elbows rather than your hands to engage your back muscles more effectively.
Use a controlled motion when lowering the barbell to maintain tension in the muscles.
Start with a lighter weight to perfect your form before progressing to heavier loads.
Maintain a strong core engagement to stabilize your body during each rep.

exercises.description: A plate-loaded machine squat in which your back rests on a pad that swings along a fixed arc while your feet stay on an angled platform. The arc lets you sink into a very deep squat with your torso supported, so the quadriceps do most of the work and the glutes help drive you out of the bottom.
instructions: Load plates onto the machine's lever and step onto the foot platform with your feet about shoulder-width apart.
Lean back against the pad, set your shoulders under the shoulder pads and grip the handles on top of them.
Straighten your legs to take the weight and release the safety lever if your machine has one.
Brace your core and bend your knees and hips to lower yourself as the pad swings down along its arc.
Go as deep as you can while your heels stay flat and your lower back stays on the pad.
Push through your whole foot to stand back up, stopping just before your knees lock.
After the last rep, engage the safety lever if there is one and step off the platform.
mistakes: Lifting the heels off the platform at the bottom
Letting the knees cave inward on the way up
Letting the lower back come off the pad and round at the bottom
Doing half reps with a heavy load instead of using the full depth the machine allows
Dropping fast into the bottom and bouncing out of it, which jolts the knees
Pushing through the toes instead of the whole foot
Locking the knees hard at the top, which takes the tension off the quads
exercises.name: Pendulum Squat
tips: Place your feet lower on the platform to focus on the quads, or a little higher to bring in more glutes.
Let your knees travel forward past your toes at the bottom; that deep knee bend is what works the quads.
Take a breath and brace before each rep, then breathe out once you pass the hardest point on the way up.
Hold the handles lightly to stay in position; do not pull on them to sink deeper.
Start light to learn the machine's arc before you add plates.
Use the same foot position every session so you can compare your weights from week to week.

exercises.description: The Pigeon Pose is a yoga exercise that primarily targets the hip flexors and glutes. It is beneficial for improving flexibility, reducing lower back pain, and enhancing overall mobility. This pose involves extending one leg behind you while bending the other leg in front of you, creating a deep stretch in the hips.
instructions: Begin in a tabletop position on your hands and knees.
Bring your right knee forward towards your right wrist. Angle your right shin under your torso and bring your right foot to the front of your left knee.
Slide your left leg back, straightening the knee and lowering the front of the thigh to the floor.
Square your hips towards the mat, ensuring they are not tilted to one side.
Inhale to lengthen your spine, and as you exhale, fold forward over your right leg, resting on your forearms or extending your arms forward.
Hold the position for 30 seconds to 2 minutes, breathing deeply.
To release, push back through the hands and lift your hips, returning to a tabletop position.
Repeat on the opposite side.
mistakes: Hips are not squared to the front, causing uneven stretch.
Front knee is not bent at a 90-degree angle, leading to improper alignment.
Back leg is not extended straight behind, reducing stretch effectiveness.
Torso is not aligned over the hips, causing imbalance.
Shoulders are hunched instead of relaxed, leading to tension.
Front foot is too close to the body, limiting hip stretch.
Back foot is not actively engaged, causing instability.
Neck is strained by looking up or down excessively.
Weight is unevenly distributed, putting stress on the front knee.
Breathing is shallow, reducing relaxation and stretch depth.
exercises.name: Pigeon Pose
tips: Keep your hips square to ensure an even stretch on both sides.
If you feel discomfort in the knee, place a folded blanket or cushion under the hip of the bent leg for support.
Focus on deep breathing to help relax into the stretch and release tension.
Ensure that the back leg is extended straight behind you with toes pointing downwards.
Avoid forcing yourself into the pose; ease into it gradually as flexibility improves.

exercises.description: Pike Push Ups are a bodyweight exercise targeting the shoulders, triceps, and upper chest. This exercise mimics the overhead pressing movement and is performed in a pike position, which increases the load on the shoulders compared to regular push-ups.
instructions: Begin in a downward dog position with your hands shoulder-width apart and your feet hip-width apart.
Walk your feet closer to your hands to form an inverted V shape with your body.
Keep your legs straight and your hips high, ensuring your back is flat.
Lower your head towards the ground by bending your elbows, keeping them pointed outwards.
Stop when your head is just above the ground, then push through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Maintain a neutral neck position throughout the movement.
mistakes: Hands placed too far apart, reducing shoulder engagement.
Elbows flaring out excessively, increasing strain on the shoulders.
Not maintaining a straight line from hips to hands, leading to poor form.
Allowing the head to drop too low, risking neck strain.
Failing to engage the core, causing a loss of stability.
Not controlling the descent, leading to a lack of muscle tension.
Inadequate range of motion, limiting shoulder activation.
Hips sagging, reducing effectiveness and increasing lower back strain.
Feet positioned too close to hands, compromising balance and form.
Rushing the movement, sacrificing control and precision.
exercises.name: Pike Push-Up
tips: Focus on keeping your core engaged to maintain balance and stability.
Ensure that your elbows are not flaring out excessively; they should be at about a 45-degree angle from your body.
If you're new to this exercise, start with a smaller range of motion and gradually increase as you build strength.
Keep your movements controlled and avoid bouncing at the bottom of the push-up.
Practice proper breathing by inhaling as you lower yourself and exhaling as you push back up.

exercises.description: The Pike Push Up Between Benches is an advanced bodyweight exercise targeting the shoulders, triceps, and upper chest. By elevating the feet on benches, this variation increases the range of motion and intensity, simulating an overhead press movement.
instructions: Position two benches parallel to each other, about shoulder-width apart.
Place your feet on one bench and your hands on the other, forming a pike position with your hips elevated.
Keep your body inverted with your legs straight and core engaged.
Lower your head towards the floor by bending your elbows, keeping them close to your body.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement, then push through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Maintain control throughout the movement and avoid arching your back.
mistakes: Placing hands too wide or too narrow, affecting shoulder engagement.
Allowing elbows to flare out excessively, reducing tricep activation.
Failing to maintain a straight line from hips to shoulders, causing lower back strain.
Not lowering head between benches, limiting range of motion.
Rushing through the movement, compromising control and stability.
Neglecting to engage core, leading to sagging hips.
Positioning feet too close to hands, reducing the effectiveness of the pike position.
Overarching the lower back, increasing risk of discomfort or strain.
Not aligning wrists directly under shoulders, causing wrist discomfort.
exercises.name: Pike Push-Up Between Benches
tips: Ensure that both benches are stable and can support your weight.
Focus on keeping your core tight to maintain balance and proper form.
Keep your elbows tucked in to engage the triceps more effectively.
Control the descent to maximize muscle engagement and prevent injury.
Breathe in as you lower yourself and exhale as you push back up.
If new to this exercise, start with a lower elevation or perform regular pike push-ups until strength improves.

exercises.description: The Pike Push Up Between Chairs is an advanced bodyweight exercise targeting the shoulders, triceps, and upper chest. It involves elevating your hands and feet on chairs, creating a pike position to increase the range of motion and intensity. This exercise requires significant shoulder strength and stability.
instructions: Place two sturdy chairs shoulder-width apart for your hands and one chair behind you for your feet.
Position yourself in a pike position with your hands on the chairs and your feet elevated on the third chair.
Ensure your body forms an inverted V shape with hips raised high.
Lower your head towards the ground by bending your elbows, keeping them slightly flared out.
Pause briefly when your head is close to the floor, then push through your palms to return to the starting position.
Maintain a neutral neck position throughout the movement.
mistakes: Feet positioned too far forward or backward, disrupting balance and reducing effectiveness.
Hands placed too wide or too narrow on the chairs, leading to poor shoulder engagement.
Head dropping too low, causing neck strain and loss of alignment.
Hips not elevated high enough, reducing shoulder activation.
Elbows flaring out excessively, increasing shoulder strain.
Insufficient range of motion, limiting muscle engagement.
Rushing through the movement, compromising control and form.
Core not engaged, leading to sagging hips and poor stability.
Failing to keep a straight line from hips to head, affecting posture and effectiveness.
exercises.name: Pike Push-Up Between Chairs
tips: Keep your core engaged to maintain balance and stability.
Focus on controlled movements to maximize muscle engagement.
Ensure the chairs are stable and won't slip during the exercise.
If you're new to this exercise, start with lower elevation or perform regular pike push-ups on the floor.
Breathe in as you lower down and exhale as you push back up.
Keep your elbows slightly bent at the top of the movement to maintain tension in the muscles.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/肩部/斜板俯卧撑

exercises.description: The Pike Push Up On Bench is a bodyweight exercise targeting the shoulders, triceps, and upper chest. It involves elevating the feet on a bench to increase the angle of the body, which shifts more emphasis onto the shoulders compared to a standard push-up.
instructions: Begin by positioning yourself in front of a bench. Place your feet on the bench and your hands on the floor, shoulder-width apart.
Walk your hands back towards the bench until your body forms an inverted V shape, with your hips elevated and head pointing downwards.
Keep your legs straight and core engaged throughout the movement.
Lower your head towards the floor by bending your elbows, keeping them slightly flared out.
Pause briefly when your head is close to the floor, then push through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Hands placed too wide, reducing shoulder engagement.
Elbows flaring out excessively, increasing shoulder strain.
Hips not elevated high enough, decreasing emphasis on shoulders.
Head looking forward instead of down, causing neck strain.
Feet positioned too far from the bench, reducing leverage and control.
Lowering body too quickly, leading to poor control and form.
Failing to engage core, causing instability and lower back strain.
Not achieving full range of motion, limiting shoulder activation.
Allowing shoulders to shrug, reducing effectiveness and increasing tension.
exercises.name: Pike Push-Up On Bench
tips: Ensure that your hands are placed firmly on the ground to maintain stability.
Focus on keeping your core tight to prevent sagging or arching of the back.
Control the movement by lowering slowly and pushing up with steady force.
Keep your elbows at a slight angle rather than flaring them directly out to reduce strain on the joints.
Adjust the height of the bench if needed to modify difficulty; a higher bench increases difficulty by shifting more weight onto the shoulders.
Breathing is crucial: inhale as you lower down and exhale as you push up.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腹肌/v形普拉提百次拍击

exercises.description: From lying on your back, raise the straight legs and torso into a high V position, passing through a hollow hold with the arms overhead. Reach the arms toward the feet and pump them in small movements while holding the V. This variation of the hundred combines abdominal tension with steady breathing.
instructions: Lie on your back with legs straight and arms beside you.
Brace your abdomen and raise the legs and shoulders into a hollow hold, reaching the arms overhead.
Raise your torso into the high V while keeping your straight legs at their raised angle, balancing through the pelvis.
Reach both arms toward your feet and keep the elbows straight.
Pump the arms in small movements while holding the torso and legs steady.
Breathe in for five pumps and out for five, then lower the body under control when finished.
mistakes: Rounding and collapsing the torso instead of holding the V.
Pulling the chin forward and straining the neck.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears.
Bending and straightening the elbows to pump the arms.
Rocking the pelvis or letting the legs shift side to side.
Rushing the entry into the V with an uncontrolled swing.
exercises.name: Pilates Hundred in V Position
tips: Reach the hands long toward the feet.
Use a small, even rhythm for the arm pumps.
Keep the leg angle high enough to hold the V steadily.
Start with fewer breathing cycles and build toward ten.
Inhale through the nose and exhale smoothly without losing abdominal tension.

exercises.description: The Pin Bench Press is a variation of the traditional bench press where the barbell is pressed from a dead stop off safety pins set at a specific height. This exercise targets the chest, triceps, and shoulders, and is particularly useful for improving lockout strength and overcoming sticking points in the bench press.
instructions: Set up a flat bench inside a power rack and adjust the safety pins to the desired height, typically just above chest level.
Lie on the bench with your eyes directly under the barbell. Ensure your feet are flat on the floor and your back is slightly arched.
Grip the barbell with a slightly wider than shoulder-width grip, ensuring your wrists are straight and elbows are directly under the bar.
Unrack the barbell and lower it slowly until it rests on the safety pins. Pause briefly to eliminate momentum.
Press the barbell upwards explosively until your arms are fully extended.
Lower the barbell back to the pins with control and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Setting the pins too high, limiting range of motion and reducing muscle engagement.
Arching the lower back excessively, leading to poor form and potential strain.
Failing to maintain shoulder blades retracted, causing shoulder instability.
Using a grip that is too wide or too narrow, affecting leverage and muscle activation.
Bouncing the bar off the pins, reducing control and increasing risk of joint stress.
Not aligning the bar with the wrists and elbows, leading to inefficient pressing mechanics.
Allowing elbows to flare out excessively, placing undue stress on the shoulders.
Neglecting to engage the core, resulting in a lack of stability and power.
Rushing the movement, compromising control and precision.
exercises.name: Pin Bench Press
tips: Ensure that the safety pins are set at a height that allows for a full range of motion without compromising form.

exercises.description: The Pin Front Squat is a variation of the traditional front squat where the barbell is set on safety pins within a power rack. This exercise emphasizes quadriceps strength, core stability, and proper squat mechanics by limiting the range of motion and allowing for a controlled pause at the bottom position.
instructions: Set the safety pins in a power rack at a height that allows you to squat to parallel or slightly below.
Position the barbell on the safety pins and stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the barbell with an overhand grip, elbows pointing forward, and position it across your shoulders, resting on your deltoids.
Engage your core and lift the barbell off the pins by extending your legs to stand up straight.
Initiate the squat by bending at the hips and knees, lowering your body until the barbell lightly touches the pins.
Pause briefly at the bottom, maintaining tension in your muscles.
Drive through your heels to extend your hips and knees, returning to a standing position.

Not engaging the core, leading to a loss of stability and potential back strain.
Failing to maintain an upright torso, resulting in excessive forward lean.
Starting the squat too low, causing the pins to interfere with the movement.
Using a grip that's too wide or too narrow, affecting bar stability and control.
Descending too quickly, which can lead to bouncing off the pins and loss of form.
Not setting the pins at the correct height, leading to incomplete range of motion.
Neglecting to keep the knees aligned with the toes, increasing knee stress.
Rising unevenly, which can cause imbalance and shift the weight improperly.
exercises.name: Pin Front Squat
tips: Ensure that your elbows remain high throughout the movement to keep the barbell stable on your shoulders.
Focus on maintaining an upright torso to prevent leaning forward excessively.
Use a controlled tempo when lowering into the squat to maximize muscle engagement.
Keep your core tight throughout the exercise to support your lower back and maintain balance.
Adjust the pin height based on your flexibility and comfort level to ensure proper depth without compromising form.

Stand under the bar with your feet shoulder-width apart and position it across your upper back, ensuring it is centered.
Grip the bar firmly with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
Engage your core, retract your shoulder blades, and maintain a neutral spine.
Lift the bar off the pins by driving through your heels and extending your hips and knees simultaneously.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower the bar back to the pins by bending your hips and knees, maintaining control throughout.

Not engaging the core, resulting in instability and poor posture.

Experiment with different pin heights to target specific weaknesses in your squat.

exercises.description: The Pistol Box Squat is a unilateral lower body exercise that targets the quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings, and core. instructions: Stand in front of a box or bench with your feet hip-width apart.
Lift one leg off the ground, extending it forward while keeping it straight.
Engage your core and maintain an upright posture.
Slowly lower your body by bending the knee of the standing leg, pushing your hips back as if sitting down.
Descend until your glutes lightly touch the box or bench.
Pause briefly at the bottom position to maintain control.
Press through the heel of the standing leg to return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions before switching legs.

Allowing the heel of the standing foot to lift off the ground, compromising balance.
Dropping too quickly onto the box, reducing muscle engagement and control.
Not fully extending the standing leg at the top of the movement, limiting range of motion.

Allowing the non-working leg to touch the ground, decreasing the effectiveness of the exercise.
exercises.name: Pistol Box Squat
tips: Ensure that your knee tracks over your toes to avoid unnecessary strain.
Keep your chest up and shoulders back throughout the movement.
Use a box height that allows you to maintain control and proper form.
Focus on engaging your core to help with balance and stability.
Start with a higher box if you're new to this exercise and gradually decrease the height as you become more proficient.
Perform the movement slowly to maximize muscle engagement and control.

exercises.description: Rest on your forearms and toes and hold one straight line from head to heels, training your abs to keep your hips from sagging. You feel it most in the front of your stomach and the sides of your waist, while your glutes squeeze to keep the hips level. The front of your shoulders, your triceps and your thighs just hold you up. All you need is a patch of floor, so it suits beginners, home workouts and the end of a session. Unlike the Bear Plank, your knees stay straight, which makes the lever longer and the hold harder.
instructions: Kneel on the floor and set your forearms down with your elbows right under your shoulders, forearms parallel and pointing straight ahead, palms flat.
Step your feet back one at a time onto the balls of your feet, toes tucked and feet close together. If you wobble, widen them to hip width.
Lift your knees until your body forms one straight line from head to heels, hips in line with your shoulders and heels, eyes on the floor just ahead of your hands.
Brace before you start the clock: ribs down toward your pelvis, tailbone tucked slightly toward your heels, glutes squeezed hard.
Push the floor away with your forearms so your chest doesn't sink between your shoulder blades, then hold still and keep taking short, quiet breaths.
The set is over as soon as your hips drop or start to rise. Lower your knees to the floor and sit back on your heels.
mistakes: Hips sagging until the lower back arches. You usually feel it as an ache low in the back. Tuck your pelvis slightly, squeeze your glutes and pull your ribs down; if the hips keep dropping, end the set or switch to the knee plank.

Piking the hips up high. It feels easier because your abs get a break. Lower them until shoulders, hips and heels line up; a mirror, or a broomstick along your back touching your head, upper back and the base of your spine, will show you.
Chest sinking between the shoulder blades, or elbows creeping out in front of the shoulders. Stack the elbows back under your shoulders and push the floor away with your forearms.
Holding your breath or sucking your belly in. Brace as if someone is about to punch you in the stomach, then keep taking short breaths behind that brace.
Chasing 3–5 minute holds while the hips slowly sink. Stop at the first break in position; once 60 seconds is clean, add weight or a harder variant instead of more time.
exercises.name: Plank
tips: Hold 30–60 seconds, 2–4 times. For a strength-style version, do 3–5 shorter holds of 10–20 seconds, squeezing everything as hard as you can, with 30–60 seconds of rest.

Add time first, then load: 5–10 seconds per hold each session while the line from head to heels stays the same. Once all your holds reach a clean 60 seconds, have a partner set a 5 kg (10 lb) plate between your shoulder blades or move to a harder variant, and drop back to 20–30 second holds.
The front of your stomach and the sides of your waist should be burning. An ache in your lower back means your hips have dropped: stop and reset instead of pushing through.

Too hard? Put your knees down and keep a straight line from head to knees, or rest your forearms on a bench. Too easy and no plate around? Lift one foot an inch or two for 5–10 seconds per side. On a hard floor, a folded towel under the elbows helps.

Substitutes: Bear Plank if your lower back complains, Hollow Body Hold for the same ab work lying on your back with no weight on the elbows, and Weighted Plank or Swiss Ball Plank once the regular plank gets easy.

exercises.description: Start in a high plank with straight arms and your hands below your shoulders. Lift one straight leg behind you while keeping your hips level, then lower the foot and change legs. Keep your trunk braced throughout, lifting only as far as you can without arching your lower back.
instructions: Start in a high plank with your hands under your shoulders, arms straight, and your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Place your feet about hip width apart for balance. Brace your abdomen, squeeze your glutes, and keep your neck neutral by looking slightly ahead of your hands.
Shift your weight gently into both hands and your grounded foot without letting your hips rotate or sag.
Keeping your lifting leg straight, raise one foot a few inches off the floor by squeezing the glute. Do not lift so high that your lower back arches.
Pause briefly, then lower the foot back to the floor with control.
Lift the opposite leg in the same way, keeping your shoulders level and hips square to the floor.
Continue alternating legs for the prescribed repetitions or time, maintaining a stable plank position throughout.

Brace your stomach, squeeze your glutes, and keep your body in a straight line from your head to your heels.

Rotate to the other side and lower the opposite hip toward the floor.

Keep your neck neutral by looking slightly ahead of your hands instead of letting your head hang.

Continue alternating between high plank and forearm plank at a controlled pace.
Change the arm you lead with regularly so both sides work evenly.

exercises.description: The Plate Bus Driver is a core and shoulder stability exercise that mimics the motion of turning a steering wheel. Return to the starting position and then rotate the plate to the right until your right hand is higher than your left.

Allowing the elbows to flare out excessively, straining the shoulders.

tips: Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid shrugging them up towards your ears.

exercises.description: Raise a plate to shoulder height with straight arms, turn it like a steering wheel both ways, then lower it: a front raise for the front and side delts. The front of your shoulders does most of the lifting, and the side delts work hard as long as the plate is up. On each turn, the shoulder of the hand going over the top takes a bit more. Your hips and chest face forward the whole time; the plate turns, your body doesn't. One plate is all you need, so it works as a shoulder warm-up or finisher at home or in a crowded gym.
instructions: Pick a plate you can grip firmly by the rim. Stand tall with your feet hip- to shoulder-width apart, knees soft and ribs down.
Hold the plate at 3 and 9 o'clock, palms facing each other and fingers wrapped around the edge, and let it rest flat in front of your thighs.
With your arms almost straight, raise the plate in an arc for about 2 seconds until your hands reach shoulder height. It tips upright on the way and ends up facing you.
Turn the plate a quarter turn to your left, like a steering wheel: your right hand goes over the top and your left hand drops to the bottom. Come back to the center.
Now a quarter turn to the right with the left hand on top, and back to the center. Belly button and chest keep pointing straight ahead, and you keep breathing.
Lower the plate in 2-3 seconds until it lies flat in front of your thighs again. One raise with both turns counts as one rep.
End the set as soon as the plate starts sinking during the turns: bring it down to your thighs first, then bend your knees to set it on the floor.
mistakes: Twisting your torso or hips to turn the plate. Keep your belly button and chest facing forward and let only your arms and the plate rotate; if your body keeps following, use a lighter plate.
Bending the elbows and pulling the plate toward your face during the turns. Keep your arms long and think of reaching the plate away from you as it rotates.
Letting the plate sink below shoulder height while you turn it. Turn it around its center at shoulder height, and stop the set once you can't hold that height.
Swinging the plate up by leaning back or snapping your hips. Knees soft, ribs down, glutes tight; take about 2 seconds to raise it, with no bounce off your thighs.
exercises.name: Plate Front Raise Drive
tips: Sets of 10-15 reps work well, 2-4 of them after your pressing or as a shoulder finisher.
Stay on the same plate until you get 15 on all of them with straight arms, full quarter turns and a slow lowering, then move up a plate and build the reps again.

Most people start with 2.5-5 kg; trained lifters often use 10 kg and rarely go past 15-20 kg. The next plate up is a big jump here, so first add a 1-2 second pause at each turn or take 3 seconds to lower.

The front of both shoulders works first, then the sides. If it shows up in your lower back or the sides of your waist, you are leaning back or twisting. Pain at the front of the shoulder as the arms come up means stop just below that height or take a lighter plate.
Dry hands or chalk help: a plate that slips out of your fingers at shoulder height lands on your feet.

Substitutes: Plate Front Raise (no turns, so you can go a little heavier; the easier option), Plate Bus Driver (the plate stays at shoulder height for the whole set; the harder one), Dumbbell Front Raise, and Barbell Front Raise for heavier loading.

exercises.description: Hold one weight plate at your side, pinching its rim between your thumb and fingers. Keep the arm long and the wrist straight as you bend your knees and hips into a squat, then stand back up. The legs move while the working hand maintains the pinch grip throughout.
instructions: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart.
Pinch the rim of one plate between your thumb and fingers.
Hold the plate at your side with a straight wrist and long arm.
Brace your trunk and bend your hips and knees to squat.
Push through your feet to stand, keeping the plate off your thigh.
Repeat under control, then lower the plate carefully and change hands.
mistakes: Hooking the fingers into the plate holes instead of pinching the rim.
Bending the wrist under the load.
Resting the plate against the thigh.
Swinging the plate as you squat.
Tilting the trunk toward the loaded hand.
Dropping the plate instead of placing it down under control.
exercises.name: Plate Pinch Squat
tips: Begin with a plate whose thickness fits your hand.
Wipe sweat from your hands before the set.
Breathe out as you stand and in as you squat.
Train both hands for the same number of sets.
Increase the number of controlled squats before adding plate weight.

exercises.description: Sit in a plate-loaded lever machine and press two independent handles forward from mid-chest to train your chest and triceps without a bar or spotter. Most of the work goes to the chest, across its whole width and hardest in the middle; your triceps finish each rep and the front delts help. Each lever carries its own plates, so a weaker arm can't hide behind the stronger one. A missed rep simply lands on the stops, which lets beginners and anyone training alone push close to failure. For quick weight changes and drop sets, the pin-loaded stack machine is the better pick.
instructions: Load the same plates on both horns. The levers move independently, so mismatched plates mean one arm pushes more than the other.
Set the seat so the handles rest level with your mid-chest, roughly at nipple height.
Sit with your hips all the way back and your back and head on the backrest. Plant your feet flat, about hip width, knees near 90°.
Take the horizontal handles overhand, knuckles up, hands a little wider than your shoulders and wrists straight over your forearms.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the pad before the first rep, and leave them pinned there until the set is over.
Press both handles along the machine's arc, which rises slightly and brings your hands closer, until your arms are almost straight. Your shoulders stay on the pad.
Take about 2 seconds to bring the handles back beside your chest, elbows just behind your torso, until you feel the stretch. Touch the bottom lightly and go again.
When the set is done, guide both handles back onto the rest stops. Don't let go of either handle until both levers are resting there.
mistakes: Handles starting at shoulder height because the seat is too low. Your front delts take over and the shoulder pinches at the bottom; raise the seat until the handles line up with your mid-chest.
Reaching for the last few inches at the top until your shoulders peel off the backrest. Stop where your arms are nearly straight, with your shoulder blades still on the pad.
One handle reaching the top before the other. Match the plates, press both at the same pace, and call the set when your weaker arm starts to lag.
Dropping into the bottom and bouncing the plates off the stops. Lower for about 2 seconds, touch lightly and press without a rebound.
Wrists bent back on the horizontal handles. Set the handle in the base of your palm, knuckles up, so the wrist sits right over the forearm.
Hips sliding forward and the lower back arching off the pad as the reps get hard. Sit all the way back with your feet flat and press with your arms, not by shoving through your legs.
exercises.name: Plate-Loaded Chest Press
tips: Put it first or second on chest day: 3–4 sets of 8–12 reps, or 5–8 for strength.
Build reps before weight. Once you get 12 on all sets at full depth with your shoulders on the pad, add the smallest plate to each lever (2 × 1.25 kg or 2 × 2.5 kg) and work the reps back up.
Log the plates per side. The lever changes the real resistance, so your numbers only compare with this same machine, not with your barbell bench.

The burn belongs across your chest, armpit to breastbone, with a clear stretch at the bottom and the triceps kicking in near the top. Feeling it mainly in the front delts? Check the seat height and whether your shoulders stay on the pad. If the front of the shoulder pinches in the stretch, raise the seat a notch or stop the handles a fist's width short of your chest.

Easier: lighter plates, or the pin-loaded machine with its smaller jumps. Harder: one-arm sets on a single lever, or 3 seconds down with a 1-second pause in the stretch. The free-weight step up is the Dumbbell Bench Press.

Substitutes: Machine Chest Press (the pin-loaded stack version, handy for drop sets), Dumbbell Bench Press for each arm moving freely, Barbell Bench Press for heavy low-rep work, and Seated Cable Chest Press when every press machine is taken.

exercises.description: The plate-loaded shoulder press is performed seated against a reclined back pad, pressing the handles from shoulder height to overhead. The machine arms guide the load while the shoulders and triceps extend the arms; keep the feet planted and lower the handles evenly with control.
instructions: Set the seat height so the handles start around shoulder level and you can grip them without reaching or shrugging your shoulders.
Load an appropriate weight evenly on both sides of the machine. Sit with your back flat against the pad, feet firmly on the floor, and your head in a neutral position.
Grip the handles with a full, secure grip. Keep your wrists straight and align your elbows slightly in front of or directly under your hands.
Brace the abdomen while keeping your back on the pad.
Press the handles upward by extending the elbows, letting the shoulder blades move naturally.
Finish with straight arms without snapping the elbows or lifting your hips from the seat.
Lower the handles slowly and under control until they return to shoulder level or to a comfortable depth with no shoulder pain.
Repeat for the planned number of repetitions. After the last repetition, return the handles fully to the starting position before releasing your grip.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows too far out to the sides instead of keeping them slightly forward and under the handles.
Arching the lower back and lifting the chest excessively to move the weight.
Using a range of motion that stops too high, without lowering the handles to a controlled bottom position.
Locking the elbows aggressively at the top instead of finishing the press with control.
Using momentum by bouncing the weight out of the bottom position.
Allowing the wrists to bend back instead of keeping them neutral and aligned with the forearms.
exercises.name: Plate-Loaded Shoulder Press
tips: Adjust the seat so the handles begin around shoulder height.
Load the same number of plates on both sides.
Check the handle movement with a light load first.
Exhale during the press and inhale during the return.
Settle the handles into their starting position before releasing them.

exercises.description: The Plyo Side Lunge is a dynamic exercise that combines lateral lunges with a plyometric jump, targeting the glutes, quadriceps, hamstrings, and inner thighs. It enhances lower body strength, agility, and balance while providing a cardiovascular challenge.
instructions: Start by standing with your feet hip-width apart and your arms at your sides.
Engage your core and take a large step to the right, bending your right knee and pushing your hips back into a side lunge position. Keep your left leg straight.
As you lower into the lunge, ensure your right knee is aligned with your right foot and does not extend past your toes.
Push off explosively with your right foot to jump back to the starting position.
Immediately step out to the left side and repeat the movement on the opposite leg.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Landing with locked knees instead of soft knees, increasing joint stress.
Failing to push hips back, leading to excessive knee strain.
Not maintaining a straight back, causing potential lower back discomfort.
Allowing the knee to cave inward, risking knee injury.
Neglecting to engage core muscles, reducing stability.
Jumping too high, losing control and balance.
Not fully extending the lunging leg, limiting range of motion.
Landing on toes instead of the whole foot, decreasing stability.
Rushing the movement, compromising form and effectiveness.
Uneven weight distribution, leading to muscle imbalance.
exercises.name: Plyo side lunge
tips: Maintain a tight core throughout the exercise to support balance and control.
Focus on landing softly on each jump to reduce impact on the joints.
Ensure that your knee does not extend beyond your toes during the lunge to protect your joints.
Keep your chest up and shoulders back to maintain proper posture.
Start with a smaller range of motion if you're new to this exercise, gradually increasing as you gain strength and confidence.
Use a mirror or ask for feedback to ensure proper form and alignment.
