Secure your thighs under the padded lever to ensure stability during the exercise.
Begin by pushing through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible, engaging your calf muscles.
Hold the top position for a moment, then slowly lower your heels back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control throughout the movement.
mistakes: Placing feet too high or too low on the platform, reducing calf engagement.
Locking knees, which shifts focus away from the calves and can cause joint strain.
Using excessive weight, leading to poor form and reduced range of motion.
Bouncing at the bottom of the movement, which decreases muscle activation.
Not fully extending the ankles at the top, limiting calf muscle contraction.
Allowing heels to drop too quickly, resulting in a lack of control.
Leaning forward excessively, which can shift the load away from the calves.
Neglecting to engage the core, causing instability and poor posture.
exercises.name: Rotary Calf Raise
tips: Ensure your knees remain slightly bent throughout the exercise to avoid unnecessary strain on the joints.
Focus on a slow and controlled movement to maximize muscle engagement and prevent injury.
Keep your core engaged to maintain stability and prevent excessive movement in other parts of your body.
Exhale as you lift your heels and inhale as you lower them back down.
Start with a lighter weight to master proper form before increasing resistance.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腹肌/旋转躯干

exercises.description: The Lever Trunk Rotation is an exercise targeting the oblique muscles and core stability. It involves rotating the torso against resistance, typically using a lever machine, to enhance rotational strength and improve core engagement.
instructions: Adjust the seat height on the lever machine so that the pivot point aligns with your midsection.
Sit down and secure your feet under the foot pads, ensuring your knees are slightly bent.
Grasp the handles firmly with both hands, keeping your elbows slightly bent.
Engage your core muscles and maintain an upright posture throughout the movement.
Slowly rotate your torso to one side, using your oblique muscles to control the motion.
Pause briefly at the end of the rotation to maximize muscle engagement.
Return to the starting position in a controlled manner.
Repeat the movement on the opposite side to complete one full repetition.
mistakes: Using momentum to swing the torso instead of controlled muscle engagement.
Allowing the hips to rotate along with the torso, reducing core activation.
Positioning the feet too far apart, limiting the range of motion.
Twisting beyond a safe range, risking strain on the lower back.
Neglecting to engage the core muscles, leading to ineffective exercise.
Holding the breath instead of maintaining a steady breathing pattern.
Leaning forward or backward, compromising spinal alignment.
Rushing through repetitions without focusing on form and control.
exercises.name: Rotary Torso
tips: Focus on using your oblique muscles rather than relying on momentum to perform the rotation.
Maintain a slow and controlled pace to ensure maximum muscle activation and reduce injury risk.
Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid shrugging them during the exercise.
Exhale as you rotate your torso and inhale as you return to the starting position.
Ensure that your hips remain stable and do not sway during the movement.
Start with a lighter weight to master proper form before increasing resistance.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/back/划船机

exercises.description: The rowing machine, also known as an ergometer, is a cardiovascular and strength training device that simulates the action of watercraft rowing. It engages multiple muscle groups, including the legs, back, arms, and core, providing a full-body workout. The machine consists of a sliding seat, footrests with straps, and a handle attached to a flywheel or resistance mechanism.
instructions: Adjust the footrests so that the straps are secure over the balls of your feet.
Sit on the sliding seat and grasp the handle with both hands using an overhand grip.
Start with your knees bent and your shins vertical, leaning slightly forward at the hips.
Push off with your legs while keeping your arms straight until they are fully extended.
Once your legs are straight, lean back slightly and pull the handle towards your lower ribs.
Reverse the motion by extending your arms first, then bending your knees to return to the starting position.
mistakes: Rounding the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Using only the arms instead of engaging the legs and core.
Leaning too far back at the end of the stroke.
Not fully extending the legs during the drive phase.
Bending the knees too early during the recovery phase.
Gripping the handle too tightly, causing unnecessary tension.
Pulling the handle to the chest instead of the lower ribs.
Rushing the recovery phase, leading to poor rhythm.
Not setting the damper setting appropriately for fitness level.
Letting the knees splay out instead of keeping them aligned.
exercises.name: Rowing Machine
tips: Maintain a straight back throughout the movement to avoid strain.
Focus on driving with your legs; they should initiate the movement.
Keep your core engaged to stabilize your body during the exercise.
Ensure smooth transitions between phases to maintain rhythm and efficiency.
Avoid hunching your shoulders; keep them relaxed and down.
Start with a low resistance setting to master technique before increasing intensity.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/负重背包行走

exercises.description: Rucking is steady walking with a loaded backpack held close to the back. The extra load increases the demand on the legs and trunk while the torso remains upright, the shoulders relaxed and the arms swinging naturally with short, comfortable steps throughout the walk.
instructions: Choose a sturdy backpack with a hip belt if possible, and place the load high and close to your back. Use a weight plate, sandbag, or tightly packed items that cannot shift during the walk.
Adjust the shoulder straps so the pack sits snugly without pulling your shoulders back; secure the load without restricting normal breathing.
Stand tall with your ribs stacked over your hips, your head neutral, and your eyes looking ahead. Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid leaning forward under the pack.
Walk at a steady, controlled pace. Let your arms swing naturally and take short, comfortable steps rather than overstriding.
Keep your trunk steady and continue breathing naturally as you walk.
mistakes: Wearing the pack too low, which pulls the torso backward and strains the lower back.
Leaving shoulder straps loose so the load shifts with each step.
Using a load that is too heavy to maintain an upright walking posture.
Leaning forward from the waist instead of keeping the ribs stacked over the pelvis.
Shrugging the shoulders and tensing the neck under the straps.
Taking long, overreaching strides instead of using controlled natural steps.
exercises.name: Rucking
tips: Choose comfortable walking shoes and socks that fit well.
Start on a flat, predictable route.
Balance and secure the contents inside the backpack.
On hills, shorten your steps and adjust the pace to the slope.
Increase either load or distance at a time, after the current route feels manageable.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/跑步

exercises.description: Running is a cardiovascular exercise that involves moving at a steady pace on foot. It enhances cardiovascular endurance, burns calories, and strengthens muscles, particularly in the legs and core. Running can be performed on a treadmill or outdoors and is adaptable to various fitness levels.
instructions: Begin with a warm-up: walk briskly or jog lightly for 5-10 minutes to prepare your body.
Set your pace: start at a comfortable speed that allows you to maintain a conversation without gasping for air.
Maintain proper form: keep your head up, shoulders relaxed, and arms bent at a 90-degree angle, swinging naturally with each stride.
Focus on your foot strike: land softly on the midfoot or forefoot to reduce impact on the joints.
Breathe rhythmically: inhale and exhale deeply through both your nose and mouth to optimize oxygen intake.
Cool down after your run: gradually decrease your speed to a walk for 5-10 minutes, allowing your heart rate to return to normal.
mistakes: Overstriding, leading to increased impact on joints.
Heel striking, causing inefficient energy transfer.
Poor arm swing, reducing momentum and balance.
Excessive forward lean, straining the lower back.
Inadequate core engagement, compromising stability.
Lack of hip extension, limiting stride length.
Neglecting foot placement, increasing risk of ankle sprains.
Inconsistent breathing patterns, affecting endurance.
Tense shoulders, wasting energy and restricting movement.
Ignoring cadence, leading to inefficient pacing.
exercises.name: Running
tips: Invest in quality running shoes that provide adequate support and cushioning to prevent injuries.
Incorporate interval training by alternating between periods of high intensity and recovery to improve speed and endurance.
Stay hydrated by drinking water before, during, and after your run, especially in hot weather.
Listen to your body and adjust your pace if you experience pain or excessive fatigue.
Include strength training exercises for the legs and core to enhance running performance and reduce injury risk.
Track your progress using a running app or fitness tracker to stay motivated and set achievable goals.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/安全杠深蹲

exercises.description: A back squat with a safety squat bar, a bar with a padded yoke and handles in front of the body. You rest the pads on your upper back, hold the handles in front of your shoulders and squat to about parallel. Your arms stay in front, which spares the shoulders, while the bar tips you forward and makes your upper back work to stay upright.
instructions: Set the bar in a rack at a height you can step under with a slight knee bend, and set the safety pins just below the bottom of your squat.
Step under the bar so the padded yoke rests across your upper back and traps, and take one handle in each hand in front of your shoulders.
Brace your core, stand up to lift the bar off the hooks and take two or three short steps back.
Set your feet about shoulder-width apart with your toes turned slightly out, and point your elbows down and forward.
Take a deep breath, brace, and bend your knees and hips together, knees moving in line with your toes.
Lower under control until your thighs are about parallel to the floor, keeping your chest up and your whole foot on the floor.
Push through your whole foot to stand up, straightening your knees and hips together, and breathe out near the top.
After the last rep, walk forward into the rack and set the bar on the hooks.
mistakes: Letting the chest drop and the upper back round as the bar pulls you forward.
Letting the knees cave in on the way down or up.
Shifting the weight onto the toes and lifting the heels.
Letting the hips rise faster than the chest when standing up.
Setting the yoke too high, on the neck, instead of across the upper traps.
Cutting the squat short, well above parallel.
Dropping fast into the bottom and bouncing out without control.
Squatting without a deep breath and a braced core, so the lower back rounds at the bottom.
exercises.name: Safety Bar Squat
tips: Center the yoke on your back before you unrack, so the bar sits level and both legs share the load.
Pull the handles down lightly to keep the pads pinned to your back and the bar from shifting.
Let your knees travel forward over your toes as you descend. It helps you stay upright under the bar.
Keep your head neutral and look straight ahead. Do not let the yoke push your head and neck forward.
Choose a stance and toe angle that let your knees follow your toes comfortably, and keep them the same on every rep.
Start lighter than your straight-bar back squat. The load sits differently, and most lifters handle less weight with this bar at first.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腹肌/熊抱沙袋行走

exercises.description: The sandbag bear hug carry trains the trunk and legs while you walk with a load held against your chest. Wrap both arms around an upright sandbag and stand tall with your ribs over your pelvis. Walk in short, steady steps, keeping the bag close and breathing without releasing your abdominal tension.
instructions: Place a sandbag on the floor and choose a clear walking path. Use a bag weight that lets you keep your posture controlled throughout the carry.
Stand close to the sandbag with your feet about hip-width apart. Squat down by bending your knees and hips, keeping your back neutral.
Wrap both arms around the sandbag and pull it tightly against your chest and upper abdomen. Keep the bag close to your body.
Drive through your feet to stand up, using your legs and hips. Brace your core, keep your chest tall, and avoid rounding your lower back.
Walk forward with short, controlled steps. Keep the sandbag hugged firmly to your torso, shoulders down, and eyes looking ahead.
Breathe steadily and maintain a strong upright position. If the bag starts to slip or your posture breaks down, stop and reset.
At the end of the distance, squat down with the bag held close and place it on the floor under control. Do not drop it unless your training area and equipment allow it.
mistakes: Holding the sandbag too low, which pulls the shoulders forward and rounds the upper back.
Letting the bag drift away from the chest.
Leaning backward to counterbalance the load.
Taking long, uncontrolled strides that cause the bag to bounce.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears.
Looking down at the bag throughout the carry, which disrupts upright posture.
exercises.name: Sandbag Bear Hug Carry
tips: Start with short carries, then extend the duration as your hold improves.
Breathe behind your brace. Take small controlled breaths without relaxing your trunk.
Turn slowly by taking several small steps rather than twisting your torso under the load.
To pick up the bag, squat or hinge with a neutral back, pull it close to your body, then stand using your legs.
Use a clear walking path and leave enough room to turn and set the bag down safely.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腿部锻炼/沙袋前弓步

exercises.description: Rest the sandbag across your upper back and hold its handles beside your neck while standing upright. Step forward and bend both knees to lower into a lunge, then push through the front foot to return to the starting position and repeat on the opposite leg.
instructions: Stand upright with the sandbag across your upper back and hold the handles beside your neck.
Brace your core and take a controlled step forward with one foot.
Lower your body by bending both knees.
Keep your front knee tracking in the same direction as your toes.
Push firmly through the heel and midfoot of your front foot to return to the starting position.
Return to a balanced stance, then repeat with the other leg and alternate sides.
mistakes: Letting the front knee collapse inward instead of tracking over the toes.
Leaning the torso forward or rounding the back under the sandbag.
Twisting or shifting the sandbag to one side during the lunge.
Putting most of the weight on the back leg instead of loading the front heel and midfoot.
Letting the front heel rise or the foot roll inward.
Rushing the descent or bouncing out of the bottom position.
exercises.name: Sandbag Forward Lunge
tips: Grip the sandbag handles with both hands before taking the first step.
Stand tall with your feet about hip width apart.
Step forward far enough that both knees can bend comfortably.
Start with a light sandbag to find a repeatable step length.
Use the same number of repetitions and the same step length on both legs.

exercises.description: The Saw Plank is an advanced core exercise that targets the abdominal muscles, obliques, and shoulders. It involves a dynamic movement that enhances stability and strength by incorporating a forward and backward sawing motion while maintaining a plank position.
instructions: Start in a forearm plank position with your elbows directly under your shoulders and your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Engage your core and maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise.
Shift your body weight forward by pushing through your toes, moving your shoulders past your elbows.
Reverse the motion by pulling back with your toes, bringing your shoulders behind your elbows.
Continue this sawing motion for the desired number of repetitions or time.
mistakes: Allowing hips to sag or rise, compromising core engagement.
Failing to maintain a straight line from head to heels.
Moving too quickly, reducing control and effectiveness.
Not fully extending shoulders forward and backward.
Holding breath, limiting oxygen flow and endurance.
Letting shoulders collapse, increasing neck strain.
Engaging lower back instead of core, risking strain.
Neglecting to align wrists under shoulders, causing instability.
Using momentum instead of controlled muscle movement.
exercises.name: Saw Plank
tips: Keep your core tight to prevent sagging or arching of the lower back.
Focus on controlled movements to maximize muscle engagement and avoid injury.
Ensure your shoulders remain stable and do not collapse during the exercise.
Breathe steadily throughout the movement to maintain endurance and control.
If you feel strain in your lower back, adjust your form or reduce the range of motion.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/chest/肩胛骨俯卧撑

exercises.description: The Scapula Push Up is an exercise that targets the muscles around the scapula, primarily focusing on the serratus anterior. It enhances shoulder stability and mobility, crucial for athletes and individuals looking to improve their upper body strength and posture.
instructions: Start in a high plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders and your body forming a straight line from head to heels.
Keep your arms straight and engage your core to maintain stability.
Without bending your elbows, retract your shoulder blades by squeezing them together, allowing your chest to lower slightly.
Protract your shoulder blades by pushing them apart, rounding your upper back and returning to the starting position.
Repeat the movement for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control throughout.
mistakes: Allowing the elbows to bend, turning it into a regular push-up instead of focusing on scapular movement.
Failing to fully protract and retract the scapulae, limiting the range of motion.
Collapsing the lower back or pelvis, losing core engagement and proper alignment.
Shrugging the shoulders towards the ears, causing tension and incorrect scapular movement.
Moving too quickly, sacrificing control and the quality of each scapular motion.
Not maintaining a straight line from head to heels, leading to improper body alignment.
Letting the head drop, causing strain on the neck and disrupting alignment.
Engaging the arms too much, reducing the focus on scapular movement.
exercises.name: Scapula Push-Up
tips: Focus on the movement of the shoulder blades rather than bending the elbows.
Keep your core engaged to prevent sagging of the hips or arching of the back.
Perform the exercise slowly to ensure full range of motion and better muscle activation.
Maintain a neutral neck position by looking slightly ahead rather than down at your hands.
Incorporate this exercise into your warm-up routine to activate the serratus anterior before upper body workouts.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腹肌/剪刀式

exercises.description: The Scissors exercise is a core-focused movement that targets the abdominal muscles, particularly the lower abs. It involves alternating leg movements that mimic the opening and closing of scissors, providing a dynamic challenge to stability and core strength.
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your legs extended and arms at your sides, palms facing down.
Engage your core by pulling your navel towards your spine and lift both legs off the ground about 6 inches.
Lift your head, neck, and shoulders slightly off the mat to engage the upper abs.
Begin the movement by lifting one leg higher while lowering the other leg towards the ground without touching it.
Alternate legs in a controlled manner, mimicking a scissor motion.
Continue alternating for the desired number of repetitions or time, maintaining core engagement throughout.
mistakes: Lower back arches off the floor, reducing core engagement.
Legs drop too low, causing strain on the lower back.
Neck and shoulders lift off the ground, leading to tension.
Legs move too quickly, compromising control and form.
Feet are not pointed or flexed, reducing muscle activation.
Core is not engaged, relying on hip flexors instead.
Hands placed under the hips, altering spine alignment.
Breathing is inconsistent, affecting performance and endurance.
exercises.name: Scissors
tips: Keep your lower back pressed into the mat to avoid strain and ensure proper form.
Maintain a steady breathing pattern; exhale as you switch legs and inhale as you hold the position.
If you feel strain in your neck, rest your head on the mat while continuing the leg movements.
Focus on slow, controlled movements rather than speed to maximize core engagement.
If you're new to this exercise, start with fewer repetitions and gradually increase as you build strength.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/back/海豹划船

exercises.description: The Seal Row is a strength training exercise targeting the upper back, specifically the rhomboids, traps, and rear deltoids. It is performed lying face down on a bench with weights, typically dumbbells or a barbell, pulled towards the chest. This exercise helps improve posture and enhances upper body strength.
instructions: Set up a flat bench elevated on blocks or platforms to allow full range of motion for the weights.
Lie face down on the bench with your chest supported and feet planted firmly on the ground.
Grip the weights (dumbbells or barbell) with an overhand grip, arms fully extended towards the floor.
Engage your core and keep your body stable throughout the movement.
Pull the weights towards your chest by retracting your shoulder blades and bending your elbows.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring maximum contraction in the upper back muscles.
Slowly lower the weights back to the starting position with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Lifting the chest off the bench, causing instability and reducing back engagement.
Using momentum to lift the weights, leading to poor muscle activation.
Allowing the elbows to flare out excessively, which can strain the shoulders.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom, limiting the range of motion.
Rounding the shoulders forward, which disengages the upper back muscles.
Pulling the weights too high, causing the wrists to bend awkwardly.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine, increasing the risk of lower back strain.
Using too much weight, compromising form and control.
exercises.name: Seal Row
tips: Ensure the bench is high enough to allow full range of motion without weights touching the ground.
Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of each rep for maximum muscle engagement.
Keep your neck in a neutral position to avoid strain; do not lift your head during the exercise.
Maintain a controlled tempo throughout to maximize muscle tension and avoid momentum.
Start with lighter weights to perfect form before progressing to heavier loads.
Breathe out as you pull the weights up and inhale as you lower them back down.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腹肌/坐姿腹部绳索卷腹

exercises.description: Sit on a flat bench with your back to a high pulley, hold a rope at your temples and curl your chest down to your thighs to train your abs with weight. Almost all the work goes to the six-pack muscle (rectus abdominis), and you'll feel it most above the navel; the obliques chip in only a little. Unlike the kneeling cable crunch, you face away from the stack and your hips stay planted on the bench, so they can't sit back and help. Choose it when kneeling bothers your knees or your hips keep drifting in the kneeling version; go kneeling when you want more load.
instructions: Clip a triceps rope to the high pulley of a cable column or lat-pulldown station. Go light at first; sitting down with the rope takes practice.
Put a flat bench in front of the column. Take the rope while standing, then sit down with your back to the stack.
Hold one rope end in each hand at your temples, palms facing each other and elbows pointing forward. The rope runs behind your head.
Sit tall near the front edge of the bench, feet flat and hip-width apart, knees at about 90°. The plates should already be lifted.
Breathe out and curl: pull your ribs toward your pelvis, tuck your chin and round your back from the top down.
Curl until your chest rests on your thighs and your elbows reach your knees. Squeeze for a second, fists still at your temples.
Uncurl over 2–3 seconds and stop the moment you sit tall. Start the next rep before the plates touch down.
To finish, sit tall and let your hands rise slowly toward the pulley until the weight rests. Then let go of the rope.
mistakes: Bench in the wrong spot. Too far out and the cable pulls you backward; right under the pulley and the rope drags up your neck. Move it until the cable hangs just behind your head and the weight stays up while you sit tall.
Pulling the rope down with your arms so your hands leave your head. Pin your fists to your temples, and drop the weight if your arms keep taking over.
Tipping forward from the hips with a flat back, so you feel it at the front of the hips instead of your stomach. Think "ribs to pelvis" and round from the upper back first.
Yanking your head down with your chin. Let your head follow your upper back as it rounds, hands at your temples and never on your neck.
Letting the stack snap you upright and leaning back past vertical with an arched lower back. Take 2–3 seconds on the way up and stop when you're sitting tall.
exercises.name: Seated Ab Cable Crunch
tips: Sets of 10–20 reps suit this lift, usually 2–4 of them taken close to failure.

Pick a range such as 12–15 and add reps at the same weight until you get 15 in all sets with a full curl and a one-second squeeze. Then add one plate, usually 2.5–5 kg, and go back to 12. Pulley ratios differ, so compare loads only on the same station.

Your stomach should work hard down the front, strongest above the navel and at the bottom of each rep. Tired arms or shoulders mean the rope is doing the pulling; a pull at the front of the hips means you're tipping forward with a flat back.
New to loaded crunches? Learn the curl on the floor with Abdominal Crunches first. Once this version feels easy, slow the return to 3–4 seconds and hold the bottom for 2 before you add a plate.
Rounding your back under load is the whole point here. If it brings on back pain, or pain running into a leg, stop and switch to a plank-type exercise.

Substitutes: Kneeling Cable Abs Crunches (same curl, heavier loads), Machine Abdominal Crunches (fixed path, nothing to set up), Standing Cable Ab Crunch (no bench needed) and Weighted Ab Crunches (just a plate and a mat).

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/腹肌/坐姿交替卷腹

exercises.description: Seated Alternate Crunches are an abdominal exercise targeting the rectus abdominis and obliques. This exercise is performed while seated, engaging the core muscles through alternating side crunches.
instructions: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat, hip-width apart.
Lean back slightly, keeping your back straight and core engaged.
Place your hands lightly behind your head, elbows wide.
Lift your right knee towards your chest while simultaneously twisting your torso to bring your left elbow towards the right knee.
Return to the starting position and repeat on the opposite side, lifting your left knee and twisting your torso to bring your right elbow towards the left knee.
Continue alternating sides in a controlled manner for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Leaning back too far, reducing core engagement.
Pulling on the neck instead of using the core muscles.
Using momentum instead of controlled movements.
Not fully rotating the torso, limiting oblique activation.
Lifting the feet off the ground, destabilizing the position.
Rushing through repetitions, sacrificing form.
Arching the lower back, increasing strain and reducing effectiveness.
Failing to engage the core muscles throughout the movement.
exercises.name: Seated Alternate Crunches
tips: Maintain a straight back and avoid rounding your shoulders during the exercise.
Engage your core throughout the movement to maximize abdominal activation.
Focus on controlled movements rather than speed to ensure proper form and effectiveness.
Exhale as you twist towards each knee, and inhale as you return to the starting position.
Keep your movements smooth and avoid jerking or using momentum.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/肩部/坐姿阿诺德哑铃推举

exercises.description: The Seated Arnold Dumbbell Press is a compound shoulder exercise that targets the deltoids, particularly the anterior and lateral heads, while also engaging the triceps and upper chest. Named after Arnold Schwarzenegger, this variation of the dumbbell shoulder press involves a rotational movement that enhances shoulder stability and muscle activation.
instructions: Sit on a bench with back support, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height with palms facing your body.
Keep your feet flat on the floor, core engaged, and back pressed against the bench.
Begin by rotating your palms outward as you press the dumbbells overhead until your arms are fully extended.
Pause briefly at the top, ensuring your elbows are not locked.
Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position while rotating your palms back to face your body.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Failing to maintain a neutral spine, leading to excessive arching of the lower back.
Not keeping the elbows in line with the shoulders during the press, causing uneven muscle engagement.
Allowing the wrists to bend backward, reducing control and increasing strain on the joints.
Rotating the dumbbells too early or too late, disrupting the fluidity of the movement.
Using momentum to lift the weights instead of controlled muscle contraction.
Not fully extending the arms overhead, limiting the range of motion and muscle activation.
Allowing the shoulders to shrug upward, disengaging the targeted muscles.
Neglecting to engage the core, resulting in a lack of stability and control.
Holding the dumbbells too far apart or too close together, affecting balance and form.
Rushing through the movement, compromising technique and effectiveness.
exercises.name: Seated Arnold Dumbbell Press
tips: Maintain a controlled motion throughout the exercise to maximize muscle engagement and reduce injury risk.
Keep your core tight to stabilize your torso and prevent arching of the lower back.
Use a weight that allows you to perform the exercise with proper form for all repetitions.
Focus on breathing steadily; exhale as you press up and inhale as you lower the weights.
Ensure your elbows stay slightly bent at the top of the movement to avoid joint strain.

alternates.zh: https://smartworkout.app/zh/健身练习库/臀部/坐姿弹力带髋外展

exercises.description: The Seated Band Hip Abduction is an exercise targeting the gluteus medius and minimus muscles. It involves using a resistance band to provide tension, helping to strengthen and stabilize the hips. This exercise is beneficial for improving hip mobility, enhancing athletic performance, and preventing injuries.
instructions: Sit on a bench or chair with your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Place a resistance band around your legs, just above your knees.
Keep your back straight and engage your core muscles.
Slowly push your knees outward against the resistance of the band, keeping your feet stationary.
Hold the position for a moment, then slowly return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Leaning too far back, reducing hip engagement.
Allowing knees to collapse inward, losing tension in the band.
Using a band with too much resistance, limiting range of motion.
Not maintaining a neutral spine, causing lower back strain.
Performing the movement too quickly, sacrificing control.
Failing to keep feet flat on the ground, destabilizing the position.
Neglecting to engage core muscles, reducing overall stability.
Allowing shoulders to hunch forward, affecting posture.
exercises.name: Seated Band Hip Abduction
tips: Ensure the resistance band is tight enough to provide adequate tension throughout the movement.
Focus on maintaining a straight back and engaged core to prevent leaning forward or backward.
Perform the movement slowly and with control to maximize muscle activation.
Keep your feet flat on the ground and avoid lifting your heels during the exercise.

exercises.description: Sit facing a low cable with your feet braced and knees slightly bent. Hold the handle with arms extended and begin tall through the spine. Pull the handle toward your lower ribs while rounding your upper back and drawing your ribcage toward your pelvis. Pause briefly in the contracted position, then slowly extend your arms and return to a controlled upright position. Keep the movement smooth, avoid jerking, and use a load that allows controlled spinal flexion.
instructions: Attach a straight bar or close-grip handle to the low cable pulley and select a light-to-moderate load that allows smooth, controlled movement.
Sit facing the cable machine with your feet braced firmly against the foot platform, knees slightly bent, and arms extended toward the handle.
Begin with your torso slightly flexed forward from the hips and upper back, allowing your shoulder blades to move apart while keeping your neck neutral.
Initiate the pull by driving your elbows back and drawing the handle toward your lower abdomen.
As you pull, gradually extend your spine to bring your torso upright, keeping your chest open and squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the movement.
Pause briefly with the handle close to your abdomen, elbows behind your body, and shoulders kept down away from your ears.
Return the handle slowly by extending your arms and allowing your torso to flex forward in a controlled manner, without rounding aggressively or losing tension in the cable.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, avoiding jerking, excessive lower-back movement, or using momentum to pull the weight.
mistakes: Using momentum by rocking the torso instead of controlling the spinal flexion and rowing phases.
Pulling mainly with the arms while failing to retract the shoulder blades and engage the back.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears instead of keeping the neck relaxed and shoulders depressed.
Rounding the spine passively and collapsing at the bottom rather than actively controlling the flexed position.
Extending the spine too early during the pull, reducing the intended flexion-row movement pattern.
Hyperextending the lower back at the end of the row instead of finishing with a neutral, controlled torso position.
Flaring the elbows excessively instead of guiding them back in a consistent path.
Using a range of motion that is too short, especially by not allowing controlled spinal flexion and shoulder protraction on the return.
Letting the weight stack slam or allowing the cable to pull the torso forward uncontrollably.
exercises.name: Seated Cable Flexion Row
tips: Set the pulley low and sit facing the cable with your feet braced securely, knees slightly bent, and the handle held with straight but not locked arms.
Begin tall with your shoulders relaxed, then allow a controlled, comfortable rounding through the upper back as you reach forward; do not force painful lumbar flexion.
Initiate the pull by drawing your shoulder blades back and down, then pull the handle toward your lower ribs or abdomen while extending back to a neutral, tall seated position.
Keep the movement smooth and coordinated rather than jerking with the lower back; the cable should stay under tension throughout the repetition.
Use a load that lets you control both the forward flexion and the return phase without swinging, leaning excessively, or losing your footing.
Keep your neck neutral and avoid shrugging your shoulders toward your ears as you pull.
Exhale during the pull and return slowly under control, allowing the spine to flex only as far as is comfortable and intended.
If you have low-back pain, disc symptoms, or discomfort during spinal flexion, use a neutral-spine seated row variation or ask a qualified professional for guidance.

exercises.description: Sit with your back to a high pulley and press a short bar from behind your head until your straight arms point forward at eye level, not at the ceiling. The long head gets the biggest stretch while the bar is behind your head, and all three heads straighten the elbows. The seat and upright back pad take balance and your lower back out of the lift, unlike the standing high-pulley version. The cable also keeps pulling once your arms are straight, where a dumbbell or EZ bar goes light.
instructions: Set one pulley of a cable station to the very top and clip on a short straight bar.
Put a bench with the back pad set upright right in front of the machine, so you sit with your back to the stack.
Take the bar overhand, hands about head-width apart, sit down and bring it behind your head. Elbows fully bent, pointing up, no wider than your shoulders.
Sit tall with your back on the pad and your feet flat and wide.
If the plates touch down with the bar behind your head, slide the bench a little farther from the machine.
Exhale and straighten your elbows until the bar is above your head. Your upper arms stay beside your head for this part.
With your elbows locked, push the bar forward in an arc until your arms point straight ahead at eye level. Hold it there for a second.
Reverse the path: raise the straight arms back over your head, then bend your elbows and lower the bar behind your head over 2–3 seconds.
To end the set, bring the bar back over your head before you let go or stand up, so the stack can't snap it into your head.
mistakes: Sitting facing the machine or hooking up the low pulley. The cable then pulls the bar forward and the second half has no resistance; sit with your back to the stack and use the top pulley.
Bringing the arms forward while the elbows are still bent. That turns the rep into a bent-arm pullover. Straighten your elbows fully over your head first, then move the straight arms.
Stopping at 90° with the bar above your head. Lower it behind your head until your elbows are fully bent, and go lighter if you can't get there.
Dropping the arms below eye level or peeling your back off the pad to finish the forward part. Stop as soon as your arms point straight ahead.
Letting the stack yank the bar back behind your head. Take 2–3 seconds on the way down and stop the weight in the stretch; the plates shouldn't touch between reps.
exercises.name: Seated Cable Horizontal French Press
tips: Sets of 10–15 reps are typical; heavier sets of 6–10 also work. Keep the same weight until all your sets reach the top of the range with the full arc and your back on the pad, then go up one plate and start again from the bottom of the range.
On two-tower stations the plate number often doesn't match what the bar feels like, so compare loads only on the same machine. If one plate is too big a jump, use the add-on weight.

With the bar behind your head you should feel a strong stretch along the back of your upper arm, up toward the armpit. In the forward part, the back of your shoulder and your lats help hold the straight arms. Nothing should show up in your lower back or neck.

Pain at the front of the shoulder or inside the elbow in the stretch? Start each rep with the bar above your head instead of behind it and go lighter. Once the stretch feels easy, pause there for 1–2 seconds to make it harder.

Substitutes: High Pulley Overhead Triceps Extension, standing with a rope, when no bench is free; Overhead Cable Triceps Extension (Bar), which finishes pointing at the ceiling; EZ-Bar Seated Triceps Extension or Dumbbell Seated Triceps Extension when every cable is taken.

exercises.description: Sit tall at a cable row station and pull a close, palms-facing handle to your upper stomach to build your lats and mid-back. With your elbows brushing your ribs, the lats do most of the pulling, followed by the lower traps and the small muscles around your shoulder blades (infraspinatus, teres minor, teres major); the middle traps, rear delts and forearms help. The neutral grip is easy on wrists and elbows and the seat spares your lower back, so it suits any level as a main back exercise. Pick it over the wider-grip cable rows when lats and a heavy stack matter more than rear delts.
instructions: Clip a close neutral-grip handle (V-bar) to the cable, sit facing the stack and put your feet on the foot plate, knees softly bent.
Hold both grips with your palms facing each other and slide back until your arms are straight and the plates you're using lift off.
Sit tall with your torso vertical, chest up, ribs down and lower back neutral. The cable runs roughly level from the pulley to your hands.
Draw your shoulder blades back first, then drive your elbows straight back along your ribs, upper arms about 20–30° from your sides.
Bring the handle to your upper stomach, just below the ribcage, elbows ending just behind your torso. Hold that squeeze for a second.
Take 2–3 seconds to let the handle forward until your arms are straight and your shoulder blades glide forward into a lat stretch.
Keep the plates off the stack until the set ends, then bend your knees and lower the handle to the foot plate with a flat back.
mistakes: Rocking: you lean forward to reach, then lean back to finish, so your hips move the stack. Keep your torso vertical and get the stretch from your shoulder blades; if the handle only reaches your stomach with a lean, drop the weight.
Pulling the handle up to your chest. Your elbows rise and flare and your shoulders creep toward your ears; aim just below the ribs and let your elbows skim your sides.
Never reaching all the way forward. Bent arms and pinned shoulder blades mean the lats never stretch, so straighten your arms and let the blades slide forward before each pull.
Yanking the elbows too far back until your shoulders roll forward and the front of the shoulder pinches. Stop with the elbows just behind your torso, shoulders down and back.
Locking your knees. With straight legs your pelvis tips back and your lower back rounds; keep a soft bend, and bend more if you still can't sit tall.
exercises.name: Seated Cable Low Row Neutral Grip
tips: Row 8–15 reps for muscle and 6–10 for strength; any heavier and the torso usually starts to rock. Add reps at the same weight until all sets reach the top of the range with a still torso, then move the pin down one plate (often 5 kg, about 10 lb; 2.5 kg on small stacks) and build the reps back up.

Expect a stretch down the sides of your back at the front of each rep and a squeeze below your shoulder blades at the finish. If your forearms give out first, keep your wrists straight, treat your hands as hooks and pull with your elbows.

Before the next weight jump, add a 2-second squeeze at your stomach or a 3-second return. Can't keep your torso still even with a light stack? Learn the pull on the Lever Low Row, where a chest pad holds you; once this version is solid, the One-Arm Low Cable Seated Row gives each side a longer reach.
Substitutes: Seated Cable Row (short straight bar, overhand), Lever Low Row, Dumbbell Neutral Grip Incline Bench Row, and Dumbbell Bent Over Row if you want a free-weight version.

exercises.description: Sit tall at a low-pulley row station and pull a short straight bar, palms down, to your upper stomach to build the middle of your back. Your middle and lower traps (between and just below the shoulder blades) and your lats take the bulk of the load, with the infraspinatus and teres muscles on the shoulder blade close behind. The seat and foot plate spare your lower back, so it works at any level. Compared with the close neutral-grip handle, the overhand bar puts more work on your middle traps and forearms and copies the grip of a barbell row.
instructions: Clip a short straight bar to the low pulley and sit facing the stack, feet on the foot plate, knees clearly bent but never locked.
Grab the bar overhand, hands about shoulder-width apart, and slide back until your arms are straight and the selected plates lift off the stack.
Sit tall on your sit bones, torso vertical, chest up. That's the start: arms long at lower-chest height, shoulder blades spread forward.
Draw your shoulder blades back first, then drive your elbows straight back along your ribs, upper arms about 15–35° out from your sides.
Finish with the bar on your upper stomach, just below the ribs, and hold a second: elbows behind your torso, shoulder blades squeezed together and down.
Let the bar travel forward over about 2 seconds until your arms are straight. Only your arms and shoulder blades move.
Keep the plates off the stack until the last rep, then bend your knees and set the bar on the foot plate with a flat back.
mistakes: Rocking: you lean forward to reach and back to finish, so your hips and lower back move the stack. Keep your torso vertical and get the stretch from your shoulder blades; if the bar only reaches your stomach when you lean back, drop the weight.
Rowing the bar to your chest. Your elbows lift and flare and your shoulders creep toward your ears; aim just below the ribs and keep your elbows close to your sides.

Bent wrists. Palms down, they tend to curl under or cock back, and your forearms quit before your back does. Point your knuckles forward, hold the bar like a hook and pull with your elbows; if your grip still goes first, use straps.

Cutting the reach short, so your arms never straighten and your shoulder blades stay pinned back. At the front of every rep let them glide forward with your chest up, then start the next pull from there.
exercises.name: Seated Cable Row
tips: Use 3–4 sets of 8–15 reps for muscle, or 6–8 for strength; much heavier than that and the overhand grip usually gives out first. Add reps at the same weight until all your sets hit the top of the range with a still torso, then move the pin down one plate (usually 5 kg, about 10 lb; 2.5 kg on small stacks) and drop back to the bottom.

Expect a stretch across your upper back at the front of each rep and a squeeze between your shoulder blades at the finish, with the backs of your shoulders and your forearms chipping in. If your lower back or biceps tire first, you're rocking or pulling with your hands instead of your elbows. A pinch at the front of the shoulder means your elbows are going too far back.

exercises.description: Sit on the floor facing a cable station and pull a rope to your face, hands ending beside your head, to build your rear delts and upper back. The rear delts work hardest. Your middle traps squeeze the shoulder blades together and the infraspinatus, a rotator cuff muscle on the back of the shoulder blade, turns your arms out at the finish; the upper traps help a little. With your legs out on the floor, nothing below the waist can help, so it's easier to learn than the standing Cable Face Pull and the setup repeats week to week. Go standing when you want more load.
instructions: Clip a rope to one pulley of a cable station and set it level with your face as you sit on the floor, usually mid-column.
Take one rope end in each hand with an overhand grip: knuckles up, palms down, hands close together, wrists straight.
Sit facing the machine, legs out in front, knees slightly bent, heels down. Scoot back until your arms are straight at face height and the plates lift.
Sit tall with your chest up and lean back about 10–20°. The cable should now run level to the pulley; that lean stays put until the set is done.
Set your shoulders down, then pull the rope toward your face with your elbows leading out to the sides at shoulder height.
Split the rope as it nears your face. Your hands finish beside your head at eye level, forearms vertical, knuckles up and back; hold a second with your shoulder blades squeezed.
Take 2–3 seconds to straighten your arms, plates still off the stack. After the last rep, scoot forward to set the weight down, then let go.
mistakes: Rowing the rope to your chin or chest. The elbows drop below your shoulders and your lats and biceps take over. Aim the middle of the rope at your nose or forehead and finish with your hands beside your head.
Leaning further back on every rep to get the weight moving. Set the slight lean before the first rep and hold it there; if your torso still rocks, take a plate off.
Shrugging, so your shoulders creep toward your ears and your neck carries the load. Pull your shoulders down before each rep, think “elbows wide and back” and lighten the stack.
Stopping with your hands in front of your face and the rope ends still together. Pull them apart until your knuckles point up and back and your forearms stand vertical beside your head.
A pulley set for standing, not sitting. Too high and it becomes a pulldown, too low and it becomes an upward row. Set it at the height of your face when seated so the cable runs level.
Sitting so close that the plates clank down between reps. Scoot back until the weight stays up with your arms straight.
exercises.name: Seated Face Pull
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 12–20 reps and stop 1–3 reps short of failure; the set is over when your hands can no longer reach head height. Push the reps up before the load. Once you get 20 in each set with a one-second hold at your face and a still torso, go up one plate (usually 2.5–5 kg) and go back to 12. That plate can be a 10–20% jump on a face pull, so expect a few sessions at each weight. Pulley ratios vary, so compare loads only on the same station.

It should land in the back of your shoulders and between your shoulder blades, and late in the rep on the back of the shoulder blade as your hands turn up. A burning neck means you're shrugging. If your biceps or lats do most of the work, you're rowing to your chest. A pinch at the front of the shoulder at the finish? Stop with your hands slightly in front of your ears and use less weight.
Tight hamstrings rounding your lower back on the floor? Bend your knees more, or sit on a low box or flat bench and raise the pulley so it's still at face height.

Substitutes: Banded Face Pull at home, as a warm-up or as the easier step; Cable Face Pull, done standing, once a 2-second hold at the finish and a 3-second return feel easy and you want more load; Lying Cable Face Pull on a bench when you want your torso fully out of it; Machine Reverse Flyes for rear delts with your chest on a pad and no rotation at the end.

exercises.description: Sit against an upright backrest and curl two dumbbells together, thumbs up, from straight arms to your shoulders to build bigger biceps and forearms. Both heads of the biceps do most of the work. Next comes the brachioradialis along the thumb side of your forearm, with the brachialis working under the biceps and your forearm muscles holding on. Doing your hammer curls seated, back on the pad, takes away the hip drive and lean-back of the standing version, so you'll use slightly lighter dumbbells but your arms do all the lifting. Many people whose wrists or elbows complain on palms-up curls find this grip easier.
instructions: Set an adjustable bench with the backrest upright, vertical or one notch back, and check that the pin is locked.
Take a dumbbell in each hand and sit at the back of the seat: back, shoulder blades and head on the pad.
Plant your feet flat, hip-width apart or a little closer, knees bent to about 90 degrees.
Let your arms hang straight beside the seat, palms facing your thighs, thumbs forward. The dumbbells hang clear of the bench and your legs.
Curl both dumbbells at the same time, thumbs leading. Your palms keep facing each other and your upper arms stay against your ribs.
Stop when your forearms are about vertical and the dumbbells are in front of your shoulders, elbows still at your sides. Hold for a second.
Lower over 2–3 seconds until both elbows are straight again, then go into the next rep without touching the seat.
To finish, lower to straight arms and set the dumbbells down beside the bench with a straight back; don't drop them.
mistakes: Leaning back off the pad to finish each rep. Keep your shoulder blades and head on the backrest from the first rep to the last, and go down one dumbbell size if you can't.

Elbows sliding forward and shoulders rolling in at the top until the curl turns into a front raise. Keep the elbows by your ribs and stop with the dumbbells in front of your shoulders, not at your chin.
Palms turning up halfway, so it becomes a regular curl. Lead with your thumbs and keep your palms facing each other from bottom to top.
Half reps at the bottom, or dumbbells bouncing off the seat or your thighs. Sit so they hang clear beside the bench and straighten your elbows fully before the next rep.
exercises.name: Seated Hammer Curl
tips: For size, 2–4 sets of 8–15 reps taken close to failure suit most people; for strength, 6–10. Keep the same pair and add reps until all sets reach 15 with your back on the pad and straight elbows at the bottom. Then move to the next pair, usually 1–2 kg per hand heavier, and build up again from 8. Losing 2–4 reps after the jump is normal at curl weights.

The front of your upper arm works, along with the top of your forearm on the thumb side and, by the last reps, your grip. If the front of your shoulder burns more than your arms, your elbows are drifting forward. Sharp pain at the elbow or the front of the shoulder means lighter dumbbells or a lower stopping point.

Can't keep your back on the pad yet? Use a lighter pair and stop with your forearms horizontal for a few sessions. When it gets easy and you don't want heavier dumbbells, lower over 3–4 seconds or pause for 1–2 seconds with the forearms horizontal on the way up.

Substitutes: Dumbbell Hammer Curl (standing, no bench, a little more weight but more swing), Dumbbell Seated Alternate Hammer Curl (same seat, one arm at a time, easier to watch each elbow), Dumbbell Incline Hammer Curl (backrest reclined, harder at the bottom), Rope Cable Hammer Curl (low pulley and rope when the dumbbells are taken).

exercises.description: Sit tall on a box or bench, lift one knee a little and keep it still while the foot swings in toward your other shin. The thigh turns outward in the hip socket, so you train hip external rotation with your own muscles instead of being pulled into a stretch. You feel the work deep in the back of the hip and in the glute, with some along the front of the thigh. It mirrors the Seated Hip Internal Rotation: there the thigh rests on the box and the foot swings out, here the knee is lifted and the foot swings in. Slow sets per side suit a warm-up before squats or lunges and any hip mobility day.
instructions: Sit tall near the front edge of a box or bench, feet flat, knees bent about 90 degrees, hands resting on the box beside your hips.
Lift the working knee a few centimetres so the foot leaves the floor.
Fix the knee at that height and in that spot; it is the pivot for every rep.
Swing the foot in toward your other shin and let the thigh turn outward in the hip.
Stop where the knee or the pelvis would start to move and hold that end for 1-2 seconds.
Swing the foot back out until it is under the knee again, at the same speed.
Finish all reps on one leg, then switch legs.
mistakes: Knee drifting sideways as the foot comes in. If the knee travels, the thigh is not turning. Picture the knee resting on a shelf and leave it there.
Leaning the torso or tilting the pelvis to get the foot further across. Sit tall with both sit bones heavy on the box.
Swinging the foot fast and letting it bounce back. Slow down so you could stop at any point of the arc.
Curling the ankle in to fake a bigger range. Let the foot hang relaxed; it simply follows the shin.
Letting the knee rise or sink during the rep. Lift it once at the start and keep it at that height.
Pushing past a pinch at the front of the hip or a strain in the knee. Stop short of it; the range grows over a few weeks of practice.
exercises.name: Seated Hip External Rotation
tips: Do 2-3 sets of 8-12 reps per side: about 2 seconds in, a 1-2 second pause, 2 seconds back. Before squats, lunges or a run, one slow set per side is enough.
For end-range strength, swap reps for holds: at the inside end, try to swing the foot further for 5-10 seconds while it stays where it is. Do 3-5 holds per side.
Test both legs at the start of the session. If one side moves less, give it an extra set.
Pair it with the Seated Hip Internal Rotation, one set of each, so both directions get the same work. Then use the range on the floor in the 90/90 Hip Switch.
Once 12 slow reps feel easy, strap a 0.5-1 kg ankle weight to the working leg.

exercises.description: Sit tall on a box or bench with the working thigh resting on it and swing the foot out to the side, just above the floor, while the knee stays put. The thigh rolls inward in the hip socket: hip internal rotation, often the most limited hip movement in lifters and the one the back leg needs in a 90/90. You feel it on the outer side of the hip, with a stretch deep in the buttock near the end. Expect less range than in the Seated Hip External Rotation, where the knee is lifted and the foot swings in. Slow sets per side fit a warm-up, a hip mobility day or a short daily routine.
instructions: Sit tall near the front edge of a box or bench, feet flat, knees bent about 90 degrees, hands on the box beside your hips.
Leave the working thigh on the box and lift that foot just off the floor.
Point the knee straight ahead and keep it in that spot for every rep.
Swing the foot out to the side and let the thigh roll inward.
Stop before the knee drifts or the opposite hip lifts, and hold the end for 1-2 seconds.
Bring the foot back under the knee at the same pace.
Do all reps on one side, then change legs.
mistakes: Knee drifting outward as the foot swings out. The thigh stops turning and the knee takes the strain. Keep the knee pointing straight ahead in one spot.
Lifting the opposite hip or leaning toward the working side to get the foot further out. Keep both sit bones on the box and the torso upright.
Working thigh lifting off the box. Leave it resting there; only the lower leg moves.
Flinging the foot out and letting it drop back. Move at the same pace both ways.
Twisting the ankle outward to fake range. The foot hangs relaxed and simply follows the shin.
Forcing through a pinch at the front of the hip or a pull on the inside of the knee. Back off to a range that feels clean and build from there.
exercises.name: Seated Hip Internal Rotation
tips: Aim for 2-3 sets of 8-12 reps per side: 2 seconds out, a short pause, 2 seconds back. Use it in the warm-up before squats, lunges or deadlifts, or as part of a mobility day.
Most people move noticeably less here than in external rotation. A clean 30 degrees with a still pelvis is worth more than a big swing.
Build end-range strength with 3-5 holds of 5-10 seconds per side at the outside end, pressing the foot outward as if to go further.
Check both sides first and add a set to the one that moves less; side-to-side gaps are common in internal rotation.
Alternate sets with the Seated Hip External Rotation, then put the new range to use in the 90/90 Hip Switch on the floor.

exercises.description: Lean back on an incline bench and curl two dumbbells up from arms hanging straight down, to train your biceps from a deep stretch. Both heads of the biceps work, and the backrest stops you from swinging the weight up. With your arms hanging behind your torso, the long head, which crosses the shoulder, gets more stretch than in most other curls, so the first third of every rep is the hardest part. Pick it over the Seated Dumbbell Curl when you want that extra stretch and can live with lighter dumbbells; it suits lifters who already curl cleanly standing.
instructions: Set the backrest to about 45–60°. The lower it goes, the deeper the stretch and the harder the curl.
Sit with your hips all the way back, feet flat and wide on either side of the bench, knees bent about 90°.
Pick up the dumbbells sitting upright, rest them on your thighs, then lean back until your back, shoulders and head touch the pad.
Let your arms hang straight down beside the seat, palms facing forward. They should hang behind your torso, clear of the bench edge.
Curl both dumbbells at once. Elbows keep pointing at the floor and upper arms stay vertical as the dumbbells arc up toward your shoulders.
Stop with your forearms about vertical and palms facing your shoulders, and squeeze for a moment. Head and back stay on the pad.
Lower on the same arc over 2–3 seconds until your arms are fully straight. Pause in the stretch, then curl again without bouncing.
When you finish, bend your elbows to bring the dumbbells back onto your thighs, sit up, and only then put them down.
mistakes: Elbows drifting forward as the dumbbells come up. The shoulder starts helping and the stretch is gone. Keep the elbows pointing at the floor, stop once your forearms are vertical, and go lighter if the elbows still wander.
Shoulders rolling forward off the pad at the bottom. Pull your shoulder blades back and lift your chest before every rep, so the arms keep hanging behind you.
Half reps that never reach straight arms. Lower until your elbows are fully straight and the arms hang vertically, pause, then curl. If you can't get there, the dumbbells are too heavy.
Dropping into the stretch and bouncing out of it. Count 2–3 seconds on the way down and come to a dead stop at the bottom before you curl again.
Setting the backrest almost upright. That's an ordinary seated curl; lower it to about 45–60° so your arms hang behind your torso.
exercises.name: Seated Incline Biceps Curl
tips: Do 2–4 sets of 8–15 reps; 10–15 suits this curl best. Add reps with the same dumbbells first. When you get 15 in every set with straight arms at the bottom, move up to the next pair, usually 1–2 kg heavier per hand, and drop back to 10.

At the bottom you should feel a strong stretch along the front of your upper arm, sometimes up into the front of the shoulder. A sharp pain there means it's time to raise the backrest a notch or go lighter.

Want it harder without heavier dumbbells? Drop the backrest a notch toward 45° and take 3–4 seconds on the way down with a one-second pause at the bottom. For an easier version, set the backrest at 60–75°.

Substitutes: Seated Dumbbell Curl (upright backrest, less stretch, easier on the shoulder, more weight), Dumbbell Incline Alternate Supinated Curl (same bench, one arm at a time with a wrist turn), Incline Cable Curl (the cable keeps pulling in the stretch) and Bayesian Cable Curl when no incline bench is free.

exercises.description: A seated core exercise done on the end of a flat bench. Leaning back on your hands, you pull your knees in toward your chest, then push your legs out until they are almost straight without putting your feet down. It works the abs, especially the lower part, and the hip flexors.
instructions: Sit on the end of a flat bench and grip its edges just behind your hips.
Lean your torso back slightly and brace your abs.
Lift your feet off the floor and extend your legs until they are almost straight.
Exhale and pull your knees in toward your chest, bringing your torso slightly forward to meet them.
Pause briefly when your knees are closest to your chest.
Inhale and push your legs back out as you lean your torso back.
Stop with your heels just above the floor and go straight into the next rep.
mistakes: Swinging the legs with momentum instead of controlling them.
Leaning back so far that the arms carry most of your weight.
Rounding the back and dropping the head toward the knees.
Putting the feet down and resting between reps.
Cutting the extension short so the knees stay bent for the whole set.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears while pressing into the bench.
Holding the breath.
Arching the lower back as the legs extend.
exercises.name: Seated Knee Tuck
tips: Keep your chest up and your back long rather than rounding over your knees.
Move from your abs: curl your pelvis toward your ribs as the knees come in.
Keep your legs together and move them at a steady, controlled pace.
Exhale as you tuck and inhale as you extend.
To make it easier, extend your legs less and lean back less.
To make it harder, straighten your legs fully and keep them lower, or hold a light dumbbell between your feet.

exercises.description: The Seated Leg Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the hamstring muscles located at the back of the thigh. It is performed using a leg curl machine where the user sits with their legs extended and curls them back towards the body against resistance. This exercise helps in strengthening and toning the hamstrings, improving knee stability and overall leg strength.
instructions: Adjust the seat and backrest of the leg curl machine so that your knees align with the pivot point of the machine.
Sit on the machine with your back firmly against the backrest and place your legs under the padded lever, securing it just above your ankles.
Grip the handles or sides of the seat for stability.
Begin with your legs fully extended in front of you.
Exhale and slowly curl your legs back by bending your knees, bringing your heels as close to your buttocks as possible.
Hold the contraction for a moment at the bottom of the movement.
Inhale and slowly return to the starting position with controlled movement, extending your legs fully.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Setting the machine seat too far back, leading to ineffective engagement of the hamstrings.
Locking the knees at the start, which can strain the knee joint.
Using too much weight, causing momentum to take over and reducing muscle activation.
Not adjusting the ankle pad to rest comfortably above the heels, leading to improper leverage.
Failing to maintain a controlled tempo, resulting in swinging or jerking motions.
Allowing the hips to lift off the seat, which reduces isolation of the hamstrings.
Not completing the full range of motion, limiting muscle engagement and effectiveness.
Pointing the toes excessively, which can shift focus away from the hamstrings.
Relying on the lower back for assistance, increasing the risk of strain.
Rushing through repetitions without proper muscle contraction focus.
exercises.name: Seated Leg Curl
tips: Ensure that your knees are aligned with the pivot point to prevent strain on your joints.
Keep your movements slow and controlled to maximize muscle engagement and reduce risk of injury.
Avoid locking your knees at the top of the movement to maintain tension on the hamstrings.
Focus on squeezing your hamstrings at the bottom of each curl for maximum contraction.
Adjust the weight so that you can perform all repetitions with proper form without compromising technique.

exercises.description: The Seated Leg Extension Machine targets the quadriceps muscles located at the front of the thigh. This isolation exercise is designed to improve strength and definition in the quadriceps, making it a staple in lower body workouts. The machine consists of a padded seat, a backrest, and a lever with a padded bar that rests on the lower legs just above the ankles.
instructions: Adjust the seat so that your knees align with the pivot point of the machine.
Sit back against the backrest and place your feet under the padded bar, ensuring it rests just above your ankles.
Grip the handles on either side of the seat for stability.
Begin by extending your legs fully while exhaling, keeping your back pressed against the backrest.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement with your legs fully extended.
Slowly lower the weight back to the starting position while inhaling, maintaining control throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
exercises.name: Seated Leg Extension Machine
tips: Ensure proper alignment by adjusting the seat so that your knees are in line with the machine's pivot point.
Keep your movements controlled to maximize muscle engagement and reduce risk of injury.
Avoid locking your knees at full extension to prevent joint strain.
Focus on using your quadriceps to lift the weight rather than relying on momentum.
Maintain a neutral spine by keeping your back against the backrest throughout the exercise.
Start with a lighter weight to perfect your form before increasing resistance.

exercises.description: The Seated Machine Trunk Rotation is an isolation exercise targeting the oblique muscles of the core. It involves rotating the torso against resistance while seated, helping to improve core strength and stability.
instructions: Adjust the seat height so that your knees are at a 90-degree angle when seated.
Sit on the machine with your back straight and feet flat on the floor.
Place your arms across your chest or hold onto the handles if available.
Engage your core muscles by pulling your navel towards your spine.
Rotate your torso to one side as far as comfortable, keeping your hips stable.
Return to the starting position in a controlled manner.
Repeat the movement on the opposite side.
Perform equal repetitions for both sides.
mistakes: Using excessive weight, leading to poor form and reduced control.
Allowing the knees to move, reducing isolation of the core muscles.
Twisting the hips instead of rotating the trunk, decreasing core engagement.
Leaning forward or backward, compromising spinal alignment.
Relying on momentum rather than controlled muscle contraction.
Failing to maintain a neutral spine, increasing stress on the lower back.
Not fully engaging the obliques, limiting the effectiveness of the exercise.
Rotating beyond a safe range of motion, risking spinal strain.
exercises.name: Seated Machine Trunk Rotation
tips: Maintain a slow and controlled motion to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid using momentum; focus on using your oblique muscles to drive the movement.
Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid hunching them during the exercise.
Ensure that your hips remain stationary throughout the rotation to isolate the core effectively.
Start with a lighter resistance to master the form before increasing weight.
Exhale as you rotate and inhale as you return to the center position.

exercises.description: Seated Reverse Circle Crunches are an abdominal exercise that targets the lower and upper abs, as well as the obliques. This exercise involves performing circular motions with your legs while maintaining a seated position, engaging your core muscles to stabilize your body.
instructions: Sit on the edge of a bench or mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Lean back slightly, keeping your back straight and core engaged.
Lift your feet off the ground, bringing your knees towards your chest.
Begin to draw a circle in the air with your knees, moving them in a clockwise direction.
Complete the desired number of repetitions, then switch to a counterclockwise direction.
Maintain controlled breathing throughout the exercise.
mistakes: Leaning back too far, reducing core engagement.
Using momentum instead of controlled movements.
Performing circles that are too wide, straining the lower back.
Not keeping feet elevated, diminishing lower abdominal activation.
Failing to maintain a straight back, leading to poor posture.
Neglecting to engage the obliques during the circular motion.
Allowing shoulders to hunch, reducing upper body stability.
Inconsistent breathing, affecting core stability and endurance.
exercises.name: Seated Reverse Circle Crunches
tips: Keep your core tight to prevent strain on your lower back.
Focus on smooth, controlled movements rather than speed.
If you find it difficult to balance, place your hands lightly on the floor beside you for support.
Ensure that your shoulders remain relaxed and away from your ears.
Start with smaller circles if you're new to this exercise and gradually increase the size as you gain strength.

exercises.description: Sit on a bench with your upper arm propped on a raised knee and rotate a light dumbbell up beside your head to strengthen your rotator cuff. The work happens at the back of the shoulder: the infraspinatus and teres minor on your shoulder blade turn the arm out, and the rear delt helps. Because the knee carries the weight of your arm, the side and front delts have little to do, so this won't build your delts. The elbow sits at shoulder height, close to overhead and throwing positions, which suits lifters who press a lot and anyone cleared to train after a shoulder problem.
instructions: Sit tall on a flat bench and put your working-side foot up on the bench beside your hip, so that knee rises high.
Keep the other foot flat on the floor and rest your free hand on that knee.
Hold a light dumbbell overhand and rest the back of your upper arm, just above the elbow, on the raised knee. Shoulder down and back.
Your elbow, bent to 90 degrees, sits at or just below shoulder height, and the forearm hangs in front of your stomach.
Keeping the elbow on the knee, turn at the shoulder so the forearm swings forward and up like a windshield wiper.
Stop when the forearm is vertical and the dumbbell is beside your head, palm facing forward. Hold for a second or two.
Take about 2 seconds to lower until the forearm points down again.
After the last rep, put the other foot up on the bench and switch the dumbbell to the other hand.
mistakes: The elbow slides off the knee or lifts away as the dumbbell rises, so the rotation turns into a raise. Bring the foot closer to your hip to raise the knee, and go lighter.
Straightening the elbow at the top and pressing the dumbbell up. The 90-degree bend stays fixed and the rep ends when the forearm is vertical: rotate, don't press.
Leaning back or twisting your torso to help the weight up. Sit tall with your chest facing forward and your free hand on the other knee; only the forearm moves.
Letting the dumbbell drop from the top. Take about 2 seconds to lower it on the same arc, and if you can't, it's too heavy.
Forcing the forearm past vertical or bending the wrist back to squeeze out a few more degrees. Finish at vertical, or earlier if it pinches, with your wrist straight.
exercises.name: Seated Shoulder External Rotation
tips: Two or three sets of 12–20 reps per arm suit this lift, with a 1–2 second hold at the top; 8–12 is about as heavy as this lift should get. Add reps first. Once both arms reach 20 in every set with the elbow still on the knee and a slow lowering, pick up the next dumbbell, usually just 0.5–1 kg (1–2.5 lb) heavier, and build the reps back up.

Working weights here are tiny, often 1–5 kg, so even 1 kg is a big jump. If the next dumbbell is too much, first stretch the top hold to 2–3 seconds or take 3 seconds to lower. Too hard as it is? Do it with no weight, or stop when the forearm points straight ahead.

The work sits behind your shoulder blade and at the back of the shoulder, most in the top half and the hold. A pinch at the front or top of the shoulder means you went too far, the elbow sits too high or the dumbbell is too heavy. If lifting the arm to shoulder height hurts even without weight, switch to the side-lying version; in a rehab program, use the range and load your clinician gives you.

Substitutes: Side Lying External Rotation, the gentler position with the elbow at your side and a good first step; Dumbbell Cuban Rotation, the same upward turn but standing, with nothing under the arm; Cable Face Pull, which trains the rear delts and external rotators together with both arms and more weight.

exercises.description: The Seated Shoulder Press Neutral Grip is an upper body exercise targeting the deltoid muscles, particularly the anterior and lateral heads, as well as engaging the triceps and upper chest. This exercise is performed using a pair of dumbbells or a specialized machine, with a neutral grip to reduce stress on the shoulder joints and enhance stability.
instructions: Sit on a bench with back support, ensuring your feet are flat on the floor and your back is straight.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip (palms facing each other) at shoulder height.
Engage your core to stabilize your torso and keep your elbows slightly in front of your body.
Press the dumbbells upward until your arms are fully extended but not locked out.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, maintaining control.
Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position at shoulder height.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Arching the lower back excessively, which can strain the spine.
Allowing elbows to flare out, reducing shoulder engagement.
Pressing the weights too far forward, missing the vertical path.
Using momentum by bouncing weights, reducing muscle activation.
Failing to keep feet flat on the floor, affecting stability.
Not maintaining a neutral wrist position, leading to wrist strain.
Lowering the weights too quickly, compromising control.
Not aligning wrists directly above elbows, reducing leverage.
Neglecting to engage the core, leading to instability.
Raising weights unevenly, causing muscle imbalance.
exercises.name: Seated Shoulder Press Neutral Grip
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain stability and prevent arching of the lower back.
Use a controlled motion to avoid using momentum, which can reduce effectiveness and increase injury risk.
Ensure that your elbows remain slightly in front of your body to maintain proper shoulder alignment.
Avoid locking out your elbows at the top to keep tension on the muscles and protect your joints.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
