exercises.description: A standing stretch for the calf of the straight back leg. With your hands on a wall and one foot a short step back, you press that heel into the floor, bend the front knee and move your hips toward the wall. It mainly targets the gastrocnemius and works well after running or calf training.
instructions: Stand facing a wall, about an arm's length away, and place both hands on it at shoulder height.
Take a short step back with one foot. Point both feet straight at the wall.
Straighten the back leg and press its heel firmly into the floor.
Bend the front knee and move your hips toward the wall until you feel a stretch in the calf of the back leg.
Keep your body in one straight line from head to back heel, with your hips facing the wall.
Hold the position for the planned time and breathe calmly.
Bring your feet together and repeat with the other leg back.
mistakes: Letting the back heel lift off the floor, which takes the stretch off the calf
Bending the back knee, which shifts the stretch away from the gastrocnemius
Turning the back foot outward instead of pointing the toes at the wall
Bending at the waist and leaving the hips behind instead of moving them toward the wall
Letting the arch of the back foot collapse inward
Bouncing in and out of the stretch instead of holding a steady position
Leaning so hard that you feel sharp pain in the Achilles tendon instead of a pull in the calf
exercises.name: Wall Calf Stretch
tips: For a deeper stretch, place the back foot a little further from the wall. If the heel starts to lift, shorten the step.
Push the back heel down and slightly back, as if you wanted to make the leg longer.
Do it barefoot or in flat shoes. A raised heel in the shoe reduces the stretch.
Breathe out slowly as you lean in and let the calf relax a little more with each breath.
Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds and do 2 or 3 sets. Give a tighter calf one extra set.

exercises.description: Stand side-on to a wall with your hands together and arms extended in front of your chest. Press your hands sideways against the wall and hold the pressure while keeping your torso facing forward. Breathe steadily, release the pressure and repeat with the other side toward the wall.
instructions: Stand side-on to a wall with your feet about hip-width apart.
Join your hands and extend your arms in front at chest height.
Set the joined hands against the wall so you can press sideways into it.
Brace your abdomen and keep your shoulders and hips facing forward.
Press your hands into the wall and hold without moving your torso, breathing steadily.
Release the pressure and repeat with the other side toward the wall.
mistakes: Rotating the torso toward the wall.
Leaning the whole body into the wall.
Arching the lower back and flaring the ribs.
Bending the elbows during the hold.
Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears.
Holding the breath while pressing.
exercises.name: Wall Pallof Hold
tips: Use moderate pressure you can maintain steadily for the whole hold.
Keep your wrists aligned with your forearms.
Use the same hand height and similar pressure on both sides.
Keep a slight bend in your knees for a stable base.
Look forward rather than at your hands.

exercises.description: A standing push-up variation in which you lean into a wall with your hands at shoulder height and press yourself back upright. Your body stays close to vertical, so you push only a small part of your body weight, which makes it suitable for beginners and for people returning to training. It works the chest, front shoulders and triceps.
instructions: Stand facing a wall about an arm's length away, with your feet about hip-width apart.
Place your palms flat on the wall at shoulder height, about shoulder-width apart, with your fingers pointing up.
Brace your abs and squeeze your glutes so your body forms a straight line from head to heels.
Bend your elbows and lean your whole body toward the wall, keeping your elbows pointing down and slightly back rather than out to the sides. Your heels can lift off the floor as you lean in.
Pause briefly when your chest is close to the wall.
Press through your palms to straighten your arms and push your body back to the upright starting position.
Do the planned number of reps at a slow, steady pace.
mistakes: Placing the hands far above or below shoulder height.
Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
Pushing the hips back and bending at the waist instead of moving the body in one straight line.
Letting the hips sag toward the wall and the lower back arch.
Stopping with the chest far from the wall and using only a short range of motion.
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears.
Falling toward the wall quickly instead of leaning in under control.
exercises.name: Wall Push-Up
tips: Spread your fingers and press through your whole palm, not just the heel of your hand.
Look at the wall between your hands so your neck stays in line with your spine.
Exhale as you press away from the wall and inhale as you lean in.
At the top, push the wall away a little more so your shoulder blades move apart.
Step your feet farther from the wall to make it harder, or closer to make it easier.
Once you can do about 20 controlled reps, move on to incline push-ups with your hands on a bench.

exercises.description: The Wall Sit is an isometric exercise that targets the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes. It involves holding a seated position against a wall without any support from a chair, engaging the lower body muscles to maintain the position.
instructions: Stand with your back against a wall and feet shoulder-width apart.
Slowly slide down the wall until your thighs are parallel to the ground, forming a 90-degree angle at your knees.
Ensure your knees are directly above your ankles and not extending past your toes.
Keep your back flat against the wall and hold this position for the desired amount of time.
To finish, slowly slide back up the wall to a standing position.
mistakes: Knees extending beyond toes, increasing knee strain.
Hips positioned too high, reducing quadriceps engagement.
Back not flat against the wall, compromising support.
Feet placed too close together, affecting balance.
Feet placed too far from the wall, reducing stability.
Neck and head not aligned with spine, causing discomfort.
Arms resting on thighs, reducing core activation.
Holding breath, leading to unnecessary tension.
Uneven weight distribution on feet, causing imbalance.
Failing to maintain a 90-degree angle at knees, reducing effectiveness.
exercises.name: Wall Sit
tips: Maintain a straight line from your head to your hips to ensure proper posture.
Engage your core muscles to help stabilize your body during the exercise.
Focus on keeping your weight distributed evenly across both feet.
Breathe steadily throughout the exercise to maintain endurance.
Start with shorter durations and gradually increase as you build strength.

exercises.description: Start in a high plank with your feet by the wall and your arms straight. Walk your feet upward and your hands toward the wall until you reach a near-vertical position you can control. Walk your hands forward and feet down to return to the plank, keeping your trunk braced.
instructions: Start in a high plank with your feet close to a clear wall. Place your hands under your shoulders and brace your core.
Walk your feet up the wall slowly while walking your hands back toward the wall. Keep your arms straight and your body tight.
Continue until you reach the planned height. Beginners can stop before vertical, while advanced athletes can bring their chest close to the wall.
At the top, push firmly through your hands, keep your ribs pulled in, and look between your hands rather than at the wall.
To come down, walk your hands forward as you lower your feet down the wall under control.
Finish in a strong high plank, then lower your knees or step away from the wall.
mistakes: Starting too far from the wall, which forces an awkward reach and loss of control.
Letting the hips sag as the hands walk closer to the wall.
Keeping the shoulders behind the hands instead of actively pushing tall through the shoulders.
Bending the elbows and collapsing through the upper back.
Failing to brace the core, causing the ribs to flare and the low back to arch.
Dropping out of the wall walk too fast instead of walking the hands and feet down under control.
exercises.name: Wall Walk
tips: Set up facing away from a clear, solid wall.
Keep your hands shoulder width apart, fingers spread wide and pressing firmly into the floor.
Walk your feet up the wall in small steps while walking your hands back toward the wall.
Keep your head neutral and look at the floor between your hands.
Start with a partial climb and increase the height as shoulder strength improves.

exercises.description: Weighted Ab Crunches are an advanced core exercise that targets the rectus abdominis by adding resistance to the traditional crunch. This exercise enhances core strength and stability, making it ideal for individuals looking to intensify their abdominal workouts.
instructions: Lie on your back on a mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against your chest with both hands.
Engage your core by pulling your navel towards your spine.
Exhale as you lift your head, shoulders, and upper back off the floor in a controlled motion.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring your lower back remains in contact with the mat.
Inhale as you slowly lower back to the starting position without letting your head touch the floor.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using too much weight, leading to compromised form and reduced muscle engagement.
Pulling on the neck with hands, causing strain and reducing core activation.
Lifting the lower back off the floor, reducing abdominal focus.
Performing the movement too quickly, sacrificing control and effectiveness.
Not fully engaging the core, relying on momentum instead.
Allowing the elbows to flare out, reducing isolation of the abdominal muscles.
Failing to exhale during the crunch, limiting core contraction.
Raising the shoulders too high, shifting focus away from the abs.
Arching the back, which can lead to discomfort and reduced efficiency.
exercises.name: Weighted Ab Crunches
tips: Choose a weight that allows you to maintain proper form throughout the exercise.
Focus on using your abdominal muscles to lift rather than pulling with your neck or arms.
Keep movements slow and controlled to maximize muscle engagement and reduce injury risk.
Avoid using momentum; each repetition should be deliberate and focused.
Ensure your breathing is steady; exhale on the exertion (lifting) and inhale on the return (lowering).
If you're new to weighted crunches, start with a lighter weight to master the technique before progressing.

exercises.description: The Weighted Back Extension is an exercise targeting the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings. It involves extending the spine against resistance, typically performed on a hyperextension bench with added weight for increased intensity.
instructions: Position yourself face down on a hyperextension bench, securing your feet under the foot pads.
Align your hips with the edge of the pad to allow for full range of motion.
Hold a weight plate or dumbbell close to your chest with both hands.
Start with your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Lower your upper body slowly towards the floor by bending at the hips, keeping your back straight.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement, then engage your lower back and glutes to raise your torso back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Hyperextending the back at the top of the movement.
Using momentum to lift the weight rather than controlled movement.
Positioning the pad too high on the thighs, reducing range of motion.
Allowing the head to drop forward, misaligning the spine.
Failing to engage the glutes and hamstrings, overloading the lower back.
Holding the weight too far from the chest, increasing strain on the back.
Rising too quickly, compromising muscle engagement and control.
Not lowering the torso fully, limiting the exercise's effectiveness.
exercises.name: Weighted Back Extension
tips: Ensure your movements are controlled and deliberate to maximize muscle engagement and minimize injury risk.
Keep your core tight throughout the exercise to maintain stability and support for your lower back.
Avoid hyperextending your back at the top of the movement; stop when your body is in a straight line.
Start with a lighter weight to master proper form before progressing to heavier loads.
Focus on squeezing your glutes and hamstrings as you lift to enhance muscle activation.

exercises.description: Weighted Bench Dips are a compound exercise targeting the triceps, shoulders, and chest. By adding weight, this exercise increases resistance, promoting muscle growth and strength. It is performed using a bench and additional weight, such as a plate or dumbbell, placed on the lap.
instructions: Sit on the edge of a bench with your hands positioned next to your hips, fingers gripping the edge.
Place your feet flat on the floor, knees bent at approximately 90 degrees.
Have a partner place a weight plate or dumbbell on your lap for added resistance.
Slide your hips off the bench, supporting your body with your arms extended.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until they form a 90-degree angle.
Press through your palms to extend your arms and lift your body back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions while maintaining control throughout the movement.
mistakes: Placing hands too far apart, which reduces tricep engagement and increases shoulder strain.
Allowing shoulders to hunch forward, leading to poor posture and reduced effectiveness.
Dropping too low, which can put excessive strain on the shoulder joints.
Using momentum to push up instead of controlled muscle contraction, reducing muscle engagement.
Failing to keep elbows close to the body, which shifts focus away from the triceps.
Not keeping feet flat on the ground, leading to instability and reduced control.
Allowing the weight to rest on the thighs instead of maintaining active engagement.
Bending wrists excessively, which can cause discomfort and reduce stability.
Neglecting to engage the core, leading to poor alignment and reduced control.
exercises.name: Weighted Bench Dips
tips: Ensure that your elbows are pointing backward and not flaring out to maintain proper form.
Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to stabilize your body.
Avoid locking out your elbows completely at the top of the movement to maintain tension on the triceps.
Start with a lighter weight to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
Maintain a controlled tempo; avoid bouncing at the bottom of the movement.
Breath in as you lower yourself and exhale as you push back up.

exercises.description: The Weighted Chin Up is an advanced upper body exercise that targets the latissimus dorsi, biceps, and upper back muscles. By adding weight, this exercise increases resistance, enhancing muscle strength and hypertrophy. It requires a chin-up bar and additional weight, typically attached via a dip belt.
instructions: Attach the desired weight to a dip belt securely around your waist.
Stand beneath a chin-up bar and grasp it with an underhand grip, palms facing you, shoulder-width apart.
Engage your core and pull your shoulder blades down and back.
Initiate the movement by pulling yourself up until your chin clears the bar.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring full contraction of the back muscles.
Lower yourself in a controlled manner until your arms are fully extended.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using excessive weight that compromises form and control.
Failing to engage the core, leading to swinging or kipping.
Not starting from a full hang position, reducing range of motion.
Pulling with the arms instead of engaging the back muscles.
Allowing the shoulders to shrug upward, increasing tension on the neck.
Not retracting the shoulder blades, leading to poor scapular stability.
Rushing through the movement without controlled tempo.
Failing to maintain a straight line from head to heels, causing body misalignment.
Neglecting to fully extend the arms at the bottom of each rep.
Letting the elbows flare out excessively, reducing bicep engagement.
exercises.name: Weighted Chin Up
tips: Ensure your grip is firm to maintain control throughout the exercise.
Focus on engaging your lats and biceps during the pull-up phase.
Keep your core tight to prevent swinging or using momentum.
Control the descent to maximize muscle engagement and prevent injury.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
Breath out as you pull up and inhale as you lower yourself down.

exercises.description: The Weighted Cossack Squat is a unilateral lower body exercise that targets the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and adductors. It involves performing a deep lateral squat while holding a weight, such as a dumbbell or kettlebell, to increase resistance and improve strength, balance, and flexibility.
instructions: Stand with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart, toes pointing slightly outward.
Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell with both hands close to your chest.
Shift your weight onto your right leg, bending the knee and pushing your hips back as you lower into a squat.
Keep your left leg straight with the foot flat on the ground or with the heel slightly raised if necessary.
Lower yourself until your right thigh is parallel to the ground or as low as your flexibility allows.
Push through your right heel to return to the starting position.
Repeat the movement on the left side.
mistakes: Leaning forward excessively, which shifts the load away from the targeted leg.
Allowing the knee to cave inward, increasing stress on the joint.
Rising onto the toes of the working leg, reducing stability and engagement.
Holding the weight too far from the body, causing balance issues.
Failing to keep the non-working leg straight, limiting range of motion.
Dropping the hips too low without maintaining control, risking strain.
Not engaging the core, leading to a lack of support and balance.
Using momentum to rise instead of controlled muscle activation.
Neglecting to keep the chest up, which can lead to rounding of the back.
exercises.name: Weighted Cossack Squat
tips: Maintain an upright torso throughout the movement to ensure proper form.
Engage your core muscles to stabilize your body and protect your lower back.
Focus on keeping your knee aligned with your toes to avoid unnecessary strain.
Start with a light weight or no weight at all to master the technique before progressing.
Perform the exercise slowly and controlled to maximize muscle engagement and balance.
Inhale as you lower into the squat and exhale as you push back up to the starting position.

exercises.description: The Weighted Dead Bug is a core strengthening exercise that enhances stability and coordination. It involves lying on your back while holding a weight and moving your arms and legs in a controlled manner to engage the abdominal muscles effectively.
instructions: Lie flat on your back on a mat with your arms extended towards the ceiling, holding a dumbbell or weight plate in both hands.
Lift your legs off the ground, bending your knees at a 90-degree angle so that your thighs are perpendicular to the floor.
Engage your core by pulling your belly button towards your spine.
Slowly lower your right arm and left leg towards the floor simultaneously, keeping your lower back pressed against the mat.
Return to the starting position and repeat the movement with your left arm and right leg.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Lifting the lower back off the floor, reducing core engagement.
Allowing the weight to pull the arms too far back, straining the shoulders.
Dropping the legs too low, causing lower back arching.
Moving the arms and legs too quickly, losing control and stability.
Holding the breath, leading to increased tension and reduced core activation.
Using too heavy weights, compromising form and control.
Failing to keep the head and neck in a neutral position, causing strain.
Not engaging the core muscles throughout the movement.
Letting the knees bend excessively, reducing the challenge on the core.
exercises.name: Weighted Dead Bug
tips: Focus on maintaining a neutral spine throughout the exercise to prevent lower back strain.
Keep movements slow and controlled to maximize core engagement.
Ensure that your lower back remains in contact with the mat at all times.
Start with a lighter weight to master the form before progressing to heavier weights.
Breathe steadily, exhaling as you lower your limbs and inhaling as you return to the starting position.

exercises.description: Lie head-down on a decline ab bench with a weight plate on your chest and curl your trunk up off the pad to load your abs over a long range. The rectus abdominis, your six-pack muscle, does the work along its whole length, and the obliques at the sides of your waist help. Because your head starts below your hips, your abs lift the plate out of a stretch, while the floor version with a plate starts from flat. It stays a crunch, not a sit-up: your lower back never leaves the pad. Move to it once 20 clean decline crunches without a plate feel easy.
instructions: Set the ab bench to a moderate decline, about 20–30°. On most benches that's a middle hole, and steeper is harder.
Sit on the short top pad, hook the front of your ankles under the foot roller and bend your knees about 90° over the edge.
While you're still sitting up, press the plate flat against your upper chest and cross your forearms over it, hands reaching toward the opposite shoulders.
Lie back slowly until your shoulder blades touch the pad. Your head is now below your hips; keep it in line, chin slightly tucked.
Breathe out and pull your ribs toward your pelvis, peeling your head, then your shoulders, then your upper back off the pad.
Stop about 45° from the bench, with your shoulder blades and mid-back up and your lower back still on the pad. Squeeze for a second.
Take 2–3 seconds to uncurl until your shoulder blades touch down, and start the next rep before your head comes to rest.
Finish by sitting up first, then set the plate down beside the bench. Light-headed? Give it a few seconds before you stand.
mistakes: Sitting up all the way to your thighs. Once your lower back leaves the pad, the rep turns into a sit-up and you feel it at the front of your hips. Stop at about 45°, shoulder blades and mid-back up.

Pulling yourself up with your legs, shins driving into the roller. The roller only holds you in place. Think ribs to pelvis, and if you can't curl without yanking on it, use a lighter plate or a flatter bench.
Pushing the plate forward or up to swing your trunk off the pad. Keep it pinned flat to your upper chest under crossed forearms, elbows low; your arms don't move.
Dropping back and bouncing your shoulders or head off the pad. Lower in 2–3 seconds, touch down lightly with your shoulder blades and curl again from a standstill.
Leading with your head: chin jammed into the plate or neck craning forward while your trunk stays flat. Leave about a fist of space between chin and plate and let your head follow your ribcage.

Setting the bench too steep for the plate. The bottom gets away from you and your lower back arches off the pad on the way down; go a hole flatter or use a lighter plate until you can lower slowly with your back down.
exercises.name: Weighted Decline Crunch
tips: Take 2–4 sets of 10–20 reps close to failure. Pick a range such as 10–15 and add reps with the same plate and bench angle until you get 15 in every set with a 1-second squeeze and a slow way down. Then take the next plate up and go back to 10. Jumps from 2.5 to 5 kg or 5 to 10 kg are big for abs, so if the next plate is too much, set the bench one hole steeper with your current plate first.

The work runs down the front of your stomach, from just below the breastbone to below the navel, hardest in the squeeze at the top and the stretch at the bottom, plus some work at the sides of your waist. A burn at the front of your hips means you're sitting up too far or pulling with your legs. Stop the set if you get sharp low-back pain or pain that travels down a leg.

Substitutes: Decline Crunch (the same bench without a plate, good for learning the range), Weighted Ab Crunches (plate on the floor, a little easier), Kneeling Cable Abs Crunches and Machine Abdominal Crunches (heavier loads in smaller steps, once plates above about 20 kg get awkward to hold on your chest).

exercises.description: Weighted dips are a compound exercise targeting the chest, triceps, and shoulders. By adding weight, you increase resistance, enhancing muscle strength and hypertrophy. This exercise is performed using parallel bars and additional weight, typically attached to a dip belt.

Grasp the parallel bars firmly with your palms facing inward.
Lift yourself off the ground by straightening your arms and support your body weight.
Lean slightly forward to engage the chest muscles more effectively.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until your upper arms are parallel to the ground.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement.
Push through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
exercises.name: Weighted Dips

Maintain a slight forward lean to target the chest muscles more effectively.
Keep your core engaged throughout the movement for stability.
Avoid locking out your elbows at the top of the movement to maintain tension on the muscles.
Control the descent to prevent strain on the shoulder joints.
Start with lighter weights to master form before progressing to heavier loads.

Slowly lower your hips back to the starting position without letting them touch the ground.

Not aligning the feet correctly, which can lead to uneven muscle activation.

Not squeezing the glutes at the top of the movement, reducing the exercise's effectiveness.
Allowing the head to lift off the ground, causing neck strain.

Keep your core engaged throughout the movement to protect your lower back.
Avoid arching your back at the top of the movement; focus on squeezing the glutes.
Control the descent to maximize muscle engagement and prevent injury.
Start with a lighter weight to master form before progressing to heavier loads.
Maintain even pressure through both heels to ensure balanced muscle activation.

exercises.description: The Weighted Hanging Leg Raise is an advanced core exercise that targets the lower abdominal muscles, hip flexors, and obliques. By adding weight, it increases the intensity and demands greater stabilization from the core and grip strength. This exercise is performed by hanging from a pull-up bar and raising the legs while holding a weight between the feet or using ankle weights.
instructions: Begin by hanging from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Ensure your body is fully extended and your feet are off the ground.
Secure a dumbbell or weight plate between your feet or use ankle weights.
Engage your core and keep your legs straight as you raise them to a 90-degree angle with your torso.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring your core is tight.

exercises.description: Lie on your back with a plate locked out overhead, lift your shoulders and straight legs, and hold the hollow shape still to build a stronger midsection. Your whole abdominal wall works to keep the lower back pinned to the mat, from the ribs down to the pubic bone and along the sides of your waist. The front of your hips holds the legs up and your shoulders hold the plate, but they only keep the shape. Move on to it once a strict bodyweight hollow of about 60 seconds feels easy: a plate at the end of your arms makes 20 seconds hard work.
instructions: Lie on your back on a mat. If you use a medicine ball (2–4 kg), squeeze it between your shins just above the ankles.
Grip a light plate (2.5–5 kg to start) by the rim, one hand on each side, and press it up over your chest, arms straight.
Tilt your pelvis back until your lower back presses flat into the mat. That contact comes first; nothing leaves the floor before it.
Curl your head and shoulder blades up, chin slightly tucked, then take the plate back until your upper arms are beside your ears.
Raise your straight legs until your heels hover 15–30 cm off the floor, the lowest height at which your lower back stays down.
Now hold still: elbows locked, legs pressed together, toes pointed. Take short breaths behind a braced stomach and don't let it bulge.
When time is up, bring the plate back over your chest first, then bend your knees, lower your legs and head and set it down.
mistakes: Lower back lifting off the mat as the legs drop or the plate goes overhead. Raise your legs or bring the plate closer to your chest until the back stays flat.
Bent elbows that let the plate drift toward your face and shorten the lever. Lock your arms with the biceps by your ears; if you can't, take a lighter plate.
Head resting on the floor, or the chin cranked onto the chest so the neck does the work. Lift your shoulder blades, keep the neck long and look up between your arms.
Legs up at about 45°, where the hold gets easy. Bring your feet down to the lowest height your lower back allows, roughly 15–30 cm off the floor.
Knees bending, legs drifting apart or the ball slipping out. Squeeze it with your inner thighs and shins, legs straight and toes pointed, or start with a smaller ball.
exercises.name: Weighted Hollow Body Hold
tips: You work in seconds here, not reps: usually 3–5 holds of 10–20 s with a plate that makes 20 s hard, or 3–4 holds of 20–40 s. Add time first. Once all your holds reach the longest time with your back still flat, go 1.25–2.5 kg heavier (or use a ball 1–2 kg heavier) and go back to the shortest.

Expect hard, even work across the front of your stomach and the sides of your waist, plus the front of your hips and the inner thighs squeezing the ball. Feeling it in your lower back means the back has come off the mat: end the set there.

Too hard? Hold the plate straight up above your chest and raise your legs higher, or bend your knees. Too easy? Lower your legs or reach further back before adding kilograms; later, try weighted hollow rocks or the dragon flag.

Substitutes: Hollow Body Hold without load to build the base, Weighted Dead Bug or Dead Bug with Ball when the long lever arches your back, and Weighted Plank if you'd rather work face down or want the same plate without the overhead reach.

Start each rep by pulling your shoulder blades back, then drive your elbows back and out, about 45–60° from your sides.
Row until your elbows pass your torso and your hands reach your lower chest. Squeeze your shoulder blades together and hold for a second.
Let the handles go forward over about 2 seconds, until your arms are straight and your shoulder blades spread. Your chest never leaves the pad.
Finish the set by guiding the handles back to their resting spot instead of letting the stack drop.
mistakes: Peeling your chest off the pad or leaning back to heave the handles in. Your breastbone stays on the pad for every rep; if it has to come off, the weight is too heavy.
Elbows tucked against your ribs. That turns it into a lat row; keep them out at about 45–60°, in line with the wide handles, and finish with your hands at your lower chest.
Short reps at the front: the arms stay bent and the shoulder blades stay pinched. Before every pull, let your arms straighten all the way and your shoulder blades slide apart.
exercises.name: Wide Grip Chest Supported Row
tips: Two to four sets of 8–15 reps suit this row, or 6–10 when strength is the goal. Add reps before weight: stay at one load until you reach the top of your range, say 3 × 12, with your chest on the pad and straight arms at the front. Then move the pin down one plate, usually 5 kg (2.5 kg with an add-on weight), or add 2.5 kg per side on a plate-loaded machine, and work up again from the bottom of the range.

Feel it between and just below your shoulder blades and across the backs of your shoulders. A burning neck means you're shrugging; if it's mostly your lats under the armpits, your elbows have drifted in to your sides.

Front of the shoulder pinching at the end of the pull? Stop your elbows level with your torso or switch to the neutral handles. If the next plate is too big a jump, make the reps harder first: hold 2 seconds at the chest and take 3 seconds on the way back.

Substitutes: Chest Supported Machine Row (neutral handles, elbows closer, more lats and more weight), Seated Cable Wide Grip Row (the same wide pull, but nothing props up your torso), and Barbell Incline Wide Grip Row or Incline Bench Dumbbell Wide Row when there's no machine.

exercises.description: The Wide Grip Lat Pulldown is a compound exercise primarily targeting the latissimus dorsi muscles in the back. It also engages the biceps, forearms, and shoulders. This exercise is performed using a cable machine with a wide bar attachment, allowing for a greater range of motion and increased muscle activation in the upper back.
instructions: Sit down at the lat pulldown machine and adjust the knee pad to fit snugly against your thighs to prevent your body from lifting during the exercise.
Grasp the bar with an overhand grip, hands placed wider than shoulder-width apart.
Lean back slightly at an angle of about 30 degrees while keeping your chest up and core engaged.
Pull the bar down towards your upper chest by squeezing your shoulder blades together and driving your elbows down and back.
Pause briefly at the bottom of the movement, ensuring maximum contraction in the lats.
Slowly release the bar back to the starting position with controlled movement, fully extending your arms.
exercises.name: Wide Grip Lat Pulldown
tips: Ensure your grip is wide enough to maximize lat engagement but not so wide that it causes discomfort or strain.
Keep your core tight throughout the movement to maintain stability and support your lower back.
Avoid using momentum; focus on controlled movements to effectively target the muscles.
Exhale as you pull the bar down and inhale as you return to the starting position.
If you experience shoulder discomfort, try adjusting your grip width or consult with a fitness professional.

exercises.description: The Wide Grip Rear Pull Up is a compound upper body exercise targeting the latissimus dorsi, trapezius, and rhomboids. This exercise emphasizes the back muscles while also engaging the biceps and forearms. It is performed using a pull-up bar with a wide overhand grip, pulling the body upwards until the chin clears the bar.
instructions: Stand under a pull-up bar and reach up to grasp it with an overhand grip, hands placed wider than shoulder-width apart.
Engage your core and retract your shoulder blades to stabilize your upper body.
Begin the movement by pulling your chest towards the bar, leading with your elbows and keeping them pointed outwards.
Continue pulling until your chin is above the bar, ensuring your back muscles are fully engaged.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, then slowly lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using momentum to swing the body instead of controlled movement.
Failing to engage the core, leading to an unstable body position.
Pulling the bar behind the neck, which can strain the shoulders.
Allowing the elbows to flare excessively, reducing lat engagement.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom of the movement.
Rounding the shoulders forward, leading to poor posture and engagement.
Pulling with the arms instead of focusing on the back muscles.
Using a grip that is too wide, reducing range of motion and control.
Not retracting the shoulder blades at the start of the pull.
Failing to maintain a neutral neck position, leading to neck strain.
exercises.name: Wide Grip Rear Pull-Up
tips: Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement to maximize back engagement.
Avoid swinging or using momentum; maintain a controlled motion throughout.
If you struggle with full pull-ups, use resistance bands for assistance or perform negative pull-ups by focusing on the lowering phase.
Ensure your grip is secure but not overly tight to prevent forearm fatigue.
Keep your body straight and avoid arching your back during the exercise.

exercises.description: The Wide Grip Standing Barbell Curl is an isolation exercise targeting the biceps brachii, particularly emphasizing the short head due to the wide grip. This exercise helps in building overall arm strength and muscle mass, enhancing the peak of the biceps.
instructions: Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a barbell with a wide grip, palms facing forward.
Ensure your grip is wider than shoulder-width to target the short head of the biceps.
Keep your elbows close to your torso and maintain a slight bend in your knees for stability.
Curl the barbell upwards by contracting your biceps, keeping your upper arms stationary.
Continue lifting until your biceps are fully contracted and the bar is at shoulder level.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, squeezing your biceps.
Slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position, maintaining control throughout the descent.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Using momentum by swinging the body to lift the barbell.
Allowing the elbows to flare out instead of keeping them close to the torso.
Curling the wrists at the top of the movement, which can strain the wrists.
Not fully extending the arms at the bottom, reducing the range of motion.

Failing to keep the core engaged, leading to instability.

Gripping the barbell too tightly, causing unnecessary forearm tension.
Allowing the shoulders to move forward, disengaging the biceps.
exercises.name: Wide Grip Standing Barbell Curl
tips: Focus on keeping your elbows stationary to maximize bicep engagement.
Avoid swinging or using momentum; control the movement for better muscle activation.
Exhale as you lift the barbell and inhale as you lower it.
Keep your core engaged throughout the exercise to maintain proper posture.
Start with a lighter weight to perfect your form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: The Wide Hand Push Up is a bodyweight exercise targeting the chest, shoulders, and triceps. By positioning the hands wider than shoulder-width apart, it emphasizes the outer portion of the pectoral muscles and increases the involvement of the anterior deltoids.
instructions: Start in a plank position with your hands placed wider than shoulder-width apart on the floor.
Keep your body in a straight line from head to heels, engaging your core and glutes.
Lower your chest towards the ground by bending your elbows out to the sides.
Stop when your chest is just above the floor, ensuring your elbows are at about a 90-degree angle.
Push through your palms to extend your arms and return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions while maintaining proper form.
mistakes: Hands placed too wide, causing excessive strain on shoulders.
Elbows flaring out excessively, reducing chest engagement.
Sagging hips, leading to lower back strain.
Incomplete range of motion, limiting muscle activation.
Neck craning forward, causing neck strain.
Lack of core engagement, resulting in unstable posture.
Dropping too quickly without control, increasing injury risk.
Hands not aligned with shoulders, causing joint discomfort.
Uneven hand placement, leading to muscle imbalance.
Failing to maintain a straight line from head to heels.
exercises.name: Wide Push-Up
tips: Ensure your hands are positioned wider than shoulder-width to target the chest effectively.
Maintain a straight line from head to heels to prevent lower back strain.
Engage your core throughout the movement to stabilize your body.
Control the descent and avoid letting your chest touch the ground.
Focus on breathing; inhale as you lower down and exhale as you push up.

exercises.description: In a deep lunge with one hand on the floor, you turn your chest and reach the other arm to the ceiling to loosen your hips and upper back in one drill. The rear leg stays straight with the knee off the floor, so you feel a stretch at the front of that hip and in the groin of the front leg. Up top, the chest and front of the raised shoulder open while the muscles around the shoulder blade (serratus anterior, infraspinatus, middle and lower traps) turn it and hold the arm up. A few slow reps per side warm you up for squats, deadlifts, overhead pressing or sprints.
instructions: From a push-up position or standing, step one foot far forward, whole foot flat, and sink your hips low. The front knee can travel well past the toes.
Straighten the rear leg: knee off the floor, heel pushed back, weight on the ball of the foot. Squeeze that glute to open the front of the hip.
Plant the hand opposite your front leg flat on the floor inside the front foot, fingers forward, and push the floor away with a straight arm.
Let your other arm hang inside the front knee, hand reaching toward the instep, while the knee stays out over your toes.
Breathe out and turn your chest toward the front leg. The free arm sweeps past your face and up in an arc until it points at the ceiling.
Follow the hand with your eyes and pause for 2-3 seconds, both arms in one line from floor to ceiling, hips low and square.
Bring the arm back down the same arc to inside the knee. Finish all your reps on this side, then switch legs.
mistakes: Letting the rear knee bend and drift to the floor while the hips rise. Push the rear heel back and squeeze the glute; if you can't hold it, do the knee-down version on purpose.
Turning the pelvis instead of the upper back. The stretch then lands in your lower back, so keep both hip bones facing the floor and stop the turn where the hips start to move.
Front knee caving in as your arm drops inside it. Press the knee out over the second toe and keep the whole foot flat.
Support shoulder sagging toward the floor or the elbow bending. Push the floor away and keep that arm straight under the shoulder.
Flinging the top arm back behind you to fake range. Finish with it vertical, stacked over the support arm: the chest turns, the arm just follows.
exercises.name: World’s Greatest Stretch
tips: For a warm-up, 3-5 slow reps per side with a 2-3 second pause at the top, for 1-2 rounds, is usually plenty. In a mobility session, do 2-3 rounds of 5 per side, or 30-60 seconds of slow reps per side.

There's no weight to add. Progress reps and pause first, up to 5 reps and one full breath at the top on each side, then depth: a longer lunge, lower hips and the rear knee closer to the floor without touching it.
Feel for two areas: the front of the rear hip and the groin of the front leg, then the chest and the front of the raised shoulder. If your lower back feels it, the turn is coming from your hips.

Easier: rear knee down on a mat and the support hand on a yoga block or a low step. The block also spares sore wrists; pressing on a fist works too. Harder: drop the same-side elbow to the instep before each rotation, or walk it, stepping into the next side every rep.

Substitutes: Lizard Pose holds the same low lunge for the hips, Kneeling Back Rotation Stretch gives you the upper-back turn without the lunge, and Lunge Stretch is a quicker hip opener when the warm-up is short.

exercises.description: Sit with your forearms supported on the machine pad and palms facing upward. Grip the handles with a supinated grip, keeping your wrists just beyond the edge of the pad. Lower the handles by extending your wrists under control, then curl them upward by flexing your wrists as far as comfortably possible. Keep your forearms and elbows still throughout the movement, using only the wrists. Avoid swinging, gripping excessively hard, or using a load that limits your range of motion.
instructions: Adjust the machine so the wrist pad supports your forearms comfortably and the handle is within easy reach when your wrists are neutral.
Sit facing the machine with your forearms resting fully on the pad, palms facing upward, and your wrists positioned just beyond the edge of the support.
Grip the handle with an underhand grip, keeping your shoulders relaxed, elbows still, and forearms firmly against the pad.
Allow the handle to roll slightly toward your fingers as you slowly extend your wrists downward, keeping control of the weight.
Curl the handle upward by flexing your wrists and squeezing your forearm muscles, bringing your palms toward your forearms.
Pause briefly at the top without lifting your forearms or using your elbows, then lower the handle slowly to repeat.
Keep the movement isolated to your wrists throughout the set and use a light enough load to maintain a full, controlled range of motion.
mistakes: Using the forearms instead of keeping them fully supported on the pad
Bending or lifting the elbows to move the weight
Turning the movement into a biceps curl by flexing the elbows
Using a grip that is too wide or too narrow to control the handle
Moving the wrists through only a short, partial range of motion
Letting the wrists drop abruptly at the bottom instead of controlling the stretch
Using momentum or bouncing the handle through the repetitions
Extending the wrists excessively at the bottom and losing a stable grip
Relaxing the fingers completely and allowing the handle to roll out of control
Shrugging the shoulders or tensing the neck during the curl
Using a load that forces rapid, jerky wrist movement
Failing to fully squeeze the forearm flexors at the top of each repetition
exercises.name: Wrist Curl on Machine
tips: Adjust the machine so the pivot point aligns with your wrists and your forearms are fully supported on the pad.
Use an underhand grip with your palms facing up, keeping your wrists in a neutral, comfortable starting position.
Keep your elbows and forearms still throughout the movement; only your wrists should move.
Lower the handle slowly by allowing your wrists to extend, without forcing an uncomfortable stretch at the bottom.
Curl the handle upward by flexing your wrists and squeezing your forearms, rather than lifting with your elbows or shoulders.
Use a controlled tempo and avoid bouncing or using momentum, especially during the lowering phase.
Choose a light to moderate load that allows full wrist movement and strict control, as the forearm muscles fatigue quickly.
Exhale as you curl the handle up and inhale as you return it under control.
Stop if you feel sharp pain, tingling, or discomfort in the wrist or elbow, and reduce the range of motion or load if needed.

exercises.description: The Wrist Push Up is a bodyweight exercise that targets the forearms and wrists, enhancing strength and flexibility in these areas. It is performed with the back of the hands on the ground, requiring balance and control. This exercise is beneficial for athletes looking to improve wrist stability and forearm endurance.
instructions: Begin by kneeling on the floor, placing your hands on the ground with the backs of your hands facing down and fingers pointing towards your body.
Ensure your wrists are directly under your shoulders and your knees are under your hips.
Engage your core to maintain a straight line from your head to your knees.
Slowly lower your chest towards the floor by bending your elbows, keeping your wrists stable.
Pause briefly at the bottom, then push through the backs of your hands to return to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Placing hands too far apart, reducing stability and control.
Allowing elbows to flare out, leading to improper engagement of wrist and forearm muscles.
Not keeping wrists aligned with shoulders, causing strain on joints.
Bending wrists excessively, increasing risk of injury.
Failing to maintain a straight line from head to heels, compromising core engagement.
Dropping hips too low, reducing core activation and increasing lower back strain.
Performing reps too quickly, sacrificing form for speed.
Not fully extending arms at the top of the push-up, limiting range of motion.
Neglecting to engage the core, leading to instability and poor form.
Allowing shoulders to collapse, reducing upper body engagement.
exercises.name: Wrist Push-Up
tips: Warm up your wrists thoroughly before attempting this exercise to prevent injury.
Start with a small range of motion if you are new to wrist push ups, gradually increasing as you build strength.
Focus on maintaining control throughout the movement to maximize effectiveness and safety.
Keep your elbows close to your body to reduce strain on the wrists.
If you experience discomfort, try adjusting the angle of your hands or reduce the number of repetitions.

instructions: Attach a weight plate to the wrist roller using a secure rope or cord.

Extend your arms fully, keeping them parallel to the ground.
Begin rolling the weight up by rotating your wrists forward, maintaining controlled movements.
Continue until the weight reaches the top, then slowly reverse the motion to lower the weight back down.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Allowing elbows to flare out, reducing wrist engagement.
Rolling with the shoulders instead of isolating wrist movement.
Leaning back excessively, compromising posture and balance.

Failing to fully extend the wrists, limiting range of motion.
Using momentum instead of controlled wrist rotation.
Neglecting to keep the core engaged, affecting stability.
Allowing the wrists to drop below shoulder level, reducing effectiveness.
exercises.name: Wrist Roller
tips: Ensure your grip is firm but not overly tight to avoid unnecessary strain.
Focus on smooth, controlled wrist movements to maximize muscle engagement.
Keep your core engaged and maintain a neutral spine throughout the exercise.
Start with a lighter weight to perfect your form before increasing resistance.
Avoid using momentum; rely on wrist strength to move the weight.
Incorporate wrist rollers into your routine 2-3 times a week for balanced forearm development.

exercises.description: This exercise targets the upper back, specifically the lats, rhomboids, and traps, while also engaging the biceps and rear deltoids. To perform, stand with feet shoulder-width apart, bend at the hips until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor, keeping your back straight. Grip a barbell with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Pull the barbell towards your lower abdomen, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement. Lower the barbell under control to the starting position. Maintain a tight core and avoid using momentum to ensure proper muscle activation and reduce injury risk. This exercise enhances back thickness and strength.
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and hold a barbell with an underhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Bend your knees slightly and hinge forward at the hips, keeping your back straight and chest up, until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor.
Let the barbell hang at arm's length in front of you with your arms fully extended.
Engage your core and pull the barbell towards your lower chest or upper abdomen by bending your elbows and squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement, ensuring your elbows stay close to your body.
Slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position with controlled movement, fully extending your arms.
Repeat the movement for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining proper form throughout.
mistakes: Using excessive momentum by swinging the torso to lift the weight
Allowing the elbows to flare out too wide instead of keeping them close to the body
Rounding the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine position
Pulling the bar too high, beyond the lower ribs, reducing lat engagement
Not fully retracting the shoulder blades at the top of the movement
Using a grip that is too wide, which shifts focus away from the targeted muscles
Performing the movement too quickly, sacrificing control and muscle activation
Allowing the wrists to bend excessively, causing strain and reducing force transfer
Not maintaining a slight bend in the knees, leading to poor stability
Lowering the bar too quickly, losing tension on the muscles and increasing risk of strain
exercises.name: Yates Row
tips: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and hold the barbell with an underhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Bend your knees slightly and hinge forward at the hips, keeping your back straight and chest up throughout the movement.
Pull the barbell towards your lower abdomen, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement.
Keep your elbows close to your body as you row the barbell upwards to maximize back engagement.
Lower the barbell in a controlled manner until your arms are fully extended, maintaining tension in your back muscles.
Avoid rounding your back or using momentum; focus on controlled, deliberate movements to prevent injury.
Engage your core to stabilize your torso and protect your lower back during the exercise.
Breathe out as you pull the barbell up and breathe in as you lower it back down.
Start with a lighter weight to master proper form before progressing to heavier loads.

exercises.description: The Zercher Squat is a compound lower body exercise that primarily targets the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and core. It involves holding a barbell in the crook of your elbows while performing a squat, which challenges stability and engages the upper body muscles for support.
instructions: Begin by setting a barbell on a squat rack at about waist height.
Position yourself under the barbell and cradle it in the crook of your elbows, keeping your arms bent and hands clasped together.
Stand up to lift the bar off the rack, maintaining a strong posture with feet shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core and keep your chest up as you initiate the squat by bending at the hips and knees.
Lower your body until your thighs are parallel to the floor or slightly below, ensuring your knees track over your toes.
Push through your heels to return to the starting position, keeping the bar secure in your elbows throughout the movement.
Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
mistakes: Allowing the knees to cave inward during the squat.
Rounding the back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Holding the bar too low on the forearms, causing balance issues.
Not engaging the core, leading to instability.
Descending too quickly, losing control of the movement.
Failing to keep the elbows high, causing the bar to shift.
Squatting too shallow, not achieving full range of motion.
Leaning too far forward, putting strain on the lower back.
Not keeping the feet flat, causing heels to lift off the ground.
Using too much weight, compromising form and control.
exercises.name: Zercher Squat
tips: Keep your core engaged throughout the movement to maintain balance and protect your lower back.
Ensure that your elbows are positioned under the bar to prevent it from slipping forward.
Focus on keeping your chest up and shoulders back to maintain an upright torso during the squat.
Start with a lighter weight to master the form before progressing to heavier loads.
Use a squat pad or towel around the bar if you experience discomfort in the elbows.
Maintain a controlled descent and ascent to maximize muscle engagement and minimize injury risk.

exercises.description: A static version of the Zercher squat: you hold a barbell in the crooks of your elbows and stay in a squat with your thighs close to parallel to the floor for a set time. Your quads and glutes hold the position, while your upper back, core and arms keep the bar tight against your body.
instructions: Set a barbell in a rack at about waist height.
Bend your knees, place the bar in the crooks of your elbows and clasp your hands in front of your chest.
Stand up to lift the bar off the rack, step back and set your feet about shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out.
Brace your core, lift your chest and keep the bar pressed against your body.
Bend your hips and knees and lower until your thighs are close to parallel to the floor.
Hold this position for the set time with your heels down, knees in line with your toes and torso as upright as you can keep it.
Push through your whole foot to stand up, then walk the bar back into the rack.
mistakes: Letting your clasped hands drop, so the bar slides out of your elbow crease toward your wrists
Rounding your upper back as the bar pulls your chest forward
Letting your knees cave inward during the hold
Shifting your weight onto your toes or lifting your heels
Slowly rising out of the squat as your legs tire instead of holding the same depth
Going deeper than you can hold with a neutral spine, so your pelvis tucks under
exercises.name: Zercher Squat Hold
tips: Start with a light bar and holds of 20 to 30 seconds, and add time before you add weight.
Wrap the bar in a pad or towel, or wear long sleeves, if it digs into your elbows.
Time the hold from the moment you reach the bottom position, not from when you lift the bar off the rack.
Take short breaths behind a braced core instead of holding your breath for the whole set.
If you can, hold inside a power rack with the safety pins just below the bar's height in the bottom position, so you can set the bar down if your legs give out.

exercises.description: The Zottman Curl is a compound exercise targeting the biceps and forearms. It combines a standard bicep curl with a reverse curl, effectively working both the flexor and extensor muscles of the arm. This exercise is performed with dumbbells and is beneficial for developing arm strength and size.
instructions: Stand upright with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with a neutral grip (palms facing inward).
Keep your elbows close to your torso and curl the weights upward by flexing your elbows, rotating your wrists so that your palms face up as you lift.
At the top of the movement, pause briefly and then rotate your wrists so that your palms face downward.
Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position with this reverse grip.
Rotate your wrists back to the neutral position to prepare for the next repetition.
mistakes: Using momentum to lift the weights instead of controlled movements.
Allowing the elbows to flare out, reducing bicep engagement.
Not fully rotating the wrists at the top and bottom of the movement.
Swinging the body to assist the curl, leading to poor form.
Failing to keep the wrists straight, causing unnecessary strain.
Lifting too heavy, compromising form and control.
Not extending the arms fully at the bottom, limiting range of motion.
Rushing through the exercise without focusing on muscle contraction.
exercises.name: Zottman Curl
tips: Maintain a controlled motion throughout the exercise to maximize muscle engagement.
Avoid swinging or using momentum to lift the weights; focus on isolating the biceps and forearms.
Keep your core engaged and back straight to maintain proper posture.
Use a weight that allows you to perform the exercise with correct form; it's better to start lighter and increase gradually.
Breath naturally, exhaling as you lift and inhaling as you lower the weights.
